# The Lineage of the Author of the Madhuri Commentary—

---

->In the noble Bharadwaja lineage, there was a most eminent man named Sudai Belauche, of the highest social rank.<-
->From him was born the famous and illustrious Mahinatha, whose son was the venerable Phani.<-

->My grandfather, Jayanatha Sharma, resided in the town named Malamajhi.<-
->He married the daughter of a nobleman from the Udighno-Maulika family, a woman named Khusi.<-

->His eldest son was the excellent Shridarshana, and the younger was Batuka.<-
->Having fathered these two sons with the daughter of Khusi, my grandfather departed for the world of the gods <note>passed away</note>.<-

->My mother was Shri Janaki, and my father was Shri Darshana, who possessed divine insight into the philosophical systems <note>original: "darshana-divya-drishtih"; a play on his name Darshana, suggesting he was a visionary scholar</note>.<-
->From these two parents, seven sons shine forth; the eldest among them is Shri Lavajha.<-

->Vishveshwara was born after him, and I, Yugeshwara, am indeed the next younger brother.<-
->Yageshwara, a leader among the wise, is my younger brother, and Rajeshwara, a physician, is younger than him.<-

->Kusheshwara is the youngest of all, an expert in medical practice and beautiful discernment.<-
->Within the pure heart of the Mithila region, in the vicinity of Mirzapur, we reside.<-

->In the Shaka year 1865 <note>approximately 1943 CE</note>, in the month of Kartika <note>original: "Urja"</note>, during the dark fortnight, on the 14th lunar day <note>Tithi</note> dedicated to Shiva, on a Friday;<-
->My mother, Shri Janaki, remembering Lord Shiva, went to the supreme abode of Shiva in the afternoon.<-

->In the month of Magha, during the bright fortnight, on a Wednesday, the 9th lunar day dedicated to the Goddess <note>Girija</note>;<-
->Having heard the nectar-like stories of the Bhagavata Purana, at the very moment the week-long recitation concluded, my father Shri Darshana went to heaven.<-

->Our sister is the compassionate and virtuous Mrs. Daijau Devi, devoted to her religious vows. We are seven brothers in total.<-

->The mother is Shri Janaki Devi and the father is the wise Shri Darshana;<-
->By their son, Shri Yugeshwar Sharma, this commentary <note>Tika</note> was composed.<-

Date:               } **Shri Yugeshwar Jha**
June 22, 1946 CE.   } **Maves-Mirzapur, Darbhanga.**

->Salutations to the Holy Ganesha.<-

# Introduction

Who among the experts of <term>Jyotishashastra</term><note>The traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note> in India does not know the name of the venerable Ganesha? Or who has not encountered his <term>Grahalaghava</term><note>Literally 'Ease of the Planets,' a famous 16th-century astronomical manual by Ganesha Daivajna</note>? Writing an introduction for it is a task in itself. || 1 ||

Ample <term>Vasana</term><note>Explanatory commentary or proofs</note> has been provided for this work by Mallari and Sudhakara, as well as by the illustrious Vishvanatha. Excellent commentaries and examples were also produced by Sita, Rama, and other Maithila scholars. || 2 ||

Yet, some of those works have become difficult to obtain, and there is a lack of modern accessibility in what is available. Therefore, being earnestly requested by groups of students and encouraged by Jayakrishna Das <insert>the publisher</insert>, || 3 ||

I have reflected upon modern mathematics and the teachings of Naradeva and others. Thus, for the benefit of students, I have written a new, simple <term>Upapatti</term><note>Mathematical proof or rationale</note> using clear language. || 4 ||

Since a seeker of knowledge cannot find a truly excellent work without the wisdom of the ancients, O masters of the craft! I have also preserved the ancient calculations performed by the venerable Vishvanatha. || 5 ||

If this work provides even a small benefit to students, my great labor will be successful. I, Yugeshwar, pray to the community of learned scholars to correct any collection of errors found herein. || 6 ||

---

Full Moon of Jyeshtha <note>The third month of the Hindu lunar calendar, typically May-June</note> } \
Year 2003 <note>Vikram Samvat era, corresponding to approximately 1946 CE</note> } \
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **Shri Yugeshwar Jha**

### ॐ Announcement ॐ

In this entire world, who does not know the name of *Grahalaghava* <note>literally "Lightness of the Planets," a famous 16th-century astronomical treatise</note>, the jewel of fame composed by the learned **Shri Ganesha**, who was the son of the illustrious **Shri Keshavacharya**—a sun to the lotus-like family of astrologers <term>Daivajna: a traditional astronomer or astrologer</term>—and who was like an incarnation of the god Ganesha himself? Even though several other astronomical systems, manuals, and instruments <note>original: "Siddhanta, Tantra, and Karana," the three classes of Sanskrit astronomical texts</note> exist today, this work is honored everywhere by the people as if it had attained a unique greatness. Indeed, seeing the scholarship in this jewel of a book—praiseworthy even by the immortals—many honorable great souls composed numerous commentaries. 

The "Three Commentaries" composed by the illustrious **Mallari**, **Vishvanatha**, and **Sudhakara Dvivedi** became universally respected and extremely helpful to scholars. For this reason, the late **Mahamahopadhyaya Shri Sudhakara Dvivedi** <note>a title meaning "Greatest of Great Teachers"</note> personally undertook its editing. However, due to the widespread circulation of this extraordinary jewel of a book accompanied by the three commentaries, the copies in the libraries of headmasters and teachers gradually became depleted <note>literally "attained emptiness"</note>. Consequently, students and teachers faced great difficulty in obtaining copies. 

Furthermore, nowadays, the mathematical portion of this book is prescribed for the *Madhyama* <note>Intermediate</note> examinations of the Government Sanskrit College of Kashi <note>Varanasi</note> and the Bihar State examinations, and the portion on proofs <term>Upapatti: rationales or mathematical demonstrations</term> is prescribed everywhere for the *Acharya* <note>Master's</note> examinations. Therefore, this book, with its two parts of mathematics and proofs, has become extremely useful. 

Even so, despite the re-publication of the book with the aforementioned three commentaries, it was observed that modern students following the current examination patterns found them difficult to engage with. Thus, the most compassionate servant of Sanskrit culture, the eminent merchant **Shri Jayakrishna Das Harikrishna Das Gupta**, earnestly requested the excellent scholar **Pandit Shri Yugeshwar Jha** to compose a commentary suited for the present time. Upon this request, that noble soul wrote the "Madhuri" commentary, adorned with explanations, proofs, and modern examples in the common language <note>referring to Hindi or accessible Sanskrit</note>, and gave it to the eminent merchant for publication.

Furthermore, I was earnestly requested by the said noble publisher to revise and edit this work. While preserving the ancient examples created by **Shri Vishvanatha Daivajna**, I have revised the language of the explanations and proofs provided by the author of the *Madhuri* commentary. Regarding the mathematical subjects in the new examples, I have completed the editing of this book by simply overseeing them, setting aside minor errors due to discrepancies.

Moreover, even during this terrible, world-encompassing Great War <note>referring to the aftermath of World War II</note>, when there is a scarcity of all goods, the kindness shown by the noble publishers for the benefit of us who depend on Sanskrit is worthy of gratitude. They and their kin deserve our thanks and are greeted with our blessings. Furthermore, we request you wise scholars to favor us—the commentator, the publisher, and the editor—by promoting the wide circulation of this book, while correcting any natural errors that may have arisen in this human undertaking, which is subject to fallibility.

---

Patna—  
Full Moon of Jyeshtha, Samvat 2003 <note>June 1946</note>

->Yours—<-
->**Chaudhary Shri Kapileshwar Shastri**<-
->Principal, Hathwa Government Shri Gyanodaya College<-
->Location—Patna<-

# Madhuri—Explanation of Symbols

> Having bowed with devotion to my parents, named Janakidarsanapriti and Janakidarsana, I am writing this *Madhuri* <note>The title of the commentary, meaning "Sweetness"</note>.
> Since the mathematical proofs and calculations herein are expressed through symbols, the nature of those symbols is clarified first.

Therefore, in this *Madhuri* commentary, I have written the proofs and calculations using symbols; thus, I shall first make those symbols clear.

Now, by these symbols, the following are respectively represented: equal $=$, unequal $\angle$ <note>original: *asaman*, likely used here for "angle" or "inequality" depending on context, but defined here as "unequal"</note>, addition $+$, subtraction $-$, multiplication $\times$, division $\div$, square $^2$, square root $\sqrt{}$, degrees $^\circ$, minutes $'$, seconds $''$, and thirds $'''$.

Namely— $=$ is the sign for equality, $\angle$ is the sign for inequality, $+$ is the sign for addition, $-$ is the sign for subtraction, $\times$ is the sign for multiplication, $\div$ is the sign for division, $^2$ is the sign for squaring, $\sqrt{}$ is the sign for the square root, $^\circ$ is the sign for degrees, $'$ is the sign for minutes, $''$ is the sign for seconds, and $'''$ is the sign for thirds.

### Now, the Definition of Multiplication—

> In the multiplication of numbers with fractional parts, the *Gomutrika* <term>Gomutrika: literally "zigzag like the flow of cow's urine," a method of distributive multiplication</term> operation should be performed. Multiply the multiplicand by the individual parts of the multiplier; their sum is the product.

In the multiplication of numbers with fractional parts, one should perform the *Gomutrika* operation. By multiplying the multiplicand separately by the parts of the multiplier and then adding them, the product is obtained.

For example—the multiplicand in signs and degrees <note>original: *rashyadi*, referring to the zodiacal notation of signs, degrees, minutes, etc.</note> is $11|5^\circ|24'|5''$ and the multiplier is $2|6|9|7$. Therefore, according to the root rule:

-> $( 11|5^\circ|24'|5'' ) \times 2$ <-
-> $( 11|5^\circ|24'|5'' ) \times 6^\circ$ <-
-> $( 11|5^\circ|24'|5'' ) \times 9'$ <-
-> $( 11|5^\circ|24'|5'' ) \times 7''$ <-
$= 22|30^\circ|48'|10''$
$= \quad 6^\circ|30'|144''|30'''$
$= \quad\quad 9'|135''|216'''|45$
$= \quad\quad\quad 7''|105'''|168|35$
**Sum**— $22|36^\circ|147'|296''|351'''|213|35$

Here, by dividing the degrees by 30 <note>to convert to zodiac signs</note> and the minutes etc. by 60, the product in signs and degrees becomes $3|8^\circ|32'|11''|54'''|33|35$.

### Now, the Definition of Squaring—

> The product of two equal numbers is the Square; the "Kriti" <note>another term for square</note> of a quantity with fractional parts.

The product of two equal numbers is a square.

For example:—Days etc. $( 2|5|35 ) ( 2|5|35 ) = 2|5|35 \times 2$
$\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad 2|5|35 \times 5$
$\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad 2|5|35 \times 35$

## Now, the procedure for extracting the square root—

> When the square root of a quantity with fractional parts is sought, there is a specific method described.
> First, multiply the first part by three thousand six hundred <note>original: "khashunya-ripu-tribhih" (zero-zero-six-three in reverse notation)</note> and find its root.
> Add one to the remainder of that root, multiply by sixty, and add the subsequent fractional part.
> Divide this by twice the root plus two; the result is the accurate root of the fractional quantity.

There is a great distinction—that is to say, a significant difficulty—in calculating the square root of numbers with fractional parts <term>savayava-anka</term><note>Numbers consisting of whole units and their sexagesimal fractions</note>. This is because **Kamalakara, in the Tattvaviveka**, stated that for non-square numbers (those with fractions), the root is geometric/linear; otherwise, a "true" root of a non-square number cannot exist. Now, multiply the first part of the fractional number by 3600 and find the root using the method of **Bhaskara** <note>Referring to Bhaskaracharya, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> starting with **"having discarded the last odd digit's square..."** and so on. Add 1 to the remainder, multiply by 60, add the next fractional part, and divide the sum by twice the root plus 2. This yields the approximate root of the fractional number.

For example, to find the square root of 63 | 50: Following the rule **"multiply the first part,"** 63 x 3600 = 226,800. Using Bhaskara's method, the root is 476 and the remainder is 224. Adding 1 to the remainder 224 gives 225. Multiplying 225 by 60 gives 13,500; adding the 50 <term>vikala</term><note>Seconds of arc or a third-order sexagesimal fraction</note> gives 13,550. Now, twice the root 476 is 952; adding 2 gives 954. Dividing 13,550 by 954 gives a quotient of 14, which is the second part of the root. Dividing the first part of the root (476) by 60, the approximate root is 7 | 56 | 14.

## Now, the description of Addition and Subtraction—

> Addition should be performed within like categories, and subtraction likewise among like categories.
> In the addition or subtraction of unlike categories, the relationship is shown by a line/sign.

Addition and subtraction occur with their own similar categories. The addition and subtraction of different categories (units) are expressed through signs/lines.

For example: In the signs etc. <note>Astronomical notation: Signs, Degrees, Minutes, Seconds</note> 3 | 11° | 21' | 35", adding the signs etc. 1 | 15° | 31' | 7" results in the sum 4 | 26° | 52' | 42". Similarly, subtracting 1 | 15° | 31' | 7" from 3 | 11° | 21' | 35" leaves a remainder of 1 | 25° | 50' | 28". Furthermore, adding the days etc. 11 | 6 | 4 | 32 to the signs etc. 1 | 27° | 35' | 6" is expressed as {( 1 | 27° | 35' | 6" ) + ( 11 | 6 | 4 | 32 )}. Likewise, subtracting the days etc. 11 | 6 | 4 | 35 from the signs etc. ( 1 | 17° | 7' | 27" ) is expressed as ( 1 | 17° | 7' | 27" ) — ( 11 | 6 | 4 | 35 ).

# ॥ Salutations to the Blessed Lord Ganesha ॥
## Composed by Ganesha Daivajna
# Grahalaghava: An Astronomical Manual
## With the commentary and examples by the eminent astronomer Vishvanatha,
## including new examples, proofs, and Sanskrit-Hindi explanations.

---

### The Author’s Auspicious Invocation —

> The speech of Keshava <note>The author's father and teacher</note> and the sacred Vedas are victorious; they generate the awakening of light <note>referring both to the stars and to spiritual enlightenment</note>. Having purified the mind through the performance of subtle calculations, though concise in words, they are filled with profound meaning and made manifest through the methods devised by his followers. ॥1॥

### Vishvanatha —

> ->Having churned the ocean of the scriptures, the teacher Ganesha, the master of astronomers,<-
> ->composed this *Grahalaghava*; to please the virtuous, I provide this explanation.<-
> ->Meditating on the son of Shambhu <note>Ganesha</note>, I, Vishvanatha, son of Divakara,<-
> ->the capable Narayana for the protection of Gokula, the best of living astronomers, [write this]. ॥ 1 ॥<-

The works composed by the venerable teacher Ganesha Daivajna were recorded in two verses by his nephew, the astronomer Nrisimha, in his own commentary on the *Grahalaghava*.

They are as follows —
> ->Having first composed the *Grahalaghava*, the small and large *Tithi-Chintamani*,<-
> ->a commentary on the *Siddhanta Shiromani*, and an explanation of the *Lilavati*;<-
> ->a commentary on the *Vrindavana*, an explanation of the *Muhurta-Tattva*,<-
> ->a definitive judgment on the true scriptures, and a fine commentary on the *Chhandarnava*... ॥ 1 ॥<-
> ->...the *Sudhiranjana*, the *Tarjani-Yantra* <note>a finger-gnomon instrument</note>, a decision on the Krishna-Ashtami festival and Holika;<-
> ->having reached his goals through these simple methods and other unprecedented works, the teacher Ganesha attained the Great Peace of Brahma. ॥ 2 ॥<-

The eminent Ganesha Daivajna—born into the noble lineage of the sage Kaushika, residing in Nandigrama near the ocean shore, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of the whole earth, who is proficient in the meaning of all scriptures, an expert in the proofs of the eighteen *Siddhantas* <note>major astronomical treatises</note>, a leader among grammarians, and clever in the essence of mathematical inquiry—desiring to compose this manual named *Grahalaghava*, first utters an auspicious invocation in the *Vasantatilaka* meter. This invocation, intended for the successful completion and propagation of the book, takes the form of a blessing and salutation directed toward the Goddess of Speech, the Vedas, and his teacher:

**"Light..."** etc. The speech or voice of Keshava, the author’s father, is victorious—it exists in a state of supreme excellence. The *Shruti* (the Veda) is also victorious. He describes its nature in the verse: "Generating the awakening of light." It generates the *Prabodha* (knowledge or awakening) of the *Jyotis* (the lights), meaning the planets, constellations, and stars. In another sense, it generates the knowledge of the Supreme Light known as Brahman. By doing what? "Having purified the mind," meaning having made the mind steady and clear. How? "Through the performance of subtle calculations." These are the astronomical operations and methods well-taught by Keshava; through their practice, specifically <unclear>the astronomical manuals mentioned such as the Graha-Kautuka</unclear> <unclear>having practiced well</unclear> the mind...

By making [the mind] steady, the awakening or knowledge of the planets and other celestial bodies occurs. In the other sense, regarding the *Shruti* <note>The Vedas, or divinely "heard" scripture</note>, it means that by performing the rituals well-spoken of in the *Vishnu-Sukta* and other hymns—namely the performance of religious duties—and by those observances, the heart is purified, and the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman arises. In the other sense, "his parts" refers to the portions of that *Shruti* or those like Ravana <note>Referring here to Vedic commentators or lineages</note>, by whose efforts in creating commentaries and expositions, it is revealed and made manifest. || 1 ||

**In the sense of Scripture (*Shruti*):**—**Ke** = in the water; **Shavah** = like a corpse, motionless; at the beginning of creation, his intellect hindered by the thought of what to do or not do, lying on the leaf of a banyan tree, licking his own toe—the child Mukunda <note>Krishna/Vishnu</note>, **Keshava**. Such is the speech of Keshava which reigns supreme. ||

Of what nature is it? It is **Gahana** = difficult to grasp, **Arthaih** = with other meanings or methods, **Purna** = well-constructed. It is **Svalpa** = brief, **Akshara** = without error/deviation. By the **Amshakritaih** = those made by the "parts" of that Keshava, i.e., accomplished by his disciples and sons, through **Upayaih** = means such as commentaries and rationales (*Vasana*), it is made manifest. Here, some explain **Gahanarthapurna** as "filled with many meanings" and **Svalpakshara** as "having very few words." That is not entirely sufficient. 1. **First Interpretation (Regarding the Deity):** The speech of **Keshava** <note>original: "Keshav" — here referring to Lord Krishna/Vishnu</note> (the young Mukunda) is supreme. Now, showing the similarity between the astronomical manual (*Karana*) and Lord Rama, the author provides an instruction for remembering them:

## Remembering Rama, who broke the bow of Shiva, whose arms shine with firm virtues,
## Who grants good fruits and took a human form; so too remember this Manual.

Now, demonstrating the equivalence between his own astronomical manual (*Karana*) and the form of Lord Rama/Vishnu, the author speaks a mangala <note>an auspicious introductory verse</note> in the *Aupachhandasika* meter: *“Paribhagnasamaurvikesachapam...”* O Astronomer! Remember Rama, who is a form of Vishnu. Also remember this *Karana*, the method for calculating planets which is about to be described. By remembering both, one attains the highest good.

In what way is he like Vishnu? **He who broke the bow of Shiva.** He broke into two pieces the bow of Lord Shiva (*Isha*) along with its string (*maurvi*). This is well-described in the story of Sita’s wedding.
In the other sense (the manual): It has **discarded the use of sines and arcs.** <note>A technical feature of this specific manual is that it simplifies calculations by avoiding complex trigonometric sine tables (Jya/Maurvi)</note>. In this manual, sines and arcs are not used.

Furthermore, how is he? **Shining with a firm necklace of virtues.** He shines with a necklace made of firm, connected virtues (qualities).
In the other sense: It shines with **firm multipliers (*Gunaka*) and divisors (*Hara*).**

Furthermore, how is he? **Having well-rounded arms.** His arms are perfectly circular and strong.
In the other sense: It contains **excellent circles (*Vritta*) and sides of triangles (*Bahu*).** <note>Refers to geometric diagrams and the "arms" or sides of right-angled triangles used in shadow calculations</note>.

Furthermore, how is he? **The giver of good fruits.** He grants the great fruit of liberation (*Moksha*).
In the other sense: It grants **accurate results** (the *Phala* or "fruits" of planetary equations, such as the Equation of the Center).

Furthermore, how is he? **Possessing a human luster.** He has accepted the form and radiance of a human being.
In the other sense: It contains the **measure of the gnomon’s shadow.** <note>The word 'Nr' (man) is a technical term for a gnomon of 12 digits, and 'Prabha' means shadow</note>. **[2]**

->**The Madhuri Commentary**<-

**Regarding Rama:** O Man! Worship that form of Vishnu through meditation. He who **broke the bow of Shiva**: he broke and divided the bow of Lord Shiva into three equal parts on the ground. **Shining with a firm necklace of virtues**: he is adorned with a necklace made of the "string" of *Sattva* (purity/goodness) which is firm and unchanging. **With well-rounded arms**: his arms provide the livelihood for all living beings. **Giver of good fruits**: he grants the desired fruits of one's actions. **Possessing human luster**: he took on the radiance of a human body. "Rama" is he in whom the yogis delight. He is the creator of the world.

**The bow of the Lord (Ishachapam)** = broken and cast aside by the **bowstring (maurvika)**. With the **sine (jiva)** <note>The Sanskrit word 'jiva' means both 'life/soul' and the geometric 'sine'</note>, he broke the mighty bow. **1st Interpretation (Devotional):** O Man! Remember the form of Vishnu, who broke Shiva's bow into three pieces upon the earth. He is adorned with the garland of the quality of goodness (Sattva-guna), the provider of livelihood to every living being, the giver of desired fruits, the one who took human form, the mover of the universe, and as beautiful as the god of love.

**2nd Interpretation (Astronomical):** O Calculator! Study this *Karana* text <note>A 'Karana' is a concise astronomical manual for practical calculations</note>. It is free from the complexities of sines (jiva) and arcs (chapa), adorned with stable dividends and divisors, contains the 'arm' (sine) calculations within beautiful verses, provides perfect knowledge of the planetary corrections, utilizes the shadow of the gnomon, and is delightful and pure. || 2 ||

### Now, the reason for beginning the book is stated:

->Though wise and great men have composed astronomical manuals,<-
->without the use of sines and arcs, no success is found in them.<-
->To create a planetary manual free from sine and arc operations,<-
->and of great simplicity, I am clearly prepared.<- || 3 ||

Now, since manuals by previous teachers already exist, why compose another? He explains the reason in the *Vasantatilaka* meter: "Though wise men..." etc. I, Ganesha, have set out to create a planetary manual that is 'clear'—meaning it brings the calculated positions into harmony with observation. Why? He says: although wise and great calculators have made manuals, in those manuals, if one discards the sine and arc, the 'success' (the completion of the mathematical goal) is not achieved. But this work is free from the operations of sines and arcs and is 'of great simplicity,' meaning it involves very few steps. Where planetary calculation starts from the beginning of the *Kalpa* <note>an immense cosmic cycle</note>, it is a **Siddhanta**; where it starts from the beginning of a **Yuga** <note>an age</note>, it is a **Tantra**; where it starts from a specific **Saka** date <note>an era, usually 78 CE</note>, it is a **Karana**. Thus, it is indicated: "I am performing the planetary calculation from the Saka era." || 3 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary

**Great (uravah)** = principal; **Wise (dhirah)** = learned men; **Manuals (karanani)** = the work of composing astronomical texts; **Although (yadyapi)**; **They made (akarshuh)** = even if they did; **But because (yasmāt)**; **In those (teshu)** = in those composed books; **Sine and Arc (jyaka-dhanuh)**; **Discarding (apasya)** = leaving aside; **Success (siddhih)** = the mathematical result; **Not (na)** = would not occur. For that reason, "I, Ganesha," am **eager (udyatah)** to **compose (kartum)** a **planetary manual (graha-prakaranam)** that is **clear (sphutam)**, **free from sine and arc operations (jya-chapa-karma-rahitam)**, and **of great simplicity (sulaghupakaram)**—meaning it has beautiful and easy operations.

In this book, Ganesha fulfills his promise by giving different names to the sines and arcs. Great scholars should consider that, in reality, he has performed all the functions of sines and arcs throughout. || 3 ||

Although great teachers created astronomical manuals, their mathematical systems do not function correctly if sines and arcs are removed. Therefore, I (Ganesha the Astrologer) am ready to create the *Grahalaghava* (Simplified Astronomy) with extremely simple operations, leaving aside the traditional sine and arc methods. || 3 ||

# Chapter 1: On Middle Motion

### Now he describes the calculation of the Ahargana <note>The "Ahargana" is the total number of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a desired date, essential for calculating planetary positions.</note>—

> Subtract 1442 from the Shaka year; divide the result by eleven. The quotient is called the *Chakra* (Cycle). Multiply the remainder by twelve and add the months elapsed since Chaitra. Set this sum in two places. To one, add twice the *Chakra* and ten; divide by thirty-three to find the *Adhimasa* (intercalary months). Add these to the sum of months. Multiply by thirty and add the elapsed lunar days (*tithis*). Add one-sixth of the *Chakra* (ignoring fractions). Set this in two places. Divide one by sixty-four to find the *Kshaya-ahas* (omitted days). Subtract these from the other to get the *Ahargana*. To find the weekday, add five times the *Chakra* to the *Ahargana* and divide by seven; the remainder counted from Monday gives the day. || 4-5 ||

Now, the calculation of the *Ahargana* is explained in two verses beginning with "Subtract 1442..." First, an example is written: From the reign of the illustrious King Vikramaditya, 1669 years have passed; likewise, in the Shaka era of King Shalivahana, 1534 years. On the full moon day of the bright half of Vaishakha, a Monday, at 54 ghatis and 10 palas, with the moon in the Vishakha nakshatra (39 ghatis, 55 palas) and the Variyan yoga (0 ghatis, 59 palas), the *Ahargana* is calculated to observe a lunar eclipse.

In this case, the Shaka year is 1534. Subtracted by "two-four-one" (1442), the resulting group of years is 92. This is divided by eleven. The quotient in one place is 8, named the *Chakra*. The remainder is 4. Multiplied by twelve, it is 48. Adding the one elapsed month from Chaitra to the desired time, it becomes 49. This is placed in two spots. The *Chakra* doubled is 16. Adding this to the 49 and adding ten, we get 75. Divided by thirty-three, the quotient for intercalary months is 2. Adding this to the 49, the total months are 51. This multiplied by thirty is 1530. The elapsed lunar days are 14. Adding these, we get 1544. Adding one-sixth of the *Chakra* (which is 1), it becomes 1545. This is placed in two spots and divided by sixty-four; the quotient for omitted days is 24. Subtracting these from the total, the civil *Ahargana* is 1521.

Now for the weekday: The *Chakra* (8) multiplied by five is 40. Adding this to the *Ahargana* (1521) gives 1561. Divided by seven, the remainder counted from Monday <note>original: "abja" (the Moon/Monday)</note> indicates the day. The result is Monday.

Now for a special rule: If the desired weekday does not result from the *Ahargana*, one should add or subtract one to match the desired day. Furthermore, if the division by eleven results in a remainder of zero, a difference of two days may occur in the resulting weekday.

### Example of this:

In Shaka 1674, on the first day of the bright half of Chaitra, the *Ahargana* is calculated for a Sunday. There, the *Chakra* is 12 and the remainder is 0. The *Ahargana* is 32. Here, Tuesday results, but Sunday is expected. In such cases, the *Ahargana* should be adjusted by subtracting or adding two.

Furthermore, there is another special rule for years containing an intercalary month. If, when calculating the *Ahargana* for months prior to the intercalary month, a higher number of intercalary months appears compared to the previous year, it should not be taken; rather, the count from the previous year should be used. For example, in Shaka 1666, on the first day of the bright half of Chaitra, a Friday. In this year, there is an intercalary Vaishakha. Calculating the *Ahargana* for the first of Chaitra: Shaka 1666 minus 1442 is 223. Divided by eleven, the *Chakra* is 20 and the remainder is 3. Multiplied by twelve, it is 36. Adding the months elapsed from Chaitra (0), it remains 36. Doubling the *Chakra* (40) and adding it gives 76; adding ten gives 86. Divided by thirty-three <note>original: "amara" (the gods/33)</note>, the intercalary months result as 2. Since this intercalary month occurs after Vaishakha, it is not accepted here; one must subtract one. Thus, the intercalary month is 1. Adding this to the 36 and multiplying by thirty gives 1110. Adding the elapsed lunar days (0) and one-sixth of the *Chakra* (3), we get 1113. Divided by sixty-four, the omitted days are 17. Subtracting these, the *Ahargana* is 1096. To match the desired Friday, one is added, making the *Ahargana* 1097. If the calculation were done with the raw intercalary months, it would be 1124; even subtracting one for the weekday would yield 1123, which is incorrect because it would cause a discrepancy in the resulting planetary positions. Therefore, an intercalary month is not accepted before it actually occurs. Conversely, in months following an intercalary month, if the calculation does not show it, it must still be included. For example, in Samvat 1669 (Shaka 1530), there is an intercalary Bhadrapada. Calculating for the first of Kartika, a Saturday: Shaka 1530 minus 1442 is 88. Divided by eleven, the *Chakra* is 8, remainder 0. Multiplied by twelve is 0. Adding 7 months from Chaitra gives 7. Doubling the *Chakra* (16) and adding it gives 23. Adding ten—

# With the Commentary on Grahalaghava

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on Grahalaghava—</header>

...that 33. Divided by the "gods" <note>original: *amaraiḥ*; a code-word for the number 33</note>, the resulting intercalary month is 1. Even if an additional intercalary month is not mathematically obtained here, it should still be taken. By doing so, the intercalary months become 2. These two are added to the quantity placed in two positions: 9, multiplied by thirty: 270, added to the elapsed lunar days: 270, added to one-sixth of the cycle: 1, resulting in 271. This is placed in two positions and divided by sixty-four; the result is 4. Subtracting this from the quantity in the other position, the count of days (*Ahargana*) is 267. To find the desired day of the week, one is subtracted, and the day-count becomes 266, which falls on a Saturday. If the day-count were calculated using only the mathematically "obtained" intercalary month, it would be 238; therefore, that would be incorrect. This is because the resulting position of the Sun and other planets would disagree with observations. Therefore, after a "clear" <note>calculated/true</note> intercalary month has occurred, even if it is not mathematically "obtained" by the simplified formula, it must be included.

This was stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A famous 12th-century astronomical text</note> by the great teacher Bhaskaracharya:

> "Whenever a 'clear' intercalary month has occurred but is not obtained by the formula, or when it is obtained but has not yet occurred;
> The wise should calculate the heap of days (*Ahargana*) by adding or subtracting one intercalary month respectively."

There is another specific rule: In the calculation of the day-count following an intercalary month, if one is counting elapsed months from Chaitra <note>the first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note>, the intercalary month itself is not counted as a separate month. However, in the middle of the day-count calculation, when taking the elapsed lunar days, the lunar days of the intercalary month must be included. Now, the method for deriving the *Brahmatulya* day-count from the *Grahalaghava* day-count is described by the venerable Ganesha Daivajña. It is as follows:

->The *Grahalaghava* day-count increased by 123,113<-
->and increased by 4,016 times the number of cycles, becomes the *Grahatulya* count. || 4-5 ||<-

### The Madhuri Commentary

"The Shaka year reduced by 1442" = the current Shaka year minus 1442. "Divided by the Lord" = divided by eleven; the "result" = the quotient, "is called the Cycle." The "remainder multiplied by the Sun" = the remainder multiplied by twelve, "added to the months starting from Chaitra" = added to the elapsed lunar months of the current year. This sum is "placed separately." From this, "added to ten" and "added to twice the cycles," "along with the intercalary months obtained by the 'gods' (33)," "multiplied by thirty" = multiplied by 30, "added to the elapsed lunar days" = including the elapsed lunar days of the desired month, "added to the sixth part of the cycle," "placed in another position." From this, "the results of dividing by sixty-four" = the number of omitted lunar days (*kshaya-tithis*), "subtracted," becomes the "heap of days" (*Ahargana*) = the collection of civil days. Here, the word *vai* is used for emphasis. "The day-count added to five times the cycles" gives the "day of the week" starting "from the Moon" <note>Monday</note>. || 4-5 ||

### The Rationale (Upapatti):

By calculating the day-count from the beginning of the *Kalpa* <note>a vast cosmic age</note> up to the desired day, the planets produced are the "mean planets" for that day. Here, the planets produced from the day-count from the beginning of the *Kalpa* until the start of this book (Shaka 1442) are called "additive constants" (*ksepa*). Similarly, the planets produced by a day-count corresponding to a cycle of eleven years are called "constants" (*dhruva*). The planets produced by the day-count from the end of a cycle to the desired day are called "planets born of the day-count" by the Teacher. By adding these together, the mean planets from the beginning of the *Kalpa* to the desired day are found. Because the work was begun in Shaka 1442, and one "cycle" is defined as eleven years, one subtracts 1442 from the desired Shaka year and divides the remainder by eleven to get the number of cycles. The remainder of the cycles is multiplied by twelve to get the solar months elapsed since the end of the year (since twelve months make a year). When the elapsed lunar months from Chaitra are added to these, it becomes the total count of months. However, this is <unclear>therefore</unclear> <unclear>consequently</unclear> even when converting solar to lunar, the remainder of the intercalary month is taken. Right here, the intercalary months are—

<note>The following section presents a mathematical ratio for calculating intercalary months (Adhimasa) based on the relationship between solar and lunar cycles.</note>

$\frac{\text{K. A. Ma.} \times \text{I. Sau.}}{\text{K. Sau.}} = \frac{\text{I. Sau.}}{\frac{\text{K. Sau.}}{\text{K. A. Ma.}}} = \frac{\text{I. Sau.}}{32 | 16 | 4}$ <note>K. A. Ma. = Kalpa Adhimasa (Intercalary months in an eon); I. Sau. = Ishta Saura (Elapsed solar months); K. Sau. = Kalpa Saura (Solar months in an eon). The value 32|16|4 represents the interval in months between intercalary additions.</note>

In place of this value (32|16|4), the Teacher <note>referring to the author of the astronomical treatise</note> has adopted the number 33. Because this divisor is larger, the resulting quotient is smaller than the true value. This difference between the true and calculated values over one cycle <term>Chakra: a specific period of years used in this system</term> equals the residual of two months. Therefore, the number of cycles is multiplied by two. Furthermore, at the commencement of this text, there was a remainder of ten months; thus, their sum constitutes the desired intercalary months. By adding these intercalary months—calculated as $\frac{\text{I. Sau.} + 2 \text{ Ch.} + 10}{33}$—to the count of solar months, we obtain the lunar months. This is because the difference between solar and lunar months is defined as the intercalary month. This month-count is multiplied by thirty and added to the elapsed lunar days <term>Tithis</term> to find the total lunar days.

Now, the desired omitted days <term>Avama: days deleted to synchronize the lunar and solar calendars</term> are calculated as:
$= \frac{\text{K. Ava.} \times \text{I. Chan. Di.}}{\text{K. Chan. Di.}} = \frac{\text{I. Chan. Di.}}{\frac{\text{K. Chan. Di.}}{\text{K. Ava.}}}$

$= \frac{\text{I. Chan. Di.}}{63 + \frac{9}{10}}$

However, the Teacher has used $\frac{\text{I. Chan. Di.}}{64}$ here due to the very small difference. But in one cycle, the omitted days actually equal $63 \frac{9}{10}$. Therefore, $64 - 63 \frac{9}{10} = \frac{1}{10}$ has been taken in excess for each cycle. By multiplying the cycle count by this $\frac{1}{10}$ and adding it to the previously calculated omitted days, we get the true omitted days. Thus, the lunar days minus these omitted days $= \text{I. Chan. Di.} + \frac{\text{Ch.}}{64}$ <note>formula simplified for calculation</note> results in the civil day-count <term>Ahargana: the number of days elapsed since a fixed epoch</term> at sunrise. This is proven because Lunar Days - Civil Days = Omitted Days.

**The derivation for determining the day of the week:**
The remainder of one cycle divided by seven is 5. Therefore, multiply the cycle count by five, add it to the desired day-count, and divide by seven. Since the day the text commenced was a Monday <note>original: "Chandra-vara"</note>, the result indicates the number of days elapsed from Monday. The reason for discarding the remainders of the intercalary and omitted days is well-explained in the standard astronomical treatises <term>Siddhantas</term>. It is not detailed here for fear of making the text too long. Thus, all is proven. || 4-5 ||

Subtract 1452 from the desired Shaka era year; the quotient when divided by 11 is called the **Cycle** <term>Chakra</term>. Multiply the remainder by 12, add the lunar months elapsed since the start of the year (Chaitra), and place this in two positions. In one position, add 10 and twice the Cycle number, then divide by 33. Add the resulting intercalary months to the months set aside in the other position and multiply by 30. To this, add the number of lunar days <term>Tithis</term> elapsed in the current month, then add one-sixth of the Cycle number. Place this in two positions. Divide one by 64 and subtract the resulting "loss days" from the other position. The result is the day-count <term>Ahargana</term> for sunrise on the desired day.

Add five times the Cycle to the day-count and divide by 7; the remainder gives the day of the week starting from Monday. || 4-5 ||

### Example—

We must calculate the *Ahargana* <term>Ahargana: the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a target date</term> for the New Moon of the dark fortnight of the month of Karttika, Friday, in the Shaka year 1758 <note>approx. 1836 CE</note>. Following the previously stated method: 1758 - 1442 = 316. Therefore, 316 ÷ 19 = a quotient of 27 and a remainder of 9. Here, 27 is the number of cycles <note>Chakra</note>. 12 × 9 = 108. From the first day of Chaitra to the New Moon of Ashvina, 6 lunar months have passed. Thus, 108 + 6 = 114. This is placed in two positions: 114 and 114. The cycle count is 27. Therefore, (27 × 2) + 10 + 114 = 54 + 10 + 114 = 178. 178 ÷ 33 = 6, which are the intercalary months <note>Adhimasa</note>. Thus, 114 + 6 = 120 months have passed. 120 × 30 = 3600. From the first day of Ashvina to the 14th day of the dark fortnight of Karttika, 29 lunar days <note>Tithis</note> have passed. Thus, 3600 + 29 = 3629 lunar days. Therefore, 37 ÷ 6 = quotient 6, remainder 1. So, 3629 + 6 = 3635. Since 3635 ÷ 64 = quotient 56, remainder 51. Because the remainder 51 is more than half, the quotient is increased by 1; therefore, 57 are the omitted days <note>Kshayah</note>. Thus, 3635 - 57 = 3578, which is the *Ahargana* (total day count).

**Determining the weekday from the Ahargana—** Cycle = 27. Therefore, 27 × 5 = 135. The Ahargana = 3578. Thus, 3578 + 135 = 3713. 3713 ÷ 7 = quotient 530, remainder 4. Counting from Monday, the 4th day is Thursday (elapsed), and the current day is Friday.

If the desired weekday is not reached when calculating from the *Ahargana*, one should add or subtract one (as appropriate). Furthermore, if an intercalary month occurred in a month prior to the one being calculated but does not appear in the calculation, one should add 1 to the obtained intercalary months. If an intercalary month is expected after the desired month but appears earlier in the calculation, one should subtract 1. See the Vishwanathi commentary for examples.

### The Rationale (Upapatti):

Here, in one cycle (11 years), by the proportion of the years of a *Kalpa* <note>a vast cosmic age</note>, the revolutions of the planets in a Kalpa are used. For the 11 years falling within one cycle, the planets are obtained in Signs etc. For the sake of ease, these are purified by the total revolutions (12) and designated as "constants" (Dhruvas). These should be understood as the Signs etc. read for those respective planets.

# Chapter on Mean Motion || 1 ||

->Now he describes the specific correction for the epochal constant (Dhruva-Kshepaka) for the planets derived from the total elapsed days (Ahargana):<-

> **The planet produced from the count of days, diminished by the constant multiplied by the number of cycles,**
> **and increased by its own epochal position, becomes the mean planet at sunrise.**
> **From the multitude of yojanas <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> situated between one's own city and the prime meridian,**
> **minutes of arc measured by one-sixth [of those yojanas] are added or subtracted for the Moon, in the west or east respectively. || 9 ||**

Now he explains the correction of the epochal constant for planets derived from the count of days. *The planet produced from the count of days*: the planet calculated according to the method to be described from the *Ahargana* <note>The total number of elapsed days since a fixed epoch</note>. *Diminished by the constant multiplied by the cycle*: subtracted by the constant (Dhruva) which has been multiplied by the number of elapsed 11-year cycles, and then *increased by its own epochal position* (Kshepaka). Thus, that planet becomes *mean at the rising of the maker of day* (at sunrise). The intention is that the planet becomes a mean planet at the time of mean sunrise in the city of Lanka <note>The theoretical city on the equator used as the zero-point for Indian astronomical longitudinal calculations</note>. This is stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note> as "The city of the ten-headed one [Lanka]," etc. 

To make this applicable to one's own location, he describes a correction: *From the multitude of yojanas...* From the total distance in yojanas existing between one's own city and the *Madhya-rekha* (the prime meridian), minutes of arc (minutes) measured by a *sixth part* (rasa-lava) should be added or subtracted for the Moon, in the west or east respectively. That is to say: if one's city is west of the prime meridian, the value is added; if east, it is subtracted. The measurement of the prime meridian was stated by Bhaskara as "The city of the demons [Lanka]." Here, this correction is made only for the Moon. Because the difference for other planets is very small, it is not performed, and thus there is no error. As stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*: "Because the difference is very small," etc. || 9 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary —<-

<term>Chakra-nighna-dhruvonah</term> = devoid of the constant multiplied by the cycle; <term>Dinagana-bhava-khetah</term> = the planet produced from the count of days; <term>Sva-kshepa-yuk</term> = joined with its own epochal position; <term>Divasakrit-udaye</term> = at sunrise; <term>Madhyamah</term> = the mean planet, it shall be. <term>Indau</term> = for the Moon; <term>Nija-nija-pura-rekhantah-sthitat</term> = from that which lies between the meridian and one's own city; <term>Yojanaughat</term> = from the sum of yojanas; <term>Rasalava-mita-liptah</term> = minutes of arc equal to one-sixth [of the yojanas]; <term>Pare prak</term> = in the west and east of the meridian respectively; <term>Svarnam</term> = addition and subtraction should be performed. The meaning is: in one's own country to the west, addition; in one's own country to the east, subtraction should be done. || 9 ||

Here is the <term>Vasana</term> <note>The underlying logic or demonstration</note> — Observing the difficulty in calculating planets from the beginning of the Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic age</note>, Ganesha <note>The author, Ganesha Daivajna</note>, calculating planets with ease, has derived the desired planets by calculating them in three parts and then summing them. There, the positions of the planets at the start of the text are given as the *Kshepaka* (epochal positions). Then, the positions for every eleven-year cycle (*Chakra*) are given as the *Dhruva* (constant), which are the remainders after subtracting full revolutions (12 signs). Then, the planets produced for the desired days after a cycle are called *Dinagana-bhava* (produced from the day-count). The sum of these becomes the mean planets at the desired sunrise from the start of the Kalpa. Here, at the start of the text:

# Commentary on the Grahalaghava

The planets related to the desired cycle = 12 × (planets from one cycle) × cycle = Constant × cycle.
Therefore, 12 × cycle - (Constant × cycle) = planets produced in the desired cycle. By adding all these, the mean planets at the desired time are found:
= Planets from the total days + (12 × cycle - Constant × cycle) + Epochal Position <note>The 'Epochal Position' or 'Kshepa' is the position of a planet at the start of a specific era.</note>. Since the full revolutions (cycles) are not needed here, we discard '12 × cycle' —
(Planets from total days - Constant × cycle) + Epochal Position = Mean planets at the desired time. Thus, the first half of the verse is proven.

Now, the planets calculated here are for the Prime Meridian <note>original: 'Rekha-desha', referring to the line passing through Ujjain</note>. To adapt them for one's local position, the longitudinal correction <term>Deshantara-samskara: a correction applied to account for the distance between the observer's location and the prime meridian</term> must be performed. Here, the author has applied the longitudinal correction only to the Moon, because its motion is very fast. For other planets, it is ignored due to their slow motion.

Now, knowing the distance in leagues <note>original: 'Yojanas'</note> between the Prime Meridian and the local place, the proportion is as follows — * If the Moon's motion in minutes is obtained for the Earth's circumference in leagues, then what is obtained for the longitudinal distance in leagues? The resulting Lunar longitudinal correction = 

(Moon's motion in minutes × Longitudinal distance) &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; (790' 35'') × Long. distance &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Long. distance
------------------------------------------------- = --------------------------- = -----------------
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Earth's circumference in leagues &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 4967 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 6

This is due to a small difference. If the local place is West of the Prime Meridian, the resulting minutes should be added to the Moon calculated from the total days. This is because the sunrise there occurs after the sunrise at the Meridian. If the local place is to the East, it should be subtracted, as the sunrise occurs before the Meridian sunrise. This is correctly stated. — The Editor. || 9 ||

By multiplying the constant of a planet by the cycle and subtracting it from the planet generated by the total days <note>original: 'Ahargana'</note>, and then adding the planet's epochal position, the mean planet at sunrise is found. Divide the distance in leagues between your location and the Prime Meridian by 6; if your location is west of the Meridian, add the resulting minutes to the Moon; if east, subtract them to find the mean Moon for your location. || 9 ||

### Example — See ahead || 9 ||

The Prime Meridian locations are those touched by the line going from Lanka to Mount Meru. For example —

### The Equator (Prime Meridian) —

> "The line touching Lanka, Ujjain, Kurukshetra, and other places, going to Meru, is called the Middle Line of the Earth by the wise." (Siddhanta Shiromani) <note>Lanka here refers to an equatorial point, not necessarily modern Sri Lanka.</note>.

### Earth's Circumference in Leagues —

> "The circumference of the Earth is said to be 4967 leagues; its diameter is 1581." (Siddhanta Shiromani) || 9 ||

Now, he describes the calculation for the mean Sun, Mercury, Venus, and Moon —

> **The Sun, Mercury, and Venus are derived from the total days minus their seventy-thousandth part;**
> **the result of the total days divided by fifteen is subtracted from the minutes to get degrees and so on.**
> **The Moon is the total days divided by 18, minus its one-hundred-and-eighty-first part;**
> **the total days divided by 140 is subtracted from the minutes to get degrees and so on. || 10 ||**

Now the method for mean Sun, Mercury, Venus, and Moon is explained. "Sva-kha-naga" etc. The total days <note>Ahargana</note> is 1921. This is placed in two spots: 1921 divided by seventy (70) gives a result of 27 degrees. The remainder is 31, multiplied by sixty (60) is 1860, divided by seventy (70) gives 26 minutes. Again the remainder is 40, multiplied by sixty (60) is 2400, [divided by] seventy (70)...

---

\* Here, the proportion should ideally use the corrected Earth circumference and corrected Moon's motion. However, since small differences are observed throughout this manual <term>Karana-grantha: a concise astronomical manual for practical calculations</term>, the proportion has been made in this manner. — The Editor.

# Chapter on Mean Motions || 1 ||
Page 13

The result obtained is in minutes of arc <note>original: "kala"</note> and so on; the seconds <note>original: "vikala"</note> are 42. Thus, the value in degrees and so on is 29; 43, 42. This must be subtracted from the total count of elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the number of days passed since the beginning of an epoch</term> which is 1521. The method is as follows: since degrees are to be subtracted from the day-count, one degree is taken from the total and converted into 60 minutes. From these, the previous minutes are subtracted to find the remaining minutes. From those, one minute is taken and converted into 60 seconds. From these, the previous seconds are subtracted to find the remaining seconds. || 10 ||

In older printed books, the example provided by the commentator Vishvanatha for this tenth verse is not found in its entirety. From the point where Vishvanatha’s example was printed, it continues: "Therefore, the value in degrees etc. is 1499; 16, 18. Again, the day-count of 1521 is divided by 150 <note>original: "kha-tithi," where 'kha' (space) is 0 and 'tithi' is 15</note>. The result in minutes etc. is subtracted from the previously obtained degrees etc. (1499; 16, 18). This gives the degrees for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus as 1499; 6, 10. Converting this to signs <note>one sign = 30 degrees</note> and degrees, we get 11 signs, 29 degrees, 6 minutes, and 10 seconds. Now, the constant for the Sun <note>the position at the start of the epoch</term> is 0; 14, 51, 11. Multiplied by 8 cycles, it becomes 0; 14, 33, 28. Subtracting the motion from the day-count (11 signs, 29; 6, 10) results in 1 sign, 14, 32, 42. Adding the solar additive constant of 11 signs, 19, 41, 0, the mean Sun, Mercury, and Venus at sunrise are found to be 1 sign, 14 degrees, 32 minutes, and 42 seconds.

Now, the calculation for the Moon: The day-count 1521 multiplied by fourteen is 21294. Its seventeenth part is 1252; 35, 18. Subtracting this from the fourteen-fold day-count (21294) gives the degrees etc. as 20041; 24, 42. Again, the day-count 1521 is divided by 240 <note>original: "kha-manu," where 'kha' is 0 and 'manu' is 24</note>, giving 6 minutes and 22 seconds <note>The text says 10; 52, likely a variant reading</note>. Subtracting this from the previous degrees (20041; 24, 42) results in 20041; 13, 50. Converting this to signs, the Moon's motion from the day-count is 8 signs, 11 degrees, 13 minutes, and 50 seconds. The Moon's constant 0; 3, 46, 11 multiplied by 8 cycles is 1; 0, 9, 28. Subtracting this from the day-count motion gives 7 signs, 11, 4, 22. Adding the lunar additive constant 11; 19, 6, 0, the mean Moon is 6 signs, 20 degrees, 10 minutes, and 22 seconds." This much should be understood. — The Editor || 10 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

"Diminished by its own seventieth part" <note>original: "svakhangalavahina"</note> means the day-count <note>original: "yuvraja"</note> minus its 1/70th part. These are the degrees <note>original: "amshakaya"</note> for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus. From their minutes, the day-count divided by 150 must be subtracted. Now, for the Moon: the day-count multiplied by fourteen <note>original: "ganamanuhati"</note> is the Moon. This is diminished by its own seventeenth part and, in the minutes, diminished by the day-count divided by 140. || 10 ||

---

### Mathematical Proof—

If the total solar motion in minutes during a Kalpa <term>a vast cosmic cycle of time</term> is obtained by the total number of civil days in a Kalpa, then what will be the motion for the desired day-count? By this proportion:

⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

$= \frac{70 \times A ( 59' \text{ } 8'' \text{ } 10''' )}{70} = \frac{A ( 4130' \text{ } 56'' \text{ } 700''' )}{70} =$

$= \frac{A ( 4139' \text{ } 31'' \text{ } 40''' )}{70} = \frac{A ( 68^\circ \text{ } 59' \text{ } 32'' )}{70} \text{ (converted by sixty)}$ <note>original: "shashtya savarnite"; this refers to the sexagesimal system where 60 seconds make a minute and 60 minutes make a degree.</note>

$= \frac{A ( 68^\circ \text{ } 59' \text{ } 32'' ) + 28'' - 28''}{70} \text{ (by adding and subtracting equals)},$ <note>original: "tulyayogaviyogat"; a common algebraic technique to complete a whole number.</note>

$= \frac{A ( 69^\circ - 28'' )}{70} = \frac{A \times 69^\circ}{70} - \frac{28'' A}{70} = \frac{A ( 69^\circ + 1^\circ - 1^\circ )}{70} - \frac{28'' A}{70}$

$= \frac{A \text{ } 70^\circ}{70} - \frac{A \text{ } 1^\circ}{70} - \frac{28'' A}{70} = A \text{ } 1^\circ - \frac{A \text{ } 1^\circ}{70} - \frac{A'}{\frac{70 \times 60}{28}}$

$= A \text{ } 1^\circ - \frac{A \text{ } 1^\circ}{70} - \frac{A'}{\frac{4200}{28}} = A \text{ } 1^\circ - \frac{A \text{ } 1^\circ}{70} - \frac{A'}{150} .$

->Because the revolutions of Mercury, Venus, and the Sun are equal, Mercury and Venus are considered equal to the Sun <note>in terms of mean motion</note>; thus, it is proven.<-

### Now, the derivation for the Moon's position—

->According to the previous method of proportion within a Kalpa <note>a vast cosmic cycle of time</note>: Mean Moon = $\frac{\text{Moon's Revolutions in a Kalpa} \times \text{A}}{\text{Civil Days in a Kalpa}}$<-

$= \frac{A \times 57753336 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60}{5477917828} = \frac{A \times 57753336 \times 12 \times 30 \times 15}{1369479457}$

$= \frac{3108668014400 \times A}{1369479457} = A ( 790' \text{ } 34'' \text{ } 54''' )$

$= A ( 13^\circ \text{ } 10' \text{ } 34'' \text{ } 54''' ) = \frac{A \times 17 ( 13^\circ \text{ } 10' \text{ } 34'' \text{ } 54''' )}{17}$

$= \frac{A ( 221^\circ \text{ } 170' \text{ } 578'' \text{ } 918''' )}{17} = \frac{A ( 223^\circ \text{ } 59' \text{ } 53'' )}{17} \text{ (due to slight difference)}$ <note>original: "svalpantarat"; indicating a rounding for mathematical convenience.</note>

$= \frac{A ( 223^\circ \text{ } 59' \text{ } 53'' ) + 7'' - 7''}{17} = \frac{A ( 224^\circ - 7'' )}{17} = \frac{A \text{ } 224^\circ}{17} - \frac{A \text{ } 7''}{17}$

$= \frac{A \times 224^\circ + 14^\circ - 14^\circ}{17} - \frac{A \text{ } 7''}{17} = \frac{A \times 238^\circ}{17} - \frac{A \times 14^\circ}{17} - \frac{A \times 7''}{17}$

$= A \text{ } 14^\circ - \frac{A \times 14^\circ}{17} - \frac{A \times 7''}{17 \times 60} = A \text{ } 14^\circ - \frac{A \times 14^\circ}{17} - \frac{A'}{\frac{1020}{7}}$

$= A \times 14^\circ - \frac{A \times 14^\circ}{17} - \frac{A'}{145} \text{ due to slight difference, thus it is proven. || 10 ||}$

By subtracting the minutes and seconds—representing the 145th part of the Ahargana <note>the total number of days</note>—from the result in degrees obtained by subtracting the 17th part of the Ahargana, <insert>Digitized by Google</insert> the positions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus are found, and the product of the Ahargana...

# Chapter on Mean Motions || 1 ||

By subtracting the 70th part of the <term>Ahargana</term> (total elapsed days) from the total degrees, and further subtracting the 150th part of that same <term>Ahargana</term> in the form of minutes, the position of the Moon in degrees etc. is obtained. || 10 ||

**Example—**

->The previously calculated <term>Ahargana</term> = 3578.<- 

Therefore, according to the verse: 3578 ÷ 70 = 51° 7' 15''. $\therefore$ 3578 - 51° 7' 15'' = 3526° 52' 45''. <note>The text has a slight calculation or printing discrepancy in the subtraction result here</note> Then 3578 ÷ 150 = 23' 51'', therefore (3526° 52' 55'') - (23' 51'') = 3526° 29' 4''. By dividing the degrees by 30, we get 117 <term>Signs</term> 16° 29' 4'', and by dividing the Signs by 12, the quotient 9 is discarded as unnecessary <note>Multiples of 12 signs represent full revolutions and are ignored in positional astronomy</note>, leaving the position of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus as 9 Signs 16° 29' 4''. Now, according to Verse 9: $\therefore$ Cycles = 37, the Sun's Constant (<term>Dhruva</term>) = 0s 1° 49' 11'', and the Sun's Additive (<term>Kshepa</term>) = 11s 19° 41' 10''. Thus, multiplying the cycles by the constant (37 x (0s 1° 49' 11'') = 0s 37° 18' 53''. 40'' = 2s 7° 11' 47''). Subtracting this from the Sun's position generated by the Ahargana: (9s 16° 29' 4'') - (2s 7° 11' 47'') = 7s 9° 17' 17''. Adding the Additive to this: (7s 9° 17' 17'') + (11s 19° 41' 10'') = 6s 28° 50' 27''. These are the positions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus at the time of sunrise.

Now, the example for calculating the Moon — <term>Ahargana</term> = 3578. $\therefore$ 14 x 3578 = 50092. $\therefore$ 50092 ÷ 17 = 2946° 35' 17''. $\therefore$ 50092 - (2946° 35' 17'') = 47145° 24' 43''. Dividing the degrees by 30 = 11 <term>Signs</term> 15° 24' 43''. Subtracting 3578 ÷ 140 = 25' 33'' from this: (11s 15° 24' 43'') - (25' 33'') = 11s 14° 59' 10'' = the Moon generated from the <term>Ahargana</term>. Again, $\therefore$ Cycles = 37, the Moon's Constant = 0s 3° 46' 11'', and the Additive = 11s 19° 16' 10''. Thus, the cycles multiplied by the constant (37 x (0s 3° 46' 11'') = 0s 111° 17' 2'' 40'' = 4s 19° 38' 47''). Subtracting this from the Ahargana-generated Moon: (11s 14° 59' 10'') - (4s 19° 38' 47'') = 6s 25° 20' 23''. Adding the Additive: (6s 25° 20' 23'') + (11s 19° 16' 10'') = 6s 14° 36' 33'', which is the mean Moon for the prime meridian.

Now, the <term>Correction for Longitude</term>—the local place is 96 <term>Yojanas</term> <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-13km</note> east of the prime meridian. Therefore, 96 ÷ 6 = 16'. By subtracting these minutes of longitude from the previously calculated Moon: (6s 14° 36' 33'') - (0s 0° 16' 0'') = 6s 14° 20' 33''. This is the true mean Moon at local sunrise. || 10 ||

### Now he describes the calculation for the Moon's Apogee and Node—

> The sum of days divided by nine is the Moon's apogee in degrees;
> To this, add the minutes obtained by dividing the constant by seventy.
> From the sum divided by nine-one-one (119) and five-four (45) separately,
> The sum of the resulting degrees and minutes is the Node, subtracted from the cycle. || 11 ||

Now he explains the <term>Calculation of the Moon's Apogee and Node</term>. Regarding "The sum of days divided by nine": The count is 1921 <note>original: "गण: १९२१"</note>, divided by nine, the result in degrees etc. is 169° 0' 0''. The count 1921 divided by seventy (<term>Khanaga</term>) <note>A Sanskrit numerical code where 'Kha' = 0 and 'Naga' = 7</note> gives 27' 23'' in minutes etc. Adding this to the minutes: 169° 27' 43'', or in Signs etc. 5s 19° 27' 43''. The Constant for the Moon's apogee is 9s 24° 49' 0''. Multiplied by 8 cycles: 0s 22° 0' 0''. Subtracting 7s 22° 0' 0'' from this: 4s 27° 29' 43''. Adding the Additive 1s 29° 53' 0'', the Moon's apogee becomes 10s 27° <unclear>42</unclear>'.

<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

### 54.43. Now, the Calculation of Rahu <note>Rahu refers to the Ascending Lunar Node.</note>.

The group <note>The *Ahargana* or number of elapsed days since the epoch.</note> is 19-1. Divided in two places: in one, divided by nineteen (19), the result in degrees etc. is 80;3;9. In the other, divided by forty-five (45), the result in minutes etc. is 33;48. The sum of these two is 80;36;57. In signs etc., this is 2;20;36;57. Now, subtracted from twelve (12) signs, the resulting Rahu is 9;9;23;3. The constant <term>Dhruva</term> <note>A fixed starting position for a specific epoch.</note> for Rahu is 7;2;50;0. Multiplied by 8 cycles, it is 8;22;50;0. Subtracted by this, it is 0;16;43;3. Added to the additive <term>Kshepaka</term> <note>A correction factor applied to the mean position.</note> 0;27;38;0, the resulting Rahu is 1;14;21;3. || 11 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary—<-

The sum of days multiplied by nine = the number of days divided by nine; the result in degrees etc. is the <term>Chandra-tunga</term> <note>The Lunar Apogee.</note>. Again, here, the minutes obtained by dividing the group by seventy should be added. Now, in two places = because it is placed in two positions; from the <term>Ghasra-sangha</term> = the number of days (*Ahargana*); by "earth-arrows" = nineteen (19); by "arrows-Vedas" = forty-five (45); from the quotient = the result obtained; the sum of the resulting degrees and minutes should be made, then it becomes <term>Agu</term> = Rahu. This Rahu must be "cycle-purified" = subtracted from twelve signs. || 11 ||

->Here is the Proof:—<-

According to the previous method, the Lunar Apogee is derived from the number of days using the ratio of the <term>Kalpa</term> <note>A vast cosmic time cycle of 4.32 billion years.</note>. Thus, the revolutions of the Lunar Apogee in a Kalpa according to the Surya Siddhanta = 488,203. The terrestrial days in a Kalpa = 1,577,917,828. Therefore, the Lunar Apogee =

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| (Kalpa Lunar Apogee Rev. $\times$ Days) | 488,203 $\times$ 12 $\times$ 30 $\times$ 60 $\times$ Days |
| ----------------------- | = -------------------------------------------- |
| Kalpa Terrestrial Days | 1,577,917,828 |

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| 488,203 $\times$ 12 $\times$ 30 $\times$ 15 $\times$ Days | 2,636,296,200 $\times$ Days |
| ----------------------------------------- | (Divided by four) = ----------------------- |
| 394,479,457 | 394,479,457 |

= ($6' 140'' 152'''$) $\times$ Days = $\frac{(6' 140'' 152''') \times 9 \times \text{Days}}{9}$ = $\frac{(1^\circ 10' 7'' 48''') \times \text{Days}}{9}$

| | | | | | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days $\times$ 7'' | Days $\times$ 48''' | Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days $\times$ 7' | Days $\times$ 48' |
| ---- + | --------- + | ---------- = | --------- + | ----------- + | -------------- |
| 9 | 9 | 9 | 9 | 9 $\times$ 60 | 9 $\times$ 60 $\times$ 60 |

| | | | | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days $\times$ 7' | Days' | Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days' |
| --------- + | ------ + | ------- = | --------- + | ----, due to slight difference. |
| 9 | 540 | 32,400 | 9 | 70 |

->Thus, the calculation of the Lunar Apogee is proven.<-

---

->Now, the Proof for the Lunar Node (Rahu):—<-

The revolutions of the Node in a Kalpa according to Aryabhata = 232,226. The terrestrial days in a Kalpa = 1,577,917,500.
By the ratio: if these are the minutes of the Node's revolutions in the Kalpa's terrestrial days, then what are they for the desired number of days? Thus is produced the Node called Rahu —

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| (Kalpa Node Rev. Min. $\times$ Days) | 232,226 $\times$ 12 $\times$ 30 $\times$ 60 $\times$ Days |
| ----------------------- | = ------------------------------------------- |
| Kalpa Terrestrial Days | 1,577,917,500 |

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| 232,226 $\times$ 12 $\times$ 30 $\times$ Days | 83,601,360 $\times$ Days |
| --------------------------- | = ------------------- = ($3' 190'' 188'''$) $\times$ Days |
| 26,298,625 | 26,298,625 |

| | | | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| ($3' 190'' 188'''$) $\times$ 19 $\times$ Days | Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days $\times$ 25' | Days $\times$ 48' |
| ------------------------- | = ----- + | ----------- + | ------------ |
| 19 | 19 | 19 $\times$ 60 | 19 $\times$ 360 |

| | | | | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days $\times$ 25' | Days $\times$ 48' | Days $\times$ 1$^\circ$ | Days' |
| ------- + | ------ + | ------- = | ----- + | ----, due to slight difference. |
| 19 | 1,140 | 68,400 | 19 | 45 |

Because the motion of Rahu is retrograde <note>original: "vilo-ma-gati"</note>, it is subtracted from the cycle (12 signs). Thus, it is proven. ||

By dividing the *Ahargana* <note>The total count of days elapsed from the start of the epoch</note> by 9, the resulting degrees and other units, when added to the minutes and further units obtained by dividing the *Ahargana* by 70, give the position of the Moon’s Apogee <note>original: "चन्द्रोच्च" (Chandrouchcha); the point where the Moon is farthest from Earth</note>. To find Rahu <note>The ascending lunar node</note>, take the *Ahargana* placed in two locations, divide them by 19 and 45 respectively, and subtract the sum of these resulting degrees and minutes from 12 Signs <note>A full circle of the zodiac</note>. || 11 ||

### Example—
*Ahargana* (A) $\div$ 9 = 3578 $\div$ 9 = 397° 33′ 20″. And 3578 $\div$ 70 = 51′ 7″.
$\therefore$ (397° 33′ 20″) + (51′ 7″) = 398° 24′ 27″ = 9 Signs 18° 19′ 24″ 27″ <note>The text uses "r" for Rashi/Signs</note> = This is the Moon’s Apogee in signs and degrees.

Again, according to Verse 9—
The constant <note>original: "ध्रुवा" (Dhruva)</note> for the Moon’s Apogee = 9 Signs 12° 45′ 100″ and the cycle count = 37.
$\therefore$ 37 $\times$ (9 Signs 12° 45′ 100″) = 333 Signs 74° 166′ 5′ 100″ = 00 Signs 199° 14′ 5′ 100″.
Subtracting this from the Moon’s Apogee generated from the *Ahargana*:
(9 Signs 18° 24′ 27″) - (00 Signs 199° 14′ 5′ 100″) = 00 Signs 126° 139′ 127″.
Adding the additive constant <note>original: "क्षेप" (Kshepa)</note> for the Moon’s Apogee (5 Signs 17° 33′ 100″):
(00 Signs 126° 139′ 127″) + (5 Signs 17° 33′ 100″) = 6 Signs 14° 192′ 27″ = The Moon’s Apogee in signs etc. at the time of sunrise.

### Calculation of Rahu—
$\because$ A $\div$ 19 = 3578 $\div$ 19 = 188° 19′ 15″ and A $\div$ 45 = 3578 $\div$ 45 = 79′ 131″ = 1° 19′ 131″.
$\therefore$ (188° 19′ 15″) + (1° 19′ 131″) = 189° 138′ 128″ = 6 Signs 9° 138′ 128″.
Subtracting this from 12 Signs gives 5 Signs 20° 121′ 132″ = Rahu generated from the *Ahargana*.
Again, the constant for Rahu in signs etc. = 7 Signs 2° 50′ 100″, cycle = 37, and additive constant = 0 Signs 27° 38′ 100″.
Thus, 37 $\times$ (7 Signs 2° 50′ 100″) = 259 Signs 74° 1850′ 100″ = 10 Signs 14° 50′ 100″.
$\therefore$ (5 Signs 20° 121′ 132″) - (10 Signs 14° 50′ 100″) = 7 Signs 5° 131′ 132″.
Finally: (7 Signs 5° 131′ 132″) + (00 Signs 27° 38′ 100″) = 8 Signs 3° 19′ 132″ = The mean Rahu at the time of sunrise. || 11 ||

### Now, the method for bringing forth the centers of Mars and Mercury—

> The day-count multiplied by ten and placed in two positions, divided by nineteen and seventy-three; the difference between the resulting degrees and minutes shall be Mars. ||
> The day-count multiplied by three, increased by its own twenty-eighth part, gives the Mercury-fast-center <note>original: "ज्ञशीघ्रकेन्द्र" (Jna-shighra-kendra); the anomaly of Mercury</note> in degrees, etc., diminished by the day-count divided by thirty-eight in minutes. || 12 ||

Now the calculation for the centers of Mars and Mercury is explained. "The day-count multiplied by ten and placed in two positions" etc. The count is 1921. Multiplied by ten, it is 19210. Placed in two positions: 19210. In one place, divided by nineteen (19), the result in degrees etc. is 1003 | 13 | 4. In the other place, divided by seventy-three (73), the result in minutes etc. is 208 | 11. The difference between these two is 790 | 3 | 13. In signs etc., this is 2 | 10 | 3 | 13. The Mars constant is 1 | 29 | 32. Multiplied by 8 cycles, it is 2 | 12 | 16. Subtracting this gives 11 | 22 | 47 | 13. Adding the additive constant 10 | 7 | 8, Mars becomes 9 | 29 | 56 | 13.

Now for the calculation of Mercury’s center. The count is 1921. Multiplied by three, it is 5763. This is placed in two positions: 5763. Divided by twenty-eight (28), the result in degrees etc. is 205 | 49 | 51. Adding this to the tripled *Ahargana* gives 5792 | 57 | 51. The count 1921 divided by thirty-eight (38) gives the result in minutes etc. as 50 | 1. Subtracting these minutes gives 5792 | 59 | 50. In signs etc., this is 1 | 19 | 59 | 50. The Mercury center constant is 4 | 3 | 27. Multiplied by 8 cycles, it is 8 | 27 | 36. Subtracting this gives 4 | 17 | 41 | 50. Adding the additive constant 8 | 29 | 33 | 0, the Mercury fast-center becomes 1 | 17 | 14 | 50. || 12 ||

[The text begins with the conclusion of a rule] ...by sixty, and in the other by "three-mountains" <note>The word 'shaila' (mountain) represents the number 7 in Sanskrit numerical notation; thus 73.</note> = seventy-three, divided. The difference between the resulting degrees and minutes is Mars. -> **Mathematical Proof** <-

If in the total days of a Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> there are a specific number of revolutions for Mars, then how many are there in the desired sum of days? Thus, the mean Mars is calculated.
Here, the revolutions of Mars in a Kalpa according to the *Aryabhatiya* <note>The 5th-century astronomical treatise by Aryabhata</note> = 2,296,824, and the total days in a Kalpa = 1,577,917,500.
Therefore, Mars = $\frac{(2,296,824 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60) \times \text{Days}}{1,577,917,500} = \frac{(2,296,824 \times 360) \times \text{Days}}{26,298,625}$
$= \frac{(826,856,640) \times \text{Days}}{26,298,625} = (31' 26'' 31''' 13'''' 36''''' ) \times \text{Days}$
$= \frac{(31' 26'' 31''' 13'''' 36''''' ) \times \text{Days} \times 19}{19} = \frac{(597' 52'' 50''' 18'''' 24''''' ) \times \text{Days}}{19}$
$= \frac{(600') \times \text{Days}}{19} - \frac{(2' 7'' 19''' 41'''' 36''''' ) \times \text{Days}}{19}$
$= \frac{10^{\circ} \times \text{Days}}{19} - \frac{10' \times \text{Days}}{73}$ <note>original: "svalpāntarāt" - due to a very small difference/approximation.</note>

Now, the revolutions of the Mercury anomaly according to the *Brahma-Siddhanta* = 1,331,699,898, and the total days in a Kalpa = 157,791,645,000. Therefore, by proportion, the Mercury anomaly = $\frac{1,331,699,898 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60}{157,791,645,000}$
$= (3^{\circ} 16' 54'' 18''') \times \text{Days} = \frac{(3^{\circ} 16' 54'' 18''') \times 28 \times \text{Days}}{28} = \frac{(92^{\circ} 53' 19'' 44''') \times \text{Days}}{28}$
$= \frac{\text{Days} \times 87^{\circ}}{28} - \frac{\text{Days} \times (44' 16'')}{28} =$
$\text{Days} \times 3^{\circ} + \frac{3^{\circ} \times \text{Days}}{28} - \frac{\text{Days} \times 1'}{28 \times 60} =$
$= \text{Days} \times 3^{\circ} + \frac{3^{\circ} \times \text{Days}}{28} - \frac{\text{Days} \times 1'}{38}$, due to approximation. Thus, all is proven. || 12 ||

### Now, the method for calculating the anomalies of Jupiter and Venus—

> The day-count divided by twelve, starting with degrees, is Jupiter; subtract from the day-count the minutes obtained by dividing by seventy.
> From the day-count multiplied by three and placed in two positions, divide by five and by one hundred and eighty-one; the sum of the resulting degrees is the fast-anomaly <note>original: "Ashukendra"</note> of Venus.

Now the calculation for the anomalies of Jupiter and Venus is explained. Regarding the "day-count" <note>original: "Dyupinda"</note>: The group 1621 divided by twelve—12—yields degrees etc. $126 | 45 | 10$. The group 1621 divided by seventy—70—yields minutes etc. $23 | 43$. Subtracting this from the degrees: $126 | 43 | 15$. In signs etc. $4 | 6 | 43 | 15$. Jupiter’s constant is $0 | 26 | 6 | 10$; multiplied by 8 cycles it is $7 | 0 | 24 | 10$. Subtracting this: $9 | 5 | 19 | 15$. Adding Jupiter’s additive constant—$7 | 2 | 16 | 10$—the result for Jupiter is $4 | 7 | 35 | 25$.

Now the calculation for Venus’s anomaly. The group 1621 multiplied by three is 4863. Placed in two positions: 4863 in one place divided by five—5—yields degrees etc. $972 | 36 | 0$. In the other place, divided by "sky-moon-mountains-moons" <note>A Sanskrit numerical code (Bhutasankhya) where sky=0, moon=1, mountain=7, moon=1, read backwards as 181</note>—181—yields degrees etc. $26 | 52 | 36$. The sum of both is $999 | 48 | 36$. In signs etc. $9 | 9 | 48 | 36$. The constant for Venus’s anomaly is $1 | 1 | 4 | 2 | 0$; multiplied by 8 cycles it is $9 | 12 | 32 | 16 | 0$. Subtracting this: $7 | 27 | 13 | 36$. Adding the additive constant—$7 | 20 | 6 | 10$—the result for Venus’s anomaly is $2 | 17 | 49 | 29$. || 13 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

"Divided by the Sun" = divided by twelve; "Day-count" = the number of elapsed days; "Starting with degrees" = the result should be in degrees etc. "From that day-count" = from the count of days; "Subtracting minutes obtained from sky-mountains" = minus the minutes obtained by dividing by seventy; then "Jupiter" = the planet Jupiter is found. "In two positions" = from the day-count placed in two spots; "Multiplied by three" = tripled; "From the day-count" = from the count of days; "By the senses" = by five; "By sky-moon-mountains-moons" = by one hundred and eighty-one (181); "The sum of obtained degrees" = the addition of the resulting degrees etc.; "Of Bhrigu" = of Venus; "Fast-anomaly" <note>original: "Ashukendra"</note> = the <term>Shighra-kendra</term> (anomaly of parallax) is produced. || 13 ||

### Example:
<margin>∴ Cycle = 37, Ahargana = 3578, Jupiter's constant (Dhruva) = 00s 26° 18' 100''</margin>
Therefore, the operation according to the verse: ∴ 3578 ÷ 12 = 298° 10' 100'', and 3578 ÷ 70 = 51' 10''.
∴ ( 298° 10' 100'' ) - ( 51' 10'' ) = 297° 19' 53'' = 9s 27° 19' 53'' = Jupiter generated from the *Ahargana*.
Again, 37 x ( 00s 26° 18' 100'' ) = 00s 962° 666' 100'' = 8s 13° 16' 100''.
∴ ( 9s 27° 19' 53'' ) - ( 8s 13° 16' 100'' ) = 1s 14° 3' 53''.
∴ ( 1s 14° 3' 53'' ) + ( 7s 2° 16' 100'' ) = 8s 16° 18' 53'' = Jupiter at the time of sunrise.

## Now, the example for the anomaly of Venus:
∴ Ahargana = 3578, Cycle = 37, the constant (Dhruva) for the anomaly of Venus = 1s 14° 02' 00'', and the additive constant (Kshepa) = 7s 20° 9' 00''. Therefore, 3578 x 3 = 10734. 10734 ÷ 5 = 2146° 48' 00'' and 10734 ÷ 181 = 59° 19' 54''. ∴ ( 2146° 48' 00'' ) + ( 59° 19' 54'' ) = 2206° 7' 54'' = 1s 16° 6' 54'' = Venus's anomaly generated from the *Ahargana*.
Again, 37 x ( 1s 14° 2' 00'' ) = 37s 51° 104' 100'' = 6s 9° 14' 100''. ∴ ( 1s 16° 6' 54'' ) - ( 6s 9° 14' 100'' ) = 7s 6° 52' 54''.
Therefore, ( 7s 6° 52' 54'' ) + ( 7s 20° 9' 100'' ) = 2s 27° 19' 54'' = The mean anomaly of Venus at the time of sunrise. || 13 ||
