### Now, he describes the calculation for Saturn—

> The number of elapsed days divided by thirty results in the degrees of Saturn.
> To this, add the result in minutes obtained by dividing the same day-count by one hundred and fifty-six. ॥ 13½ ॥

Now he explains the method for bringing forth <term>Saturn</term><note>Sanskrit: Shani</note>. "Divided by thirty" etc. Given the day-count <term>Ahargana</term><note>The number of days elapsed since the beginning of the epoch</note> is 1621, divided by 30, the quotient in degrees and so on is 54° 2' 0". This same day-count 1621 is divided by 156. The result in minutes and so on is 10' 23". Adding this to the previous result gives 54° 12' 23". In signs and degrees, this is 1 Sign, 24° 12' 23". The <term>constant</term><note>Dhruva: a fixed value for a specific epoch</note> for Saturn is 7s 16° 42' 0". Multiplied by the number of completed cycles, it is 0s 53° 6' 0". Subtracting this gives 11s 16° 16' 46". Adding the <term>additive constant</term><note>Kshepaka: an initial position value</note> of 9s 21° 21' 0", the resulting Saturn is 11s 7° 38' 46". ॥ 13½ ॥

### The Madhuri Commentary —

**Divided by thirty** = divided by 30; **Day-count** = the number of elapsed days; **Divided by one hundred and fifty-six** = the day-count divided by 156; **Add the result in minutes** = add the quotient obtained in minutes; **Degrees etc.** = starting with degrees; **Saturn** = the planet Saturn; **Shall be** = is produced. ॥ 13½ ॥

### Here is the Proof —

If the total cycles of Saturn in a <term>Kalpa</term><note>An immense cosmic time period of 4.32 billion years</note> are obtained from the total days in a Kalpa, then what is obtained from the desired elapsed days? Thus, the mean Saturn (according to the <term>Aryabhatiya</term><note>The foundational astronomical treatise by Aryabhata, c. 499 CE</note>) is:
Saturn = $\frac{\text{146564} \times \text{12} \times \text{30} \times \text{60} \times \text{A}}{\text{1577917500}}$ = $\frac{\text{52763040} \times \text{A}}{\text{26298625}}$
$= (\text{2}' \text{। 00}'' \text{। 23}''' ) \text{A} = \frac{(\text{2}' \text{। 00}'' \text{। 23}''' ) \text{A} \times \text{30}}{\text{30}} = \frac{(\text{60}' \text{। 19}'' \text{। 30}''' )}{\text{30}}$
$= \frac{\text{A} \times \text{1}^\circ}{\text{30}} + \frac{(\text{11}'' \text{। 30}''' )' \text{A}}{\text{30} \div \text{60}} = \frac{\text{A} \times \text{1}^\circ}{\text{30}} + \frac{\text{A'}}{\frac{\text{30} \times \text{६०}}{(\text{11।30})}} = \frac{\text{A} \times \text{1}^\circ}{\text{30}} + \frac{\text{A} \times \text{1'}}{\text{156}}$
due to the very small difference. Thus, the entire calculation for Saturn is proven. ॥ 13½ ॥
By adding the result of the day-count divided by 156 (in minutes) to the result of the day-count divided by 30 (in degrees), the position of Saturn in degrees etc. is found. ॥ 13½ ॥

### Example —

$\therefore$ Day-count = 3578, Cycles = 37, Saturn's Constant = 7s 15° 42' 00"
and the Additive Constant = 9s 15° 21' 00". $\therefore$ 3578 $\div$ 30 = 119° 16' 00", and 3578 $\div$ 156 = 22' 56". $\therefore$ (119° 16' 00") + (22' 56") = 119° 38' 56" = 3s 29° 38' 56" = Saturn generated from the day-count. Again, as before, 37 $\times$ (7s 15° 42' 00") = 259s 555° 1554' 00" = 2s 10° 54' 00". Therefore, (3s 29° 38' 56") - (2s 10° 54' 00") = 1s 18° 44' 56". $\therefore$ (1s 18° 44' 56") + (9s 15° 21' 00") = 11s 4° 5' 56" = Mean Saturn at the time of sunrise. ॥ 13½ ॥

### Now, he states the motion in minutes of the Sun and others. "Go-na Gaja" etc. The meaning is clear. || 14-15 ||

->The Excellent Explanation—<-

**Go-ksha** <note>A mnemonic code where 'Go' = 9 and 'Ksha' = 5, read right-to-left as 59</note> = fifty-nine minutes, **Gaja** <note>Literally 'elephants', representing the number 8</note> = eight seconds (59' 8"), is the **Sun's motion** = the daily motion of the Sun. **Abhra-go-shva** <note>0, 9, 7</note> = seven hundred ninety minutes, **Pancha-agnaya** <note>5, 3</note> = thirty-five seconds (790' 35"), is the motion of **Shashin** = the Moon. Then = following that, six minutes, **Ilabdhaya** <note>1, 4</note> = forty-one seconds (6' 41"), is the **motion of the Apogee** = the motion of the Moon's highest point.

Three = three, **Ku-shashina** <note>1, 1</note> = eleven, in minutes etc. (3' 11") is the motion of **Rahu** <note>The North Lunar Node</note>. **Indu-rama** <note>1, 3</note> = thirty-one, **Tarka-ashvina** <note>6, 2</note> = twenty-six (31' 26") is the motion of **Asraja** = Mars. **Ardha-dik-shma** <note>6, 8, 1</note> = one hundred eighty-six, minutes = minutes, **Jina** <note>24</note> = twenty-four, seconds, is the **motion of Mercury's anomaly** <term>Mercury's anomaly: The motion of Mercury relative to its mean position</term>. **Shara** <note>5</note> = five, **Kham** <note>0</note> = zero (5' 0"), is the motion in minutes etc. of **Guru** = Jupiter. **Adri-guna** <note>7, 3</note> = thirty-seven (37' 0"), minutes, is the motion of Venus's anomaly = the motion of the anomaly of Venus. Two = (2' 0") minutes, is the motion of **Shani** = Saturn. The meaning is that these planets travel daily according to these stated proportions in their mean motion. || 14-15 ||

->The Proof—<-

If the total minutes of a planet's revolutions in a Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle of time</note> are divided by the total terrestrial days in a Kalpa, then the result is the motion for one day. That indeed is the mean motion. For example—if the minutes of the Sun's revolutions in a Kalpa are divided by the terrestrial days in a Kalpa, the resulting motion of the Sun in minutes etc. is:

---
$ \frac{4,320,000 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60 \times 1}{1,577,917,828} = \frac{4,320,000 \times 3 \times 30 \times 60 \times 1}{394,479,457} $

$ \frac{388,800,000 \times 60}{394,479,457} = \frac{23,328,000,000}{394,479,457} = 59' 8'' , 15''' $ <note>The final fraction represents thirds/sixtieths of a second</note>
---

The teacher Khandacharya did not include the final fraction because the difference is negligible; therefore, Sun's Motion = 59' 8". In this way, the motion of all planets is derived. Thus, it is proven. || 14-15 ||

59' 8" is the motion of the Sun; 790' 35" of the Moon and 6' 41" of the Moon's Apogee (mean motion).
3' 11" of Rahu; 31' 26" of Mars; 186' 24" of Mercury's anomaly; 5' 00" of Jupiter; 37' 00" of Venus's anomaly and 2' 00" of Saturn is the mean motion. || 14-15 ||

# Page 23
## Chapter on Mean Motions || 1 ||

> The center of Venus is found by taking the average of the Aries <note>likely referring to the Brahma school</note> and half-Aries <note>likely referring to the Arya school</note> positions; these planets thus attain equality with observation. With these perfected values, one should announce the timing of eclipses, religious duties, political affairs, and auspicious ceremonies. || 16 ||

Now, the author explains the unification of calculation and observation through planets derived from different schools. "The Sun is of the Solar school" <note>Saurapaksha</note> and so on. Here, for the unification of calculation and observation, the Sun is calculated according to the Solar school in all instances. The lunar apogee <note>vidhucca</note> is also taken from the Solar school. The Moon, diminished by 9 minutes of arc <note>9'</note>, is taken from the Solar school. Jupiter is taken according to the Arya school. Mars and Rahu <note>the ascending node</note> are both born of the Arya school. Mercury’s center is taken from the Brahma school. In the Arya school, Saturn is taken with the addition of five degrees. The center of Venus is established by taking the average of the Brahma and Arya schools; the mean of their sum results in observational accuracy. In this manner, these planets attain "sight-equivalence" <note>drktulyata</note>, meaning the unification of calculation and observation. Seeing the "heavy labor" <note>jadakarma</note> required to calculate planets from so many different sources, the Teacher <note>Ganesh Daivajna</note> composed this text for the sake of brevity and ease. In this book, one should use these perfected planets to announce eclipses <note>parva</note>, religious duties <note>dharma</note>, political ethics <note>naya</note>, and auspicious works <note>satkarya</note>. One should announce eclipses, religious acts, policy, and auspicious works like marriages and thread ceremonies. Because at any given time, only that which creates harmony between calculation and observation is acceptable, as it fits the reality. || 16 ||

->Thus ends the illustration of the Chapter on Mean Motions of the Grahallaghava,<-
->composed by Vishvanatha Daivajna, son of Shri Divakara Daivajna.<-

**Sun** = the Sun; **Lunar Apogee** = the highest point of the Moon; **Moon minus nine parts** = the Moon devoid of nine minutes of arc; **Solar** = belonging to the *Surya Siddhanta*; **But/Again** = furthermore; **Jupiter** = the planet Brihaspati; **Mars and Rahu** = the planet Mars and the ascending node; **Arya-born** = belonging to the *Aryabhata Siddhanta*; **Mercury’s center** = the fast-moving center <note>shighra-kendra</note> of Mercury; **Mars** <note>here referring to the Brahma school calculation</note> = belonging to the *Brahma Siddhanta*; **With five parts** = including five degrees; **Saturn** = the planet Shani; **In the Arya** = in the *Arya Siddhanta*; **Venusian center** = the fast-moving center of Venus; **Midpoint of Aries-half** = fits the average of the results from the Brahma and Arya schools. **Thus** = in this way; **These** = the planets; **Sight-equivalence** = equality between calculation and visual observation; **Attain** = they go to/reach. **By the perfected** = by those calculated; **By them** = by the planets; **Eclipses, duties, policy, and auspicious acts** = eclipses, fasts, ethics, and initiation ceremonies; **Should announce** = should be used in practice. || 16 ||

### The Mathematical Rationale:

Observation itself is the proof here. In the calculation of all mean planets, I have accepted this very verse and have established the "explanation of causes" <note>vasana</note> based on the revolutions <note>bhagana</note> and civil days <note>kudina</note> calculated in those respective schools. || 16 ||

The Sun, the lunar apogee, and the Moon minus 9 minutes are according to the *Surya Siddhanta*; Jupiter, Mars, and Rahu are according to the *Arya Siddhanta*; the center of Mercury is according to the *Brahma Siddhanta*; Saturn plus 5 degrees is according to the *Arya Siddhanta*; and the center of Venus is the average of the *Brahma* and *Arya* schools—these result in observational accuracy. One should perform eclipses, religious duties, policy, and auspicious works only using the planets calculated through these specific schools. || 16 ||

# Chapter 2: On the True Positions of the Sun and Moon

---

->First, he describes the values for the Base, the Complement, and the Sun’s Apogee:<-

> The Base is that which is less than three signs; if greater than three, it is the difference from six; if greater than nine, it is the difference from the Circle. Three signs minus the Base is the Complement. Each set of three signs constitutes a Quadrant. The Sun’s Apogee is seventy-eight degrees. ॥ 1 ॥

Now the chapter on calculating the true positions of the Sun and Moon and the five limbs of the calendar <note>The Panchanga</note> is explained. First, for the purpose of clarifying the planets, he explains the knowledge of the Base <term>Bhuja: the arc of a circle used in sine calculations</term>, the definition of the Quadrant <term>Pada</term>, and the Sun’s Apogee <term>Mandocca: the point where a planet is farthest from Earth</term>. **"Less than three signs"**: If the center <note>the anomaly</note> or the planet's position is less than three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, that itself is the Base. If it is higher than three signs up to nine, it should be subtracted from or compared with six signs <note>180 degrees</note>; the remainder is the Base. If it is greater than nine signs, then it should be subtracted from the Circle <note>12 signs or 360 degrees</note> to find the Base. **"Minus the Base"**: Three signs minus the Base is the **Complement** <term>Koti: the perpendicular side of the right triangle</term>. Each set of three signs is one **Quadrant**. This means: the first three signs are the Odd Quadrant, the second is Even, the third is Odd, and the fourth is the Even Quadrant. The Sun’s Apogee is **seventy-eight degrees** (78°). This means two signs and eighteen degrees. ॥ 1 ॥

->The "Madhuri" Commentary—<-

· **Less than three signs** = less than three signs, is the **Base**. This means the value of the Base is always less than three signs. If the center is **greater than three signs**, then use **six** = six signs; **difference** = one should find the difference. If **greater than nine** = more than nine signs, then subtract from the **Circle** = twelve signs. The remainder is the Base. **Minus the Base** = three signs without the Base is the **Complement**. **By threes** = by groups of three houses <note>Zodiac signs</note>, **each one** = one by one, is called a **Quadrant**. Thus there are four Quadrants in the Circle. **Seventy-eight** = 78, **degrees** "78 = 2 signs, 18°" is the Sun’s Apogee. ॥ 1 ॥

->Mathematical Proof—<-

Since there are twelve signs and four quadrants in a circle, there are three signs in one quadrant. In this regard, the method of bringing forth the Base is easy following Bhaskara’s rule: "In an odd quadrant use the elapsed part, in an even quadrant use the part to be elapsed." Since the sum of the Base degrees and Complement degrees is three signs, the rule "Three signs minus the Base is the Complement" is appropriate.

Since the Base is less than three signs, it is no wonder that values greater than 90 degrees or greater than nine signs are respectively subtracted from the half-circle or the full circle to result in a value less than three signs. At the time of composing this text, the Teacher established the Sun’s Apogee at 78° and recorded it as a constant, because the motion of the Apogee is extremely slow. ॥ 1 ॥

<margin>A Base is less than 3 signs. If the Base is between 3 and 6 signs, subtract it from 6. If between 6 and 9, subtract 6 from it. If between 9 and 12, find the difference from 12.</margin>

---

However, in calculations, the Apogee etc., should be according to the specific time, because it is moving. For example, now the Sun’s Apogee is 3 signs, 11 degrees, 16 minutes, and 32 seconds. As stated in the *Sarvananda-karana*: "The Apogee of the Lord of Day <note>the Sun</note> is signs etc. 3, 11, 16, 32." — Thus says the Editor.

# Chapter on the True Position of the Sun || 2 ||
<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>Chapter on the True Position of the Sun || 2 ||</header>
<sig>4 Pr. La.</sig>

From this, the <term>Bhuja</term><note>The arc of the sine, or the longitude within a quadrant</note> is formed. Subtracting the Bhuja from 3 signs results in the <term>Koti</term><note>The complement of the arc, similar to a cosine arc</note>. Every 3 signs constitute one <term>Pada</term><note>A quadrant or "foot" of the circle</note>. Thus, in the 12 signs of the zodiac, there are 4 quadrants. The Sun’s <term>Mandocca</term><note>Apogee; the point where the planet is farthest from Earth and moves slowest</note> is 78 degrees, which is 2 signs and 18 degrees. || 1 ||
**Example:** See the following 2nd verse. || 1 ||

---

->Now he describes the <term>Mandakendra</term><note>Anomaly; the angular distance from the apogee</note> and the method for calculating the Sun’s <term>Mandaphala</term><note>Equation of Center; the correction needed to find the true position from the mean position</note>:<-

**The Apogee diminished by the planet's position is called the Anomaly (Kendra) by the wise.**
**When this Anomaly begins with Aries or Libra, the correction (Phala) is respectively added or subtracted for the Sun.**
**The degrees of the Anomaly's Bhuja are subtracted from 20 and then multiplied by those same degrees; this result is set aside.**
**That result is then divided by 57 minus one-ninth of itself; the result is the correction in degrees and minutes. || 2 ||**

The Apogee (<term>Mandocca</term>) should be reduced by the planet's position; this is called the Anomaly (<term>Kendra</term>) by the wise. For example: when the planet is subtracted from the Apogee, it becomes the <term>Mandakendra</term> (Anomaly of the slow motion); when the planet is subtracted from the <term>Shighrocca</term> (Apex of quick motion), it becomes the <term>Shighrakendra</term>. In the six signs beginning with Aries (the first half of the zodiac), the correction is positive (added). In the six signs beginning with Libra, it is negative (subtracted). Now, the Sun's Anomaly should be calculated as stated.

For example: The Sun's Apogee is 2 signs 18°. The Sun's position 1 sign 4° 13' 42" is subtracted from it, resulting in the Sun's Anomaly: 1 sign 13° 46' 18". The <term>Bhuja</term> of this is 1 sign 13° 46' 18". This must be converted into degrees. As a general rule: multiply the signs by 30 and add the degrees below. Doing so, the degrees are 43° 46' 18". One-ninth of this is 4° 51' 48". Subtracting this from 20 (<term>Nakha</term>) <note>The word 'Nakha' means nails, a traditional Sanskrit numerical code for 20</note> gives 16° 8' 12". This is multiplied by the planet's degrees (43° 46' 18"), resulting in 73° 36' 52". This is set in two places. One-ninth of 73° 36' 52" is 8° 10' 49". Subtracting this from 57 (<term>Nageshu</term>) <note>A code for 57: Naga (mountains) = 7, Ishu (arrows) = 5</note> gives 48° 49' 11". The value set aside is divided by this. The dividend is 269012 and the divisor is 175766. From this division, the correction in degrees is 1° 30' 28". Since the Anomaly is in the Aries-half, this is added to the Sun's position. The corrected Sun is 1 sign 5° 44' 10". || 2 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary —<-

"Diminished by the planet" means without the planet. The Apogee which <unclear>is</unclear> <gloss>the circle</gloss> is known by the name Anomaly. The name Manda...

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

...is meant; by the **wise** = by the learned, it is **declared** = called the **anomaly** <note>Sanskrit: *kendra*; the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note>. The meaning is that the **apogee** <note>Sanskrit: *mandocca*</note> of a particular planet, when subtracted by that planet's position, becomes the **anomaly** of that planet. In the anomalies beginning with **Aries** and **Libra** <note>The first and second halves of the zodiacal circle</note>, the result is respectively **positive and negative** = addition and subtraction. This means in Aries-etc., it is an addition, and in Libra-etc., it is a subtraction.

Now, the **anomaly of the Sun** must be processed. The **degrees of the anomaly's arc** <note>Sanskrit: *bhuja-bhāga*</note> are multiplied by **twenty** <note>Sanskrit: *nakhāḥ*, literally "fingernails," a traditional term for 20</note> which has been reduced by one-ninth of those same degrees; these are placed **separately** = in a different place. These are then **divided** = partitioned by **fifty-seven** <note>Sanskrit: *naga-iṣu*, literally "mountains (7) and arrows (5)" read right-to-left</note> reduced by that same one-ninth. Then the resulting **degrees etc.** = portions etc., shall be the **Sun's equation of center** <note>Sanskrit: *manda-phala*</note>. || 2 ||

### Here is the Rationale:—

<margin>(1)</margin>
Let the **radius** <note>Sanskrit: *trijyā*</note> = 120. The **maximum solar equation** = 125/57 degrees. The **Sun's anomaly degrees** = *k*. Therefore, according to the **Method of Sripati** <note>An 11th-century mathematician/astronomer</note>, the **Sine of the Sun's anomaly** = *Sine(k)*:

$$ \frac{(180 - k) \times k \times 120}{10125 - \frac{(180 - k) \times k}{4}} = \frac{(180 - k) \times k \times 480}{40500 - (180 - k) \times k} $$

$$ = \frac{\frac{(180 - k)}{9} \times \frac{k}{9} \times 480}{\frac{40500}{9 \times 9} - \frac{(180 - k)}{9} \times \frac{k}{9}} = \frac{(20 - k/9) \times k/9 \times 480}{500 - (20 - k/9) \times k/9} \dots \dots (a) $$

->Now the proportion: If by the Sine of the anomaly as the radius, the maximum equation is (125/57) degrees, then what is it by the desired Sine of the anomaly?<-

The resulting **Sun's equation** = *S.E.* = $\frac{\frac{125}{57} \times \text{Sine}(k)}{120}$. If the value of the Sine of the anomaly from equation (a) is substituted, then:

$$ S.E. = \frac{\frac{125}{57} \times (20 - k/9) \times k/9 \times 480}{120 \times (500 - (20 - k/9) \times k/9)} $$

$$ = \frac{\frac{125}{57} \times (20 - k/9) \times k/9 \times 4}{500 - (20 - k/9) \times k/9} = \frac{\frac{500}{57} \times (20 - k/9) \times k/9}{500 - (20 - k/9) \times k/9} $$

---

(1) The Method of Sripati is as follows:
> "The degrees of the arc and its complement, multiplied together, are then multiplied by 180,800 <note>original: *kha-nāga-candra*, literally 0-8-1</note>... These, multiplied by the radius and divided... are the Sines of the arc and its complement." <note>This is a Sanskrit verse describing an approximation formula for the Sine function, similar to Bhaskara I's formula.</note>

<note>The vocabulary list below defines the technical terms used in the Sanskrit text.</note>
<term>Anomaly (Kendra)</term>: The angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee).
<term>Equation of Center (Manda-phala)</term>: The correction applied to a planet's mean position to find its true position.
<term>Radius (Trijyā)</term>: In Indian trigonometry, often calculated with a specific value like 120 or 3438.
<term>One-ninth (Navamāṃśa)</term>: A division by nine used here as a mathematical simplification.

# Chapter 2: On the True Longitudes of the Sun and Moon

$$ \frac{( 20 - \frac{K}{9} ) \frac{K}{9}}{\frac{500}{57} - ( 20 - \frac{K}{9} ) \frac{K}{9}} = \frac{( 20 - \frac{K}{9} ) \frac{K}{9}}{57 - \frac{( 20 - \frac{K}{9} ) \frac{K}{9}}{9}} , \text{due to a slight difference.} $$
<note>original: "svalpāntarāt". The author notes that the denominator 500/57 is approximated as 9 to simplify the calculation for the practitioner without losing significant accuracy.</note>

Thus, the rationale for the rule beginning with "the <term>anomaly</term><note>kendra: the angular distance of a planet from its apsis</note> subtracted from the degrees of the planet's <term>arm</term><note>bhuja: the arc used in sine calculations</note>" is established.
The proof for the first half of the verse is easily understood by observing the geometry of the <term>eccentric circle</term><note>prativṛtta: a circle whose center is offset from the Earth to account for varying planetary speeds</note> model. See the diagram below.

By subtracting the planet's position from its <term>apogee</term><note>mandocca: the point where the planet is furthest from Earth and moves slowest</note>, the remainder is the <term>mean anomaly</term><note>mandakendra</note> of that planet. If the anomaly begins with Aries <note>the first six signs</note>, the correction is additive; if the anomaly begins with Libra <note>the latter six signs</note>, the correction is subtractive.

Subtract the <term>ninth part</term><note>navamāṃśa</note> of the degrees of the Sun's "arm" from 20. Multiply the remainder by that same ninth part and set the result in two places. Subtract the first from 57. Divide the second by this remainder; the resulting degrees and minutes are the Sun's <term>equation of center</term><note>mandaphala: the correction applied to the mean longitude to find the true longitude</note>.

**Example:** The Sun's apogee = 78° <note>Note: The text likely means 2 signs 18° or similar, but provides 78°</note> = 218°. Therefore, the Sun's mean anomaly = (218°) — (Sun = 6 signs 28° 15' 17") = 7 signs 19° 19' 43". Again, according to Verse 1, the "arm" = (7 signs 19° 19' 43") — 6 signs = 1 sign 19° 19' 43". In degrees, this is 49° 19' 43".
Its ninth part is 49° 19' 43" ÷ 9 = 5° 27' 45". Subtracting this from 20 gives 20° — (5° 27' 45") = 14° 32' 15". Multiplying this by the previous ninth part: (5° 27' 45") $\times$ (14° 32' 15") = <meta>text obscured by watermark</meta>

### Multiplication by the Gomutrika Method —
<note>The "Gomutrika" or "cow's zigzag" method is a traditional Indian mathematical technique for multiplying multi-part numbers (degrees, minutes, seconds).</note>

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| { 14° 32' 15'' X 5°, } | { 70 160 75 } |
| { 14' 32'' 15''' X 27' } | = { 378 864 405 } |
| { 14'' 32''' 15'''' X 45'' } | { 630 1440 675 } |

Sum = 70 | 538 | 1569 | 1845 | 675. By dividing the minutes and further units by 60 <note>original: "tastita," meaning reduced or refined by the modulus</note>, the Sun's <term>Manda Phala</term> <note>Equation of Center: the correction needed to account for the elliptical orbit</note> in degrees etc. = 1° 11' 15''. Since the <term>Kendra</term> <note>Anomaly</note> begins with Libra, this result is negative <note>subtractive</note>. Therefore, subtracting it from the Mean Sun, the corrected Sun <note>original: "Samskrta Ravi"</note> = (6s 28° 50' 17'') - (1° 11' 15'') = 6s 27° 39' 2''. ॥ 2 ॥

->Now he describes the calculation for the Moon's correction —<-

> Thirty <note>original: "Kharama," a numerical code where Kha=0, Rama=3</note> is multiplied by the Moon's anomaly sine <note>Kendra-dor</note> minus one-sixth of itself. This is placed separately and divided by fifty-six <note>original: "Rasakshai," Rasa=6, Aksha=5</note> minus one-twentieth of that [previous value]. The result is the correction in degrees. By these two corrections, the Sun and Moon become "clear" <note>true/accurate</note>. ॥ 3 ॥

(Introduction) From verse nineteen to verse twenty, the examples are not written here. They are written after verse twenty-three. This was done by the Teacher <note>the author, Ganesha Daivajna</note> because the mathematical presentation arises more naturally in that order. ॥ 3 ॥

### Madhuri Commentary —

**Of the Moon** <note>Vidhoh</note> = of the Moon which has been refined by the three corrections of <term>Chara</term> <note>ascensional difference</note>, <term>Bhujantara</term> <note>equation of time</note>, and <term>Deshantara</term> <note>terrestrial longitude</note>. **Multiplied by the anomaly sine minus one-sixth** = multiplied by the degrees of the anomaly sine minus its sixth part. **Thirty** <note>Kharama</note> = the number 30. **Separately** = placed in a different position. **Minus one-twentieth** = minus a twentieth part of that. **By fifty-six** <note>Rasakshai</note> = by the number 56. **Divided** = when divided, then for the Moon, **the result in degrees** = the correction starting with degrees occurs. **By these two** = by these two corrections, **refined** = having the calculation applied, **the Sun and Moon** = the Sun and the Moon, **become clear** = become "true" or mathematically accurate. ॥ 3 ॥

### Mathematical Rationale —

Here, the Radius <term>Trijya</term> = 120. The maximum Moon correction = 5°. The sine of the anomaly = <term>Ke-jya</term>. Now the proportion: if for the Radius-sine we get the maximum correction, then for the desired anomaly-sine, what is the result?
Moon's Correction = (5° X Sine of Anomaly) / 120.

Now, according to the method of Sripati <note>an 11th-century mathematician</note>, the Sine of Anomaly is:
Sine = [ (180 - K) * K * 120 ] / [ 10125 - ( (180 - K) * K / 4 ) ]

[...Mathematical derivation follows...]

= [ (30 - K/6) * K/6 * 480 ] / [ 1125 - (30 - K/6) * K/6 ] ......... (1)

# Chapter 2: On the True Longitude of the Sun and Moon

Here—(1) By this, the Moon's equation <note>Sanskrit: *chandraphala*; the correction applied to mean position to find true position</note> derived from the Sine of the Anomaly <note>Sanskrit: *kendra*</note> is:

[Mathematical Table/Derivation]
<note>The text shows a derivation simplifying the formula for the Moon's equation. It uses the number 120 as the radius (Trigyan) and 480 as a multiplier related to the maximum equation.</note>

$$ \frac{5 \times (30 - \frac{K}{6}) \frac{K}{6} \times 480}{120 \times \{ 1125 - (30 - \frac{K}{6}) \frac{K}{6} \}} = \dots = \frac{(30 - \frac{K}{6}) \frac{K}{6}}{56 - \frac{(30 - \frac{K}{6}) \frac{K}{6}}{20}} $$

...due to the small difference. Thus, it is proven. || 3 ||

Divide the degrees of the Moon's anomaly by 6; subtract this quotient from 30 and multiply the remainder by that same quotient. Place this result in two positions. In the first position, divide by 20 and subtract the resulting degrees and minutes from 56. Divide the value in the second position by this remainder. The result is the Moon's Equation of the Center <note>Sanskrit: *mandaphala*</note> in degrees and minutes. By applying these corrections, the Sun and Moon become "True" <note>Sanskrit: *spashta*; their observed positions in the sky</note>. || 3 ||

### Example—See after Verse 7. || 3 ||

### Now, he describes the True Motion of the Sun and Moon—

> The degrees of the cosine of the anomaly, subtracted from and then multiplied by eleven-twentieths, [gives a value]. For the Sun, this is divided by thirteen; for the Moon, it is multiplied by two and increased by its own eighth part. This is added to or subtracted from the mean motion depending on whether the anomaly is in the six signs beginning with Cancer or Capricorn; that is the True Motion. || 4 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

<margin>"In the six signs beginning with Cancer or Capricorn" means when the anomaly is in the half-circles starting with Cancer or Capricorn. "Of the anomaly" refers to the anomaly of the equation of center. "Subtracted from and multiplied by eleven-twentieths" means multiplied by eleven after subtracting one-twentieth of the cosine degrees. "Eleven" refers to the number eleven. "For the Sun" means the Sun's [motion]. "Divided by thirteen" means divided by the number 13. "For the Moon" means the Moon's [motion]. "Multiplied by two" means doubled. "With its own eighth part" means added to its own eighth portion. "In the motion" refers to the mean motion. "Addition and subtraction" should be done respectively. Then, "that" motion becomes "True" or accurate. || 4 ||</margin>

### Here is the Rationale:

Let the Sun's maximum motion correction = $8/9$, the Moon's maximum motion correction = $273/4$, the degrees of the cosine of the anomaly = $Kco$, and the Radius = 120. Then, according to the method of *Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Shri Sudhakara* <note>Sudhakara Dvivedi, a famous 19th-century mathematician/astronomer</note>, the Sine of the Cosine of the Anomaly is:
$Sine(Kco) = (11 - \frac{Kco}{20}) \frac{Kco}{20} \times 4 \dots (1)$.

---

<note>* The method of Mahamahopadhyaya Pandit Shri Sudhakara is as follows:</note>
> The degrees of the sine multiplied by eleven minus one-twentieth of itself, then multiplied by four and divided by 120, gives the Sine <unclear>of the arc</unclear>. This is the Sine of the side with a small margin of error, according to the scholars of astronomy.

# Page 30
## Commentary on the Grahalaghava

Therefore, the proportion is as follows: if the maximum velocity correction for the Sun <note>original: "ravi-parama-gati-phalam"</note> is 9/4 <note>2.25 minutes of arc</note> when the cosine of the anomaly <note>term: "kendra-koti-jya" — the trigonometric cosine of the planet's angular distance from its apogee</note> is equal to the radius <note>term: "trijya" — the standard radius used in Indian trigonometry, here 120 units</note>, then what would it be for a given cosine of the anomaly?

The resulting Solar velocity correction <note>original: "ravi-gati-phalam"</note> = $\frac{\frac{9}{4} \times \text{cosine of anomaly}}{120}$. 

Here, substituting the value for the cosine of the anomaly from equation (1):
Solar velocity correction = $\frac{4 \times \frac{9}{4} \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}}{120}$ = $\frac{9 \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}}{120}$
= $\frac{(11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}}{\frac{120}{9}}$ = $\frac{(11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}}{13}$ <note>This is an approximation for ease of calculation</note>, due to the slight difference.

Similarly, the Lunar velocity correction = $\frac{\frac{273}{4} \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20} \times 4}{120}$
= $\frac{273}{120} \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20} = (2 + \frac{33}{120}) \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}$
= $(2 + \frac{3}{11}) \times (11 - \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}) \frac{\text{cosine}}{20}$, due to the slight difference. Thus, the rule is proven. || 4 ||

---

### Explanation of the Positive and Negative Nature of Velocity Correction

Now, the rationale <note>term: "vasana" — the underlying logic or geometric proof</note> for the positive and negative application of the velocity correction is discussed. First, what is "velocity" <note>term: "gati"</note> and what is "velocity correction" <note>term: "gati-phala"</note>?

As stated by Bhaskara <note>referring to the 12th-century astronomer Bhaskara II</note>:
> "The true velocity is the difference between the true positions of a planet on two successive days at the same time."

This means the difference between today's and tomorrow's positions of a planet at the same time is called its velocity. The difference between two mean positions is the mean velocity <note>original: "madhya-gati"</note>, and the difference between two true positions is the true velocity...

# Chapter 2: On the True Motion of the Sun and Moon

The difference between the positions is the true motion. In this context, when the difference is taken between the true positions of a planet for yesterday and today, it results in the difference between the two days' "equations" <note>Equation (Phala) refers to the correction applied to mean motion to find true motion</note>. This means that by applying the "motion correction" (Gati-phala)—which is the difference between the equations of two consecutive days—to the mean motion (the difference between yesterday's and today's mean positions), the true motion is obtained. Therefore, the difference between today's and yesterday's equations is the motion correction. Here, since the planet's apogee is the reference for the "anomaly" (Kendra), in the signs starting with Aries, the positive correction decreases; in Capricorn, the negative correction increases; in Cancer, the positive correction increases; and in Libra, the negative correction decreases. Thus, when calculating the difference between today's and yesterday's equations, the motion correction remains negative in the six signs starting from Capricorn and positive in the six signs starting from Cancer.

This is established as stated; for visual proof, one should examine the diagram of the eccentric circle. <margin>Editor's note.</margin>

**In the quadrants starting with Cancer and Capricorn, divide the degrees of the "complementary arc" (Kotyansha) of the anomaly by 20. Place this quotient in two places. Subtract the first from 11. Multiply the remainder by the second value. If it is the Sun's anomaly, divide this product by 13. If it is the Moon's, double it and add its own sixth part. These results are the motion corrections for the Sun and Moon respectively. By adding or subtracting this motion correction to their respective mean motions, the True Motion is obtained. || 4 ||**

**Example—** The previously mentioned Sun's anomaly = 7s 19° 9' 43". Its "base sine" (Bhuja) = 1s 19° 9' 43".
$\therefore$ 3s — (1s 19° 9' 43") = 1s 10° 50' 17" = 40° 50' 17" = Sun's complementary arc (Kotyansha).
$\therefore$ (40 50 17) ÷ 20 = 2° 12' 31". Then 11 — (2° 12' 31") = 8° 47' 29".
Now, multiply (8° 47' 29") $\times$ (2° 12' 31") using the "cow's urine" method <note>Gomutrika: a traditional zig-zag multiplication method</note>—
> 8 47 29 $\times$ 2 = 16 15 58
> 8 47 29 $\times$ 12 = 16 15 58 <note>Note: The OCR shows repeated values; this is the step-by-step calculation of arc-minutes and seconds</note>
> 8 47 29 $\times$ 31 = 24 8 17 6 19

The sum = 16 13 0 41... converting this and dividing by 13 gives the quotient 1' 24" = Sun's motion correction. Because the anomaly is in the Cancer quadrant, we add this to the Sun's mean motion of 59' 8". (59' 8") + (1' 24") = 60' 32", which is the Sun's True Motion.

**For the Moon's motion, see after the 7th verse. || 4 ||**

### ->Now he describes the Equinoctial Shadow and the Ascensional Differences:<-

> When the Sun, including the precession of the equinoxes, is at the beginning of Aries, the shadow at midday is the Equinoctial Shadow (1).
> Place that value in three places; multiply them by ten (10), eight (8), and ten (10) respectively. Divide the last one by three (3). These are the three segments of the ascensional difference. || 5 ||

Now he explains the knowledge of the Equinoctial Shadow (Palabha) and the calculation of the segments of ascensional difference (Charakhanda). "When the Sun is at the beginning of Aries": when the Sun, adjusted for precession (Sayana), is at zero degrees of Aries, the shadow cast by a twelve-digit gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar used for timekeeping</term> at midday is the Equinoctial Shadow. That shadow value should be placed in three positions. Multiply them in order by **ten (10), eight (8), and ten (10)**. The last result is divided by three. These become the three segments of ascensional difference. || 5 ||

### ->The Madhuri Commentary—<-

When the Sun, including the precession of the equinoxes, has reached the beginning of Aries, the midday—

# With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava

<page-num>32</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

<term>Dharbhā</term> <note>original: "Dharbhā"</note> = the shadow at midday; that is the shadow. <term>Palabhā</term> <note>The equinoctial midday shadow of a 12-digit gnomon</note> = the latitude-shadow. That <term>Palabhā</term> should be placed in <term>three positions</term> <note>original: "triṣṭhā"</note> and multiplied by ten, by <term>serpents</term> <note>The word "bhujanga" (serpent) is a Sanskrit numerical symbol for 8</note> (eight), and by ten. The last value, when divided by three, results in the <term>half-Chara segments</term> <note>original: "carārddhāni"; these are components used to calculate the difference in rising times between the equator and a specific latitude</note> || 5 ||

### Here is the Derivation:—

Following the method "The sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow," for a latitude-shadow of one digit, the <term>Chara segments</term> for the three signs <note>Aries, Taurus, Gemini</note> are calculated as 10, 8, and 3 + 1/3 (which is 10/3). These are derived from the rule "multiplied by ten, elephant (8), and seven-zero (70)..." etc. Therefore, the proportion is: if these are the Chara segments for one digit of latitude-shadow, what will they be for the desired latitude-shadow? Thus, the <term>Chara segments</term> are proven || 5 ||

The name of the midday shadow of the gnomon on the day the Sun (with precession) is at the beginning of Aries is the Palabhā. By placing this in 3 positions and multiplying respectively by 10, 8, and 10, and dividing the last position by 3, the Chara segments are produced || 5 ||

**Example:** The Palabhā of Mithila is 5 digits and 54 minutes.
Therefore: ($5;54$) $\times 10$; ($5;54$) $\times 8$; ($5;54$) $\times 10/3$ = $50;540$, $40;432$, $590/3$.
Converting these to the standard base of 60, we get 59, 47, and $197/3$ = 197 <note>The text shows a calculation resulting in the specific Chara segments for the location of Mithila</note> || 5 ||

### Now he describes the calculation of the Chara time:—

> **The sum of the half-Chara segments corresponding to the signs of the "arm" of the Sun (with precession) is added to the product of the remaining degrees and the next segment, divided by thirty.**
> **This result is the Chara; it is added or subtracted when the Sun is in the six signs starting with Libra or Aries, and the reverse at sunset || 6 ||**

Now the calculation of Chara is described. "Syāt" etc. The "arm" <note>the distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note> of the Sun (with precession) is taken. The sum of the Chara segments corresponding to those signs should be made. How? The degrees remaining in the current sign are multiplied by the "bhogya" (the next Chara segment), and the product is divided by thirty (30). This is added to the previous sum to get the Chara. That Chara is additive (positive) when the Sun is in the six signs starting with Libra, and subtractive (negative) when in the six signs starting with Aries. At sunset, it is the opposite: subtractive in Libra etc., and additive in Aries etc. || 6 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary:—

**The sum of the half-Chara segments...** = the sum of the Chara segments equal to the signs of the Sun's "arm" including precession; **from the product of the degrees and the next segment** = from the result of multiplying the degrees by the next segment; **divided by thirty** = including the result of the division by thirty, **it becomes the Chara**. **When the Sun** = in the Sun, **is in the six signs starting with Libra or Aries** = the Chara is **added or subtracted** = respectively added to or subtracted from the planet. **At sunset** = at the time of the Sun setting, **the opposite** = the reverse operation should be done || 6 ||

### Here is the Derivation:—

If thirty degrees give one Chara segment, what do the desired degrees give? By this proportion, the Chara (1) is found by adding the segments for the completed signs. It is positive in Libra etc., and negative in Aries etc. At sunset, it is the reverse. All this is clear simply by observing the nature of the celestial sphere. Thus it is proven || 6 ||

---

<insert>
( 1 ) Now, what is this thing called "Chara"? The planets calculated here are those as they rise at Lanka (the equator). The vertical/horizontal difference between the horizon of Lanka and one's own local horizon is called Chara. In the Northern Hemisphere, because the local horizon is below the Lanka horizon, the Chara should be subtracted at sunrise and added at sunset. This is because rising happens earlier and setting happens later at the local station. In the Southern Hemisphere (starting from Libra), because the local horizon is above the Lanka horizon, the Chara should be added at sunrise and subtracted at sunset. Since rising happens later and setting happens earlier there, this is correctly stated. Now—

# Chapter 2: On the True Longitudes of the Sun and Moon

In the arc of the tropical <note>Sayana: including the precession of the equinoxes</note> Sun, take the sum of the "ascensional difference segments" <term>Chara-khandas: segments used to calculate the variation in rising times</term> corresponding to the number of signs. To this, add the 30th part of the "remaining segment" <note>Bhogyakhanda</note> multiplied by the degrees and minutes of the current sign to find the total ascensional difference. When the Sun is in the six signs beginning with Libra or Aries, apply this value as an addition or subtraction respectively. However, at sunset, the addition and subtraction operations are reversed. || 6 ||

**Example:** Precession <note>Ayanamsha</note> = 21° 33' 31". The Sun previously corrected by the equation of center <note>Mandaphala</note> = 6s 27° 30' 52". Therefore, (6s 27° 30' 52") + (21° 33' 31") = 7s 19° 4' 23" = Tropical Sun. Its arc <note>Bhuja</note> = (7s 19° 4' 23") - 6s = 1s 19° 4' 23". Thus, for 1 sign passed, the first segment is 59. Next, multiplying the remaining segment 47 by the degrees 19° 4' 23" gives 896' 26" 1"'. Dividing this by 30 gives 29, which added to the passed segment 59 results in 59 + 29 = 88" <note>seconds of arc</note>. This correction of 1' 28", according to verse 7, is added to the Sun's seconds because the Sun is in the signs starting from Libra. The True Sun = (6s 27° 30' 52") + (1' 28") = 6s 27° 32' 20". || 6 ||

### Now, regarding the Precession and corrections for the Sun and Moon:

> This ascensional difference should be applied as a negative correction to the seconds of the Sun; for the Mean Moon, apply twice that value divided by nine to the minutes.
> The Sun’s equation of center, divided by twenty-seven, should be applied to the Moon’s degrees. The Shaka era year minus four hundred and forty-four, divided by sixty, gives the Precession. || 7 ||

Now he describes the correction of the ascensional difference and the precession. "This ascensional difference should be applied": the calculated value should be added or subtracted as appropriate to the seconds <note>Viliptikas</note> of the Sun. Twice that value divided by nine should be applied to the minutes <note>Kalas</note> of the Mean Moon. The Sun's equation of center <note>Mandaphala</note> divided by twenty-seven should be applied to the degrees of the Mean Moon, following the same additive/subtractive logic as the Sun. For the desired Shaka year, subtract 444 from the Shalivahana era year. Divide the remainder by sixty; the result is the Precession <note>Ayanamsha</note>.

In Kashi <note>Varanasi</note>, the equinoctial shadow is 5.49 and the ascensional segments are 57, 46, and 19. The Shaka year is 1534. Subtracting 444 from this leaves 1090. Divided by 60, the Precession is 18° 10'.

**Calculation of Ascensional Difference:** Tropical Sun = 9s 5° 44' 10" + 12s 3° 54' 10" <unclear>textual variation</unclear>. Its arc is 2s 23° 54' 10". The sum of segments for the passed signs is 57. The remaining segment 46 multiplied by the degrees 23° 54' 10" equals 1099' 32" 40"'. Divided by thirty, it is 36. Adding this to the passed segment 57 gives a total correction of 93. Since the tropical Sun is in the first six signs starting from Aries, this is subtracted. The True Sun becomes 9s 5° 42' 37".

**Calculation of the True Moon:** The correction of 93 doubled is 186; divided by nine, the result is 20' 40". Subtracting this from the Mean Moon 6s 21° 10' 24" gives 6s 19° 49' 44". The Sun's equation of center is positive 11° 30' 28". Divided by twenty-seven, the result is 0° 3' 21". Adding this to the corrected Moon gives 6s 19° 53' 5". The longitudinal distance <note>Deshantara</note> for Kashi, east of the prime meridian <note>Ujjain</note>, is negative 64 yojanas. Its equivalent in minutes is 10' 40". Subtracting this from the previously corrected Moon 6s 19° 53' 5" results in the Moon corrected by three factors: 6s 19° 42' 25".

Now he describes the Moon's equation of center and its correction. "From the Moon's anomaly...": The Moon's apogee <note>Uchcha</note> is 10s 14° 55' 43". Subtracting the Moon 6s 19° 42' 25" gives the Moon's mean anomaly 3s 25° 12' 18". Its arc is 2s 4'...

### Now he describes the clarification of velocity.

Regarding the anomaly: The Sun's mean anomaly is 1s 23° 46' 18". Its sine-equivalent <note>bhujā</note> is 1s 23° 46' 18". This subtracted from three signs gives the cosine-equivalent <note>koṭi</note> of 1s 26° 13' 42". Its degrees are 46;13;42. Divided by twenty (20), the result is 2;18. Eleven <note>original: "rudrāḥ"</note> minus this is 8;42. These are multiplied by twenty <note>original: "khāśvi"</note> degrees: 20;0. Divided by the specific divisor 13, the result is 1;32. Because the anomaly begins with Capricorn, the Sun's equation of motion is subtractive. The mean velocity 59;8 minus this results in the True Solar Velocity of 57;36.

### Now the means for calculating Lunar Velocity.

There, the Moon's mean anomaly is 3s 06° 12' 18". Its sine-equivalent is 0s 14° 47' 42". This subtracted from three signs gives the cosine-equivalent of 0s 25° 12' 18". These degrees 25;12;18 divided by twenty (20) are 1;15. Eleven minus this becomes 9;45. These multiplied by twenty degrees are 193;11. Doubled, they are 386;22. Adding its own sixth part 43;3, it becomes 28;29 <note>Calculation adjusted for context</note>. Because the anomaly begins with Cancer, the Moon's equation of motion is additive. The mean velocity 790;36 plus this results in the True Lunar Velocity of 819;05. // 7 //

->The Madhuri Commentary<-

That = the previously mentioned, the ascensional difference <term>Cara: the difference between the celestial and terrestrial equator</term>, in the Sun <note>original: "aruṇe"</note>, in seconds of arc <note>vilititkāsu</note>; in the Mean Moon, twice divided by nine in minutes of arc <note>kalāsu</note>, is to be applied <note>deyam</note>. The result = divided by twenty-seven, the Sun's Equation of Center <note>dyumaṇiphalam</note>, is to be applied to the Moon's degrees. Then = thereafter, the current Shaka year minus 444 <note>original: "vedābdhyabdhyūnaḥ"</note>, <unclear>the era</unclear> = the desired Shaka year, combined with the ascensional difference and divided by sixty, shall be the Precession of the Equinoxes <term>Ayanāṃśa</term>. // 7 //

->Here is the Rationale<-

It is assumed that the Sun's velocity in minutes = 60, and the Moon's velocity in minutes = 800. Then the proportion: If for the minutes of a day and night <note>3600</note> the Sun's velocity is obtained, then for the minutes of ascensional difference <note>CP</note>, what is it? The resulting minutes of ascensional difference = $\frac{60 \times CP}{3600}$. This multiplied by sixty becomes seconds of ascensional difference = $\frac{60 \times 60 \times CP}{3600}$ = CP. The Sun corrected by this becomes accurate for its local rising.

And so, by the proportion of the Moon's velocity: $\frac{800 \times CP}{3600} = \frac{2 \times CP}{9} =$ the lunar minutes related to the ascensional difference.

->Now another proportion<-

If for a day and night the Moon's velocity is obtained, then for the time-breaths <term>Asu: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</term> arising from the Sun's Equation of Center <note>RF</note>, what is it? The lunar minutes related to the Sun's Equation = $\frac{800 \times RF \times 60}{21600}$. Divided by sixty, the lunar degrees related to the Sun's Equation = $\frac{800 \times RF \times 60}{21600 \times 60} = \frac{800 \times RF}{21600} = \frac{RF}{27}$. The Moon corrected by these according to the celestial hemisphere becomes accurate for its local rising.

## Chapter 2: On the True Positions of the Sun and Moon

> Since in the Saka year 444 there was an absence of precession <note>original: "ayanāṃśābhāvaḥ"; the point where the tropical and sidereal zodiacs coincided</note>, and the annual motion of precession is one minute <note>1'</note>, therefore the number of years elapsed since the said Saka year divided by sixty gives the degrees of precession. Thus, everything is proven. || 7 ||

That *Chara* <note>ascensional difference</note> should be applied to the seconds of the Sun; twice the *Chara* divided by 9 should be applied to the minutes of the Mean Moon; and the 27th part of the Sun's *Mandaphala* <note>equation of center/correction for elliptical orbit</note> should be applied to the degrees of that same Moon. Subtracting 444 from the desired Saka year and dividing the remainder by 60 gives the *Ayanamsha* <note>value of precession</note>. || 7 ||

**Example** — Desired Saka Year = 1858. Therefore, 1858 — 444 = 1414. 1414 ÷ 60 = 23° 34' = these are the precession values for the beginning of the current year.

### Calculation of the True Moon —

According to the sixth verse, the positive *Chara* 88 was multiplied by 2 and divided by 9: $ \frac{88 \times 2}{9} $ = 19' 13''. This was added to the Mean Moon (already corrected for terrestrial longitude) 6s 14° 10' 23'', resulting in the "twice-corrected" Moon: 6s 14° 29' 56''. Now, according to verse 2, the Sun's *Mandaphala* is negative 1° 19' 25''. Dividing this by 27 gives a quotient of 0° 2' 50'', which is subtracted from the twice-corrected Moon. The "thrice-corrected" <note>triphala-samskrta</note> Moon is (6s 14° 29' 56'' — 0° 2' 50'') = 6s 14° 27' 6''.

Now we calculate the Moon's *Mandaphala* <note>correction for the Moon's anomaly</note>. Subtracting the thrice-corrected Moon 6s 14° 27' 6'' from the Lunar Apogee <note>Chandroccha</note> 6s 14° 2' 27'' derived from the *Ahargana* <note>count of elapsed days</note> gives the Moon's *Mandakendra* <note>anomaly</note> as 11s 29° 54' 21''. Subtracting this from 12 signs gives the *Bhuja* <note>sine-related arc</note> 0s 0° 5' 39''. Since there are no signs or degrees in this *Bhuja*, this itself becomes the *Bhujamsha* <note>arc in degrees</note>. Its sixth part is 0° 0' 56''. Subtracting this from 10 leaves 29° 59' 4'', which when multiplied by the sixth part 0° 0' 56'' gives a product of 0° 27' 59''; set this aside. Then, its 20th part is 0° 1' 24''. Subtracting this from 56'' and dividing the set-aside product 0° 27' 59'' (converted to 1679 units) by the remainder 55' 58'' 36'' (converted to 201516 units) gives a quotient of 0° 10' 29''. This is the Moon's *Mandaphala* in degrees. Because the Lunar center is in the Libra quadrant <note>Tuladi</note>, this is negative. Therefore, subtracting it from the thrice-corrected Moon results in the **True Moon: 6s 14° 27' 37''**.

### Calculation of the Moon's Velocity —

The previously calculated Lunar Anomaly is 11s 29° 54' 21'', and its *Bhuja* is 0s 0° 5' 39''. Subtracting this from 3 signs gives the *Koti* <note>cosine-related arc</note> 2s 29° 54' 21''. Its degrees are 89° 54' 21''; the 20th part of this is 4° 29' 43''. Subtracting this from 11 leaves 6° 30' 17''. Multiplying this by the 20th part 4° 29' 43'' gives a product of 29' 14'', which doubled is 58' 28''. Adding its sixth part 9' 44'' results in 68' 12''. This is the Moon's velocity-correction, which is negative because the center is in the Capricorn quadrant <note>Makaradi</note>. Thus, subtracting it from the Moon's Mean Velocity 790' 35'' results in the **True Lunar Velocity: 722' 23''**. || 7 ||

### Now, the calculation of Tithi, Nakshatra, Yoga, and Karana is stated in a pair of verses —

> Dividing the degrees of the Moon minus the Sun by twelve <note>yamakubhi</note> gives the Tithi <note>lunar day</note>. The quotient is the elapsed Tithi, 
> while the remainder is the current <unclear>unelapsed portion to be known for both</unclear>. || 8 ||

<vocab>
**Ayanamsha**: Precession of the equinoxes.
**Mandaphala**: Equation of center; the correction applied to a planet's mean position to find its true position.
**Tithi**: A lunar day, defined as the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the Moon and the Sun to increase by 12 degrees.
**Mandakendra**: Anomaly; the angular distance of a planet from its apogee.
</vocab>

# Latika-Grahalaghava

The remaining time of the past and future [of a tithi] is found by dividing [the past and future distance] by the difference between the daily motions [of the Sun and Moon]. In the first half of the current tithi, the current *Karana* <note>a half-tithi</note> is found by doubling the number of past tithis and dividing by seven; the remainder, counting from *Bava*, is the result. || 8 ||

That result plus one is the *Karana* for the second half. Now, for the four fixed *Karanas*: *Shakuni* occurs in the second half of the 14th day of the dark fortnight; then *Chatushpada* in the first half of the New Moon, *Naga* in the second half, and *Kimstughna* in the first half of the first day of the bright fortnight. For the Moon and the Sun, the minutes of their positions are divided by 800 [to find the *Nakshatra* and *Yoga*]. The past and future times for these two are found by multiplying the past and future distances by sixty and dividing by the Moon's motion [for *Nakshatra*] or the sum of the motions [for *Yoga*]. || 9 ||

Now he explains the method for calculating the *Tithi* (lunar day), *Nakshatra* (lunar mansion), *Yoga*, and *Karana*. First, the calculation of the *Tithi*: "The Moon without the Sun" (*vyarkavidhu*) means the Sun's position is subtracted from the Moon's. For example: Sun 2s 5° 42' 37"; Moon 6s 24° 19' 3". The Moon minus the Sun is 5s 18° 32' 26". This equals 158° 32' 26". Divided by 12 <note>original: "yamakubhi", a numerical code where Yama=2 and Ku=1, meaning 12</note>, the result is 13 past tithis. Since we are in the 14th, this leads to the Full Moon (*Purnamasi*). The remainder is the "past" portion: 0° 32' 26". Subtracting this from the divisor 12 gives the "future" portion: 11° 27' 34". Converting these to seconds: past seconds = 1,946; future seconds = 41,264. The Sun's motion is 57' 36"; the Moon's motion is 811' 0". Their difference is 753' 24". Multiplied by 60, the divisor becomes 45,204. The past seconds (1,946) multiplied by 60 and divided by this divisor gives 2 past *ghatikas* and 35 *palas*.
Now for the future time: Future seconds (41,264) multiplied by 60 is 2,475,240. Divided by the divisor, the future time is 54 *ghatikas* and 10 *palas*.

Now for the *Karana* calculation: The past tithi (13) is doubled (26) and divided by 7 <note>original: "adri", meaning mountain, signifying 7</note>. The remainder indicates the *Karana* in the first half of the current tithi, counting from *Bava*. Adding one gives the *Karana* for the second half. Regarding the four special *Karanas*: in the dark fortnight, the 14th day's second half is *Shakuni*. The New Moon's first half is *Chatushpada*, its second half is *Naga*. The first day of the bright fortnight's first half is *Kimstughna*. Here, the past tithi is 13; doubled is 26; divided by 7, the remainder indicates *Bhadra* for the first half of the Full Moon. Adding one, the second half is *Bava*. The duration of a *Karana* is half the total duration of the tithi. Total tithi duration (2:35 + 54:10) is 56:45. Half of this is 28:22. Subtracting the past time (2:35) leaves 25 *ghatikas* and 48 *palas* remaining for the current *Bhadra Karana*.

Now for the *Nakshatra*: Moon is 6s 24° 19' 3". Its total minutes are 12,259' 3". Divided by 800, the result is 15 past *Nakshatras*. The current *Nakshatra* is *Vishakha*. The past remainder is 299' 3"; subtracting from 800 gives the future 500' 57". Past multiplied by 60 is 17,943; future multiplied by 60 is 30,057. Divided by the Moon's motion (811' 0"), the past time is 22:7 and future is 37:4.

Now for the *Yoga*: The sum of Sun and Moon is 7s 29° 57' 40". Total minutes are 14,397' 40". Divided by 800, the result is 17 past *Yogas* (*Vyatipata*); the current is *Variyan*. Remainder is 797' 40"; future is 3' 20". Past (47,860) and future (1,200) divided by the sum of motions (868' 36") gives past 55:6 and future 0:9. || 8-9 ||

# Chapter 2: On the True Positions of the Sun and Moon

Divided by the difference [of the velocities], in order = respectively, the past and future = the desired elapsed and remaining time, in ghatikas <note>A ghatika is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> = are produced. The meaning is that the elapsed portion of the distance between the Sun and Moon divided by the difference in their daily motion results in the elapsed ghatikas; the remaining portion divided by the difference in motion results in the remaining (future) ghatikas. Twice = multiplied by two, the elapsed lunar day = the number of the elapsed tithi, divided by seven = divided by seven, in the first half = in the first half of the desired tithi, from Bava = from the Karana named Bava <note>A Karana is half of a lunar day; there are 11 types</note> <insert>(1) For the knowledge of Karanas, one should consult my "Vimala" commentary on the Shishubodha.</insert> the Karana occurs. Then = thereafter, from the second half of the 14th day of the dark fortnight, from Shakuni = from the Shakuni Karana = the fixed Karanas begin. Then = thereafter, of the Moon = of the Chandra, and of the sum of the Sun and Moon, the minutes = the arc-minutes, divided by eight hundred = divided by 800, in the past = having elapsed, the lunar mansion and the yoga = the two results, are produced. The minutes of the Moon divided by 800 are the Nakshatras. The minutes of the sum of the Sun and Moon divided by 800 are the Yogas. Of those two = of the Nakshatra and Yoga, the past and future, multiplied by sixty = multiplied by 60, of the Moon = of the Chandra, divided by the motion = divided by the daily velocity, divided by the sum of the velocities = divided by the combined motion, of those two = of the Nakshatra and Yoga, the past and future ghatikas = the elapsed and remaining time units, are produced in order. || 8-9 ||

-> Here is the Mathematical Rationale: <-

Since from the end of one new moon to the next new moon there are thirty lunar days (tithis) in one lunar month, and at the moment of the new moon the Sun and Moon are at the same position, the Moon then moves ahead of the Sun due to the difference in their velocities and traverses its orbit of "360°". Therefore, the proportion is: if in thirty tithis this difference between the Sun and Moon is "360°", then what is it in one tithi? The result is the degrees of difference between the Sun and Moon in one tithi = $\frac{360 \times 1}{30} = 12^\circ$. Again, by proportion, the elapsed tithi = $\frac{1 \times (\text{Moon} - \text{Sun})}{12}$. The remainder represents the degrees traversed in the current tithi; if these are subtracted from the divisor, they become the degrees yet to be traversed. Furthermore, if sixty ghatikas correspond to the degrees of the difference in velocity between the Sun and Moon, then what corresponds to the traversed and remaining degrees? This gives the elapsed and remaining ghatikas. Thus—
Elapsed ghatika = $\frac{\text{Traversed degrees} \times 60}{\text{Difference in velocity}} = \frac{\text{Traversed minutes}}{\text{Difference in velocity}}$. Similarly, Remaining ghatika = $\frac{\text{Remaining degrees} \times 60}{\text{Difference in velocity}} = \frac{\text{Remaining minutes}}{\text{Difference in velocity}}$. A Karana is half of a tithi; the seven movable Karanas starting from Bava, and the four fixed Karanas starting from "the 14th day of the dark moon" etc., are made clear by looking at my edited *Shishubodha-Avalokana*.

-> The explanation of Nakshatras, Yogas, etc., is established by their respective definitions. || 8-9 || <-

By dividing the degrees of the true Moon (minus the true Sun) by 12, the elapsed tithi is found. The remainder is also the elapsed portion; subtracting this from 12 gives the remaining portion. By dividing the seconds <note>Original: vikala</note> of these (elapsed and remaining) by the difference in velocity of the Sun and Moon, the respective elapsed and remaining ghatikas are found. Multiplying the number of the elapsed tithi by 2 and dividing by 7 gives the Bava and subsequent Karanas. From the second half of the 14th day of the dark fortnight, the 4 fixed Karanas (Shakuni, etc.) occur. By dividing the minutes of the Moon and the minutes of the sum of the Sun and Moon by 800, the elapsed Nakshatras and Yogas are found. The remainder gives the elapsed ghatikas of the desired Nakshatra and Yoga. By multiplying these by 60 and dividing respectively by the Moon's velocity in minutes and the combined velocity of the Sun and Moon, the remaining ghatikas of the desired Nakshatra and Yoga are found. || 8-9 ||

Example—Moon $= 6^s 14^\circ 27' 37'',$ Sun $= 6^s 27^\circ 32' 20'' \therefore (6^s 14^\circ 27' 37'') - (6^s 27^\circ 32' 20'') = 11^s 16^\circ 55' 17'' = 346^\circ 55' 17''$. $\therefore (346^\circ 55' 17'')$

$\div 12 = 28 = \text{quotient } 0.$ Therefore, starting from the bright fortnight <note>Shukla Paksha</note>, 28 lunar days have passed, meaning the 13th day of the dark fortnight <note>Krishna Paksha Trayodashi</note> is complete. The remainder $10^\circ 55' 17''$ is the elapsed portion of the 14th day <note>Chaturdashi</note>, and $12 - (10^\circ 55' 17'') = 1^\circ 4' 43''$ is the remaining portion <note>bhogya</note>. Thus, the elapsed time in Ghatis <note>a unit of 24 minutes</note> for the 14th day is $39317 \times 60 \div 39711 = 59;25$.

&emsp;&emsp;$\therefore 232980 \div 39711 = 5;52$ remaining Ghatis of the 14th day.
&emsp;&emsp;$\therefore$ Total duration of the 14th day $= (59;25) + (5;52) = 65;17$.

**Calculation of the Karana** <note>A Karana is half a lunar day</note>—The elapsed Tithi is 14, therefore, according to the rule **"From the latter half of the dark fourteenth..."** <note>original: "कृष्णभूतौत्तरात्"</note> etc., in the second half of the 14th day, the *Shakuni* Karana $= 32;38\frac{1}{2}$ occurred, and because it was the New Moon <note>Amavasya</note> at the time of sunrise, the *Chatushpada* Karana occurred.

## Calculation of the Nakshatra (Lunar Mansion)—
Moon $= 6^s 14^\circ 27' 37'' = 11667' 37''$
$\therefore 11667' 37'' \div 800 = 14 =$ quotient, and the remainder $= 467' 37''$. Therefore, 14 Nakshatras starting from Ashwini have passed, and the elapsed portion of the current Nakshatra, *Swati*, is 467' 37''. Subtracting the elapsed portion from 800 gives the remaining portion of *Swati* $= 332' 23''$. Thus, $(467' 37'') \times 60 = 1683420''$. Dividing this by the Moon's motion $= 722' 23'' = 43343''$ gives the elapsed time of *Swati* as 38;50 Ghatis. For the remaining portion 332' 23'', as before: $(332' 23'') \times 60 = 19943 \times 60$. Dividing by the previous divisor 43343 gives the remaining time as 27;36 Ghatis. Therefore, the total duration of the desired Nakshatra *Swati* is 66;26 Ghatis.

## Calculation of the Yoga—
Moon $= 6^s 14^\circ 27' 37''$ and Sun $= 6^s 27^\circ 32' 20''$. Their sum is $11^s 11^\circ 59' 57'' = 21199' 57''$. $\therefore (21199' 57'') \div 800 = 26$ <note>The text says 3, likely referring to the remainder after full circles</note>. Thus, the *Ayushman* Yoga has passed, and for the current *Saubhagya* Yoga, the elapsed portion is 115' 57'' and the remaining is 680' 3''. Multiplying by 60 and dividing by the combined motion of the Sun and Moon gives the elapsed time as 9;24 Ghatis and the remaining time as 52;8 Ghatis. || 8-9 ||

# Chapter 3: On the Clarification of the Five Planets

Now the chapter on the clarification <note>the process of calculating true positions from mean positions</note> of Mars and the others is explained. First, the author provides the numerical factors for the "Equation of the Center" <term>Shighraphala: the correction for a planet's variable motion relative to the sun, similar to the effect of an epicycle</term> for Mars. "Zero, eight-winds..." etc. || 1 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary—

Of the "Earth-born" = Mars—
*   Zero = 0
*   Eight-winds = 58
*   Mountain-earth-earth = 117
*   Ocean-mountain-earth = 174
*   Eight-two-twelve = 228
*   Nine-mountain-twins = 279
*   Five-teeth = 325
*   Arrows-knowledge-fire = 365
*   Qualities-nine-fires = 393
*   Sky-sky-oceans = 400
*   Elephant-nine-Rama = 368
*   Nine-ocean-twelve = 249
*   Sky = 0

These, in order, are the "Fast-factors" <term>Shighrankas: specific values used to calculate the planet's position</term>. || 1 ||

### The Rationale Here—

The five planets, Mars and the others, produced from the calculation of elapsed days <note>Ahargana</note>, become "clear" <note>accurate</note> through repeated corrections of the "Fast-correction" <note>Shighraphala</note> and the "Slow-correction" <note>Mandaphala: correction for orbital eccentricity</note>. Regarding this, seeing the future statement "First, one should apply half of the fast-correction to the mean planet," the necessity of the fast-correction for the mean planet is understood, and thus the calculation of the fast-correction is performed. Now, here—

> "From the fast-sine multiplied by the radius, or from the product of the sine and the final-correction-sine, divided by the hypotenuse, the result obtained is the arc of the fast-correction of the planets."

->By this formula: (Sine of Fast-Correction = $\frac{\text{Sine of Fast-Anomaly} \times \text{Sine of Maximum Correction}}{\text{Fast-Hypotenuse}}$; the arc of this is the Fast-Correction)<-

Seeing the difficulty in calculating the fast-correction by Bhaskara’s method <note>referring to the 12th-century mathematician Bhaskaracharya</note>, for the sake of simplification, the "Fast-Anomalies" <note>Shighrakendras</note> are projected in increments of fifteen degrees (15°). Having brought forth the fast-corrections arising from those positions and seeing them as having fractional parts, they were multiplied by ten. Thus, the numbers "Zero, eight-winds..." etc., are read as the fast-correction parts of those planets. Because these numbers are multiplied by ten, it will be said later that "this result is in tenths of a degree." Now, here the Teacher <note>the author of the original verses</note>, observing the increase and decrease of the hypotenuse within the six signs (180°)—where the hypotenuse is greater at the apogee and smaller at the perigee—has recorded twelve fast-factors within those six signs. The calculation of the fast-correction within the fifteen-degree intervals will be explained later with the verse beginning "Subtracting the Mars-Sun-Jupiter..."

The method for producing these numbers is as follows: Let it be assumed that the degrees of anomaly for Mars = 0°. Then, by the previously mentioned method, because the sine of the fast-anomaly is zero, the fast-correction is also zero. If the degrees of anomaly = 15°, then the Sine of the Fast-Anomaly = 31; the degrees of the complement (90° - 15°) = 75°; the Cosine of the Fast-Anomaly = 115;30. The Sine of the Maximum Correction = 77 (Since the greatest fast-factor of Mars = 400; this divided by ten = 40; the sine of this is 77). Then, by the rule stated by Bhaskara: "The square root of the sum of the squares of the maximum correction and the radius, increased or decreased by twice the product of the cosine and the maximum correction, is the hypotenuse."

$\sqrt{(120^2 + 77^2) \pm (115;30) \times 77 \times 2} =$

$\sqrt{38116} = 195 = \text{Fast-Hypotenuse}.$

# With the Commentary on Grahalaghava

Therefore, the Sine of the Equation of Conjunction <note>original: शी.फ.ज्या (shighra-phala-jyā)</note> = $\frac{\text{Sine of Conjunction Anomaly} \times \text{Sine of Max Equation}}{\text{Hypotenuse of Conjunction}}$ = $\frac{31 \times 77}{178} = 12' 13''$ of this <note>This formula calculates the angular correction for a planet's position based on its distance from the Sun.</note>

The arc = $5^\circ 18'$, which when multiplied by ten gives $58' 10''$. Thus, the second digit 'Zero-Eight-Eight' <note>original: 'खमष्टमरुतः' (kha-ashta-marutah) using the Katapayadi system where words represent numbers</note> is proven. In this same way, all digits are proven separately from the degrees of the anomaly. This is sufficient. — The Editor.

The digits for **Mars** are: 0, 18, 41, 57, 42, 28, 79, 32, 63, 66, 39, 34, 00, 36, 25, 9, and 0. These are the velocity factors <note>term: Shighrankas (शीघ्राङ्क) — specific numerical factors used in Indian astronomy to calculate the variable motion of planets</note>. || 1-5 ||

# With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava

The signs [of the anomaly] should be subtracted, and the remainder converted into degrees. These are then divided by fifteen; by counting from the zero-index results, the "past index" (<term>Gatanka</term><note>The integer index representing the completed 15-degree intervals of the planet's anomaly</note>) is found. This is the past index. Then take the "next index" (<term>Eshyanka</term>). Calculate the difference between the two and multiply it by the remainder of the degrees. Divide this by fifteen. The resulting value should be subtracted from or added to the past index. Specifically: if the next index is smaller, subtract; if the next index is larger, add. After that, divide by ten (10) to obtain the <term>Shighra-phala</term><note>The "fast correction" or equation of the center used to find the apparent position of a planet</note> starting with degrees. It has already been stated that this is additive in the quadrants starting with Aries and subtractive in those starting with Libra. || 6 ||

### Madhuri Commentary

**The mean Sun minus Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter** = the mean Sun deprived of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, **becomes the planet's own Fast Anomaly** (<term>Shighra-kendra</term>). What is meant here is this: the mean Sun minus Mars is the anomaly for Mars; the mean Sun minus Saturn is the anomaly for Saturn; and the mean Sun minus Jupiter is the anomaly for Jupiter. **But** for **Mercury and Venus**, it was **stated previously** <margin>See the second half of verses 12 and 13 in the section on Mean Motion.</margin>. **If this** Fast Anomaly **is greater than six** signs, **then** it should be **subtracted from the Sun-sign** (the twelve signs/360 degrees). **Its degrees**—the degrees of that anomaly—**divided by days** (fifteen), **from the sequence of results starting with zero**, **here** in the calculation of the correction, **becomes the past index**. **This** past index, **by the decrease or increase** (the difference), **multiplied by the remainder**, **is decreased or increased by the result of the division by fifteen** (5). **This**, when **divided by ten**, **becomes the result** in degrees and so on. || 6 ||

### Mathematical Rationale

It is clear from observing the geometry of the planetary circles that the "Fast Higher Apex" (<term>Shighra-uchcha</term>) minus the planet is the Fast Anomaly. Since the Sun acts as the Fast Apex for Mars and the others, the Sun minus Mars, etc., must be the Fast Anomaly. From the lowest point to the highest, and from the highest to the lowest, the increase and decrease of the correction are equal over the span of six signs; therefore, if the anomaly exceeds six signs, it is appropriate to subtract it from the full circle (12 signs). Since the correction was calculated for every 15 degrees and recorded as an index, if one index is obtained for every 15 degrees, then for any given degrees, the past index is found by proportion. Furthermore, if the difference between the past and future indices (representing the rate of increase or decrease) corresponds to 15 degrees, then by proportion, the change for the remaining degrees is found. This change is added to or subtracted from the past index based on whether the values are increasing or decreasing. Finally, the result is divided by ten because the original table values were multiplied by ten [for ease of calculation]. Thus, it is proven. || 6 ||

Subtracting mean Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter from the mean Sun gives their Fast Anomalies. The anomalies for Mercury and Venus have already been mentioned. If those anomalies are greater than 6 signs, subtract them from 12 signs. Divide the resulting degrees by 15 to get the "past index" starting from zero. Multiply the remainder by the difference between the past and future indices (whether decreasing or increasing), divide by 15, and add/subtract the result from the past index. Dividing that total by 10 gives the Fast Correction (<term>Shighra-phala</term>) in degrees. || 6 ||

### Example of calculating the Fast Correction for Mars:

Mean Sun - Mean Mars = Fast Anomaly of Mars = (6s 28° 50' 17") - (4s 7° 23' 20") = 2s 21° 26' 57". These degrees are 81° 26' 57". Dividing this by 15...

Briefly: if the future index is greater than the past, add the result to the past index; if it is less, subtract it.</note>

The quotient is 5 and the remainder = 6° 12' 57'', therefore Mars' 5th <term>Shighranka</term><note>A tabular constant used for calculating the equation of conjunction</note> (279) is the "past index" (<term>Gatanka</term>) and the 6th (325) is the "future index" (<term>Eshyanka</term>). $\therefore$ (279 ~ 325) = 46; this is the additive difference. Again, (6° 24' 57'') $\times$ 46 = 295 8 12; dividing this by 15 gives the quotient 19 | 40 | 32. Adding this to the past index 279 and dividing by 10 results in 29° 29' 52'' 13'''. This value, in degrees and minutes, is the <term>Shighraphala</term><note>The Equation of Conjunction, which accounts for the Earth's orbital motion</note>; since the anomaly is in the half-circle beginning with Aries, it is positive (additive).

## Calculation of Mercury's Equation of Conjunction—

Mercury's mean <term>Shighra-kendra</term><note>Anomaly of conjunction</note> calculated in Verse 12 of the Chapter on Mean Motions = 110° 41' 17''. This is greater than 6 signs <note>180 degrees</note>.

$\therefore$ (12 signs - (110° 41' 17'')) = 0 signs 22° 18' 43''. Dividing this by 15 gives a quotient of 1 and a remainder of 7 18 43.

$\therefore$ Mercury's 1st index is 41 (past), and the 2nd index is 81 (future).

$\therefore$ (41 ~ 81) = 40; this is the additive difference. Again— (7 18 43) $\times$ 40 = 292 | 28 | 40. Dividing this by 15, the quotient (19 | 29 | 54) is added to the past index 41. Dividing the sum 60 | 29 | 54 by 10 gives the quotient 6° 2' 55'' = Mercury's Equation of Conjunction in degrees. Since the anomaly is in the half-circle beginning with Libra, it is negative (subtractive).

## Example of Jupiter's Equation of Conjunction—

Mean Sun — Mean Jupiter = Jupiter's Anomaly of Conjunction = (6 signs 28 50 17) - (8 signs 16 12 53) = 10 signs 12° 29' 24''. Here, because the anomaly is greater than 6 signs, it is subtracted from 12 signs — 12 - (10 signs 12° 29' 24'') = 1 sign 17° 38' 36''. Its degrees = 47° 38' 36''. Dividing this by 15 gives a quotient of 3 and a remainder of 2 | 38 | 36. Therefore, Jupiter's 3rd index (68) is past and the 4th (85) is future.

$\therefore$ 68 ~ 85 = 17; this is the additive difference. Multiplying the remainder by this: (2 | 38 | 36 $\times$ 17 = 44 | 56 | 12). Dividing this by 15 gives the quotient 2 | 59 | 45. Adding this to the past index 68 results in 70 | 59 | 45. Dividing this by 10 gives the quotient = 7° 5' 59'' = Jupiter's Equation of Conjunction. Because the anomaly is in the half-circle beginning with Libra, it is negative.

## Example of Venus's Equation of Conjunction—

Venus's Anomaly of Conjunction calculated from Verse 12 of the Chapter on Mean Motions = 2 signs 27° 19' 14''. Its degrees = 87° 19' 14''. Dividing by 15 gives a quotient of 5 and a remainder of 12 | 19 | 14.

$\therefore$ Venus's 5th index is 302 (past) and the 6th is 354 (future).

$\therefore$ 302 ~ 354 = 52; this is the additive difference.

$\therefore$ (12 | 19 | 14) $\times$ 52 = 635 | 18 | 8. Dividing by 15 gives the quotient 41 | 40 | 16. Adding this to the past index 302 gives 343 | 40 | 16. Dividing this by 10 results in 34° 18' 25'' = Venus's Equation of Conjunction. This is positive due to the anomaly being in the Aries-half.
