# On the Grahalaghava with Commentary

The elapsed time <note>Ishtakala: the time passed since sunrise</note> is found by adding the time passed for the Ascendant <note>Lagna: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>, the remaining time for the Sun, and the rising times of the zodiac signs situated between them (the Ascendant and the Sun). || 4 ||

**Example —** Clear Sun 6s 27° 30' 52'', Precession <note>Ayanamsha: the angular distance between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note> 21° 33' 31'', Tropical Sun 7s 19° 4' 23'', Elapsed time 2' 4'' = 124''. The remaining degrees of the Tropical Sun 30° - (19° 4' 23'') = 10° 55' 37''. Multiplying this by the rising time of Scorpio (347) gives 3791.38.59. Dividing this by 30, the result is 126, which is the remaining time. This cannot be subtracted from the elapsed time of 124''; therefore, multiplying the elapsed moments <note>Pala: a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> by 30 (124 x 30 = 3720) and dividing by the rising time of Scorpio (347), the result 10° 43' 13'' is added to the Sun 6s 27° 30' 52'', resulting in the first Ascendant 7s 8° 14' 5''.

-> Example of calculating the elapsed time from the Ascendant: <-

First Ascendant 7s 20° 11' 57'', Clear Sun 6s 27° 30' 52'', Precession 21° 33' 31''. The Tropical Ascendant is 8s 11° 45' 28'' and the Tropical Clear Sun is 7s 19° 4' 23''. Therefore, multiplying the degrees passed of the Tropical Ascendant (11° 45' 48'') by the rising time of Scorpio (347) gives 4081.52.36. Dividing by 30, the time passed for the Ascendant in moments is 136. Multiplying the remaining degrees of the Tropical Sun (10° 55' 37'') by the rising time of Scorpio (347) gives 3791.38.59. Dividing by 30, the result for the Sun's remaining time in moments is 126. Since there are no signs between them (the Sun and the Ascendant), the intermediate signs are 0. Thus, 136 + 126 = 262 = 4 Ghatis 22 Palas, which is the elapsed time. || 4 ||

-> Now, he speaks of a special case in calculating the Ascendant: <-

> If the Ascendant and the Lord of the Day <note>The Sun</note> are in the same sign, the difference of their degrees multiplied by the rising time and divided by thirty <note>literally "sky-fire" (kha-agni), a numerical code for 30</note> is the elapsed time. If the rising [Ascendant] is less than the Sun, it should be subtracted from the full day and night; at night, the Ascendant is calculated from the Sun plus six signs at the desired time. || 5 ||

When the Tropical Ascendant and Sun are in the same sign, he explains the method for calculating the elapsed time with "If...". Tropical Ascendant 9s 28° 37' 60''; Tropical Sun 9s 23° 53' 25''. Their difference in degrees is 4° 44' 35''. Multiplying this by the rising time of Taurus (293) gives 1290.0'.39. Dividing by thirty (30), the resulting elapsed time in moments is 47. Dividing by sixty, the elapsed time in Ghatis etc. is 0.47.

He then explains the method when the Ascendant is less than the Sun with "If from the Sun...". When in one sign the rising [Ascendant] is less than the Sun in degrees, the elapsed time is calculated by the difference of their degrees multiplied by the rising time, etc. That elapsed time is the time remaining until the next sunrise from the moment this Ascendant was calculated. This means it is the remaining time until the second sunrise. That remaining time should be subtracted from the sixty Ghatis of the full day and night; the result is the elapsed time from sunrise. This means it is the time at which this Ascendant was calculated. If the Ascendant is being calculated at night, the Ascendant should be calculated from the Sun plus six signs <note>Adding 180 degrees to find the point opposite the Sun</note> at the desired time.

**Example of this:** Elapsed Ghatis from sunrise: 59. Mean Sun: 9s 4° 3' 42''. Motion: 59' 8''. The Sun moved by these 59 Ghatis: 9s 5° 11' 60''. Anomaly <note>Mandakendra</note>: 9s 12° 48' 10''. Equation of Center <note>Mandaphala</note> is additive: 1° 28' 12''. The Sun corrected by this: 9s 6° 40' 42''. With the final multiplier 96, the corrected instantaneous Sun is 9s 6° 39' 7''. Tropical and with six signs added: 7s 24° 49' 7''. As stated, the rising time is 59. These are the 59 elapsed Ghatis. Subtracting the length of the day (33.10), the elapsed Ghatis from [sunset] are 25.50. The remaining time is 59. Subtracting 2550 moments from the elapsed 25.50, the remainder is 14.11. As before, the Ascendant is 8s 21° 37' 11''.

Now, an example of [the Ascendant] being less than the Sun. Tropical Sun: 9s 24° 49' 7". Tropical Ascendant: 9s 25° 47' 11". By the rule "multiplied by the rising..." the calculated time is 59. The remaining time is 1. This is subtracted from the 60 <term>Ghatis</term> <note>A Ghati is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 Ghatis make a full day/night cycle</note> of the day and night, resulting in the actual time from sunrise: 59. || 5 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

If (meaning: should it be), in one sign (meaning: occupying the same zodiacal sign), the body and the lord of the day (meaning: the Ascendant and the Sun) are situated, then "multiplied by their difference in degrees" (meaning: multiplied by the degrees of interval between them), "the rising" (meaning: the rising period or <term>Udayamana</term> of that sign), "divided by thirty" (meaning: divided by 30), the result shall be the <term>Istakala</term> (desired time). But, again, if the "rising" (meaning: the Ascendant) is "less than the Sun" (meaning: smaller in value), then the calculated time must be "subtracted from the day-night" (meaning: subtracted from the 60 Ghati measure of a full day); then the true time elapsed since sunrise is found. Furthermore, if it is night, at one's desired time, the "Ascendant from the Sun with six signs" (meaning: the Ascendant should be calculated using the Sun's position plus six signs, following the method for elapsed time). || 5 ||

### Here is the Rationale:—

The rising time of the sign where the Sun resides = U.Ka. The degrees of interval between the Sun and the Ascendant in that sign = An. If the Sun and the Ascendant are in the same sign, then the time corresponding to the degrees between the Sun and the Ascendant is the desired time. Therefore:
<gloss>4</gloss>
$$\text{Desired Time} = \frac{\text{U.Ka.} \times \text{An.}}{30^\circ}$$
Thus, the calculated time, if the Ascendant is less than the Sun, is subtracted from sixty Ghatis; the remaining time of the night is the true desired time—this is clear to those who know geometry. Since "within the interval of the eastern and western horizons on the ecliptic there are six signs," the first is the Ascendant and the seventh is the Setting Ascendant. As stated in the *Goladhyaya* (Chapter on the Sphere):

> "Where the ecliptic meets the horizon, that point is called the Ascendant. In the east, it is the Ascendant; on the western horizon, it is the Setting Ascendant; and in the north-south [meridian], it is the Midheaven." Thus, it is proven. || 5 ||

If the Ascendant and the Sun are in the same sign, then multiply the difference in degrees between them (Ascendant and Sun) by the rising time in <term>Palas</term> <note>A Pala is 1/60th of a Ghati, or 24 seconds</note> of that sign and divide by 30; this will be the **Istakala** (time elapsed since sunrise). If the Ascendant is less than the Sun, subtract the Istakala from the 60 Ghatis of the day and night to get the true Istakala. Or, if the time is during the night, add 6 signs to the clear Sun and calculate the Ascendant from that. || 5 ||

-> Now, he describes the definitions of the Spheres and Solstices, and the calculation of day/night length and latitude: <-

> The Northern and Southern Spheres <note>Golas</note> occur when the planet is in the six signs starting from Aries and Libra respectively. The Solstices <note>Ayanas</note> occur in the six signs starting from Capricorn and Cancer. Fifteen ghatikas <note>360 minutes</note> increased or decreased by the ascensional difference <note>charapala</note> is the half-day length in the two spheres. Subtracting that half-day from thirty (30) gives the half-night <note>nishardha</note>. Doubling these gives the total duration of day and night.

<margin>Example:</margin> Fifteen ghatikas (15) plus the ascensional difference (93) for a Northern Sphere Sun equals a half-day of 16 | 33. Doubling this gives a day length of 33 | 6. Multiplied by five, it is 28 | 45. The square of the shadow is 33 | 3. One-tenth of this is 3 | 18 | 18. Subtracting this from the five-fold shadow gives the southern latitude of $25^\circ 26' 42''$. These are always southern. || 6 ||

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems <note>original: "Tri-praśnādhikāra". This chapter deals with the determination of time, place (latitude), and direction using a gnomon.</note>

### Here is the proof:—

Because the region of the ecliptic <note>the sun's path</note> encompassing the six signs starting from Aries is situated to the north of the celestial equator, these six signs constitute the **Northern Hemisphere**. Conversely, because the six signs starting from Libra are situated to the south of the celestial equator, they constitute the **Southern Hemisphere**. Due to the movement of the Sun toward the north and south directions while situated in the six signs starting from Capricorn and Cancer respectively, these movements are called the **Northern and Southern Solstices** <note>original: "Ayana". The text notes that the word "Ayana" is derived from the root "Ay," meaning "to go."</note>. Know and consider that the Teacher <note>likely referring to Bhāskara II</note> has provided these meaningful designations here.

It is clear that the duration from the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle up to the upper meridian is **half-day**; and the duration up to the intersection with the lower meridian is **half-night**.

In the Northern Hemisphere, the segment of the diurnal circle from the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle to the upper meridian represents half-day. Within this, the measure of the segment from the intersection of the horizon and the diurnal circle to the intersection of the equatorial horizon <note>original: "Unmaṇḍala"</note> and the diurnal circle is the **ascensional difference** <note>original: "Cara-kāla"; the difference between the actual sunrise and 6:00 AM</note>. From the intersection of the equatorial horizon and the diurnal circle to the meridian, the duration is 30 ghatikas <note>12 hours; 1 ghatika = 24 minutes</note>. As stated by Bhāskara:
> "The duration of the segment of the diurnal circle between the equatorial horizon and the local horizon is the ascensional difference."
Therefore, in the Northern Hemisphere: 30 + Ascensional Difference = Half-day.
In the Southern Hemisphere: 30 - Ascensional Difference = Half-day.
By the inverse of this, the measure of half-night is obtained.

<column-break/>

Now, by proportion, the Sine of Latitude <note>original: "Akṣajyā"</note> = (Equinoctial Shadow × Radius) / Equinoctial Hypotenuse.
By a simplified method, the degrees of latitude <note>original: "Akṣāṃśa"</note> are:
= (Equinoctial Shadow × Radius) / (Equinoctial Hypotenuse × 2) = (Equinoctial Shadow × 120) / (√[Shadow² + 12²] × 2).
If the shadow is 1 digit, then the degrees of latitude:
= (Shadow × 120) / (√[1 + 144] × 2) = (Shadow × 120) / (√145 × 2) ≈ (Shadow × 120) / (12 × 2) = (Shadow × 60) / 12.

Here, if the numerator and denominator are reduced, then by a slight approximation, the degrees of latitude = (Shadow × 49) / 10.
= [Shadow × (49 + 1 - 1)] / 10 = [Shadow × (50 - 1)] / 10 = [Shadow × (50 - Shadow)] / 10 <note>This is a simplified rule of thumb for calculating latitude from the shadow cast at noon during the equinox</note>.
= (Shadow × 50) / 10 - (Shadow²) / 10 = (Shadow × 5) - (Shadow² / 10).
This is proven. This logic applies to a place with a one-digit equinoctial shadow. || 6 ||

If the Sun is in the six signs starting with Aries or Libra, it is respectively the Northern or Southern Hemisphere. Similarly, if the Sun is in the six signs starting with Cancer or Capricorn, it is respectively the Northern or Southern Solstice. By adding or subtracting the ascensional difference <note>original: "Carapala"</note> to 15 ghatikas <note>6 hours</note> in the respective hemispheres, one gets the half-day; subtracting the half-day from 30 ghatikas gives the half-night. Multiplying the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "Palabhā"</note> by 5 and subtracting one-tenth of the square of the shadow gives the degrees of latitude. This latitude is always for the southern direction. || 6 ||

**Example—** The tropical Sun <note>original: "Sāyana Sūrya"</note> is at 7 signs, 19°, 14', 23'' (Scorpio). Therefore, it is the Southern Hemisphere and Southern Solstice. The ascensional difference is 12'' = 1.32. Thus, 15 - (1.32) = 13.28 <note>half-day in ghatikas</note>.

# Latika's Commentary on Grahallaghava

Half-day, and 30 — (13:28) = 16:32 is the half-night. Therefore (13:28) x 2 = 26:56 is the total day duration <note>dinamana</note> and (16:32) x 2 = 33:4 is the total night duration <note>ratrimana</note>.

Equinoctial shadow <note>palabha</note> = 6, therefore 6 x 5 = 30. 6 squared = 36.
Therefore 36/10 = 3.36, so 30 — (3.36) = 26.24. This is always the latitude <note>akshansha</note> of the southern direction, 26° 24'. || 6 ||

->**Now he describes the calculation of the elapsed/remaining time and the equinoctial hypotenuse —**<-

> The time passed in the east and the time remaining in the west is the "elevated" time <note>unnata</note>; the half-day minus that is the "bent" time <note>nata - hour angle</note>.
> Twelve plus one-twenty-fifth of the square of the equinoctial shadow results in the equinoctial hypotenuse in inches. || 7 ||

Now he explains the definitions of "elevated" <note>unnata</note> and "bent" <note>nata</note> time and the knowledge of the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>akshakarna</note>. Regarding "The time passed...": From sunrise until midday is the eastern half, called the eastern hemisphere <note>prak-kapala</note>. From midday until sunset is the western half, called the western hemisphere <note>apara-kapala</note>. In the eastern hemisphere, the time in minutes <note>ghatikas</note> that has passed since sunrise is called "elevated." In the western hemisphere, the time remaining in the day is "elevated." In the eastern hemisphere, the "bent" and "elevated" times are eastern; in the western hemisphere, they are western. The half-day <note>dyukhanda</note> minus that "elevated" time is the "bent" time.

**Example:** Elapsed minutes from sunrise = 10:30. Being in the eastern hemisphere, the eastern "elevated" time is 10:30. The half-day 16:33 minus this results in the eastern "bent" time of 6:3. The equinoctial shadow is 5:49. Its square is 33:3:49. One-twenty-fifth of this is 1:19. Twelve <note>original: "Martanda" - a name for the Sun, here representing the number 12</note> plus this results in the equinoctial hypotenuse in inches: 13:19. || 7 ||

->**Madhuri Commentary —**<-

Passed = elapsed time; East = in the eastern hemisphere; Remaining = time to go; West = in the western hemisphere. Elevated time = "In the eastern hemisphere, the minutes passed from sunrise; in the western hemisphere, the minutes remaining in the day are the elevated time." This also applies at night. Minus that = subtracted from the elevated time; Half-day = midday; Bent = becomes the "bent" time <note>hour angle</note>. Twelve plus one-twenty-fifth of the square of the equinoctial shadow: Twelve = the number 12; Inches = measured in inches; Equinoctial hypotenuse = the Palakarna. || 7 ||

->**Mathematical Proof —**<-

During the day, the "elevated" time is the duration on the diurnal circle above the horizon. The "bent" time is the duration on the diurnal circle from the Sun to the meridian. Thus, the definition of "elevated" and "bent" time as "passed in the east and remaining in the west" is quite clear.

Now, in a right-angled triangle where 12 is the vertical side <note>koti</note>, the equinoctial shadow is the base <note>bhuja</note>, and the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse <note>karna</note>: the sum of the squares of the base and vertical side equals the square of the hypotenuse.
Thus, (Equinoctial Hypotenuse)² = (Shadow)² + 12² = 1² + 144 = 145 <note>using a 1-inch shadow example</note>.

Therefore, Equinoctial Hypotenuse = $\sqrt{145}$ = 12 + 1/24. Because the difference is very small, the Teacher has accepted 25 in place of 24. Therefore: Hypotenuse = 12 + (Shadow² / 25). This is proven. || 7 ||

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the relationship between direction, place, and time in Indian astronomy.</note>

The time elapsed since sunrise is the **elevated time** <note>Sanskrit: *unnata-kāla*</note>. By subtracting the elevated time from half the day's duration, the **meridian distance** <note>Sanskrit: *nata-kāla*, literally "bent time," the time distance from the sun to the local meridian</note> is found. This calculation of meridian distance and elevated time should also be performed for the night. By adding the twenty-fifth part of the square of the **equinoctial shadow** <note>Sanskrit: *palabhā*, the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> to 12, the **hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow** <note>Sanskrit: *palakarṇa*</note> in digits and its fractions is obtained. || 7 ||

**Example—** If the elapsed time of the day is 4;22 <note>expressed in *ghatis*, where 1 ghati = 24 minutes</note> and half the day is 13;28. Therefore, 4;22 is the elevated time and (13;28) - (4;22) = 9;6 is the meridian distance before noon. The same logic applies to the night.
Since the equinoctial shadow = 6, therefore 6² = 36. 36 / 25 = 1;26.
Therefore, 12 + (1;26) = 13;26, which is the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow in digits. || 7 ||

### Now, the calculation of the divisor for the purpose of finding the shadow:

->**One hundred and fourteen, increased or decreased by the ascensional difference divided by five in the northern and southern hemispheres respectively,**<-
->**is the "divisor." Then, half the square of the meridian distance increased by half a ghati is known as the "equalizer."**<-
->**If the meridian distance exceeds thirteen and a half, that excess multiplied by four is subtracted from it**<-
->**to make the "equalizer" accurate. The divisor minus that equalizer, divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse, is the "desired divisor." || 8 ||**<-

Now the calculation of the divisor is explained. Regarding "One hundred and fourteen" <note>Sanskrit: *vedeśāḥ*, a numerical code where *veda* = 4 and *īśa* = 11</note>: The **ascensional difference** <note>Sanskrit: *cara*, the difference between the tropical and equatorial day</note> is 93; divided by five, the result is 18;36. Because the Sun is in the northern hemisphere, 18;36 is added to 114, making the divisor 132;36. The meridian distance is 6;3, which, when increased by half a ghati (0;30), becomes 6;33. The square of this is 42;94;9. Divided by two, it becomes the "equalizer" <note>Sanskrit: *samākhya*</note> 21;47. If the meridian distance were greater than 13.5, one would subtract 13.5 from it, multiply the remainder by four, and subtract that result from the equalizer to make it "accurate." Since here the meridian distance is less than 13.5, the equalizer remains as it is. An example of this will be shown further on.

Now the calculation of the "desired divisor" <note>Sanskrit: *abhimata-hāra*</note>: The divisor 132;36 minus the equalizer 21;47 is 111;19. Divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse 13;19, the result is the desired divisor 8;20. || 8 ||

### Madhuri Commentary

**Increased or decreased by the ascensional difference divided by five =** added to or subtracted from the *palas* of the ascensional difference divided by five. **One hundred and fourteen =** 114. **In the northern and southern hemispheres =** in the North and South celestial halves. **Divisor =** the mean divisor. **Then =** thereafter. **Square of the meridian distance increased by half a ghati =** the square of the meridian distance plus 30 minutes. **Half =** divided by two. **Equalizer =** known as the time-knower or "equal." **If =** provided that. **From thirteen and a half =** from 13.5. **Meridian distance =** the measure of time from the meridian. **Which =** by how much. **Exceeds =** is greater. **That =** that excess amount. **Multiplied by four =** times four. **Subtracted from it =** minus that. **This =** this. **Equal =** becomes the accurate equalizer. **With that =** minus the equalizer. **Divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse =** divided by the *palakarṇa*. **Divisor =** the mean divisor becomes the **desired divisor.** || 8 ||

### Here is the Proof:

In the northern and southern hemispheres, the radius increased or decreased by the sine of the ascensional difference is the *Antyā* <note>the total sine of the day-arc</note>; this is clear from observing the nature of the celestial sphere. Here, the teacher has assumed the Radius = 114, therefore *Antyā* = Radius ± Sine of ascensional difference = 114 ± Sine of ascensional difference.
Since, due to small difference, Sine of ascensional difference ≈ (Ascensional difference in *palas* × 2) / 10 = (Ascensional difference) / (10/2) = (Ascensional difference) / 5. Therefore, *Antyā* = 114 ± (Ascensional difference / 5).

This *Antyā* is accepted here by the name "divisor." When the versed sine of the meridian distance is subtracted from it, it becomes the "desired *Antyā*." The versed sine of the meridian distance is treated here as the "time-value." <unclear>And so, Cosine of meridian distance - Cosine of meridian distance = \sqrt{Radius^2 - Sine of meridian distance^2}</unclear>

# On the Grahalaghava with Commentary

Therefore, the Versed Sine of the hour angle = $Versin(H)$ = Radius — ($\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \sin(H)^2}$)

$= 114 - (\sqrt{114^2 - \sin(H)^2}) = 114 - 114 + \frac{\sin(H)^2}{114 \times 2}$
<note>The commentator is using a mathematical approximation where $R - \sqrt{R^2 - x^2} \approx \frac{x^2}{2R}$. Here, the Radius is taken as 114 units.</note>

$= \frac{\sin(H)^2}{114 \times 2} = \frac{(\text{Hour Angle in ghatis} \times 6 \times 2)^2}{114 \times 2} = \frac{(\text{Hour Angle})^2 \times 36 \times 4}{114 \times 2}$

$= \frac{(\text{Hour Angle})^2 \times 36}{38 \times 2} = \frac{(\text{Hour Angle})^2}{2} (1 + \frac{8}{38}) = \frac{(\text{Hour Angle})^2}{2} (1 + \frac{1}{4})$ approximately $\frac{(\text{Hour Angle} + \frac{3}{4})^2}{2} = \text{Sama (The Equalizer).}$

This "Sama" value is accurate when the <term>Nata-kala</term><note>Hour angle or time from noon, measured in ghatis (1 ghati = 24 minutes).</note> is less than 13.5 ghatis. If it is greater than that, a difference of 4 arises for every additional ghati. Therefore, by multiplying the difference in ghatis by four and subtracting it from the previously calculated Sama, the true Sama is clearly obtained. Thus, the derivation is proven. || 8 ||

In the Northern and Southern hemispheres, by respectively adding to or subtracting from 114 the 5th part of the <term>Charapala</term><note>Ascensional difference measured in vinadis.</note>, the <term>Hara</term> (Divisor) is found. Half of the square of the hour angle (increased by half a ghati) is the <term>Sama</term>. If the hour angle exceeds 13.5 ghatis, multiply the excess by four and subtract it from the previous Sama to get the corrected Sama. Subtract the Sama from the Hara and divide the result by the <term>Akshakarna</term><note>Hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow.</note>; the quotient is the <term>Ishta-hara</term> (Desired Divisor). || 8 ||

**Example—** <term>Charapala</term> is 92, <term>Nata-kala</term> (hour angle) is 9;6 and the <term>Sayana</term> (tropical) Sun is 7s 19° 4' 23". Here the Sun is in the Southern hemisphere, therefore: $\frac{92}{5} = 18;24.$

$114 - (18;24) = 95;36 = \text{Hara.}$ $(9;6) + (00;30) = 9;36.$ Its square $= 92;9;36.$ Therefore $\frac{92;9;36}{2} = 46;4;48 = \text{Sama.}$ Since the hour angle does not exceed 13.5, 46;4;48 remains the corrected Sama.

Subtracting Sama 46;4 from Hara 95;36, the remainder is 49;32. Dividing this by the <term>Palakarna</term> (equinoctial hypotenuse) 13;26, the quotient 3;41 is the <term>Ishta-hara</term>. || 8 ||

### Now he describes the calculation of the Dividend, Desired Hypotenuse, and Desired Shadow—

> Multiply the equinoctial shadow by ten, divide the ascensional difference by this, square the result and double it. Add its own fifth part and add two; this is the Dividend. The hypotenuse in digits is the Dividend divided by the Desired Divisor. The square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the gnomon is the Desired Shadow. || 9 ||

Now the knowledge of the <term>Bhajya</term> (Dividend), <term>Ishta-karna</term> (Hypotenuse), and <term>Ishta-chhaya</term> (Shadow) is explained. This, added to its own fifth part 1;2, becomes 6;14. Adding two <note>original: "yugma" meaning the number 2</note>, the Dividend becomes 12;14. This, divided by the intended Divisor 8;20, gives the Hypotenuse in digits as 1;29. Its square is 2;7;50. The square of the gnomon (12) is 144. Their difference is 63;50. The square root of this should be taken; that will be the Desired Shadow. Regarding the method of finding the square root of a fractional number: wherever the square root of two fractional parts is to be found, the upper digit is multiplied by sixty and added to the lower digit, then multiplied by sixty again. Thus, it is reduced twice by sixty. Then, "discarding from the last odd place" <note>A reference to the traditional square root algorithm</note>, find the root. # Chapter on the Three Problems || 4 ||

The result obtained by dividing [the remainder] by the doubled [root] plus two should be placed below the root. The upper digit should be divided by sixty once. This yields the precise root for a number with fractional parts. In this way, for a number with fractional parts, the process of multiplying by sixty should be performed four times. The root obtained as described should be divided by sixty twice. This same logic should be understood for further steps. Here, the process should be done six times for an even power, not for an odd power. The difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the sun <note>original: *arkavarga*; here referring to the gnomon of 12 digits</note> is 63;50. To find the precise root, this was converted by sixty twice, resulting in 229800. From this, the root as described is 469. The remainder of the root is 369. Adding one, it is 360. Divided by sixty, it is 21600. This is combined with zero seconds. Dividing by the doubled root 998 plus two (totaling 960 <note>The text shows a slight calculation or transcription discrepancy in the divisor</note>), the result is 22. Placed below the root, it becomes 479;22. Divided by sixty, the root becomes 7;59;22. This itself is the **desired shadow** <term>Iṣṭacchāyā: the length of the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at a specific time</term> 7;59;22. 

If the root of a fractional number is taken as it is, an error occurs. If the square of such a root is taken, it does not return to the original squared number; for this reason, the "as-is" root of a fractional number should not be accepted. Here is an example: Suppose the desired value is 0;29. Its square is 0;6. The "as-is" upper digit is 0. The root is 0. The remainder is 9;6. By the "adding one" method, the result is 33. This does not equal the assumed desired value. Alternatively, if the desired is 0;30, its root is 0;36 and its square is 0;20. Thus, in small numbers, a large difference occurs. In large numbers, it might occasionally coincide, but for this reason, the root should not be taken by that method. It must be taken according to the previously stated method. || 9 ||

---

### Madhuri Commentary—

->The ascensional difference in seconds multiplied by ten and divided by the equinoctial shadow, squared, doubled, increased by its own fifth part, and added to one hundred and fourteen, becomes the **Dividend** <term>Bhājya</term> here. The Dividend divided by the **Desired Divisor** <term>Iṣṭahara</term> results in the **Hypotenuse** <term>Karṇa</term> in digits etc., for the calculation of the shadow. From the difference of the squares of the Hypotenuse and the Sun (12), the square root is the **Desired Shadow** <term>Iṣṭabhā</term>. || 9 ||<-

---

### Here is the Proof:

Since Sine of Declination <note>original: *krāñjyā*</note> = $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Day-Radius}^2}$. Earth-Sine <note>original: *kujyā*</note> = $\frac{\text{Sine of Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Day-Radius}}{\text{Radius}}$.

Because of the similarity between the triangles formed by (Sine of Declination, Earth-Sine, Sine of Amplitude) and (12, Equinoctial Shadow, Equinoctial Hypotenuse):

Earth-Sine = $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{12}$ = $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times \sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{Day-Radius}^2}}{12}$. 

Squaring both sides:

(Earth-Sine)$^2$ = $\frac{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 - \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Day-Radius}^2}{144}$ = $\frac{\text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 \times \text{Day-Radius}^2}{\text{Radius}^2}$.

$\therefore \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 - \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Day-Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 = 144 \times \text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 \times \text{Day-Radius}^2$.

$\therefore \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 = 144 \times \text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 \times \text{Day-Radius}^2 + \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Day-Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2$

$= \text{Day-Radius}^2 (144 \times \text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 + \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2)$. 

$\therefore \frac{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2}{144 \times \text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 + \text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2}$

$= \text{Day-Radius}^2 = \frac{\text{Radius}^2 \times \text{Radius}^2}{\frac{144 \times \text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2}{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2} + \frac{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2 \cdot \text{Radius}^2}{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2}} = \frac{\text{Radius}^2 \times \text{Radius}^2}{\frac{\text{Sine Asc. Diff.}^2 \times 144}{\text{Eq. Shadow}^2} + \text{Radius}^2}$

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems

= **Dividend / Desired Divisor**. Therefore, in this triangle formed by 12 <note>the standard length of a gnomon in Indian astronomy</note>, the shadow, and the hypotenuse of the shadow, the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the vertical side will indeed be the shadow, which is the horizontal side. This is thus proven. || 9 ||

By dividing the <term>Chara</term><note>ascensional difference, or the difference between the length of day and night</note> by the product of ten and the <term>Palabha</term><note>the equinoctial midday shadow</note>, then doubling the square of the result, adding one-fifth of itself and 114, the **Dividend** is obtained. By dividing this Dividend by the **Desired Divisor**, the hypotenuse in digits and other units is found. The square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and 12 is the shadow. || 9 ||

### Madhuri Commentary

**The sum of the squares of the Sun's shadow** = from the sum of the squares of twelve and the shadow, **the root** = the square root, **the hypotenuse** = shall be the hypotenuse of the shadow.
**The dividend divided by that** = the dividend divided by the hypotenuse, **the desired** = the intended, **divisor** = shall be the divisor. **Diminished by the product of that and the equinoctial hypotenuse** = the result of multiplying the intended divisor by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>The equinoctial hypotenuse is the shadow hypotenuse at the equator during the equinox</note> is subtracted from the **middle** = middle **divisor**. **Multiplied by two** = doubled, **if** = if it is, **greater than 194** = greater than one hundred and ninety-four, then **from this** = from this value, set aside, **increased by the result of dividing the value minus 194 by three** = added to the result obtained by subtracting one hundred and ninety-four and dividing by three, **of that** = of that sum, **the root** = the square root, **diminished by half a ghati** = minus half a ghati, **the face of the ghati** = the time in ghatis etc., **the hour angle** = shall be the hour angle. 10

### Here is the Derivation:

In a right-angled triangle where 12 is the vertical side, the shadow is the base, and the shadow-hypotenuse is the hypotenuse: **"The sum of the squares of the base and the vertical side is equal to the square of the hypotenuse." Thus, Hypotenuse$^2$ = 12$^2$ + Shadow$^2$.**

$\therefore$ Shadow Hypotenuse = $\sqrt{12^2 + \text{Shadow}^2}$. $\because$ Hypotenuse = $\frac{\text{Dividend}}{\text{Intended Divisor}}$ $\therefore$ $\frac{\text{Dividend}}{\text{Hypotenuse}}$ = Intended Divisor.

Thus, by the previous logic, the Correction = $\frac{3}{8}$ ( Hour Angle + $\frac{1}{2}$ )$^2$. Intended Divisor = $\frac{\text{Divisor} - \frac{3}{8} ( \text{Hour Angle} + \frac{1}{2} )^2}{\text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse}}$

$\therefore$ Intended Divisor $\times$ Equinoctial Hypotenuse = Divisor $-$ $\frac{3}{8}$ ( Hour Angle + $\frac{1}{2} )$ $^2$. By rearranging, $\frac{3}{8}$ ( Hour Angle + $\frac{1}{2} )$ $^2$ =
Divisor $-$ Intended Divisor $\times$ Equinoctial Hypotenuse. $\therefore$ ( Hour Angle + $\frac{1}{2} )$ $^2$ = ( Divisor $-$ Intended Divisor $\times$ Equinoctial Hypotenuse ) $\times$ $\frac{8}{3}$. Taking the square root of both sides:
Hour Angle + $\frac{1}{2} = \sqrt{(\text{Divisor} - \text{Intended Divisor} \times \text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse}) \times \frac{8}{3}}$. By rearranging:
Hour Angle = $\sqrt{(\text{Divisor} - \text{Intended Divisor} \times \text{Equinoctial Hypotenuse}) \times \frac{8}{3}} - \frac{1}{2}$.

Furthermore, according to the rule "If the hour angle is more than 13.5" etc.:

Correction = $\frac{3}{8} ( \text{Hour Angle} + \frac{1}{2} )^2 - ( \text{Hour Angle} - 13 \frac{1}{2} ) \times 4$

$= \frac{( \text{Hour Angle} + \frac{1}{2} )^2}{\frac{8}{3}} - \frac{( 2 \times \text{Hour Angle} - 27 ) \times 4}{2}$

$= \frac{(\frac{2 \times \text{Hour Angle} + 1}{2})^2}{\frac{8}{3}} - ( \frac{2 \times \text{Hour Angle} - 27}{2} ) \times 4$

$= \frac{4 \times \text{Hour Angle}^2 + 4 \times \text{Hour Angle} + 1}{4 \times \frac{8}{3}} - ( 4 \times \text{Hour Angle} - 54 )$

$= \frac{4 \times \text{Hour Angle}^2 + 4 \times \text{Hour Angle} + 1 - ( 32 \times \text{Hour Angle} - 432 )}{8}$

$= \frac{4 \times \text{Hour Angle}^2 - 28 \times \text{Hour Angle} + 433}{8}$ (By adding and subtracting 46 to balance).

## Now, he describes the calculation of the precise declination—

> **Forty, eighty, one hundred and seventeen, one hundred and fifty-one, one hundred and eighty-one,**
> **two hundred and six, two hundred and twenty-four, two hundred and thirty-six, two hundred and forty; from the planet**
> **with the precession of the equinoxes, find the degrees of the arc. The number corresponding to the tens-place of those degrees is the "past" value. Multiply the remainder by the difference between that and the "next" value;**
> **divide by ten and add to the past value. That total, divided by ten, is the declination in degrees and so on, in its own direction. || 11 ||**

Now he explains the method for finding the declination <note>original: "Kranti"</note>. These are the <gloss>*</gloss> segments. Starting with "forty," there are nine segments.
Namely: 40, 40, 37, 34, 30, 27, 18, 12, 4. The Sun is at 2 signs, 15 degrees, 24 minutes, 49 seconds. Adding the precession <note>Ayanamsha</note> of 18;10, it becomes 3 signs, 3 degrees, 34 minutes, 2 seconds, 49 seconds. Its arc degrees <note>Bhujamsha</note> are 93;34;49. Divided by ten, the result is 9, which are the "past segments," totaling 181. The remainder is 3;34;49.
Multiplying by the "future segment" 26, we get 109;5;15. Divided by ten, the result is 10;54;32. Adding this to the sum of past segments 181, we get 191;54;32. Dividing by ten, the declination in degrees etc. is 19;11;27. Since the Sun (with precession) is in the northern hemisphere, the direction is North.

Now he explains the calculation of declination by another method. "Forty," etc.: 40, 80, 117, 151, 181, 206, 224, 236, 240.

Example for this: The arc degrees of the Sun with precession are 93;34;49. Divided by ten, the result is 9. The "past number" corresponding to this is 181. Subtracting this from the "future number" 206 leaves 25. <gloss>Multiplying the remainder 3;34;49 by this [25] gives 109;5;15.</gloss> Divided by ten, the result is 10;54;32. Adding this to the past number 181 gives 191;54;32. Divided by ten, the declination in degrees etc. is that same 19;11;27. || 11 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary—

-> Forty = 40; Eighty = 80; Mountains-Earth-Ground = one hundred and seventeen (117); <-
-> Organs-Eyes-Moon = one hundred and fifty-one (151); Earth-Bearers = one hundred and eighty-one (181); <-
-> Six-Sky-Eyes = two hundred and six (206); Jinas-Ashvins = two hundred and twenty-four (224); <-
-> Limbs-Transformations = two hundred and thirty-six (236); Sky-Oceans-Ashvins = two hundred and forty (240). <-
These are the segments of declination. Now, "from the planet with precession" <note>Sayana</note>, the "past number" of the declination segment is equal to the tens-place of the arc degrees. "That" refers to the past number; "from the next value minus that" means the next number minus the past number; "multiplied by the remainder" means multiplied by the remaining degrees...

The result combined with the quotient of ten = including the result multiplied by ten, divided by ten = divided by ten, its own direction = the declination of the tropical planet's sphere, beginning with degrees = degrees and so on, is the declination <note>original: "apama"</note> || 11 ||

### Here is the Geometrical Proof:—

At the intersection of the spheres <note>the equinox</note>, at an interval of three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, the maximum distance between the celestial equator and the ecliptic is the maximum declination. Its sine is the maximum sine of declination ($49 \frac{7}{9} = 48$ <term>Sva-units</term><note>A specific unit of measurement used in this manual</note>). Here, the illustrious Ganesha has calculated the declination for every ten degrees at the equinox, multiplied them by ten, and recorded them as "segments" <note>tabular differences</note>. These are nine within the span of three signs. In the ecliptic there are ninety degrees, in the celestial equator there are ninety degrees, and in the polar circle there are the degrees of maximum declination—this is one triangle. The degrees of the ten-degree arc, its equatorial degrees, and its declination degrees—this is the other. By constructing the sine-area of these two triangles, a proportion is established due to their similarity. There, the Radius = 120, the Maximum Sine of Declination = 48, and the Sine of $10^{\circ}$ = 21. Therefore, the Sine of Declination for $10^{\circ} = \frac{48 \times 21}{120} = \frac{7 \times 48}{40} = \frac{7 \times 12}{10} = \frac{84}{10} = 8$ Sva-units. Since a sine divided by two is approximately equal to its arc for small values, the declination degrees for $10^{\circ} = \frac{8}{2} = 4$. Multiplied by ten, $4 \times 10 = 40$. Thus, the first segment is 40. This applies everywhere. The proof for the second half is easy to understand, so why expand the writing? Thus it is proven || 11 ||

The segments of declination are respectively 40, 80, 118, 151, 181, 206, 224, 236, and 240. By dividing the <term>Bhujāṃśa</term><note>the degrees of the planet's longitude measured from the nearest equinox</note> of the tropical Sun by 10, the quotient will be the "passed index" <note>original: "gatāṅka"</note>. Subtract the passed index from the "next index" <note>original: "agrimāṅka"</note>; multiply the remainder by the remaining degrees of the arc and divide by 10. Add this result to the passed index and divide the total by 10 again; this will be the declination in the direction of the tropical Sun's hemisphere || 11 ||

### Example:—

For a tropical Sun at 7 signs, 19°, 4', 23", using the method "subtract two signs from the third," etc., the arc degrees are 49° 4' 23". Dividing by 10 gives a quotient of 4 and a remainder of 9° 4' 23". Therefore, the 4th segment (151) is the passed index and the next (181) is the next index. Subtracting the passed index 151 from the next index 181 leaves 30. Multiplying this by the remaining arc 9° 4' 23" gives 272° 11' 30". Dividing by 10 gives 27° 13' 9". Adding this to the passed index 151 gives 178° 13' 9". Dividing this by 10 again results in a declination of 17° 49' 18" in the southern direction, as the tropical Sun is in the southern hemisphere || 11 ||

### Now, the calculation for Rough Declination:—

> With six, six, five, four, four, three, and one, the sum of the segments corresponding to the planet's arc degrees divided by fifteen, combined with the next segment multiplied by the remaining degrees and divided by fifteen, gives the declination in degrees for easy practical use || 12 ||

Now, for the sake of simplification, the method for finding the rough declination is stated. "Six, six..." etc. 6, 6, 5, 4, 4, 3, 1. The arc degrees of the tropical Sun are 53° 2' 41". Divided by fifteen, the quotient is 3. The sum of the passed segments for this amount is 17 <note>6+6+5</note>. The next segment is 4. Multiplying by the remainder 8° 2' 41" <note>Note: The text says 9.2.41, likely a slight calculation variant or scribal error</note> gives 36° 12' 44". Divided by fifteen, the result is 2° 24' 53". Adding this to the sum of passed segments (17) results in a declination of 19° 24' 53" in degrees. This is for the purpose of "easy practical use" <note>original: "sukha-saṃvyavahāra"</note> || 12 ||

### The "Madhuri" Commentary:—

Or = alternatively, with six, six, five, four, four, three, one = with these values, segments = the tabular differences, the sum of segments equal to the fifteenth parts of the tropical planet's arc degrees, combined with the next segment multiplied by the remainder and divided by fifteen, then for the sake of simplification = for ease, beginning with degrees = degrees etc., the declination = the declination, is found ||

->### Here is the Proof:<-

Here also, as before, the declination degrees were calculated for every fifteen degrees from the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic <note>the vernal equinox</note> up to three signs <note>90 degrees</note>. By subtracting each from the one below it, six rough declination segments were established. They are as follows: Sine 15° = 31. Maximum Sine of Declination = 48. Radius = 120. Therefore, by the previous rule of proportion, the Sine of Declination at 15° = $\frac{\text{Sine 15}^\circ \times \text{Max Sine Declination}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{31 \times 48}{120} = \frac{31 \times 4}{10} = \frac{124}{10} = 12 \text{ (with a slight difference)}$. This value divided by two results in the declination at 15° = $\frac{12}{2} = 6 = \text{the first segment}$. Similarly, Sine 30° = 61. Therefore, Sine of Declination at 30° = $\frac{61 \times 48}{120} = \frac{61 \times 4}{10} = \frac{244}{10} = 24 \text{ approx}$. Thus, the declination at 30° = $\frac{24}{2} = 12$. Therefore, $12 - 6 = 6 = \text{the second segment}$. This continues for all. From this, calculating the desired declination is easy; thus it is proven. || 12 ||

Alternatively, using these segments 6, 6, 5, 4, 2, and 1: divide the degrees of the <term>longitude</term><note>specifically the 'arm' or distance from the nearest equinox</note> of the Sun (including precession) by 15. To the sum of the segments corresponding to the quotient, add the result of multiplying the remainder by the next segment and dividing by 15. This will give the rough declination in degrees etc., for easy practical use. || 12 ||

**Example—**The Sun with precession is at 7 signs, 19°, 4', 23". Its <term>longitude</term><note>bhujāṃśa: the arc distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note> is 49°, 4', 23". Dividing this by 15 gives a quotient of 3. The sum of the first 3 segments (6, 6, 5) is 17. The remainder is 4°, 4', 23". Multiplying this by the next segment (4) gives 16°, 17', 32". Dividing this by 15 gives 1°, 5', 10". Adding this to the sum of the previous segments (17) results in a southern rough declination of 18°, 5', 10". || 12 ||

->**Now he describes the method for finding the longitude from the declination:<-**

> **Then one should subtract the segments; the remainder multiplied by fifteen and divided by the next [segment],**
> **Added to the number of subtracted segments multiplied by fifteen, becomes the degrees of the longitude. || 13 ||**

Now he describes the <term>longitude calculation</term><note>bhujāṃśānayana: finding the angular distance from the equinox</note> by the inverse method from the declination degrees, saying **"Then the segments..."** The declination calculated by the small segments is 19; 24; 43. Subtracting the first two segments (6+6) from this, the remainder is 7; 24; 43. Subtracting the third segment (5) from this, the remainder is 2; 24; 43. Multiplied by fifteen <note>original: tithighna</note>, it is 36; 10; 45. Divided by the next segment (4), the result is 9; 2; 42. The number of fully subtracted segments (3) multiplied by fifteen is 45. Adding the previous result to this, the Sun's longitude degrees become 54; 2; 42. || 13 ||

->### The Madhuri Commentary:<-

**Then (tataḥ)=** from the declination degrees. **The segments (dalāni)=** the segments mentioned in the intermediate verse. **Should subtract (śodhayet)=** should take away. **The remainder multiplied by fifteen (tithighnaśeṣaṃ)=** the product of the remainder and the number fifteen. **Divided by the next (apyahṛt)=** divided by the subsequent segment value. **Added to the number of subtracted segments multiplied by fifteen=** together with the product of the count of fully subtracted segments and fifteen. Then **the longitude degrees (dorlavāḥ)=** the degrees of the 'arm' <note>longitude</note> **come to be. || 13 ||**

->### Here is the Proof:<-

Since one declination segment is taught for every fifteen degrees, the count of the "completed" declination segments is known by subtracting the segment values from the given declination as much as possible. The remainder is handled by proportion. If the next segment corresponds to fifteen degrees, then how many degrees does the remainder correspond to? This gives the degrees related to the remainder. Furthermore, if one segment count corresponds to fifteen degrees, then how many degrees do the total completed segments correspond to? The sum of these two results in the longitude degrees; thus it is proven. || 13 ||

<header>Chapter 4: On the Three Problems (Direction, Place, and Time) </header>

According to the possibility, by subtracting the segments from the **rough declination** <note>original: *sthūla krānti*; an approximate value used in initial calculations</note>, multiply the remainder by 15. Divide the product by the "Fire-Mark" <note>a numerical code or *bhūta-saṅkhyā* where 'Fire' represents the number 3</note>, and to the resulting degrees, add the product of 15 and the number of segments subtracted; this will be the **longitude of the arm** <note>original: *bhujāṃśa*; the angular distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note>. || 13 ||

**Example—** In the rough declination of 18° 5' 19", subtracting the sum of the three segments (6 + 6 + 5 = 17), the remainder is 1° 5' 19". Multiplying this by 15 gives 16° 17' 30". Dividing this by the "Fire-Mark" (3), the resulting degrees etc. are 4° 18' 23". Adding the product of the number of segments (3) and 15 (which is 45) to this, the longitude of the arm in degrees is 49° 18' 23", and in signs etc., it is 1 sign, 19° 18' 23". || 13 ||

### Now, he describes the method for finding the rough declination from the length of the day—

> The difference between half the day and fifteen <note>15 ghatis, representing 6 hours or a quarter of a day</note>, converted into minutes of time, is the **ascensional difference** <note>original: *caram*; the difference between the actual rising of the sun and the equatorial rising</note>. Then, increased by its own eighth part and divided by the **equinoctial shadow** <note>original: *akṣaprabhā*; the shadow of a gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>, the result is the Sun's declination in degrees when increased by twenty-five minutes. These are respectively South or North depending on whether the half-day is smaller or larger than fifteen. || 14 ||

Now, to demonstrate the logic without needing the Sun's position, he describes finding the rough declination from the midday point. **Half-day** is 16 [ghatis] 33 [palas]. **Fifteen** is 15. Their difference is 1 [ghati] 33 [palas]. Multiplied by sixty, this becomes the ascensional difference in seconds of time (*palas*), which is 93. This, increased by its own **eighth part** <note>original: *gajabhāga*; 'elephant-part' where elephant represents 8</note> (11 | 37 | 30), becomes 104 | 37 | 30. Divided by the equinoctial shadow (5 | 45), and converting the units, the dividend is 376650 and the divisor is 20700. The result obtained is 18° 11' 44". These, when increased by twenty-five minutes, become the Sun's **declination degrees**: 18° 36' 44". Based on whether the half-day is smaller or larger than fifteen, they are South or North respectively. For example: if the half-day is less than fifteen ghatis, it is South; if more, it is known as North. Since this half-day is greater than fifteen, the declination is North. || 14 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

**The difference between half-day and fifteen** = the interval between the midday and fifteen ghatis; **converted into minutes of time** = its value in *palas*; **is the ascensional difference** = the *carapala*. **Then** = afterwards; **increased by its own eighth part** = including its own one-eighth; **divided by the equinoctial shadow** = divided by the *palabhā*; the **ascensional difference** [becomes] **the Sun's declination degrees** = the degrees of the Sun's declination. **Increased by twenty-five minutes** = added to twenty-five minutes of arc; **these** = the Sun's declination degrees; **depending on the half-day's smallness or largeness relative to fifteen ghatis**; **respectively** = in order; **are South or North** = belonging to the Southern or Northern hemispheres. It should be understood that if the day-measure is less than fifteen, the declination is South; if the day-measure is more than fifteen ghatis, the declination is North. || 14 ||

### Here is the Proof:—

By the previous logic, the half-day in either hemisphere = Midday = 15 $\pm$ Ascensional Difference (*cap.*).

$\therefore$ Midday $\sim$ 15 = *cap*. Now, $\frac{cap}{10}$ = degrees of ascensional difference. Doubling them (due to small difference) gives the **Sine of ascensional difference** <note>original: *carajyā*</note> =

*Sine of ascensional difference* = $\frac{cap \times 2}{10}$ = $\frac{cap}{5}$. Now, by the proportion of the terrestrial latitude-field, the **Sine of declination** <note>original: *krāntijyā*</note> = $\frac{12 \times \text{Earth-Sine}}{\text{Shadow}}$. Here, the teacher has assumed the Earth-Sine <note>original: *kujyā*</note> and the Sine of ascensional difference to be equal due to the small difference. Therefore, Sine of declination = $\frac{12 \times \text{Sine of ascensional difference}}{\text{Shadow}}$ = $\frac{12 \times cap}{\text{Shadow} \times 5}$

# On the Commentary of Grahalaghava

If 10 degrees are obtained by a sine equal to 21, then what is obtained by the sine of declination? Thus, the degrees of declination are:
$\frac{10 \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{21}$ = $\frac{10 \times 12 \times \text{Chapa}}{21 \times \text{Palabha} \times 5}$ = $\frac{120 \times \text{Chapa}}{105 \times \text{Palabha}}$. Here, the numerator and denominator are divided by 15 =

$\frac{8 \times \text{Chapa}}{7 \times \text{Palabha}}$ (Self-evident) = $\frac{\text{Chapa}}{\text{Palabha}} (\frac{8}{7}) = \frac{\text{Chapa}}{\text{Palabha}} (1 + \frac{1}{7}) = \frac{\text{Chapa} + \frac{\text{Chapa}}{7}}{\text{Palabha}}$. 

Here, due to the slight error <note>original: "svalpāntara-doṣavaśāt", referring to the approximation in the sine-table</note> and for the sake of achieving a more accurate result, the Teacher <note>Ganesha Daivajna, the author</note> has added 25 minutes. In the context of the precision required for planetary combat <note>planetary conjunctions</note>, these are added or subtracted as South or North according to the experts of the celestial sphere. || 14 ||

The difference between the midday length and 15 is the *Charapala* <note>ascensional difference in time units</note>. Adding its own eighth part to it and dividing by the *Palabha* <note>the equinoctial midday shadow</note>, then adding 25 minutes to the result, gives the declination. If the midday length is less than 15 *dandas*, the declination is South; if more, it is North. || 14 ||

**Example**—Midday is 13;38 and the *Palabha* is 6. Therefore, subtracting the midday 13;38 from 15 gives 1;22 *ghatis*, which is 82 *palas* as the *Charapala*. Dividing this by 8 gives a quotient of 10;30. Adding this [to 82] gives 92;30. Dividing this by the *Palabha* of 6 gives a quotient of 15° 25'. Adding 25 minutes to this results in a declination of 15° 40'. Since the midday was less than 15, the declination is in the South direction. || 14 ||

### Now he describes the Zenith Distance and Altitude at Midday—

> The combination of declination and latitude results in the zenith distance; ninety minus that results in the altitude. Those degrees of declination which arise from the middle of the day, calculated by small segments, are called the *Parakhya*. || 15 ||

**Now he describes the calculation of declination without using segments.**
The *Dhriti* (18) multiplied by the remainder of the ten-part of the *Bhujamsha* <note>longitude degrees</note> of the planet with its precession, then divided by 72... <note>The text continues with the specific algebraic steps for the sine-approximation</note>

With precession: The *Bhujamsha* of the Sun with precession is 54;24;5. Its tenth part is 5;26;26. Subtracting this from *Dhriti* (18) leaves 12;33;34. This is multiplied by the tenth part: 68;49;99. This is placed in two positions. Divided by 72, the result is 0;57;23. Subtracting this from 4;30 leaves 3;33;37. Dividing the separate value by this, the result in degrees of North declination is 19;8;59. Wherever the declination of a planet is to be calculated, it should be done by this first method.

### Now he describes the calculation of Zenith Distance and the *Parakhya*.

> The combination of declination and latitude is the zenith distance. These midday values are divided by six and squared. Added to a constant and divided by two, then subtracted from 114, the result is the *Parakhya*.

Here, "combination" <note>term: *samskriti*, meaning algebraic processing</note> should be understood as addition if in the same direction and subtraction if in different directions. The North declination is 19;6;40 and the South latitude is 25;26;32. Because they are in different directions, the difference is the South zenith distance: 6;20;2. These are the midday values. 6;20 divided by six gives 1;3;20. The square of 1;3;20 is 1;6;52. Adding the constant gives 2;10;19. Divided by two, the result is 1;5;9. Subtracting this from 114, the *Parakhya* is 112;54;51.

Now he describes the calculation of altitude and *Parakhya*. By the combination of declination and latitude, the South zenith distance is 6;20;2. Ninety (90) minus the zenith distance gives the altitude: 83;39;58. These are the midday values. Then, the declination degrees of the altitude calculated by small segments is the *Parakhya*. The altitude is 83;39...

### Chapter on the Three Problems || 4 ||

58. The declination <note>original: "krānti"</note> calculated from these small segments <note>referring to sine-table intervals</note> is 23° 34' 39". This is given the technical name **Maximum Constant** <note>original: "parākhya"; literally "called the highest/other"</note>.

Now, the method for finding the instrument degrees <note>zenith distance as measured on an instrument</note> from the hour angle <note>time from noon</note>:

> Add 30 to the hour angle, multiply by 15, and divide by half the duration of the day. Square this result, multiply by the "Maximum Constant," and divide by 114. Add 228, subtract twice the "Maximum Constant," and take the square root. Multiply by 6 and subtract 3, and the result will be the instrument degrees of the hour angle.

**Example calculation:**
Hour angle <note>time from noon</note> is 6;3 <note>6 ghatis, 3 palas</note>. Added to 30, it becomes 36;33. Multiplied by 15, it is 98;15. Divided by half-day duration 16;33, the result is 5;56,11. Squared, it is 39;14,26. Multiplied by the "Maximum Constant" 112;54,55, it is 3979;91,49. Divided by 114, it is 34;95,15. Added to 228, it is 262;95,15. Subtracted by twice the "Maximum Constant" (225;49,50), the remainder is 37;45,28. Its square root is 6;12,0. Multiplied by 6, it is 37;12,0. Subtracting 3, the instrument degrees of the hour angle are 33;32,0. Where the instrument relates to the hour angle, the "Maximum Constant" derived from the zenith distance should be taken. Where it relates to the altitude, the "Maximum Constant" derived from the altitude degrees should be taken.

Next, he describes the inverse method to find the hour angle from the instrument degrees:

> Add 3 to the instrument degrees and divide by 6. Square the result. Add twice the "Maximum Constant," subtract 228, and multiply by 114. Divide by the "Maximum Constant" and take the square root. Multiply by the half-day duration and divide by 15. Subtract 30 from this, and the result is the hour angle in units of time <note>ghatis and palas</note>.

**Example calculation:**
Instrument degrees are 33;32,0. Plus 3 is 36;32,0. Divided by 6, the result is 6;5,20. Its square is 37;44,28. Added to twice the "Maximum Constant" (225;49,50), it is 263;34,18. Subtracting 228, the remainder is 35;34,18. Multiplied by 114, it is 3979;17,12. Divided by the "Maximum Constant" 112;54,55, the result is 35;14,25. Its square root is 5;56,10. Multiplied by the half-day duration 16;33, it is 98;16. Divided by 15, the result is 6;33. Subtracting 30 <note>adjustment for the epoch</note>, the hour angle in ghatis etc. is 6;3. || 15 ||

---

-> **The Madhuri Commentary** <-

The refinement of declination and latitude = the algebraic combination of declination degrees and latitude degrees, which results in the zenith distance <note>original: "natāṃśāḥ"</note>. Subtracting that from 90 gives the altitude degrees <note>original: "unnatāṃśāḥ"</note>. These zenith and altitude degrees are those occurring at midday <note>meridian passage</note>. From that midday altitude, using the "small segments" method mentioned in verse 12, the resulting declination value is called the **Maximum Constant** <note>parākhya</note>. || 15 ||

---

-> **Rationale / Proof** <-

At midday, the arc on the meridian from one's own zenith to the intersection of the ecliptic and the meridian (the planet's position) is the zenith distance. The arc on the meridian from the intersection of the ecliptic and meridian (the planet's point) to the intersection of the meridian and the horizon is the altitude. The arc from the zenith to the intersection of the celestial equator and the meridian is the latitude. The arc from the planet's point on the meridian to the celestial equator is the declination. This is the established terminology. By this: Zenith Distance + Altitude = 90°. Therefore, 90° - Zenith Distance = Altitude. It is clear from observing the armillary sphere <note>original: "golāvalokana"</note> that the zenith distance is found by the sum or difference of declination and latitude depending on whether they are in the same or opposite directions. (See the diagram).

In calculating the sine of the altitude using the "small segments," the sine of the zenith distance relative to the ecliptic is found; the author has used the term "Maximum Constant" <note>parākhya</note> as a technical convention to maintain the consistency of the mathematical procedure. || 15 ||

# Page 67
## Commentary on the Grahalaghava

---

![A geometric diagram of a celestial quadrant illustrating astronomical coordinate systems, featuring arcs labeled 'diurnal circle' and 'horizon', with points representing the Earth and Zenith.]

The combination of the **degrees of declination** <term>Krāntyaṃśa: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term> and the **latitude** <term>Akṣāṃśa: the angular distance of a place north or south of the earth's equator</term> (their **sum** if in the same direction and their **difference** if in different directions) results in the **zenith distance** <term>Natāṃśa: the angular distance from the zenith</term>. Subtracting the zenith distance from 90 degrees gives the **altitude** <term>Unnatāṃśa: the angle of the sun above the horizon</term>. These values (zenith distance and altitude) are calculated for midday. The declination derived from this zenith distance using the "short-table" method is referred to as **'Para'** <note>original: "पर" - a specific technical term used in this text for a corrected sine value</note>. || 15 ||

**Example:** The southern declination is 17° 49' 18" and the latitude is 24° 24'. Since both are in the same (southern) direction, their sum is 42° 13' 18", which is the zenith distance. Subtracting this zenith distance from 90, the remaining 47° 46' 42" is the midday altitude. From this, using the short-table method (starting with the mnemonic "ṣaṭpadviviṣuddhaṃdī" etc.), the declination is 17° 12' 27", which is the 'Para' value. || 15 ||

### Now, the method for calculating the hypotenuse at a desired time from the elapsed altitude-time:

> Multiply the desired elapsed altitude-time by ninety and divide by half the day-length. From the resulting degrees, find the declination. Multiply this by the stated 'Para' value; divide the number 6912 by that product to find the hypotenuse (ear-length). || 16 ||

Now, another method for calculating the desired hypotenuse <term>Karṇa: literally 'ear', referring to the hypotenuse of the shadow cast by a gnomon</term> is explained. "Multiply by ninety": At the desired time, the elapsed altitude-time is 10;30. Multiplied by ninety (90), it is 945;0. Divided by the midday half-day length of 16;33, the result is 57° 9' 26". From this, using the short-table method, the declination is 201;54;28. The stated 'Para' is 23;35;39. Multiplying by this, the declination-product is 476;53;19. Dividing the constant 6912 <note>original: "रविनवषट्" - a numerical code where Ravi=12, Nava=9, Shat=6, read right-to-left or as a composite</note> by this, the result is the latitude-hypotenuse in digits, etc., which is 14;39. || 16 ||

### Madhuri Commentary:

**Desired** = at the desired time; **Elapsed altitude-time** = the time in ghatis <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> etc. since sunrise; **Multiply by ninety** and then **Divide by half-day** = divide by the measure of midday. Then, **From the resulting degrees** = from the obtained degrees etc.; **Declination** = the sine of declination; **This** is **Multiplied by the stated Para** = multiplied by the aforementioned 'Para' value. **Divided by that** = divided by that product; **6912** = six thousand nine hundred and twelve. **Or else** = by another method; **Hypotenuse** = the shadow's hypotenuse is produced. || 16 ||

### Mathematical Rationale:

Here, the Radius <term>Trijyā</term> = 24.
If at the time of midday (half-day), 90 degrees of altitude are obtained, then at the desired elapsed time, what would it be? By this proportion, the degrees of the interval from the midday point for the desired time = $\frac{90 \times \text{Desired Altitude Time}}{\text{Half-Day}}$. Using the short-tables, the sine of this declination-interval is the desired declination. Furthermore, the midday gnomon <term>Śaṅku</term> of thirty-three is treated as the 'Para' value. Therefore...

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems

Where the radius is taken as 120 <note>original: "विंशतित्रिज्या" - likely referring to a standard radius of 120 units used in these calculations</note>, the desired gnomon shadow $= \frac{\text{Maximum Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination}}{24}$. Then, by the proportion of the terrestrial sphere: The hypotenuse of the shadow <term>Chaya-karna<gloss>The hypotenuse formed by the gnomon and its shadow</gloss></term> =

$\frac{\text{Radius} \times 12}{\text{Gnomon}} = \frac{24 \times 12}{\text{Gnomon}} = \frac{24 \times 12}{\frac{\text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination}}{24}} = \frac{24 \times 12 \times 24}{\text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination}} = \frac{6912}{\text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination}}$

Thus, the proof is established. || 16 ||

By dividing the product of 90 and the "elevated time" <note>time elapsed since sunrise</note> by the half-day duration, one obtains the degrees. The declination derived from these degrees is multiplied by the "Maximum Shadow" <term>Para<gloss>The maximum shadow at a specific latitude</gloss></term>; dividing 6912 by this product yields the hypotenuse of the shadow. || 16 ||

**Example** — Using the previously calculated elevated time of 4 ghatis and 23 palas <note>approx. 1 hour 45 minutes</note>, converted to a single unit as 262. Multiplying 262 by 90 = 23580. Dividing this by the half-day duration of 13 ghatis and 28 palas (808 palas) gives the result in degrees as 29° 10' 59". Multiplying this by the Maximum Shadow (1772;28) gives 1044311 (or 376980 in simplified units). Dividing 6912 (scaled as 24883200) by this result yields a hypotenuse of 66;00 digits <term>Angulas<gloss>Traditional Indian unit of measurement, roughly a finger-breadth</gloss></term>. || 16 ||

### Now, calculating the desired elevated time from the hypotenuse:

-> The number 6912 divided by the hypotenuse and then divided by the Maximum Shadow yields the declination. <-
-> From that, the degrees of the arc multiplied by the half-day and divided by ninety gives the desired elevated time. <- || 17 ||

Now, the method for calculating the elevated time from a given shadow hypotenuse is explained in reverse. "The number 6912" <note>original: "Tarani-nava-rasa" - Tarani (12), Nava (9), Rasa (6) read right-to-left as 6912</note> divided by a hypotenuse of 14;29 gives 477.64. Dividing this by the Maximum Shadow value of 23.36 gives the declination. After converting the fractions (Dividend 1798057, Divisor 85179), the resulting declination is 201;14;28. From this, using the sine-to-arc method, the degrees of the arc are 57° 9' 56". These are multiplied by the half-day (16;33) = 946.54. Dividing by ninety (90) yields the desired elevated time of 10 ghatis and 30 palas. || 17 ||

### Madhuri Commentary:

**Divided by the hypotenuse** = divided by the desired shadow hypotenuse. **Tarani-nava-rasa** = the number 6912. **Divided by the Maximum Shadow** = divided by the *Para* value. **Declination** = the solar declination. **From that** = from the declination, **Degrees of the arc** = the degrees of the sine-arc. **Multiplied by the half-day** = multiplied by the measure of half the daylight duration. **Divided by ninety** = divided by 90. **Desired** = at the desired time, **Elevated** = the time elapsed since sunrise. || 17 ||

### Mathematical Proof:

$\because$ **Hypotenuse** $= \frac{6912}{\text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination}}$
$\therefore \text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Desired Declination} \times \text{Hypotenuse} = 6912$

$\therefore$ **Desired Declination** $= \frac{6912}{\text{Max Shadow} \times \text{Hypotenuse}}$
From the declination, the degrees of the arc are found, which represent the degrees of time elapsed. Then, by proportion: if 90 degrees corresponds to the half-day duration, then what does the desired degree of the arc correspond to? $\frac{\text{Half-day} \times \text{Desired Degrees}}{90} = \text{Elevated Time}$. Thus, it is proven. || 17 ||

Dividing 6912 by the hypotenuse and then by the Maximum Shadow yields the declination. Dividing the product of its arc-degrees and the half-day by 90 gives the desired elevated time. || 17 ||

Now, he explains the calculation of elapsed time when the degrees of altitude from the instrument are known. "The desired..." etc. For the desired instrument degrees of 95;45,48, the declination by the small segments is 19;92,13. Multiplied by 24 <note>original: "Jina"</note> it is 476;53,12. Divided by the value called "Para" 223;43,39, the result is 20;12,33,6. From this, the arc degrees are 87;51,66. Multiplied by the half-day 16;33, it is 1451. Divided by 90 <note>original: "Kha-nava"</note>, the result is the elapsed ghatikas in the eastern hemisphere: 10;30. || 18 ||

-> Madhuri Commentary <-

These "desired instrument degrees" = the chosen degrees on the instrument; "from that" = from those; "declination" = solar declination; "this" = that; "multiplied by twenty-four" = multiplied by 24; "divided by the maximum" = divided by the maximum divisor; "from that" = from the quotient; by the rule "then the parts etc.," the "arc degrees" = degrees of the sine; "multiplied by the half-day" = [multiplied by the half-day duration]; "divided by ninety" = divided by 90; "east west" = in the eastern and western; "hemispheres"; "respectively" = in order; "past and remaining" = time gone and time to come; "ghatikas" = measures of time = "elapsed time"; these are produced. || 18 ||

-> Here is the Proof <-

Here, the Radius = 24.

Having derived the declination from the degrees obtained by the instrument, then by proportion, the Sine of Altitude is:
(Declination × Radius) / Maximum = (Declination × 24) / Maximum.

The arc of this will be the arc degrees <note>Bhujāṃśa</note>. Again, by proportion, the elapsed time is:
(Half-day × Arc degrees) / 90.
Whether this is the time past since sunrise or the time remaining until sunset in the eastern and western hemispheres becomes perfectly clear by observing the nature of the celestial sphere; thus, it is proven. || 18 ||

By calculating the declination from the altitude degrees obtained by the instrument, multiplying this declination by 24 and dividing by the "Para" constant, one takes the resulting arc degrees, multiplies them by the half-day, and divides by 90. The result will be the elapsed time in ghatikas, representing time past in the eastern hemisphere and time remaining in the western hemisphere. || 18 ||

**Example —** From instrument degrees 45° 14' 34", using the mnemonic "Pad-yapa-ni..." the declination is 17° 13' 53". Multiplying by 24 gives 409;33,12. Dividing by the "Para" 177;12,27 gives a quotient of 2;38,36. Using the rule "then subtract the parts," the arc degrees are 74;00,15. Multiplying by the half-day 13;24 gives 991;35. Dividing by 90, the result is the elapsed time in the eastern hemisphere: 11 ghatikas and 16 minutes <note>11;16</note>. || 18 ||

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems (Direction, Place, and Time)

The declination degrees 20;13,36 multiplied by the maximum declination <note>original: "para" (23;27,32)</note> equals 476;53,12. Dividing this by 24 <note>The "Siddha" or "Jina" number used in sine calculations</note> results in 19;52,33. From this, by applying the rule "then subtract the halves," etc., the resulting degrees of the arc <note>term: Bhujāṃśa (the arc of the sine used in spherical trigonometry)</note> are 55;45,48. || 19 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

->The elapsed time in ghatikas <note>1 ghatika = 24 minutes</note> = the risen time. Multiplied by ninety and divided by the measure of half the day,<-
->the result is degrees (risen degrees). The declination degrees produced from that,<-
->multiplied by the maximum declination and divided by 24, then following the previously stated method of<-
->"then the halves," etc., the resulting degrees of the arc are, at that desired time, the degrees of altitude shown by the instrument.<-
->These are the instrument-altitude degrees. || 19 ||

### Mathematical Rationale—

According to the logic of the previous verse (18), the risen time (T) = (Half-day × Arc-degrees) / 90.

Therefore, T × 90 = Half-day × Arc-degrees. Thus, Arc-degrees = (T × 90) / Half-day. From this, the declination degrees are to be calculated.

Then, the Sine of the Gnomon <note>term: Śaṅku (the vertical pillar of a sundial)</note> = (Declination × 24) / Maximum Declination. Therefore, Gnomon × Maximum Declination = Declination × 24.

Thus, (Gnomon × Maximum Declination) / 24 = the declination obtained by the instrument. The arc of this value will be the instrument-altitude degrees; this is proven. || 19 ||

<note>The following paragraph is a Hindi explanation of the Sanskrit logic above</note>
By dividing the product of 90 and the risen ghatikas by the half-day, the degrees are obtained. Calculating the declination from these degrees, multiplying it by the maximum declination, and dividing by 24, one applies the rule "then subtract the halves" to find the arc-degrees, which represent the altitude degrees on the instrument at the desired time. || 19 ||

### Example—

The product of risen ghatikas 11;6 and 90 is 999;00. Dividing this by the half-day 13;28 gives the degrees 74;10. From this, the declination is 23;50,00. Multiplying this by the maximum declination 17;12,27 <note>Note: The value of 'para' varies by system</note> gives 410;6,43. Dividing this by 24 gives 17;5,15. From this, the arc-degrees are 45;14,41. This is the altitude degree of the instrument. || 19 ||

### Now, finding the Hypotenuse from Instrument Degrees, and vice versa—

> The declination degrees arising from the instrument degrees [divided into] 288 <note>original: "vasu-ibha-dasrāḥ" (8-8-2 in reverse notation)</note> shall be the hypotenuse here.
> Those [288] divided by the hypotenuse shall be the declination; from that, the arc-degrees or the instrument degrees are found. || 20 ||

Now he describes the method for finding the desired hypotenuse <note>term: Karṇa (the hypotenuse of the shadow triangle)</note> from the instrument-altitude degrees, and then finding the altitude degrees from the hypotenuse. "Arising from instrument degrees": Using the small segments of the instrument degrees 55;45,48, the declination degrees are 19;52,33. Dividing 288 by this, the result is the desired hypotenuse in digits <note>term: Aṅgula</note>, etc., which is 14;29,38. Dividing 288 by the desired hypotenuse 14;29,38, the result is the declination 19;52,33. From this, by the rule "then the halves," etc., the arc-degrees become the instrument-altitude degrees 55;45,48. || 20 ||

Here, in the calculation of the hypotenuse, 288 is divided by the declination degrees produced from the instrument degrees. 288 = <unclear>288</unclear> <insert>Shri Kailashananda Mission Trust's Vani Vilas Collection Digitized by eGangotri</insert>
