<page-num>41</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

These = eight, eight, and two <note>original: "vasv-aṣṭa-dastrāḥ" - a numerical code where Vasu=8, Aṣṭa=8, and Dasra=2, signifying 288</note> (two hundred eighty-eight), is the declination <term>apama: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term>; therefore, from the declination, the arm-degrees <note>sine components</note> are derived by the rule "then the halves," etc., which become the instrument-degrees <term>yantrāṃśa: degrees measured on an astronomical instrument, usually representing altitude</term>. || 20 ||

### Here is the Proof —

Here, the Radius = 24. The declination of the instrument-degrees = the Gnomon <term>śaṅku: a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow for measurement</term>. Then, by the proportion of the terrestrial sphere, the Shadow-Hypotenuse <term>chāyā-karṇa: the distance from the top of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term> = (Radius x 12) / Gnomon

= (24 x 12) / Declination of instrument-degrees = 288 / Declination of instrument-degrees. Or, Declination of instrument-degrees = 288 / Shadow-Hypotenuse. It is proven that the arm-degrees of the declination of the instrument-degrees are indeed the instrument-degrees. || 20 ||

In this context, dividing 288 by the declination degrees produced from the instrument-degrees gives the hypotenuse; and dividing 288 by the hypotenuse gives the declination arising from the instrument-degrees. From this, by the method of "then subtract the halves," the resulting arm-degrees become the solar altitude degrees produced by the instrument. || 20 ||

**Example—** For a solar altitude of 45° 14' 34" from the instrument, using the "six, six, five, four" <note>a mnemonic for sine tables</note> method, the declination is 17° 3' 5". Dividing 288 by this gives a quotient of 16;52,40, which is the hypotenuse. Dividing 288 by this hypotenuse gives a declination of 17° 3' 50". From this declination, by the "then the halves" method, the altitude degrees produced by the instrument in the form of arm-degrees become 45° 14' 22". || 20 ||

### Now, the Determination of Directions is described—

> On a leveled circle, the shadow-tip of a gnomon placed at the center
> Respectively enters and exits; these are the West and the East.
> From those two, the North and the South are established by the "Fish." || 21 ||

Now, for the construction of tubes, sacrificial pits, or pavilions, the method for determining directions is stated. "On a leveled circle," etc. On ground made level by water or other means, a circle is drawn. The tip of the shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon placed at the center, where it **enters** the circle in the morning <note>the western half of the circle</note>, a mark should be made; that is the West direction. Where it **exits** the circle in the afternoon, that becomes the East direction. From those two marks, East and West, the North and South are established. This is what is meant: A circle <note>arc</note> should be drawn from the East mark toward the West mark. Another circle should be drawn from the West mark toward the East mark. When this is done, a fish-shape <term>matsya: the vesica piscis shape formed by two intersecting arcs</term> is seen. The cord passing through the mouth and tail of the "fish" is the North-South line. || 21 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary—

**On a leveled circle** = situated on leveled ground; **in a circle** = in a circle made by a desired compass; **of a gnomon placed at the center** = of a twelve-digit gnomon fixed at the center point; **the shadow-tip** = the mark of the shadow's end; **where** = at which mark it **enters** = makes its entrance, and **exits** = goes out; **there respectively** = in that order, the **West** and **East** directions occur. **From those two** = from the West and East marks, from the **established fish** = from the fish-line, the **North** and **South** directions arise. || 21 ||

### Here is the Proof—

Assuming the Sun's motion in declination to be zero for a single day, the line connecting the entry and exit shadows is the East-West line. The perpendicular line at its midpoint is certainly the North-South line. To establish this perpendicular, the Teacher <note>the author, Ganesh Daivajna</note> has utilized the production of the "fish-line." This logic is approximate, but when the Sun is at the beginning of Aries <note>the vernal equinox</note>, because the difference is slight, <unclear>it is very close to the reality</unclear>. <unclear>The wise should consider this; enough with criticism.</unclear> || 21 ||

G. S. S.

# Chapter 4: On the Three Problems

"On a level ground, smooth as the surface of water, draw a circle. Place a gnomon <note>a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow</note> at the center of this circle. The two points where the shadow of the gnomon enters and exits the circle are, in order, the West and East directions. The North and South directions are established from these points by means of the 'fish' line <note>an ancient geometric method of drawing a perpendicular by intersecting two arcs, which creates a fish-like shape</note>." || 21 ||

Circle of southern inclination

->Now, he describes the method for determining the 'Bhuja' <term>Bhuja: the base or side of a right-angled triangle, here representing the north-south distance of the shadow</term> and the directions:<-

> Or, the product of the degrees of the Sun's declination and the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow, multiplied by the hypotenuse of the desired shadow and divided by 360, results in the 'Bhuja' in the direction of the Sun. This is then adjusted by twice the equinoctial shadow in the southern direction.
> In the circle formed by the shadow, this should be applied like a full chord from the tip. The line connecting the center to the midpoint of that Bhuja is the North-South line, while the rope placed at the center of the half-Bhuja is the East-West line. || 22 ||

Now, he explains another method for determining directions and the Bhuja. "Or" indicates an alternative method. One should take the declination of the Sun and multiply it by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow <term>Akshakarna: the hypotenuse of the shadow cast at noon on the day of the equinox</term>. This product is multiplied by the hypotenuse of the desired shadow <note>the shadow measured at any specific time</note> and divided by 360. The result is the Bhuja in the direction of the Sun (based on the tropical longitude). This Bhuja is then adjusted by twice the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha: the length of the shadow at noon on the equinox</term> in the southern direction. This means if the directions are the same, they are added; if different, the difference is taken. The result is the corrected Bhuja.

This Bhuja should be applied in the circle formed by the shadow, starting from the tip, like a full chord. This is what is meant: draw a circle with a cord equal to the desired shadow from the center. Place the gnomon at the center. Mark the point where the tip of the gnomon's shadow touches the circle. From that mark, if the Bhuja is southern, it should be laid out toward the north from the shadow tip like a full chord. When this is done, the resulting Bhuja is known as the North-South line. The rope connecting the center to the midpoint of the Bhuja becomes the East-West line.

**Example:**
Sun: 11s 14° 2' 37" | Motion: 57' 36"
Time elapsed from sunrise: 10:30 | Calculated Sun: 11s 14° 2' 41"
From this, the declination calculated is North 11° 16' 40".
Equinoctial hypotenuse: 13;19. Their product: 264;22,54.
This multiplied by the shadow hypotenuse 15;29 is 3668;59,08.
Divided by 360, the Bhuja is 10;12.
Since the tropical Sun is in the Northern hemisphere, this is North.
Twice the southern equinoctial shadow (9;49) is 19;30.
Adjusted due to different directions (subtraction), the corrected Bhuja is South 9;2.

->Madhuri Commentary:<-

Or = alternatively; Product of Sun's declination and equinoctial hypotenuse = the multiplication of the Sun's declination and the equinoctial shadow's hypotenuse; Multiplied by shadow hypotenuse = to be multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow; Divided by 360 = divided by <unclear>four times ninety</unclear> (360); Sun's direction = relating to the solar sphere.

<meta>This page continues the technical demonstration of calculating the cardinal directions (North, South, East, West) using the shadow of a gnomon, specifically focusing on the mathematical derivation of the 'Bhuja' (sine of the amplitude/base).</meta>

<page-num>86</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

The **Bhuja** <note>The 'arm' or base of the triangle, representing the distance of the shadow from the East-West line</note> is the side. This, when adjusted by the equinoctial shadow in the southern direction, becomes the adjusted side. In the circle produced by the shadow, it should be applied as a full chord from the tip of the shadow to the center point. At that time, that side becomes the North-South line. A cord fixed at the center of the half-side circle becomes the East-West line. || 22 ||

->Here is the mathematical proof:<-

Since for a radius of 573, the sine of one degree = 10, then for a radius of 120 <note>The standard radius used in this system</note>, the sine of one degree:
$= \frac{10 \times 120}{573} = \frac{1200}{573} \approx \frac{72}{35}$ <note>original: "svatpāntarāt" - with a slight difference</note>. Therefore, by proportion, the sine of declination $= \frac{\text{Declination} \times 72}{35}$.

Then, by the proportion of the latitude-triangle, the amplitude in the radius-circle $= \frac{\text{Hypotenuse of Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{12} = \frac{\text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Decl.} \times 72}{35 \times 12}$.

The shadow-amplitude $= \frac{\text{Amplitude} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times 72 \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{120 \times 35 \times 12} = \frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow} \times 72}{50400}$
$= \frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{\frac{50400}{72}} = \frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{700}$. 

Therefore, the solar celestial side = Amplitude $\pm$ Equinoctial Shadow.
$= \frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{700} \pm \text{Eq. Shadow}$. Doubling this, 2 $\times$ Side $= \frac{2 \times \text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{700} \pm 2 \times \text{Eq. Shadow} =$
$\frac{\text{Decl.} \times \text{Hyp. Lat.} \times \text{Hyp. Shadow}}{350} \pm 2 \times \text{Eq. Shadow}$.

From this, the method for establishing the East-West and North-South lines is easily understood and thus proven. || 22 ||

Alternatively, multiply the degrees of the Sun's declination by the hypotenuse of latitude, then multiply by the hypotenuse of the shadow, and divide by 350; this gives the side of the Sun's celestial direction. This side should be adjusted by twice the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> in the southern direction. By applying this as a full chord from the tip of the gnomon's shadow located at the center of the circle generated by the shadow's radius, the North-South line is formed. The line connecting the midpoint of the side and the center of the circle will be the East-West line. || 22 ||

**Example—** The declination of the Sun (with precession) at 7s 19° 4' 23" is 17° 49' 18". Multiplying this by the hypotenuse of latitude 13;26 gives 239;24;15. Multiplying this by the shadow hypotenuse 29;00 gives 6942;43;15. Dividing by 350, the result is 19;50;11. Since the Sun is in the southern hemisphere, this is the southern side. Adding this to twice the equinoctial shadow (6 $\times$ 2 = 12), the corrected side becomes 31;50;11. || 22 ||

->Now, he speaks of the degrees of direction for the sake of orientation:<-

> The difference between the day-measure and thirty, multiplied by eleven,
> If the day is short or long, it is South or North respectively;
> This is the declination derived from the instrument's degrees.
> Multiplied by eight, the sum of both, the difference from ninety degrees—
> From that declination-vision, the degrees of the side are known as twenty. || 1 ||

<page-num>67</page-num>

Now, he describes another method for determining the direction by calculating the degrees of the azimuth <note>The horizontal angle of a celestial object from a cardinal point</note>. Regarding the "Day-measure": The day-measure is 32;36 <note>expressed in ghatis, where 60 ghatis = 24 hours</note>. The "Sky-multipliers" <note>a technical term for the number 30</note> are 30. The difference between these two is 2;36. Multiplied by "Shiva" (11), it becomes 28;36. Since the day-measure is greater than thirty, the direction is North. The instrument degrees are North 55;45;54. The declination <note>the angular distance of a body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of these instrument degrees must be calculated. This is "not-North," meaning it is South. Using the small table of sines, the South declination for the instrument degrees 55;45;54 is 19;52;3. Because they are in different directions, the sum of the two is 14;13;47. Multiplied by eight (8), it is 113;50;56. Ninety (90) and the instrument degrees 55;45;54 have a difference of 34;14;6. The declination of this difference using the small table is 13;24;44. Dividing the eight-fold product by this, the result is 8;29;16. From this, by subtracting the halves etc., the calculated "arm-degrees" <note>the sine of the arc</note> become the degrees of the azimuth: 22;13. **[Verse 23]**

## The Madhuri Commentary—

**Multiplied by Shiva** means multiplied by eleven. **The difference between the day-measure and the sky-multipliers** means the difference between the day-measure and the number thirty. **In the day** means during the daytime; **less or more** means if it is less or more than thirty, the direction is **South or North** respectively. **Then**, the **declination of the instrument degrees** means the declination produced from the degrees on the instrument; this is **"always"** not-North, i.e., South. **Eight-fold** means multiplied by eight. **The combination of both** means the calculation involving the two. **Divided by the declination arising from the difference between ninety and the instrument degrees** means divided by the declination produced from the difference of 90 and the instrument parts. **From that** result, the **arm-degrees** which are obtained are **known as the degrees of the azimuth**. **[Verse 23]**

## Here is the Proof:—

In this case, the Equinoctial Shadow <term>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> = 4, the Radius <term>Trijya</term> = 120, the Sine of Amplitude <term>Agra</term> = A, and the Projection of the Gnomon <term>Shankutala</term> = Shanta. Alternatively, the Radius is 24.
$\because$ A $\pm$ Shanta = Base <note>Bhuja</note>, or, $\frac{\text{Base}}{\text{Sine of Zenith Distance}} = \frac{\text{Sine of Azimuth}}{\text{Radius}}$.
$\therefore \frac{\text{Base} \times 24}{\text{Sine of Zenith Distance}} = \text{Sine of Azimuth} =$
( A $\pm$ Shanta ) $\frac{24}{\text{Sine of Zenith Distance}}$ ........... ( 1 )

By the proportion of the terrestrial latitude: Shanta = $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Gnomon}}{12} = \frac{4 \times \text{Gnomon}}{12} = \frac{\text{Gnomon}}{\frac{12}{4}} = \frac{\text{Gnomon}}{3}$ ........ (a).

In this right-angled triangle of twelve, the Equinoctial Shadow, and the Equinoctial Hypotenuse, "the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse." Thus, the square of the Equinoctial Hypotenuse = $144 + \text{Palabha}^2 = 144 + 16$.
$\therefore$ Equinoctial Hypotenuse = $\sqrt{144+16}$ = 13 approximately.
By the previous logic, the Ascensional Difference in ghatis <term>Charaghati</term> = Day-ghatis $\sim$ 15.
$\therefore 2 \times \text{Charaghati} = \text{Day-measure} \sim 30 = \text{Difference}$.
$\therefore \text{Charaghati} \times 60 \times 2 = 2 \times \text{Ascensional Difference in pranas} = 60 \times \text{Difference}$.

---
$\therefore \text{Ascensional Difference in pranas} = 30 \times \text{Difference}$. Again, by the logic of Verse 14, Declination = $\frac{\text{Pranas} + \frac{\text{Pranas}}{8}}{\text{Palabha}}$
---
$= \frac{30 \times \text{Diff} + \frac{\text{Diff} \times 30}{8}}{\text{Palabha}} = \frac{30 (\text{Diff} + \frac{\text{Diff}}{8})}{4} = \frac{30 \times 9 \times \text{Diff}}{4 \times 8}$.
If for one degree the Sine is $\frac{72}{35}$, then for the degrees of declination, the Sine of Declination = $\frac{(\text{Diff} \times 30 \times 9)}{4 \times 8} \times \frac{72}{35}$.

$= \frac{Degrees \times 15 \times 9 \times 9}{2 \times 35} = \frac{Degrees \times 3 \times 81}{2 \times 7} = \frac{Degrees \times 243}{14}$ | If for a base of twelve <note>the standard 12-digit gnomon</note> the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow is given, then by this sine of declination, what is the result? Thus is produced the *Agra* <term>Agra: the amplitude of the sun at the horizon</term> $= \frac{Hypotenuse \times Sine\ of\ Declination}{12} = \frac{13}{12} \times \frac{(Degrees \times 243)}{14}$

Thus is produced the transformed *Agra* $= \frac{521 \times Degrees \times 24}{28 \times 120}$

$(1)$ When equations (a) and (b) are substituted, the Sine of Azimuth <term>Dig-jya: the sine of the horizontal angle from the cardinal points</term>

$= (\frac{Degrees \times 521}{140} \pm \frac{Gnomon}{3}) \frac{24}{Radius} = (\frac{Degrees \times 1563}{140} \pm Gnomon) \frac{8}{Radius} =$

$\frac{(Degrees \times 11 \pm Gnomon) \times 8}{Radius}$ |

$\because Radius = (90 - Instrument\ Degrees) Sine$ |

$\therefore Sine\ of\ Azimuth = (Degrees \times 11 \pm Gnomon) \frac{8}{(90 - Instrument\ Degrees) Sine}$ | The arc of this value will be the degrees of azimuth. This is thus proven. || 23 ||

When the difference between the length of the day and 30 is multiplied by 11, if the result is less than 30, the direction is South; if more, it is North. The direction of declination produced from the instrument degrees is always South. By dividing the combination of those two (multiplied by 8) by the difference between 90 and the declination produced from the instrument degrees, the resulting side-degrees are the degrees of azimuth. || 23 ||

->Example<-

The difference between the day-length 26;56 and 30 is 3;4. Multiplying this by 11 gives 33° 44'. Since the day-length was less than 30, this result is in the South direction. From the instrument degrees 45;14;34, the South declination is 17° 3' 53". Adding these gives 50° 47' 53". Multiplying this by 8 gives 406;23;44. Dividing this by the declination of the difference between 90 and the instrument degrees (44;45;26), which is 16° 55' 18", the result is 24;19;10. From this, the side-degrees are 75;4;4, which is the azimuth. || 23 ||

->Now he describes the method for finding directions from the azimuth degrees:<-

> When the quadrant instrument is placed on level ground so that it touches the center of the tip of the azimuth degrees,
> the shadow of the plumb-line or the shadow of a needle placed at the center will indicate the directions on the instrument. || 24 ||

Now he describes the method for finding directions. "On level ground": on ground made level like water, when the quadrant instrument (a triangular instrument) is placed, one should count the previously mentioned azimuth degrees from the horizon. When the shadow of the plumb-line or the shadow of a needle <term>Ishika: a small rod or pointer</term> placed at the center touches that point, the directions will be established on the instrument. When the instrument is placed thus, the East-West line is formed. From that, the North and South directions arise. || 24 ||

<header>Chapter 4: On the Three Problems (Direction, Place, and Time)</header>

### Madhuri Commentary—
At the end-point of the azimuth <note>the horizontal angle of a celestial body</note> on the quadrant instrument—that is, the two points consisting of the azimuth tip and the center—the shadow of the plumb-line, or rather, the shadow of the stylus <note>a small rod or needle</note> located at the center, touches [the markings] in such a way that when the quadrant instrument (the circle-quadrant) is placed on level ground (leveled with water), the directions on the instrument—East, West, South, and North—become established. || 24 ||

### The Rationale (Vasana)—
On the horizon, the distance between the East-West line and the vertical circle is the azimuth, whether North or South. By marking those same degrees of azimuth on the quadrant instrument, the knowledge of the azimuth-tip mark is obtained. Since the shadow always falls exactly on the line of sight, the azimuth degrees on the quadrant instrument between the East-West shadow line are exactly the same. Therefore, the two arms (sides) of the instrument should be understood as the East-West and North-South directions. || 24 ||

[Hindi translation of the above]: When the shadow of the plumb-line on level ground, or the shadow of the stylus (wood) at the center of the instrument, touches the center and the azimuth-tip mark of the quadrant, the directions produced on the instrument are established. That is, the two arms of the quadrant should be known as East-West and North-South. || 24 ||

### Now he describes the calculation of the Base (Bhuja) and Perpendicular (Koti) for the purpose of fixing the sighting tube:

**The clear declination multiplied by the desired hypotenuse and the equinoctial hypotenuse, divided by seven hundred (700), is the Base in the direction of the declination. When adjusted by the equinoctial shadow in the southern direction, it becomes the "clear" Base; the square root of the difference between the squares of that [Base] and the shadow is the Perpendicular.** || 25 ||

Now, to demonstrate one's skill in the royal assembly, he describes the calculation of the Base and Perpendicular for fixing the sighting tube <note>Nalika-bandhana; a method for aligning a tube to view a specific planet</note>. Regarding "The declination...": the planet for which the tube-fixing is being done must first be processed by the "visibility correction" (Drig-karma) which will be explained later. Its "clear" (corrected) declination, adjusted by the celestial latitude (Shara), must be calculated. That is multiplied by the "desired hypotenuse" (Ishta-karna). This is what is meant: the time elapsed in the day for the planet is found using the methods previously mentioned in the chapter on planetary shadows. The measure of the clear half-ascensional difference (Chara-dala) is calculated. From the planet's clear declination, the altitude is determined. From that altitude, the desired hypotenuse is calculated. The clear declination is then multiplied by this calculated hypotenuse.

**An Example of this:** In the Vikrama year 1669, Shaka 1534, on the full moon day of the bright half of the month of Vaishakha, Monday, at 57 ghatis <note>1 ghati = 24 minutes</note> after sunrise, the tube-fixing for Mars (Bhauma) is performed. There, the previously calculated mean Sun at morning is 1s 4° 13' 42". Its motion is 59' 8". Mars is 10s 0° 26' 4".

Now, the clarification: The Sun's anomaly of the center (Manda-kendra) is 1s 12° 50' 8". The equation of center (Manda-phala) is additive: 2° 28' 55". The adjusted Sun is 1s 6° 38' 47". The ascensional difference (Chara) is subtractive: 96. The clear Sun is 1s 6° 37' 11". The anomaly of the apex (Shighra-kendra) for Mars is 3s 4° 44' 48". Half the equation of the apex is additive: 16° 22' 58". The adjusted Mars is 10s 17° 49' 2". The anomaly of the center is 5s 12° 41' 58". The equation of center is additive: 3° 11' 45". Mars adjusted by the equation of center is 10s 23° 44' 49". The anomaly of the apex is 3s 12° 25' 3". The equation of the apex is additive: 3° 26' 45". The clear Mars is 11s 6° 37' 29".

Now, the calculation of the visibility correction (Drig-karma). There, the hypotenuse is 11;48,47. From the "Manda-spashta" etc., the Southern declination is 23° 44' 59". The celestial latitude (Shara) in digits etc. is South 46' 14" 34"'. From Mars minus three signs, the Southern declination is 23° 47' 29". The latitude of the place (Akshansha) is South 27° 26' 45". From their processing, the Southern zenith distance (Natansha) is 49° 51' 11". The visibility correction minutes are additive: 118' 45". Mars adjusted by that is 11s 8° 36' 13". From this, the Southern declination is 21° 9' 39". Adjusted by the celestial latitude, the clear Southern declination becomes 3° 3' 33". The desired time is 57 ghatis.

# On the Grahalāghava with Commentary

Page 107

Day duration: 33:10. Remaining time for the Sun's passage: 59. Ascendant: 0s 16° 23' 21". The stated Ascendant is 30. For Mars, adjusted by the <term>Drik-karma</term><note>A correction for the visibility of a planet based on its latitude</note>, the remaining time of passage is 18. According to the rule "from the eastern visibility correction," etc., the time elapsed in the day for Mars is 4:29. The southern ascensional difference (<term>Chara</term>) from the adjusted Mars is 6. By the rule "divided by 24 and multiplied by the equinoctial shadow," etc., the southern result is 8. The clear southern ascensional difference is 14. The day duration is 29:32. From the clear declination, using the rule "the square of the declination and latitude," etc., the zenith distance is 28° 28' 56". The altitude is 61° 31' 46". From this, the value called <term>Para</term> is 21:23:54. From the planet's daily motion 4:29, using the rule "the daily motion is the remainder," etc., the altitude is 4:29. From this, multiplying by ninety, the "desired altitude" is calculated. Altitude 4:29 multiplied by 90 is 403:30. Divided by the midday half-day 14:46, the result in degrees is 17° 19' 37". From this, the declination is 10° 42' 36". Multiplied by the <term>Para</term> value 21:23:54, it is 227:6:37. Dividing this by the fixed divisor 6912, the result is the "desired hypotenuse" (<term>Ishta-karna</term>) 30:26. Thus, with the established hypotenuse 30:26, the clear declination 3:13:3 is multiplied, resulting in 92:51:0. Multiplying by the equinoctial hypotenuse 13:59, it becomes 1296:16:48. Dividing by 700 (<term>kha-kha-adri</term>), the "base" (<term>Bhuja</term>) is 1:59. Since the declination is southern, this base is southern; adjusted by the southern equinoctial shadow 5:45, the "clear base" becomes 7:43. The square of that base must be taken. From the desired hypotenuse, using the rule "the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and twelve," the "desired shadow" is calculated. Its square is taken. The square root of the difference between those two squares is the "perpendicular" (<term>Koti</term>). Square of the base: 56:9. Desired hypotenuse: 30:26. Its square: 926:11. Square of twelve: 144. The square root of their difference is the desired shadow: 27:96. Square of the shadow: 782:8. The difference between the square of the shadow and the square of the base: 725:53. Its square root is the perpendicular: 26:96:0. || 26 ||

### Mathematical Proof

Here, <term>Declination</term> = Dec; <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> = ESh; <term>Equinoctial Hypotenuse</term> = EH; <term>Desired Shadow Hypotenuse</term> = SH. Then, by the logic of the previous verse (22), the double base in the form of a full sine is:
2 $\times$ Base = $\frac{\text{Dec} \times \text{SH} \times \text{EH}}{350} \pm 2\text{ESh}$

$\therefore$ Base = $\frac{\frac{\text{Dec} \times \text{SH} \times \text{EH}}{350} \pm 2\text{ESh}}{2} = \frac{\text{Dec} \times \text{SH} \times \text{EH}}{700} \pm \text{ESh}$

$\because$ Base $\pm$ ESh = Clear Base. $\therefore$ Clear Base = 
$= (\frac{\text{Dec} \times \text{SH} \times \text{EH}}{700} \pm \text{ESh} )$. Here, from the shadow hypotenuse, the square root of the difference between the squares of the base and the hypotenuse is the <term>Perpendicular</term> (<term>Koti</term>) on the east-west line; the rest is easy to understand. Thus, it is proven. || 25 ||

<insert>The declination multiplied by the desired hypotenuse and the equinoctial hypotenuse, divided by 700, gives the base in the direction of the declination. By adjusting that base with the southern equinoctial shadow (addition/subtraction), the clear base is found. Subtracting the square of that clear base from the square of the shadow and taking the square root gives the perpendicular. || 26 ||</insert>

# Chapter on the Three Problems || 4 ||

The <term>Equinoctial Hypothenuse</term> <note>original: "Akshakarna"; the hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow</note> 13:26 multiplied by 9142 gives 6920:20:18. Dividing this by 700, the <term>Base</term> <note>original: "Bhuja"; the north-south side of a right-angled triangle</note> in the northern direction is 953. By adjusting this with the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> <note>original: "Palabha"</note> of 6, the result is 353, which is the corrected Base. The square of the Shadow 28:28 is 797:4, and the square of the corrected Base 353 is 154. The difference between these is 782:0, the <term>Square Root</term> of which is 27:57, which is the <term>Upright</term> <note>original: "Koti"; the east-west side of the triangle</note>. || 25 ||

-> Now, the construction of the sighting tube is described: <-

> Having determined the directions, if the planet is in the west, place the Upright facing west; if the planet is in the east, place it facing east. From the point of the Upright, place the Base in its own direction, and between them, place the shadow. Through a tube placed along a string extending from the center point to the tip of the gnomon at the end of the shadow, one should observe the planet in the sky. Or, through a tube placed along a string extending from the center point to the tip of the shadow of a man (gnomon) standing at the center, one should observe the planet in the water. || 26 ||

Now the construction of the sighting tube is explained. "Having determined," etc. After determining the directions on ground leveled with water, draw a circle with a radius equal to the shadow at the desired time and mark the cardinal points. Then, from the center point, if the planet is in the western hemisphere, place the <term>Upright</term> facing west. If the planet is in the eastern hemisphere, place the Upright facing east. From the end of the Upright, place the <term>Base</term> in its own direction like a chord, and between the Base and Upright, place the shadow diagonally. This itself is the hypotenuse. Thus, a triangular figure is formed. One should observe the planet in the sky through a tube placed along a string going from the center point to the tip of the shadow. This is what is meant: A <term>Gnomon</term> <note>original: "Shanku"; a vertical rod used for measuring shadows</note> of twelve digits should be placed at the tip of the shadow. A string should be fixed with two sticks, running from the center point of the circle to the top of that gnomon. By looking through a tube placed along that string at the specific time the Base etc. were calculated, one sees the planet in the sky.

Now, for seeing the planet in water, the <term>Placement of the Tube</term> is described. "In the water," etc. One should see the planet in the water through a tube placed along a string going from the center point to the tip of the shadow of the gnomon standing at the center. It is done like this: From the base where the gnomon is placed, lead a string downward to the tip of the gnomon's shadow. The tube should be placed along that string. At the tip of the shadow, a vessel filled with water should be placed. Looking down into the water there, the planet is seen. Having performed all these steps—determining directions and placing the tube—one must observe at that exact time. This should be demonstrated after careful consideration to please a noble king. || 26 ||

### Thus ends the illustration of the Chapter on Shadows of Ascendants, etc., in the Graha-Laghava, composed by Vishvanatha Daivajna, son of Shri Divakara Daivajna. || 4 ||

Directions = the cardinal points; Having determined = having known through the science of directions; Planet in the west = a planet situated in the western hemisphere; Facing west = oriented toward the west; Planet in the east = a planet situated in the eastern hemisphere; Facing east = oriented toward the east; From the point = from the center point of the circle; Upright; From this = from the Upright; In its own direction = in its respective direction; Place the Base; Between them = in the interval between the center and the Base; The shadow = the radiance; Should place. The shadow is the square root of the sum of the squares of the previously calculated Upright and Base. <header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

The observed shadow at the desired time, being connected to the hypotenuse of the shadow <note>original: "chhayakarna"</note>, falls upon the center point. Therefore, from the perspective of the center, one is able to easily view the celestial body located at the top of the gnomon <note>original: "shanku"</note> through a tube <note>original: "nalika"</note> attached to that hypotenuse; this is logical. Having determined the directions through the knowledge of orientation: if the planet is in the western hemisphere, face west; if in the eastern hemisphere, face east. From the center point, mark the upright <note>the "koti" or vertical side of the triangle</note>; from there, mark the base <note>the "bhuja" or horizontal side</note> in its respective direction, and between these two, draw the shadow. One should observe the sky through a tube along the string connected between the center point (the tip of the shadow) and the head of the gnomon. Alternatively, one should observe the planet in water through a tube along the string connected between the head of the gnomon at the center and the tip of the shadow.

Here, the Teacher <note>Ganesha Daivajna, the author</note> has demonstrated the clarity of the tube-attachment method to fulfill his promise made in the verses beginning with "Even the solar Sun and the Moon..." In reality, for their own convenience in calculating planets, authors occasionally adopted approximate methods. Furthermore, because a great deal of time has passed since the composition of this text, there is now a discrepancy between the planets as calculated by these formulas and the planets as observed through instruments. Modern astronomers should reflect upon this. || 26 ||

->First, he describes the method for calculating the instantaneous position of a planet:<-

The resulting degrees should be subtracted from or added to the planet's position. If the days have passed, it should be subtracted; if the days are yet to come, it should be added. # Chapter 5: On Lunar Eclipses

The meaning is that the calculation should be made for the specific moment in time. There is a particular distinction here: for both lunar and solar eclipses, one must take the duration of the Full Moon or New Moon as given in the <term>Panchanga</term><note>The traditional Hindu almanac</note> in <term>ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatikas make a full day</note>. With these ghatikas, the mean positions of the Sun, Moon, Moon’s apogee, and <term>Rahu</term><note>The ascending lunar node, essential for eclipse calculations</note> are to be adjusted. After that, the true positions must be calculated. 

From the positions of the Sun and Moon, the duration of the <term>tithi</term><note>A lunar day, or 1/30th of a lunar month</note> is to be determined. These should be added to or subtracted from the time given in the almanac. For example: when the elapsed lunar day is the 14th or 29th, one must calculate the remaining time until the current Full Moon or New Moon; this time is added to the almanac's phase-time. When the elapsed lunar day is the 15th or 30th, one calculates the time already passed in the first lunar day of the next fortnight; this is subtracted from the almanac's time. This results in the <term>Parvanta</term><note>The exact moment of the opposition or conjunction</note>. The planets are then moved according to these elapsed or remaining ghatikas to find their positions at the exact moment of the eclipse's peak.

### Example:
In the year 1677 of the Vikrama era (1542 of the Shaka era), on Wednesday, the Full Moon of the bright half of the month Margashirsha, the time was 38 ghatikas and 11 palas. The Rohini mansion lasted 9 ghatikas and 8 palas. The Yoga was 10 ghatikas and 6 palas. To find the lunar phase, the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The count of elapsed days since the start of the epoch</note> is 636. The cycle is 9. From this, the mean positions at dawn are:
*   **Sun:** 8 signs, 0°, 8', 59"
*   **Moon:** 12 signs, 5°, 11', 57"
*   **Moon’s Apogee:** 10 signs, 3°, 37', 5"
*   **Rahu:** 7 signs, 28°, 25', 27"

Adjusting for the 38 ghatikas and 11 palas of the lunar day:
*   **Sun:** 8s 0° 46' 36" | **Moon:** 2s 3° 43' 4" | **Apogee:** 10s 3° 41' 20" | **Rahu:** 7s 28° 55' 27"

**True Calculation:** The Sun's mean anomaly is 6s 17° 13' 24". The equation of center is negative 0° 39' 4". The Sun corrected by the equation is 8s 0° 7' 32". The precession of equinoxes is 18° 18'. The ascensional difference is positive 114. The corrected Sun is 8s 0° 9' 26". The velocity correction is positive 2' 3". The true velocity is 61' 11". The Moon, corrected by three factors, is 2s 3° 56' 18". The Moon's mean anomaly is 7s 21° 45' 22". The equation of center is negative 4° 20' 22". The true Moon is 2s 29° 36' 6". The velocity correction is positive 33' 30". The true velocity is 824' 5". 

In this case, the elapsed lunar day is the 14th. The remaining time is 2 ghatikas and 37 palas. Adding this to the almanac time (38:11) gives the exact moment of opposition (<term>Parvanta</term>) at 40:48. Adjusting the planets for these remaining 2:37 ghatikas, the positions at the moment of opposition are:
*   **Sun:** 8s 0° 12' 56" | **Moon:** 2s 0° 22' 2" | **Rahu:** 7s 28° 26' 18"

## Madhuri Commentary —

The planet's daily motion multiplied by the elapsed or remaining days, divided by sixty, and then subtracted or added to the planet's position, gives the planet for the desired time. Similarly, the motion multiplied by the elapsed or remaining ghatikas and divided by sixty gives the minutes of arc to be added or subtracted to find the planet at the desired moment.

## Rationale —

The logic here is easily understood through two proportions. First: if the planet's motion in one day is X, then what is the motion for the given number of elapsed/remaining days? This gives the arc-minutes for those days. These are divided by sixty to convert to degrees. Second: if the planet's motion occurs over 60 ghatikas, what is the motion for the specific elapsed/remaining ghatikas? By combining these, adding to the sunrise position if the time has passed, or subtracting if the time is yet to come, the planet at the desired time is found. Mathematically:

-> (Daily Motion × Elapsed Days / 60) ± (Daily Motion × Elapsed Ghatikas / 60) <-

Planet ± [formula above] = Planet at desired time. <note>For retrograde planets, the addition and subtraction are reversed because they move backward.</note> This is logically sound due to their reverse motion.

By taking the product of the planet's velocity and the elapsed/remaining days and dividing by 60, and then adding or subtracting the resulting degrees etc. from the planet, the instantaneous position is found. Similarly, using the planet's velocity and the elapsed...

By dividing the product of the remaining time in ghatis <note>A ghati is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> by 60, the resulting minutes of arc are either subtracted from or added to the planet's position to find the instantaneous position of the planet. || 1 ||

**Example:** We are to calculate the lunar eclipse for Thursday, the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phalguna, in the Shaka year 1862 (Samyat 1997, 1348 AD). Therefore, on Saturday, the second day of the dark fortnight of Chaitra, the mixed value is 44;46,57. At that time, the true Sun is at 11 signs, 1 degree, 50 minutes, and 30 seconds <note>11s 1° 50' 30"</note>; its motion is 59' 46"; Rahu <note>The North Node of the Moon</note> is at 5s 11° 16' 43" with a motion of 3' 11"; and the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the shift of the vernal equinox</term> is 29° 37' 42". 45 Gh. P.

These planets must be brought to the end of the full moon time (Purnanta) at 28;49 on Thursday, the full moon of the bright fortnight of Phalguna. The elapsed time is 12;30 and the remaining is 57;3. By subtracting the desired time 5;28,49 from the row 7;44,46, the negative motion for the elapsed days is 2;15,57. Multiplying this by the Sun's motion of 59' 46": first, multiplying by 2 days gives 119;32; dividing by 60 gives 1 degree 59 minutes 32 seconds. Subtracting this from the Sun's position at the mixed time (11s 1° 50' 30") results in 10s 29° 50' 58". Again, multiplying the Sun's motion by the 15;57 remaining time gives 4;68,42; dividing by 60 gives 7 minutes 42 seconds. Subtracting this from the previous remainder (10s 29° 50' 58") gives the true Sun at the end of the full moon as 10s 28° 36' 30". Similarly, the Moon at the end of the period is 4s 29° 35' 16" with a motion of 84;22, and Rahu is 5s 11° 23' 56". || 1 ||

->Now, he describes the certainty of the eclipse and the calculation of the latitude (Shara):<-

### Thus, if at the end of the period, the degrees of the arm of the Sun minus Rahu are less than fourteen, an eclipse is possible.
### Those degrees multiplied by eleven and divided by seven give the latitude in digits and its fractions. || 2 ||

Now he explains the knowledge of the possibility of an eclipse and the calculation of the latitude. *Thus:* In the manner previously mentioned, the Moon and Sun are calculated. At the end of the period—the end of the full moon—they are at the same degrees and minutes but six signs apart. At the end of the new moon, they are equal in signs, degrees, and minutes.
As stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A famous 12th-century text by Bhaskara II</note>:
"At the moment of the full moon's end, they are equal in degrees etc. [six signs apart], and at the end of the new moon, they are equal even in signs."
Here, the word "period" (Parva) should be understood to mean both the full moon and the new moon. There, the degrees of the "arm" <term>Bhuja: the angular distance from the nearest node</term> of the Sun-minus-Rahu must be calculated. "Sun-minus-Rahu" means the Sun from which Rahu has been subtracted. It refers to the distance between the Sun and the Node. The "arm" (sine-related arc) of that should be taken. If those degrees are less than "Indra" (fourteen), then there is a possibility of an eclipse. This means an eclipse occurs. This applies to lunar eclipses; for solar eclipses, if the degrees of the arm in the northern hemisphere are less than fourteen, or in the southern hemisphere less than eight, then a solar eclipse occurs, as will be explained later. Those degrees are multiplied by "Shankura" (eleven). Then they are divided by "Shaila" (seven); the result is in digits (Angulas). The remainder multiplied by sixty and divided by seven gives the fractions of a digit (Vyangulas). Thus, the latitude (Shara) is in digits etc. The direction of the latitude is the same as the hemisphere in which the Sun-minus-Rahu resides.
Example: Sun 8s 10° 12' 6"; Rahu 7s 28° 23' 18"; Sun-minus-Rahu 0s 15° 48' 48". Its "arm" degrees are 15° 48' 48". <note>The text notes this is less than 14 in the rule, though the example numbers here seem to slightly exceed it or are used for demonstration</note>. Since it is near fourteen, an eclipse is possible. The degrees 15;48,48 multiplied by 11 = 191;46,48. Divided by 7, the result for the latitude is 2 digits 10 fractions. Since the Sun-minus-Rahu is in the northern hemisphere, the latitude is North. || 2 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary:<-

*At the end of the period* = "In a lunar eclipse at the end of the full moon, and in a solar eclipse at the end of the new moon; *thus* = by the method of 'the motion multiplied by the elapsed or remaining days,' having calculated the planets, if the <unclear>degrees are less than fourteen</unclear> of the arm of the Sun deprived of Rahu, then of the eclipse = of the period..."

The possibility = there is a possibility [of an eclipse]. Those = stated = degrees, multiplied by eleven, divided by seven, the result is the <term>celestial latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *shara* (arrow), used here to mean the angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic</note> in digits and so on, belonging to the sphere of the Sun minus Rahu <note>Rahu is the ascending node of the Moon; subtracting its position from the Sun's helps determine the distance from the node</note>. As the *Amarakosha* dictionary states: "Prishatka, Bana, Vishikha... these are synonyms for an arrow." This becomes the latitude. || 2 ||

Similarly, if the <term>arm</term><note>Sanskrit: *bhuja*, the distance from the nearest node</note> of the Sun minus Rahu is less than 14 degrees, there is a possibility of an eclipse occurring at the end of the lunar fortnight <note>the Full Moon</note>. Multiplying those degrees of the "arm" by 11 and dividing by 7 gives the latitude in digits for the direction of the sphere of the Sun minus Rahu. || 2 ||

**Example:** Subtracting Rahu (5 signs, 11°, 23', 56") from the Sun at the end of the fortnight (10 signs, 28°, 36', 30") results in the Sun minus Rahu being 5 signs, 17°, 12', 34". By the method of "subtracting three signs from the arm" etc., the degrees of the arm are 12° 47' 26". Since this is less than 14, an eclipse is possible during this Full Moon. Multiplying the arm (12° 47' 26") by 11 gives 130° 41' 46"; dividing this by 7 results in a latitude of 20 digits, 55 minutes, and 58 seconds in the northern sphere (since the Sun minus Rahu is in the northern hemisphere). || 2 ||

### Now, the Calculation of the Disks of the Sun, Moon, and Earth's Shadow —

> The disk of the Sun is one-fifth of its motion minus fifty-five, plus ten.
> The disk of the Moon is its motion divided by seventy-four.
> The disk of the Earth's shadow, in digits, is three times the Moon's disk,
> plus its own eleventh part, minus eight. || 3 ||

Now the calculation of the solar and lunar disks and the Earth's shadow is explained. Regarding motion: The Sun's motion is 61' 11". <note>The text here seems to follow a specific commentary's arithmetic</note> Twice that is 122' 22". Divided by eleven, the result is the Sun's disk in digits: 11' 7". The Moon's motion is 794' 9"; divided by seventy-four, the result is the Moon's disk in digits: 10' 48". This lunar motion of 794' 9" is reduced by 796 <insert>calculation note</insert>... [The text continues with complex ratios for the Earth's shadow]. The Earth's shadow <note>Sanskrit: *bhābha*</note> is 28.90 digits. This is also the diameter of Rahu <note>In ancient Indian astronomy, the Earth's shadow was often identified with the body of Rahu during a lunar eclipse</note>. || 3 ||

### The "Madhuri" Commentary —

The disk of the Sun (*ushnago*) is one-fifth of its motion minus fifty-five, plus ten. Then, the motion of the Moon (*sitarucho*—the one with cool rays) divided by seventy-four is the lunar disk. That same lunar disk multiplied by three, added to its own eleventh part, and reduced by eight, is certainly the disk of the Earth's shadow (*kshmābhā*) in digits. || 3 ||

# Chapter 5: On Lunar Eclipses

In an eclipse, the Earth’s shadow <note>Sanskrit: *bhūbhā*</note> covers the Moon, and the Moon covers the Sun. In common worldly parlance, it is said that the eclipse is caused by Rahu <note>the celestial demon/node</note> due to a boon granted by Brahma.
As stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*:
> "The shadow of the Earth, moving in the path of the Sun, covers the Moon; and the Moon, moving in its path, covers the solar orb. This dark form acts thus by the boon of Lord Shiva; this is not contradictory to any sacred scriptures."

O Astronomer! Calculate the "half-sum of the diameters of the obscurer and the obscured" <term>mānaikyakhaṇḍa: the sum of the radii of the two celestial bodies involved</term>. He who covers is the "obscurer" <note>chādaka</note>. That which is fit to be covered is the "obscured" <note>chādya</note>. One must take the sum of the measures of these two orbs and divide it by two. In a lunar eclipse, the obscurer is the Earth's shadow and the obscured is the Moon. Half their sum is the *mānaikyakhaṇḍa* for a lunar eclipse. In a solar eclipse, the obscurer is the Moon and the obscured is the Sun. Half their sum is the *mānaikyakhaṇḍa* for a solar eclipse. From that half-sum, subtract the "latitude" <term>śara: the celestial latitude or angular distance from the ecliptic</term> previously calculated in digits <note>angulas</note>. The remainder is the "covered portion" <note>channa</note>, which is the magnitude of the eclipse. If the latitude cannot be subtracted from the half-sum <note>i.e., if the latitude is greater than the sum of the radii</note>, it is logically proven that no eclipse occurs. If you subtract the measure of the obscured orb from this "covered portion," the remaining part is the "total obscuration" <note>khagrasa</note>. This represents the extent of the total eclipse. In a lunar eclipse, the "obscured" is the Moon's orb; in a solar eclipse, it is the Sun's orb.

**Example:** The obscurer (Earth's shadow) is 28;10. The obscured (Moon's orb) is 11;07. Their sum is 39;17. Half of this is the *mānaikyakhaṇḍa* 19;38. Subtracting the latitude 2;50, the magnitude of the eclipse is 16;48. Subtracting the obscured orb 11;07 from the covered portion 16;48, the total obscuration <note>khagrasa</note> is 5;41. || 4 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary—

The Moon covers the Sun (*arka*); the Earth's shadow (*bhūbhā*) covers the Moon (*vidhu*). Calculate the half-sum of the diameters of the obscurer and the obscured. Subtract the latitude (*śara/bāṇa*) from that half-sum; the result is the magnitude of the eclipse (*channa*). The remainder after subtracting the obscured orb from the magnitude is the measure of total obscuration (*khacchannaka*). || 4 ||

### Mathematical Rationale:—

The rationale for this is easily understood through the methods mentioned in the *Surya Siddhanta*, such as "The Moon is the obscurer of the Sun; the instantaneous lunar latitude and the measures of the obscured and obscurer..." etc. Why labor further in writing it out? This is the direction. || 4 ||

The Moon covers the Sun and the Earth's shadow covers the Moon. By subtracting the latitude from the half-sum of the obscurer and obscured orbs, the magnitude of the eclipse is found. If the magnitude of the eclipse is greater than the obscured orb, the amount of that excess is called the total obscuration (*khagrasa*). || 4 ||

**Example:** In a lunar eclipse, the obscurer (Earth's shadow) orb is 29;08 and the obscured (Moon) orb is 11;22. Their sum is 40;30. Half of that is 20;15. Subtracting the latitude 18;34 from 20;15, the remainder is 1;41, which is the magnitude of the eclipse. Here, the magnitude 1;41 is less than the Moon's measure 11;22, therefore no total eclipse occurred.

### Example of Total Obscuration:—

If the magnitude of the eclipse is 13;42 and the Moon's orb is 11;22, then by taking the difference between the Moon's orb 11;22 and the magnitude 13;42, the remainder 1;40 will be the measure of the total obscuration. || 4 ||

### Now, the duration of the eclipse and the duration of totality:—

### Add the latitude to the half-sum of the diameters, multiply by ten,
### then multiply by the magnitude of the eclipse; take the square root, and subtract one-sixtieth.
### Divide by the Moon's [relative] motion; this is the duration in ghatikas.
### Similarly, calculate the duration of totality using the difference of the half-diameters. || 5 ||

<page-num>108</page-num>
<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

**Now he describes the calculation of the duration of the eclipse and the duration of totality in ghatikas <note>A ghatika is a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. "By the sum of the radii..."** The half-sum of the radii <term>Manaikya-khanda: the sum of the radii of the obscuring body (Earth's shadow) and the obscured body (the Moon)</term> is 19;38. Added to the arrow <term>Ishu or Shara: the celestial latitude of the Moon</term> which is 2;50, it becomes 22;28. Multiplied by ten, it is 224;40. Multiplied by the obscured portion <term>Chhanna: the magnitude of the eclipse</term> of 16;48, it results in 3775;24. This is converted twice by sixty <note>A process of sexagesimal normalization</note> to 135,897,440. Its square root is 66,126. This, reduced by its own sixth part (10,154), is 55,972. Divided by the Moon's disk <term>Glau-bimba: the diameter of the Moon</term> of 1197, the result is the duration of the eclipse in ghatikas: 4;36. In the same way as the duration, the totality <term>Marda: the period during which the Moon is completely within the shadow</term> should be calculated using the difference between the half-disks and the total obscuration. This is what is meant: the difference between the halves of the two disks should be taken. In a lunar eclipse, take the difference between the half-disks of the Moon and the Earth's shadow; in a solar eclipse, the difference between the disks of the Sun and Moon. "Total obscuration" refers to the state of being completely swallowed.

**Example:** The Moon's disk is 1197. The Earth's shadow disk is 28;10 <note>Note: These values use different units/scales common in Sanskrit astronomical texts</note>. The half-disk of the Moon is 5;33. The half-disk of the Earth's shadow is 14;5. Their difference is 8;32. Added to the arrow (latitude) of 2;50, it is 11;22. Multiplied by ten, it is 113;40. Multiplied by the total obscuration of 5;41, it is 636;0. This, converted twice by sixty, is 2,325,600. Its square root is 1525. This, reduced by its own sixth part (4;14), is 1520. Divided by the Moon's disk of 1197, the result is the duration of totality in ghatikas: 1;14. || 5 ||

# The Madhuri Commentary—

By the arrow = by the latitude; added = joined with; multiplied by ten = ten times; the half-sum of the radii = the sum of the radii of the obscurer and the obscured; multiplied by the obscured = multiplied by the magnitude of the eclipse; from this; the root = the square root; reduced by its own sixth part = minus one-sixth of itself; divided by the Moon's disk = divided by the lunar diameter <gloss>“Glau, Mriganka, and Kalanidhi are synonyms for the Moon” according to the Amarakosha dictionary</gloss>; this = the quotient; in ghatikas etc. = starting with the measures of time; the duration = shall be the duration of the eclipse in ghatikas. Likewise = in that manner; by the difference of the half-disks and the total obscuration = using the difference of the obscurer/obscured disks and the measure of total immersion; the totality = "one should know" the duration of totality. || 5 ||

# Here is the Proof (Rationale):—

<margin>Moon's Motion / 74</margin>
Let the half-sum of the radii = $H$. Moon's Disk = $D$. $\therefore$ Moon's Motion = 74 $\times$ Moon's Disk.
<margin>74</margin>

$\because$ Since: Half-sum — Latitude = Magnitude of Eclipse ($E$). Therefore, according to the method stated by Bhaskara <note>Referring to Bhaskara II, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> "From the squares of the sum and difference of the semi-diameters," etc., the square of the duration minutes = $H^2 \times 9 - L^2 \times 9 = 9 (H^2 - L^2) = 9 (H + L) (H - L) = 9 (H + L) \times E$. Therefore, by proportion, the square of the duration in ghatikas =

$$ \frac{60^2 \times 9 (H + L) E}{(\text{Moon's Motion} - \text{Sun's Motion})^2} = \frac{3600 \times 9 (H + L) E}{(74 \times D - \text{Sun's Motion})^2} $$

$$ = \frac{360 \times 9 \times 10 (H + L) E}{(74 \times D - \text{Sun's Motion})^2} = \frac{3240 \times 10 (H + L) E}{(74 \times D - \text{Sun's Motion})^2} $$

Taking the square roots of these —

$$ \text{Duration in Ghatikas} = \frac{54 \times \sqrt{10 (H + L) E}}{(74 \times D - \text{Sun's Motion})} $$

$$ = \frac{54}{74} \times \frac{\sqrt{10 (H + L) E}}{D - \text{Sun's Motion}/74} = \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{\sqrt{10 (H + L) E}}{D - 71} = $$

$$ = \frac{\sqrt{10 (H + L) E}}{D} \times (1 - 1/6) = (1 - 1/6) \frac{\sqrt{10 (H + L) E}}{D} $$

$$ \frac{(\sqrt{10 (\text{Sum of Radii} + \text{Latitude})}) \text{Eclipse Measure} - \frac{\sqrt{10 (\text{Sum of Radii} + \text{Latitude})} \text{Eclipse Measure}}{6}}{\text{Lunar Diameter}} = \text{Result. Thus it is proven. || 5 ||} $$
<note>The formula calculates the duration of the eclipse in ghatis (1 ghati = 24 minutes). The "Sum of Radii" refers to the combined semi-diameters of the Earth's shadow and the Moon.</note>

Add the celestial latitude <term>Shar</term> to the half-sum of the diameters <term>Manaikyakharda</term>, multiply by ten, and then multiply by the measure of the eclipse <term>Grasamana</term>. Take the square root of this product, subtract one-sixth of that root from itself, and divide the remainder by the diameter of the Moon <term>Chandravimba</term>. The resulting quotient is the duration of the eclipse in <term>Ghatis</term> and so on. Similarly, using the square root of the difference between the diameters of the obscured and the obscurer bodies, the duration of totality <term>Marda Ghati</term> is found. || 6 ||

**Example—** The Earth's shadow diameter is 29;8 and the Moon's diameter is 11;32. Their half-sum is 20;15. Adding the latitude 18;34 gives 38;49. Multiplying this by 10 gives 388;10. Multiplying this by the eclipse measure 11;41 results in 453;25. The square root of this is 25;33. Subtracting its sixth part 4;15 leaves a remainder of 21;18. Dividing this by the Moon's diameter 11;32, the quotient is 1;52 <term>Ghatis</term>, which is the duration of the eclipse <term>Sthitikala</term>.

Similarly, the difference between the Earth's shadow 29;8 and the Moon's diameter 11;32 is 17;46. Half of this is 8;53. Adding the latitude 18;34 gives 27;41. Multiplying by 10 gives 276;50. Multiplying by the total eclipse measure 1;40 gives 444;43. The square root is 21;6. Subtracting its sixth part 3;31 leaves 17;35. Dividing by the Moon's diameter 11;32, the quotient is 1;33 <term>Marda Ghati</term> (half-duration of totality). || 5 ||

->**Now he describes the calculation of the contact, separation, duration, and totality—**<-

> The duration, placed in two positions, is decreased and increased by seconds of time <term>Palas</term> equal to twice the degrees of the Sun's longitude minus Rahu's longitude. This occurs when that value is less than twelve or six signs. If it is greater, the operations are reversed. Thus, the durations for the beginning (contact) and end (separation) are found, and the same applies to the half-duration of totality. || 6 ||

Now the calculation for contact, separation, duration, and totality is explained. "By pairs" means the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu <term>Vyagu-bhujamsha</term> should be doubled. The previously mentioned duration, placed in two spots, should be decreased and increased by that many <term>Palas</term> (seconds). Under what condition? When the value is less than six signs or twelve signs from the Sun. If it is more, do the opposite. In this sequence, the durations for the beginning (contact) and the end (separation) are established. The same method applies to calculating totality <term>Marda</term>. Whether it is less or more than six signs should be understood by the signs and degrees. For example: starting from 11 signs and 16 degrees of the Sun minus Rahu up to zero signs, it is considered less than twelve signs. From 0 signs and 1 second up to 14 degrees, it is considered more than twelve. Similarly, from 5 signs 16 degrees to 6 signs, it is less than six signs; from 6 signs to 14 degrees beyond, it is more than six signs.

**Example:** The duration in <term>Ghatis</term> is 4;36. The Sun's mean position minus Rahu is the <term>Vyagvarka</term>. The degrees are 14;8;48. Doubled, this is 3 <note>original: "3" likely refers to the resulting adjustment in Palas</note>. Because the Sun minus Rahu is greater than twelve signs, the contact duration becomes 4;39 (by addition). The separation duration becomes 4;33 (by subtraction). The totality <term>Marda</term> is 1;54. Adding the doubled degrees as <term>Palas</term>, the immersion totality <term>Sammilana-marda</term> becomes 1;57. Subtracting them, the emersion totality <term>Moksha-marda</term> becomes 1;51. || 6 ||

# On the Khetakagrahalaghava

These two <note>referring to the results of the calculation</note> are the durations of the **contact** and the **release** <note>original: *sparsha-moksha-kaline sthiti*</note>. That is to say, in one instance it is the duration of the beginning of the eclipse, and in the other, it is the duration of the end. If the "Sun minus Rahu" <note>the distance of the Sun from the lunar node</note> is greater than six signs, it is calculated one way; otherwise, it is the reverse. The same logic applies to the **total obscuration** and **reappearance** <note>original: *sammilana-unmilana*</note> durations. || 6 ||

-> **Here is the mathematical proof:** <-

Let the degrees of the "arm" <note>the sine-like component of the orbital position</note> be represented as *Vibhu*. Then, by the previous method, the "arrow" <note>the latitude of the planet</note> is: $\frac{Vibhu \times 11}{7}$. Now, following the method taught by Bhaskara <note>referring to the 12th-century mathematician Bhaskaracharya</note>—"from the latitude, multiplied by the latitude and divided by four," etc.—the value of the correction in *palas* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> is: $\frac{5 \times Latitude}{4}$ =

$\frac{Vibhu \times 11 \times 5}{4 \times 7} = \frac{Vibhu \times 55}{28} = Vibhu \times 2$ <note>approximately</note>. The remainder is easy to understand. Thus, it is proven. || 6 ||

If the "Sun minus Rahu" <term>Vyagu: The position of the Sun after subtracting the position of the ascending node (Rahu)</term> is less than 12 or 6 signs, then by subtracting and adding the *palas* (equivalent to twice the degrees of the "arm") to the two durations, one obtains the specific durations for the **contact** and **release**. If the *Vyagu* is greater than 12 or 6 signs, then by adding and subtracting (the reverse), one obtains the durations for the contact and release respectively. || 6 ||

**Example:** (Sun - Rahu) = *Vyagu* = 5 signs, 17°, 00', 34". This is less than 6 signs. Therefore, doubling its "arm" degrees (12° 59' 26") gives 25 *palas*, 58 *vipalas*, 52 *vipalas*. By subtracting and adding this to the duration of 11 *ghatis* 52 *palas*, we get the **contact duration** of 11:27 and the **release duration** of 12:17. Similarly, subtracting the same from the total obscuration time of 11:33 gives the **immersion** <note>start of totality</note> at 11:08, and adding it gives the **emergence** <note>end of totality</note> at 11:58. || 6 ||

-> **Now, the calculation for the time of contact and other phases:** <-

> The end of the *tithi* <note>lunar day</note> is the middle of the eclipse. This, when subtracted and added to the two specific durations, gives the times for the **beginning** and the **end** of the eclipse. Similarly, using the durations of total obscuration, the times for the **covering** and **uncovering** of the disk are found. || 7 ||

Now he explains the method for finding the times of the middle of the eclipse, the contact, the release, the immersion, and the emergence. "The end of the *tithi*" refers to the calculated end of the lunar day, which is the **middle of the eclipse** <note>the moment of maximum obscuration</note>. That middle time, when subtracted by the contact duration and added to the release duration, gives the times for the "mouth" and "cessation." The "mouth" of the eclipse is the **contact** <note>first touch</note>. The "cessation" is the **release** <note>final touch</note>. Contact is the start of the obscuration; release is the absence of obscuration. In the same way, using the two durations of total obscuration, the **immersion** and **emergence** are found. Immersion is the total covering of the orb in a total eclipse. Emergence is the start of the orb's liberation from the shadow.

**Example:** The end of the *tithi* (middle of the eclipse) is 40:48. Subtracted by the contact duration of 4:39, the **time of contact** is 36:09. Added to the release duration of 4:33, the **time of release** is 45:21. The middle time 40:48 subtracted by the immersion duration of 11:57 gives the **time of immersion** as 28:51. Added to the emergence duration of 21:09, the **time of emergence** is 61:57.

# Chapter 5: On the Lunar Eclipse

### The Madhuri Commentary —

This moment, the end of the lunar day <note>original: "tithi-viratih"</note>, is the middle of the eclipse <note>original: "grahasya madhyah"</note>. That middle time of the full moon, when decreased and increased by its own duration of contact and release <note>the time from first contact to the middle, and middle to last contact</note>, results in the times of the beginning and the end of the eclipse. Similarly, by subtracting and adding the durations of total obscuration <note>original: "sammilana-unmilana-marda"</note>, the times of the start of totality and the end of totality are found. || 7 ||

### The Rationale Here —

> "At the end of the true lunar day, one should declare the middle of the eclipse," etc. Following the method stated in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit astronomical text</note>, the explanation of this is quite simple; what is the use of further elaboration? Thus, it is proven. || 7 ||

The end of the lunar day is the middle of the eclipse. By subtracting and adding the duration of the eclipse <note>the half-duration</note> to this, the respective times of first contact <note>start</note> and release <note>end</note> are obtained. Likewise, by subtracting and adding the duration of totality <note>original: "marda-kala"</note> to the middle time, the times of the start of totality <note>immersion</note> and the end of totality <note>emergence</note> are found in sequence. || 7 ||

### Example —

By subtracting the contact duration of 1:27 from the lunar day end time of 28:49, the contact time is 27:22. By adding the release duration of 2:17 to the lunar day end time, the release time is 31:06.

Similarly, by subtracting the immersion duration of 1:08 from the lunar day end time of 28:49, the immersion time is 27:41. By adding the emergence duration of 1:58, the emergence time is 30:47. || 7 ||

### Now, the calculation of the eclipse magnitude at a desired time —

> The desired time multiplied by the obscured portion and divided by the duration; that, plus one and a quarter, is the desired magnitude of the eclipse. || 8 ||

Now he speaks of calculating the magnitude at a desired time <note>original: "ishta-grasa"</note>. "Multiplied by the obscured": The maximum magnitude of the eclipse is multiplied by the "desired time" (the time elapsed since contact or remaining until release, which must be less than the half-duration). That should be divided by the duration. If the desired time is after the first contact, divide by the contact duration. If it is before the release, divide by the release duration. The result, when increased by "one and a quarter" <note>1.25 or 1:15 in sexagesimal</note>, becomes the desired magnitude of the eclipse. One should note that the time after contact is "contact-desire" and the time before release is "release-desire."

### Example —

The chosen desired time after contact is 2 hours <note>original: "ghati"</note>. Multiplied by the magnitude 16:48, it equals 33:36. Divided by the contact duration of 4:39, it equals 7:13. Adding one and a quarter (1:15), the resulting magnitude at the desired time is 8:28. || 8 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary —

The multiplication of the magnitude at the middle of the eclipse and the desired time <note>original: "pihita-hata-ishtam"</note>, divided by the duration <note>original: "sthiti-vihritam"</note>, plus one and a quarter <note>original: "sa-charana-bhu-yuk"</note>, equals the desired magnitude of the eclipse in digits <note>original: "angula"</note> at that specific time. || 8 ||

### The Rationale Here —

If one wishes to know the magnitude of the eclipse at a time between the contact and the middle, or between the release and the middle, the proportion would usually be: "If the full magnitude is obtained in the full duration, how much is obtained in the desired time?" However, observing the coarseness/inaccuracy resulting from a simple proportion, the author has added one and a quarter as a correction factor to account for the variation. What more need be said? Thus, it is proven. || 8 ||

By dividing the product of the total magnitude and the desired time by the duration, and adding 1 + 1/4 (1:15) to the result, the magnitude at the desired time is found. || 8 ||

## With the Commentary on Grahalaghava

**Example:** If one wishes to find the <term>Ishta Grasa</term><note>The "desired obscuration" or magnitude of the eclipse at a specific moment.</note> at 3 <term>Ghatis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> after the moment of first contact:

The magnitude can be similarly calculated for the duration of the clearance (latter half) of the eclipse. || 8 ||

### Now, the method for calculating the Ayana Valana:

**The Sun, increased or decreased by three signs, is added to the degrees of precession. In Solar and Lunar eclipses respectively, using the segments measured by seven, five, and one (7, 5, 1), the deflection is found like the calculation of <term>Chara</term><note>Ascensional difference.</note>. Its direction is the same as the hemisphere of the Sun so modified. || 9 ||**

Now the calculation of <term>Valana</term><note>Deflection or "aspect" of the eclipse, used to determine the orientation of the eclipsed part on the disk.</note> is explained. In the case of a Solar eclipse, add three signs to the Sun's longitude. In a Lunar eclipse, subtract three signs from the Sun's longitude. Add the <term>Ayanamsha</term><note>The degrees of the precession of the equinoxes.</note> to this. From this result, calculate the segments using the values 7, 5, and 1, just as described in the method for calculating <term>Chara</term>. This result is the <term>Ayana Valana</term>. Its direction (North or South) is determined by the hemisphere in which the modified Sun (with precession) is located.

**Example:** The Sun is at 8s 0° 12' 6". Because this is a Lunar eclipse, subtract 3 signs, resulting in 5s 0° 12' 6". Adding the precession of 18° 18' gives 5s 18° 30' 6". The <term>Bhuja</term><note>The distance from the nearest equinoctial point.</note> is 10° 11' 29" 54'''. Since the sign position in the Bhuja is zero, the first segment (7, 5, 1) is not fully reached. The remainder 11;29,54 is multiplied by the first segment (7), giving 80;29,18. Dividing by thirty, the result is 2;40. Adding this to the previous segments (which was 0), the total deflection is 2;40. Since the modified Sun is in the Northern hemisphere, the direction is North. || 9 ||

### Madhuri Commentary:

In the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, the Sun—increased or decreased by three signs and added to the degrees of precession—is used. From this Sun, using the segments equal to seven, five, and one (7, 5, 1) and following the method for calculating <term>Chara</term>, the <term>Ayana Valana</term> is produced, following the direction of the hemisphere of that modified Sun. || 9 ||

### Mathematical Rationale:

Here, the <term>Trijya</term><note>Radius of the circle, taken here as 120.</note> = 120, the <term>Jinajya</term><note>Sine of the maximum declination (obliquity of the ecliptic), taken here as 48.</note> = 48. The planet plus three signs is the subject. The <term>Dyujya</term><note>Radius of the diurnal circle.</note> of the planet with precession = 113.
Then, by proportion, the Sine of Declination (<term>Kranti-jya</term>) of the planet plus three signs = $\frac{60 \times \text{Jinajya}}{\text{Trijya}} = \frac{60 \times 48}{120}$. Then, if this is the Sine of Declination in the circle of the Radius, what will it be in the circle of the diurnal radius? The resulting deflection = $\frac{60 \times 48}{113}$.

$\therefore$ The degrees of deflection = $\frac{30 \times 48}{113}$. Furthermore, if there are 360 degrees of deflection, then in the 32-minute disk of the Moon, what are the degrees of deflection? = $\frac{30 \times 48 \times 32}{113 \times 360}$. Multiplying by six, we get the author's deflection units = $\frac{30 \times 48 \times 32 \times 6}{113 \times 360} = \frac{24 \times 32}{113} = \frac{768}{113} = 7$ approximately. In this way, the other segments are derived.

Since at the time of the full moon (Lunar eclipse), the Sun = Moon + 6 signs, therefore Sun - 3 = Moon + 3. Thus, the Sun minus three signs is indeed the Moon plus three signs. Because the Sine of Declination of the Moon plus three signs in the diurnal circle is the <margin>Moon's Ayana Valana. This arises from the geometry of the field; the Sine of Declination of the Sun plus or minus three signs is the Ayana Valana of the Moon.</margin>

# Chapter on Lunar Eclipses || 5 ||

...must indeed be the sine. Therefore, the declination sine of the Sun, when the tropical three signs are subtracted, becomes the deflection sine of the Moon. The reasoning for calculating the segments <note>original: "khandaka"</note> has been shown right here, thus it is proven. || 9 ||

In the eclipse of one's own (the Sun) and the Moon: by sequentially adding and subtracting 3 signs from the Sun, adding the precession of the equinoxes <term>ayanāṃśa: the shifting of the celestial equator</term>, and using the segments 7, 5, 1—similar to the method for calculating the ascensional difference—the result obtained is the deflection of the direction of the Sun's pole (the equinoctial deflection). || 9 ||

**Example—** From the true Sun at 10s 28° 36' 30", subtracting 3 signs gives 7s 28° 36' 30". Adding the precession of 21° 37' 43" results in the tropical Sun minus three signs in the southern hemisphere = 8s 19° 14' 13". The base <note>original: "bhuja"</note> is 2s 10° 14' 13". Here, the sign position is 2; therefore, among the segments 7, 5, 1, the elapsed segments are 7 and 5. Multiplying the remaining 20' 14" 13"' by the next segment 1, and dividing by 30, the quotient 00' 40" is added to the sum of the elapsed segments (7 + 5 = 12). The resulting southern deflection (equinoctial deflection) is 12° 40'. || 9 ||

->Now he describes the calculation of the latitudinal deflection:<-

> The deflection is obtained from the planet's position in the quadrant as stated before, divided by the latitude and the equinoctial shadow.
> North and south, in the east and west respectively; the two are combined or subtracted to find the result in the quadrants. || 10 ||

Now the connection. Now he speaks of the second deflection, its refinement, and its application. "From the quadrant..." etc. There, the method for calculating the hour angle <note>original: "nata"</note> at the middle of the eclipse is as follows: The mean Rahu <note>the ascending node</note> at the end of the phase should be subtracted from the mean Moon at the end of the phase. Thus, the "Moon minus Rahu" <note>original: "vyaguvidhu"</note> is calculated. Its base degrees should be determined. From this, the latitude <note>original: "śara"</note> is calculated using the rule "those degrees multiplied by the divisors," etc. The <term>visibility corrections: dṛkkarmakalā</term> should be calculated using the upcoming rule "from the three signs previously subtracted," etc. Thus, the Moon refined by the visibility correction is prepared. The rising sign <note>ascendant</note> is calculated from the Sun at the end of the phase. The time elapsed since moonrise is calculated using the rule from the upcoming chapter on planetary shadows, "the previous sight-correction of the celestial body," etc. The ascensional difference <note>original: "cara"</note> is calculated from the Moon refined by visibility corrections. Using the upcoming method "divided by twenty-four," etc., the true ascensional difference is made. From the true ascensional difference, the midday point is calculated. That becomes the Moon's midday. The hour angle is found from the difference between the elapsed time and the midday.

**Example of this:** Moon 2s 0° 9' 2". Rahu 7s 28° 32' 18". Moon minus Rahu 6s 2° 48' 44". Its base degrees are 1° 48' 54". The latitude is South 2° 50'. The Moon without the sign-indicator is 1s 10° 9' 2". From this, the declination is South 4° 36' 59". The terrestrial latitude is South 28° 26' 43". From the refinement of these two, the southern hour angle degrees are 30° 2' 49". From this, the visibility correction minutes are additive: 4' 58". The refined Moon is 2s 0° 16' 59". The length of the day is 26.92. The time of the end of the phase is 40.48. The ghatikas <note>units of 24 minutes</note> elapsed since sunset are 15.36. The Sun at the end of the phase is 8s 0° 12' 6". The remaining time is 116. The ascendant is 4s 18° 14' 54". The remaining time for the visibility-corrected Moon is 119. The elapsed time of the ascendant—the sum of these is 188. Adding Cancer (352) and Leo (349) gives 879. Divided by sixty, it is 14.39. Subtracting nine seconds, the time elapsed since moonrise is 14.36. The northern ascensional difference from the visibility-corrected Moon in ghatikas etc. is 1.54. The latitude in digits is 2.90. Multiplied by the equinoctial shadow (9.49), it is 16.10. Divided by 24, the result in minutes is South 0.40. Because the latitude is south, the ascensional difference ghatikas are refined by this, becoming the true northern ascensional difference ghatikas 1.53.20. Adding fifteen ghatikas to these, the Moon's midday is 16.53. Because this process is tedious and the difference is small, it should be understood that the Sun's midnight is the same as the Moon's midday. The desired time 14.36 subtracted from the Moon's midday results in 2.17, the eastern hour angle. When the elapsed time is subtracted from the midday, it is the eastern hour angle. In the reverse subtraction, it becomes the western hour angle. This is the primary method for calculating the hour angle at the end of the phase in a lunar eclipse. Alternatively, one can calculate it from the Sun's night-half after sunset at the end of the phase...
