# Commentary on the Mahā-lāghava

Midday is the point from which "Nata" <note>hour angle or zenith distance</note> is measured. From midday until midnight is the first half of the night; from midnight until midday is the western half. The definitions of East and West are to be understood as reversed in a solar eclipse compared to a lunar eclipse.

As it is said:
> From the middle of the day until the end of the third part <note>sunset</note>, they call it the Eastern hemisphere.
> From then until the end of the day <note>sunrise</note> is the Western hemisphere for the Moon; for the Sun, these are reversed during an eclipse.

Thus, the calculated Middle-Nata is East 2;27. This is divided by "the senses" <term>Vishaya: the number 5</term>. The result in signs is 0. The remainder 2;27 is multiplied by thirty, giving 60;81;0. Dividing the lower part by sixty, the result added to the high part becomes 73;30. Again dividing by 5, the result is 14 degrees. The remainder 3;30 multiplied by sixty and divided by five gives 42 minutes. The remainder multiplied by sixty and divided by five gives 1 second. Thus, the result in signs etc. is 0;14;42;1. Then, as previously stated in the rule "the sum of the sine of the latitude and the ascensional difference," the motion should be calculated using the "mountain-arrow-moon" <term>157</term> parts of the earth's radius. Here, there is no correction for the precession of the equinoxes. He states the result:

The deflection <note>Valana</note> divided by five becomes North or South. When? When the Nata is respectively East or West. The meaning is: if the Nata is East, the deflection is North; if the Nata is West, the deflection is South. The "culture" <note>Samskriti: algebraic combination</note> of both deflections—addition if in the same direction, subtraction if in different directions—that combination divided by "the flavors" <term>Rasa: the number 6</term> gives the "Valana-steps" <note>Valanānghraya</note>.

The result from the Middle-Nata divided by five is 0;14;42;1. From this, the deflection is 3;26;48. Multiplied by the "Palabhā" <note>equinoctial shadow</note> of 6;49, it becomes 19;43. Divided by five, the resulting deflection is North 3;56, because the Nata was East. The previously calculated deflection was North 2;47. The combination of both is 6;36. Divided by six, the Valana-steps are North 1;6.

## Now, the method for knowing the Nata to calculate deflection when the eclipse begins at sunrise or ends at sunset:

> If the contact etc. of the Moon occurs when the day is remaining or has passed, the difference between that and the midday is the Nata. For the Sun, it is the half-night minus the remaining night. These are respectively the East and West Nata for the sake of establishing the deflection.

If the contact etc. <note>contact, middle, or separation</note> of the Moon occurs when the day is remaining, or when the day has passed. By "etc." we mean the middle of the eclipse and the liberation <note>end</note>. When the Moon rises eclipsed in the evening or sets eclipsed in the morning: whatever ghatikas <note>units of 24 minutes</note> remain in the day or have passed, the difference between that and the midday <note>Dyudala</note> must be calculated. That is the East or West Nata. If time remains in the day, it is East Nata; if time has passed, it is West Nata. For the Sun, if contact occurs when the night is remaining or passed: the Sun is eclipsed at sunrise if the night is remaining, and eclipsed at sunset if the night has passed. Whatever portion of the night remains or has passed at contact, that is subtracted from the "night-segment" <note>Nishāshakala: half-night</note>. The remainder is the East or West Nata for the sake of establishing the deflection. In cases other than these definitions, the Nata is calculated as "passed or remaining is East." || 10 ||

-> The Madhuri Explanation <-

Now = thereafter. From the Middle-Nata = the Nata at the time of the middle of the eclipse. From the result of dividing by the "senses" <note>5</note> = from the signs etc. divided by five. As stated = using the full method described. The deflection, brought by the "Pala" = multiplied by the equinoctial shadow. Divided by the "Aksas" <note>5</note>. During the time of East or West Nata. Respectively = in order. North-South = the directions. The deflection = the latitudinal deflection <note>Aksha-valana</note>. Here = in the calculation of the eclipse time. Divided by "the flavors" <note>6</note>. The combination of both = the combination of the ayana (precessional) and aksha (latitudinal) deflections. The definition of "Samskara" <note>combination</note> is: addition in the same direction, subtraction in different directions. The steps = the quarters of the deflection. || 10 ||

## The Mathematical Proof:

Let the Nata-ghatikas = Na.Gha. According to the statement in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The definitive ancient Indian astronomical text</note>: "The sine of the latitudinal deflection is the sine of the latitude multiplied by the sine of the Nata..."

Sine of Latitudinal Deflection = (Sine of Latitude × Sine of Nata) / **...................(1)**

# Chapter on the Authority of Lunar Eclipses || 5 ||

$\because$ The degrees of zenith distance = <term>Nata-ghati</term><note>The time elapsed since the planet was at the meridian, measured in ghatis (1 ghati = 24 minutes).</note> $\times$ 6. Therefore, the degrees of zenith distance in signs and degrees = (Nata-ghati $\times$ 6) / 30 = Nata-ghati / 5. The sine of the zenith distance = Sine (Nata-ghati / 5) $\dots$ (a). By the proportion of the terrestrial sphere, the Sine of Latitude = (Radius $\times$ Equinoctial Shadow) / <term>Hypotenuse of the Shadow</term><note>The hypotenuse of a 12-digit gnomon and its equinoctial shadow.</note> = (120 $\times$ Equinoctial Shadow) / 13 $\dots\dots\dots$ (b).

Now, by substituting equations (a) and (b) into equation (1), the Sine of Latitude Deflection =

((Sine (Nata-ghati / 5)) $\times$ (Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ 120) / 13. Therefore, the degrees of deflection = [((Sine (Nata-ghati / 5)) / (Radius $\times$ 2)] $\times$ [(Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ 120 $\times$ 6) / 13] =

[((Sine (Nata-ghati / 5) $\times$ Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ 120 $\times$ 6 $\times$ Sine of Maximum Declination)] / [120 $\times$ 13 $\times$ 2 $\times$ Sine of Maximum Declination]. If this is the deflection for the total degrees, then for the lunar disk which consists of 32 minutes, the resulting degrees of deflection on the lunar sphere =

[(Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ 120) / (13 $\times$ 48)] $\times$ [(Sine (Nata-ghati / 5) $\times$ 6 $\times$ Sine of Maximum Declination $\times$ 32) / (120 $\times$ 2 $\times$ 360)] = (Equinoctial Shadow $\times$ Precessional Deflection) / 5.

$\because$ Since it was previously multiplied by six and then divided by six, it remains unchanged; thus, it is proven. || 10 ||

Thus, by dividing the <term>Madhyanata</term><note>The mean hour angle or time from the meridian.</note> time by 6, the resulting value in signs and degrees is used to find the deflection as per the previous method. Multiply this by the <term>Palabha</term><note>The length of the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox.</note> and divide by 6; the result is the North or South Latitude Deflection depending on whether the object is East or West of the meridian. By refining these deflections (adding them if in the same direction and subtracting if in opposite directions) and dividing by 6, the "Deflection-Digit" (<term>Valanangri</term>) is obtained. || 10 ||

**Example—** True Sun 10s 28° 36' 30", Precession 21° 37' 43", Mid-day 14:43, Mid-night 15:37. The difference between mid-day and the middle of the eclipse is 28;0;0 as before. Therefore, dividing the hour angle by 5 gives the result in signs and degrees as 5s 18° 0' 0". Treating this as the <term>Sayana</term><note>The longitude including the correction for the precession of the equinoxes.</note> Sun, its <term>Bhuja</term><note>The distance from the nearest equinoctial point.</note> is 0s 24° 0' 0". Thus, the upcoming segment is 7; multiplying the remainder 24° by 7 gives 168. Dividing this by 30 gives 5;36. Multiplying this by the Equinoctial Shadow (6) gives 33;36. Dividing by 5 gives 6;43, which is the North Latitude Deflection. Because the Precessional Deflection is 12;40 and the Latitude Deflection is 6;43 in opposite directions, their difference is 5;57. Dividing this by 6 gives the South "Deflection-Digit" (<term>Valanangri</term>) as 00;59. || 10 ||

Now, he speaks of the directions of the first contact and other phases—

->Multiply the half-sum of the diameters by the deflection and divide by sixty; the square root of that... the directions of the obscured portion are stated. To the left or right, North or South, apply the deflection-digits to the digits of the eclipse; this gives the direction at the middle of the eclipse, or the remainder of the total obscuration. || 11 ||<-

<header>With the Commentary on the Mahālaghava—</header>

Now he describes the "total obscuration" and the "steps of total obscuration." **By half the sum of the diameters**, etc. From the **product of sixty and the obscuration** <note>original: "kha-shad-ghna" (60 multiplied)</note> divided by the **half-sum of the diameters**; the square root of that result provides the **directional steps** <note>term: angri (literally 'foot' or 'step', here referring to a specific angular unit or coordinate for mapping the eclipse)</note> of the obscured portion. Now, if it is a total obscuration, then that value increased by **one and a half** (1;30) is said to be the **directional steps of the total obscuration**.

**Example:** The obscuration <note>term: grāsa (the portion of the orb swallowed/obscured)</note> is 16;48. Multiplied by sixty: 1008. Divided by the half-sum of the diameters 19;38, the result is 51;20. The square root of this is 7;9, which are the **steps of the obscured portion**. The total obscuration is 51;41; adding one and a half (1;30) results in 7;11, the **steps of the total obscuration**.

Now, with half a verse, he explains the knowledge of the direction of the middle of the eclipse. **Clockwise and counter-clockwise**, etc. A desired circle should be drawn and marked with the directions. There, from the **direction of the latitude** <note>term: śara (arrow/latitude of the planet)</note>, one should apply the directional steps arising from the southern or northern deflection <note>term: valana (variation/deflection)</note> clockwise or counter-clockwise. Here, within each direction, four steps are to be known. If the steps arising from deflection are southern, then from the direction of the latitude, they should be applied **clockwise** (in the natural order). If they are northern, then from the direction of the latitude, they should be applied **counter-clockwise** (reverse order). A mark should be made there. In that direction, the **middle of the eclipse** occurs. In the opposite direction—facing the middle of the eclipse—is the total obscuration. The remainder is to be known as the remainder of the eclipse. || 11 ||

->### Madhurī Commentary<-

**From the product of sixty and the obscuration** = from the multiplication of sixty and the measure of the obscuration; **divided by the half-sum of the diameters** = divided by half the sum of the eclipsed and eclipsing orbs; **the root** = the square root; then **the directional steps** = the steps in the direction of the obscuration; **are said** = are stated. **From the difference of their halves** = from half the difference of the eclipsed and eclipsing orbs; **from the total obscuration** = from the full eclipse; **the steps arising from total obscuration** = the steps in the direction of the total eclipse; are stated. Now, **from the direction of the latitude** = from the direction of the "arrow" (latitude); **the steps arising from southern or northern deflection** = the steps of the north-south deflection; **respectively clockwise and counter-clockwise** = in direct and inverse order; **one should apply** = should perform the placement; then the **middle of the planet** = the middle of the eclipse period occurs. In the **other direction** = in the different direction; the **total obscuration** = the full eclipse, or the **remainder** = the remaining measure of the orb occurs. || 11 ||

->### Here is the Proof:<-

Since there are 8 directional steps, in place of the square of the directions (64), the Teacher has taken **60** due to the relative scale. Therefore, if for an obscuration equal to the half-sum of the diameters one obtains the square of the directions (60), then by proportion, what would the square of the steps be for the desired obscuration? The square root of this will indeed be the directional step of the desired obscuration. The steps for total obscuration are to be calculated; there, the measure of the steps for total obscuration comes close to the measure of the total obscuration plus one and a half. Enough with useless effort; the point is proven. || 11 ||

Multiplying the obscuration by 60 and dividing by the half-sum of the diameters, the square root of the quotient is the <term>grāsāṅghri</term> (obscuration-step). And by adding 1;30 to the total obscuration, the total obscuration-step is found. When the direction of deflection is south or north, by applying the deflection-steps from the direction of the latitude—clockwise and counter-clockwise respectively—the middle of the eclipse is found. And in the reverse direction, the total obscuration or the orb-remainder is found. || 11 ||

**Example:** Obscuration measure 5;38 multiplied by 60 is 338. The sum of the Moon's orb 11;22 and the Earth's shadow 29;8 is 40;30; its half is 20;15. Dividing 338 by 20;15 (converted to 1215 minutes) gives a quotient of 10;56, the square root of which is 3;22, the deflection-step. Because it was previously inclined, apply this from the direction of the latitude in a clockwise order. Adding 1;30 to the total obscuration 1;40, the total obscuration-step becomes 3;10. || 11 ||

->### Now he describes the knowledge of the directions of contact and immersion:<-

> From the middle, with the steps of the obscured portion, forward and backward in the opposite direction, are the contact and immersion of the Moon.

From the point of total obscuration, by the quarters of the obscured portion applied to the west and east, the immersion and emersion of the Moon occur. || 12 ||

Now he describes the knowledge of the directions for the first contact, last contact, immersion, and emersion. "From the middle" means from the direction of the middle of the eclipse. By the quarters of the obscured portion applied to the east and west, the first and last contacts of the Moon occur. This means that from the middle of the eclipse, the contact is at the east and the release (last contact) is at the west. For the "hot-rayed one" <note>the Sun</note>, it is the opposite: the release is at the east and the contact is at the west. "From the total obscuration" means from the point of total darkness, by the quarters of the total obscuration applied to the west and east, the stages called immersion <term>sammīlana: the moment the body is fully covered</term> and emersion <term>unmīlana: the moment it begins to reappear</term> occur. From the point of total obscuration, immersion is toward the west and emersion is toward the east. The opposite of this <note>for the Sun</note> would be immersion in the east and emersion in the west. Here the Teacher <note>Ganesha Daivajna, the author</note> mentions that a total solar eclipse may occasionally occur. || 12 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary —

From the middle = from the middle of the eclipse; by the quarters of the obscured parts = by the quarters in the direction of the eclipse; East = in the eastern direction; West = in the western direction; of the Moon = of the lunar orb; the first and last contacts occur. For the hot-rayed one = for the Sun; it is reversed = the contacts are opposite to the Moon. From the total obscuration = from the point of total darkness; applied = performed; by the quarters of total obscuration = by the quarters in the direction of total eclipse; West and East; of the Moon; immersion and emersion occur. || 12 ||

### The Mathematical Proof —

In a lunar eclipse, the Moon is the body to be obscured and the Earth's shadow is the obscurer. Because the body to be obscured <note>the Moon</note> moves eastward, the Moon naturally enters the Earth's shadow from the eastern side. Therefore, the Moon's first contact is in the east and its release is in the west. As stated by Bhaskara <note>the famous 12th-century astronomer Bhaskaracharya</note>:

> "The Moon, traveling eastward, enters the interior of the Earth's shadow..."

All of this is perfectly clear; why "grind the already ground flour" <note>an idiom meaning to repeat the obvious</note>? Everything is easily understood. || 12 ||

The first contact and release of the Moon occur respectively in the east and west directions at a distance equal to the quarters of the eclipse from the middle point. For the Sun, the contact and release are in the opposite directions. And from the point of total obscuration, immersion and emersion occur in the west and east directions respectively. || 12 ||

Composed by Yugeshwara. Commentary in Sanskrit by Kapileshwara.
In this chapter on Lunar Eclipses, the 'Madhuri' commentary reaches completion. || 6 ||

Here, the assumed nonagesimal is 8s 2° 46' 17" and the Sun is 8s 5° 26' 26". Their difference is 0s 2° 40' 9". From this, the parallax is known to be negative. At that corrected end of the lunar day, the middle of the eclipse occurs; thus, the corrected end of the phase is 12;53. || 1-2 ||

<header>Chapter 6: On the Authority of Solar Eclipses</header>

In the *vitribha* <note>the nonagesimal, or the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> = at the nonagesimal degree, respectively, in the *tithi* <note>lunar day</note> = at the lunar day, the addition or subtraction of the parallax (*lambana*) should be performed. If the nonagesimal is greater than twelve <note>referring to signs or specific arc measurements</note>, the parallax is added; if the nonagesimal is less than twelve, the parallax is subtracted from the lunar day. This is the meaning. || 1-2 ||

->Here is the mathematical proof:<-

Let the mean zenith distance = **n**, and the difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun = **vi-am**. Then—

> "Multiply the difference between the Sun and the nonagesimal by one hundred and forty, and subtract the square of that difference.
> Divide this by one hundred; this is designated as the dividend (*bhajya*). Then, take the square of the mean zenith distance multiplied by three.
> Divide that by nine hundred and sixty-eight, and add eleven; this becomes the divisor (*hara*).
> Divide the dividend by the divisor; the resulting quotient in *ghatis* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and so on is the clear parallax."

According to the method stated in the *Karana-Rahasya* <note>a "Secret of Astronomical Calculation" text</note>, the parallax in *ghatis* =

The reasoning for addition and subtraction is easily understood through the method of Bhaskara <note>referring to Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> starting with "When the Sun is less than that or more than that..." and so on. At the end of the new moon (*amanta*), the longitudinal difference between the line of sight of an observer at the Earth's center and an observer on the Earth's surface is called *lambana* (parallax). In a solar eclipse, because of the difference in the orbits of the obscured (Sun) and the obscurer (Moon), the observer at the Earth's center sees the Sun covered by the lunar disk at the exact moment of the new moon; however, at that same time, the observer on the Earth's surface sees the Moon displaced (parallactically) in its own orbit. Therefore, the parallax in the Moon's orbit is the interval between the lines of sight from the Earth's center and the Earth's surface passing through the Sun's disk; <unclear>parallax is meaningful because the Moon is separated by such a difference in the lines of sight...</unclear>

# On the Ease of the Lati Method —
<page-num>120</page-num>

That is remembered as parallax. In the lunar eclipse, however—because the earth's shadow <note>the obscurer</note> and the moon <note>the obscured</note> are at the same distance from the earth's center, observers at the center of the earth and on the surface see the moon eclipsed by the earth's shadow at the same time. Therefore, it is established that there is no parallax in a lunar eclipse. || 1-2 ||

The zenith distance is found by the combination <note>samskara</note> of the declination of the nonagesimal <note>vitribhalagna: the point 90 degrees behind the rising sign</note> at the time of the new moon and the local latitude. 
If the 12th part of the square of this value is greater than 2, then subtract 2 from the square, add half of the remainder to the square, and add 12 to find the divisor <note>hara</note>. If the square is less than 2, simply add the square to 12 to find the divisor. 
Subtract one-tenth of the degrees of difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun from 14; multiply the remainder by that same tenth part, and divide by the aforementioned divisor. The result is the parallax <note>lambana</note> in units of ghatis <note>1 ghati = 24 minutes</note> and so on. 
If the nonagesimal is greater or less than the Sun, add or subtract the parallax from the time of the new moon <note>amanta ghati</note> respectively to find the corrected time of conjunction. || 1-2 ||

Calculation for a solar eclipse on Wednesday, the 15th day of the dark fortnight of the month of Agrahayana, Samvat 1667, Shaka 1532 <note>December 1610 CE</note>, during the Mula lunar mansion (51;12). 
Year-count: 90; Cycles: 8; Intercalary month: 1; Omitted lunar days: 15; Total elapsed days <note>ahargana</note>: 1005. 
Mean Sun at sunrise: 8s 5° 39' 25"; Moon: 8s 5° 17' 33"; Lunar Apogee: 8s 17° 7' 21"; Rahu <note>Ascending Node</note>: 2s 11° 41' 59". 
Adjusted for the time 12;36 ghatis: Sun: 8s 5° 51' 50"; Moon: 8s 3° 56' 34"; Apogee: 8s 17° 8' 45"; Rahu: 2s 11° 41' 19".

True Sun: 8s 5° 25' 57" with a daily motion of 61' 15". From this, the True Moon: 8s 5° 20' 41" with a motion of 726' 30". 
Adding the correction for the new moon (0;26) to the time 12;36 gives the time of conjunction as 13;2. 
At the moment of conjunction: True Sun: 8s 5° 26' 25"; Moon: 8s 5° 26' 20"; and Rahu: 2s 11° 41' 18".

The Ascendant <note>lagna</note> at conjunction: 11s 2° 46' 17"; the Nonagesimal <note>vitribhalagna</note>: 8s 2° 46' 17". 
Its southern declination is 23° 38' 10" and the southern latitude is 25° 26' 42". Their sum <note>samskara</note> is 49° 4' 52". 
The 22nd part of this is 2° 13' 51", the square of which is 4;58. 
Since this is greater than two: (4;58) - (2;00) = 2;58. 
Adding half the remainder (1;29) to the sum of the square and twelve (16;58) results in a divisor <note>hara</note> of 18;27.

Sun (8s 5° 26' 25") <note>difference</note> Nonagesimal (8s 2° 46' 17") = 2° 40' 8". 
One-tenth of this (0;16) subtracted from 14 leaves 13;44. 
Multiplying 13;44 by that tenth part (0;16) gives 3;39. 
Dividing this by the divisor 18;27 gives the parallax in time as 0;11 ghatis. 
Since the nonagesimal is less than the Sun, subtracting the parallax 0;11 from the conjunction time 13;4 results in the parallax-corrected conjunction time of 12;53. || 1-2 ||

->Now he describes the correction for parallax in latitude:<-

> Parallax multiplied by thirteen gives the minutes of arc; this is added to or subtracted from the moon's node like the lunar day. From this comes the latitude. 
> Then, parallax multiplied by six gives the degrees; with these, the nonagesimal is adjusted, and from that, the zenith distance is found again. || 3 ||

Now he describes the correction for parallax in latitude. "Multiplied by thirteen" etc. 
The parallax 0;11 multiplied by thirteen becomes 2' 23" of arc. 
The node <note>drgyu</note> is 9s 23° 42' 57". 
Since the parallax was subtracted from the lunar day, it is also subtracted from the node; thus the parallax-corrected node is 9s 23° 42' 45". 
Its sine-arc is 6s 17° 16'. From the rule "multiplied by the given degrees" etc., the latitude <note>shara</note> is produced as 9' 54". 
Because the Sun (minus Rahu) is in the northern hemisphere, the parallax is northern. 
0;11 multiplied by six becomes 1° 6' in degrees. <gloss>The nonagesimal is placed separately</gloss> <unclear>illegible</unclear> because the parallax is negative, it is subtracted accordingly.

### The Madhuri Commentary—

The product of the three-digit parallax <note>original: "trikunidhanavilambanam"</note> equals the product of thirteen and the parallax; these are the minutes of arc <term>kalā: 1/60th of a degree</term>. Just like the correction for a lunar day <term>tithi</term>, the Sun minus the ascending node <term>vyagu: the Rahu-less Sun</term> should be increased or decreased by these minutes of parallax. From this adjusted value, the celestial latitude <term>śara: literally 'arrow'</term> is to be calculated. **"This is the meaning,"** <insert>of the rule</insert>. Then, the parallax multiplied by six results in degrees. By adding or subtracting these degrees to the nonagesimal <term>vitribha-lagna: the point 90 degrees behind the rising point</term>, the zenith distance <term>natāṃśa</term> is to be derived.

### Here is the Mathematical Proof:

Let the parallax in time (ghatis, etc.) = *ghalaṃ*, and the motion of the Moon with the node = *sa.caṃ.ga*. At the moment of the new moon, the Sun and Moon are equal in signs, etc.; therefore, Sun - Node = Moon - Node. Since the node's cycle is subtracted, the Sun minus the node becomes the argument for latitude. Now, by the proportion of motion, the minutes of parallax are:
(Moon's motion × parallax in time) / 60 = (790 × *ghalaṃ*) / 60 = 13 × *ghalaṃ* (approximately).
Again, by the proportion of degrees, the degrees of parallax are:
(360° × *ghalaṃ*) / 60 ghatis = 6 × *ghalaṃ*.
The reasoning for the correction is clear to those who know the sphere <term>golavid: an astronomer/cosmographer</term>. Thus, it is proven.

Multiplying the parallax by 13 gives the minutes of arc. Like a lunar day correction, this should be added to or subtracted from the "Rahu-less Sun" to calculate the celestial latitude. Multiplying the parallax by 6 gives the degrees. Depending on whether the parallax is positive or negative, this should be added to or subtracted from the nonagesimal to calculate the zenith distance (via the adjustment of declination and latitude).

### Example:

Multiplying 10 and the parallax 00 | 11 gives 2 minutes and 33 seconds. Subtracting this from the Rahu-less Sun 5 | 23 | 44 | 17 (since the parallax is negative) results in the parallax-adjusted Sun 5 | 23 | 42 | 44. From its base sine 6 | 17 | 15, using the method **"multiplied by that, divided by the gnomon, divided by seven,"** etc., the northern latitude comes to 0 | 54 because the Sun is in the northern hemisphere. Similarly, multiplying 6 and the parallax 0 | 21 | 1 gives 1 degree and 6 minutes. Subtracting this from the nonagesimal 8 | 2 | 46 | 17 (due to negative parallax) gives 8 | 1 | 40 | 17. By adjusting its southern declination 23 | 34 | 35 with the latitude 25 | 26 | 42 (addition), the southern zenith distance becomes 49 | 1 | 17.

### Now, the method for calculating the parallax in latitude (nati):

> The zenith distance divided by ten, subtracted from eighteen, and multiplied by that same tenth part...
> Subtract that from six degrees plus eighteen minutes; those are the degrees.
> This is the parallax in latitude in its own direction; adjusted by this, the latitude in digits <term>aṅgula</term>
> becomes clear, from which the duration and obscuration of the eclipse are found. || 4 ||

Now he describes the calculation of the parallax in latitude <term>nati</term>. "The zenith distance..." etc. The zenith distance is 49 | 1 | 17. Divided by ten, the result is 4 | 55. Eighteen minus this result is 13 | 5. Multiplying this by the same 4 | 55 gives 64 | 11 minutes. Set these aside. These are then subtracted from six degrees plus eighteen minutes <note>original: "sadhṛtiliptaiḥ ṣaḍbhir"</note>. Specifically, from the six degrees increased by eighteen minutes, the result in minutes and seconds obtained from the rule "zenith distance divided by ten..." etc., should be subtracted <unclear>minutes</unclear> <note>Modern digital watermark obscures some characters</note> <unclear>zenith distance</unclear> six parts—

# Page 122
## In the *Laghiprahladaghava*—

One should be taken. When the result in minutes of arc <note>original: "kala"</note> exceeds sixty, then it is divided by sixty to get degrees. Here, 10 <note>likely referring to the divisor for zenith distance</note> should be subtracted from the degree position. By this, those values placed separately are the dividends; the result is the parallax in latitude <term>Nati: the shifting of the moon's apparent position due to the observer's location on Earth</term> in fingers <note>original: "angula"</note> and so on, in the direction of the zenith distance. The latitude <term>Shara: literally 'arrow', refers to the celestial latitude of the moon</term> in fingers, corrected by this, becomes the "clear" or corrected latitude. From this corrected latitude, the duration <note>sthiti</note>, the obscuration <note>chhanna</note>, and so on should be calculated as previously stated. The result in minutes is 64' 11". By this, these 6° 18' are reduced to 5° 3' 49". By this, the 64' 11" placed separately are divided; the result is the parallax in fingers, etc., which is 13;16 South. Because the zenith distance is South, the latitude in fingers corrected by the parallax becomes the clear South latitude: 2;52. By the rule "the motion multiplied by two," etc., the Sun's disk is 11;8, the Moon's disk is 9;49, and the semi-sum of the diameters <note>manaika-khanda</note> is 10;28. The magnitude of the eclipse <note>grasa</note> is 8;6.

Now, the calculation of the duration <note>sthityanayana</note>: The semi-sum of the diameters 10;28 is added to the latitude 2;52, totaling 13;20. This is multiplied by ten: 132;20. This is then multiplied by the magnitude 8;6, resulting in 1039;30. This is converted twice by sixty <note>standard sexagesimal calculation</note> to 37,432,200. Its square root is 32;54. This 32;54 is set aside. One-tenth of it, 3;17, is subtracted from the value set aside, leaving 26;52. Divided by the Moon's disk 9;49, the result is the duration in ghatikas <note>1 ghatika = 24 minutes</note> and so on: 2;44;4.

->The *Madhuri* Commentary<-

"Eighteen and the Moon <note>181</note> multiplied by the zenith distance degrees divided by ten..." = The zenith distance degrees divided by ten, subtracted from and multiplied by eighteen, should be "held separately." By six degrees and eighteen minutes reduced by that = by those six degrees with eighteen minutes of arc reduced by the value held separately, those same values = those held separately, are "attained" = divided. Then, in "its own direction" = the direction of the zenith distance, the "fingers etc." = starting with fingers, "parallax" <note>nati</note> occurs. "Corrected by this" = adjusted by the parallax, "it" = the mean latitude in fingers, becomes "clear" = the distinct "arrow" or latitude. "Here" = in a solar eclipse, "from this" = from the clear latitude, the "duration, obscuration, etc." = the duration, magnitude, and immersion should be known. || 4 ||

->Here is the Mathematical Proof<-

It is assumed that 3 minutes of arc <note>kala</note> = 1 finger <note>angula</note>. The maximum parallax in latitude <note>panaka</note> = 48' 45". The radius <note>trijya</note> = 120. The sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic point ninety degrees from the ascendant <term>Vitribha-nata-jya: the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal</term> at the end of the conjunction = the "special sine" <note>vijya</note>. The zenith distance of the nonagesimal = "vibham." Therefore—

> "The degrees of the arc and its complement, multiplied together and by 180, then divided by their own fourth part subtracted from 10125... those multiplied by the radius and divided, the result is the sine and cosine even without using sine tables."

According to this method by Shripati <note>an 11th-century astronomer</note>, the sine of the nonagesimal zenith distance = $\frac{( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD} \times \text{Radius}}{10125 - \frac{( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD}}{4}} =$

$\frac{( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD} \times 120}{40500 - ( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD}} = \frac{( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD} \times 120 \times 4}{40500 - ( 180 - \text{ZD} ) \text{ ZD}}$. Here, the divisor and dividend are reduced by a factor of one hundred, then the sine of the nonagesimal zenith distance becomes:

$\frac{( 18 - \frac{\text{ZD}}{10} ) \frac{\text{ZD}}{10} \times 120 \times 4}{405 - ( 18 - \frac{\text{ZD}}{10} ) \frac{\text{ZD}}{10}} ............... ( A )$

Furthermore, if the maximum parallax is obtained by the radius, then what is obtained by the desired sine of the nonagesimal zenith distance? By this proportion, the parallax in minutes = $\frac{\text{Max Parallax} \times \text{Sine of ZD}}{\text{Radius}} = \frac{( 48' 45" ) \times \text{Sine of ZD}}{120}$. This is divided by three...

# Chapter 6: On Solar Eclipses

Parallax in latitude <note>original: "nati"</note> in digits <note>original: "angula"</note> etc. = $\frac{48|5}{3} \times \frac{Sine\ of\ Zenith\ Distance}{120} = \frac{( 16|2 ) \times Sine\ of\ Zenith\ Distance}{120}$

Here, by substituting the form of the Sine of the Zenith Distance of the Nonagesimal <note>The "Nonagesimal" is the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant; its zenith distance determines the parallax in latitude.</note> (a), the Parallax in Latitude of the Nonagesimal in digits etc. =
$\frac{( 16|2 ) \times 4 \times (18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10} \times 120}{405 - (18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10} \times 120}$

= $\frac{( 64|8 ) \times (18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{405 - (18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}$ = $\frac{(18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{\frac{405}{64|8} - \frac{(18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{( 64|8 )}}$

= $\frac{(18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{\frac{24300}{3888} - \frac{(18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{3888}}$ = $\frac{(18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}{(6|25) - (18 - \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}) \frac{Zenith\ Dist.}{10}}$

---

->Due to the small difference [between values]. Thus, it is proven. || 4 ||<-

Divide the degrees of zenith distance <note>original: "natamsha"</note> by 10; subtract the quotient from 18 to find the remainder. Multiply this remainder by the quotient and place the result in two positions. Subtract the value in the first position from 6° 15'; divide the value in the second position by this remainder. The result will be the Parallax in Latitude <note>original: "nati"</note> in the direction of the zenith distance. By applying this correction to the celestial latitude <note>original: "shara"</note>, the corrected latitude <note>original: "spashta-shara"</note> is obtained. From this corrected latitude, one should calculate the duration <note>original: "sthiti"</note>, the magnitude of the eclipse <note>original: "grasa"</note>, and the end of the eclipse <note>original: "moksha"</note> etc., here in the context of a solar eclipse. || 4 ||

**Note** — In the first three verses, an ancient example of a solar eclipse was given; however, considering it particularly useful, a modern example of a solar eclipse is also written here.

**Example** — In the Shaka year 1863, Samvat 1998, Year 1941 AD, on the Sunday of the dark fortnight of the month of Ashvin, at the time of the New Moon <note>original: "amavasya"</note>: the time was 11 *ghatis* and 10 *palas* <note>Traditional units of time: 1 ghati = 24 minutes</note>. The Uttara Phalguni constellation <note>original: "nakshatra"</note> was at 35 *ghatis* 37 *palas*, and the Shubh Yoga was at 2 *ghatis* 56 *palas*. On this day, to observe the solar eclipse, using the method "Subtract the number of the Moon, the Vedas, and the King from the Shaka year and divide by the Lord" etc., the Cycle <note>original: "chakra"</note> was 38 and the Total Days <note>original: "ahargana"</note> were 1336. From this, the Mean Sun for that day was 5s 6° 37' 58", Mean Moon 5s 14° 56' 23", Lunar Apogee <note>original: "chandrocca"</note> 0s 0° 6' 40" 45"', and Mean Rahu <note>The ascending node of the moon</note> 4s 9° 2' 42".

Now, through all the calculations for the end of the New Moon <note>original: "amantakalika"</note> for the region of Mithila: True Sun 5s 4° 19' 38" with a daily motion of 58' 35"; True Moon 5s 4° 21' 59" with a daily motion of 790'; True Lunar Apogee 0s 6° 40' 45"; True Rahu 5s 9° 14' 38"; Precession of Equinoxes <note>original: "ayanansha"</note> 21° 38' 11" 34"'; the first Ascendant <note>original: "lagna"</note> at the end of the New Moon 7s 3° 8' 6"; the Meridian Ecliptic Point <note>original: "virahika"</note> 7s 15° 57'; and the Nonagesimal <note>original: "vittribhalagna"</note> 4s 4° 16'.

From the tropical <term>Sayana</term> sun with the precession removed <note>original: "Sayana Viraharka"</note> 4 | 24 | 46 | 17, and following the method of **"forty-eighty"** etc., the Northern declination <term>Kranti</term> is 13 | 28 | 39. The equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha</term> is 5 | 54. Multiplying this by 5 gives 29 | 30; subtracting its tenth part 2 | 57 results in the Southern latitude <term>Akshansha</term> of 26 | 33. Because the directions are different, the difference between the latitude and declination results in a Southern zenith distance <term>Natansha</term> of 12 | 4 | 21. Squaring its 22nd part 0 | 35 | 39 gives 0 | 21 | 10; adding 12 to this results in the divisor <term>Hara</term> 12 | 21 | 10. The difference between the nonagesimal <term>Vitribhalagna</term> 4 | 3 | 8 | 6 and the true Sun <term>Spashta Surya</term> 5 | 4 | 19 | 38 is 31 | 11 | 32 degrees. Dividing this by 10 gives a quotient <term>Labdhi</term> of 3 | 7. Subtracting this from 14 leaves a remainder of 10 | 53. Multiplying the quotient 3 | 7 by its tenth part results in 33 | 55 | 11; dividing this by the divisor <term>Hara</term> gives a negative quotient (since the nonagesimal is less than the Sun) for the parallax in longitude <term>Lamban</term> of 8 | 22 <term>Ghati</term> <note>A Ghati is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. Subtracting this parallax from the lunar day <term>Tithi</term> 11 | 10 results in the true time of conjunction <term>Amanta Ghati</term> 2 | 48. || 1-2 ||

Multiplying the parallax 8 | 22 by 13 gives 108 | 46 (in minutes etc.). Subtracting this from the Rahu-corrected longitude <term>Vyugu</term> results in the parallax-adjusted Rahu 0 | 1 | 16 | 24. From its base sine <term>Bhujansha</term> 1 | 16 | 24, and following the rule **"multiplied by thirty, divided by the gnomon..."** etc., the Northern celestial latitude <term>Shara</term> (since Rahu is in the Northern hemisphere) is 2 | 00 | 3 in digits <term>Angula</term>. Multiplying the parallax 8 | 22 by 6 gives 50 | 12 in degrees. Subtracting this from the nonagesimal 4 | 3 | 8 | 6 results in the parallax-adjusted nonagesimal 2 | 12 | 56 | 6. From its base sine 72 | 56 | 6, the Northern declination is 22 | 45 | 58. The difference between this and the Southern latitude 26 | 33 results in a Southern zenith distance of 3 | 47 | 52. || 3 ||

Dividing the Southern zenith distance 3 | 47 | 52 by 10 gives a quotient of 0 | 22 | 47. Subtracting this from 18 leaves a remainder of 17 | 37 | 13. Multiplying the quotient 0 | 22 | 47 by its tenth part gives 6 | 41 | 27 in minutes. Subtracting this from 6<gloss>°</gloss> 18<gloss>'</gloss> leaves a remainder of 6 | 11 | 33. Dividing the previous product by this remainder gives the Southern parallax in latitude <term>Nati</term> (as the zenith distance is South) of 1 | 3 digits. Subtracting this from the Northern celestial latitude 2 | 00 | 3 digits results in the true celestial latitude <term>Spashtashara</term> of 0 | 57 | 3 digits in the Northern direction.

Following the rule **"degrees from the motion of the sun and moon..."** etc., the solar disc <term>Bimba</term> is 10 | 43 digits and the lunar disc is 10 | 41 digits. Their semi-sum <term>Manaikyakhanda</term> is 10 | 42. Subtracting the true celestial latitude 0 | 57 | 3 from this gives the magnitude of the eclipse <term>Grasa</term> as 9 | 44 | 27 digits. Adding the semi-sum 10 | 42 and the true latitude gives 11 | 39 | 3. Multiplying this by 10 gives 116 | 30 | 30. Multiplying this again by the magnitude of the eclipse gives 1134 | 53 | 18. Taking the square root of this, 33 | 41, and subtracting its sixth part 5 | 37 leaves a remainder of 28 | 4. Dividing this by the lunar disc gives the duration of the eclipse <term>Sthiti</term> as 2 | 37 <term>Ghatis</term>. || 4 ||

# Chapter 6: On Solar Eclipses

->Chapter 6: On Solar Eclipses<-

Degrees: 16 | 24. The nonagesimal <note>The "vitribha" or the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note>: 8 | 2 | 56 | 17. Placed separately: 8 | 2 | 56 | 17. Subtracting one part: 7 | 16 | 22 | 17. In another place, adding it: 8 | 19 | 10 | 17. When calculating the contact (beginning), it is subtracted; for the release (end), it is added; thus the nonagesimals for contact and release are determined. In this manner, moving from the calculated end of the lunar day (tithi) by the duration of the half-duration (sthitighatika) to find the times of contact and release is taught for the sake of simplicity. However, this is somewhat approximate. Now, for the precise method: the Sun's position at the end of the tithi should be adjusted by the motion corresponding to the half-duration to find the Sun's position at contact and release. For contact, the motion is subtracted; for release, it is added. Thus, the middle of the conjunction (amavasya) is adjusted by the half-duration in one place (subtraction) to find the time of contact. In the other place, it is added to find the time of release. From these, the ascendant (lagna) should be calculated. Subtracting three signs from that gives the nonagesimals for contact and release. From these, the parallax (lambana) <note>The difference in the apparent position of the Sun as seen from the Earth's center versus the observer's location</note> must be calculated.

First, the parallax from the subtraction is calculated. Nonagesimal: 7 | 16 | 22 | 17. Its southern declination: 21 | 24 | 39. Adjusted by the latitude: 26 | 26 | 42, the resulting southern zenith distance is 46 | 51 | 21. Its double-sine part: 2 | 7. Squared: 4 | 28. Separately: 4 | 28. Minus two: 2 | 28. Halved: 1 | 14. Added to the separate value: 5 | 42. With twelve added, the divisor becomes 17 | 42. The Sun at the end of the phase: 8 | 6 | 26 | 21. Motion: 61 | 19. Adjusted by the half-duration 2 | 44, the Sun at contact becomes: 8 | 5 | 43 | 38. The nonagesimal at contact: 7 | 16 | 22 | 17. The difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun: 0 | 11 | 5 | 21. Its degrees: 11 | 5 | 21. Its tenth part: 1 | 5 | 6. Subtracted from fourteen: 12 | 54. These multiplied by ten: 22 | 59. Divided by the divisor 17 | 42, the resulting negative parallax in ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> is 1 | 17.

Next, the parallax for the time of release is calculated. The nonagesimal increased by those degrees: 8 | 19 | 10 | 17. Its southern declination: 23 | 42 | 28. Adjusted by latitude, the southern zenith distance is 49 | 9 | 10. Its double-sine part: 2 | 24. Squared: 4 | 59. Separately: 4 | 59. Minus two: 2 | 59. Halved: 1 | 29. Added to the separate value: 6 | 28. With twelve added, the divisor is 18 | 28. The Sun at the time of release: 8 | 6 | 29 | 12. The nonagesimal at release: 8 | 19 | 10 | 17. The difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun: 0 | 13 | 41 | 5. Its degrees: 13 | 41 | 5. Its tenth part: 1 | 22. Subtracted from fourteen: 17 | 16. Divided by the divisor, the resulting positive parallax in ghatikas is 0 | 56.

The middle of the conjunction is decreased and increased by the half-duration. Adjusted by those two parallaxes, the times of contact and release are found. The middle conjunction minus the half-duration, adjusted by the contact parallax, is the time of contact. The middle conjunction plus the half-duration, adjusted by the release parallax, is the time of release. Previously, the middle time of the conjunction adjusted by the middle parallax should be known; though not explicitly stated, this is understood by the wise. Middle conjunction: 13 | 4. Minus half-duration 2 | 44: 10 | 20. Adjusted by contact parallax 1 | 17, the time of contact is 9 | 3. Middle conjunction: 13 | 4. Plus half-duration 2 | 44: 16 | 48. Adjusted by release parallax 0 | 56, the time of release is 16 | 45.

->The Madhuri Commentary<-

The collection of duration = the duration multiplied by six, these are the degrees. Placed separately = placed in two ways. The nonagesimal = the nonagesimal ascendant. By those = by the degrees of duration multiplied by six, subtracted and added = having performed subtraction and addition. From these = from the subtraction and addition, those = the two parallaxes that exist. By them = by those two parallaxes, the middle conjunction decreased and increased by the duration = the middle conjunction minus and plus the duration ghatikas, adjusted = processed, "then," respectively = in order, these = these two, of contact and release = of the beginning and end of the eclipse, the times, they shall be. || 5 ||

->Rationale/Proof<-

From the two nonagesimal ascendants, which are the tithi minus and plus the duration, the two resulting parallaxes are applied to the tithi minus and plus the duration; these are the times of contact and release. <unclear>And thus, for the easy understanding of the student, the teacher has provided these two nonagesimal methods...</unclear>

The <term>Duration Ghatis</term> <note>Sanskrit: sthiti-ghati; the time from the start of the eclipse to the maximum point</note> are processed. Multiplied by six, they become the <term>Duration Degrees</term>. By subtracting these from the <term>Nonagesimal</term> <note>Sanskrit: vitribha-lagna; the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> at the moment of the new moon, the Nonagesimal for the moment of contact is found; by adding them, the Nonagesimal for the moment of liberation (end) is found. This is established. || 5 ||

By multiplying the <term>Duration</term> by 6, the result is in degrees. By subtracting and adding this to the <term>Nonagesimal</term>, one sequentially finds the <term>Nonagesimal</term> for the moment of contact and the moment of liberation. By calculating the <term>Parallax</term> <note>Sanskrit: lambana; the difference in the apparent position of the sun as seen from the Earth's surface vs. center</note> from this Nonagesimal and applying it to the middle time (minus the duration and plus the duration), the corrected clear time of contact and clear time of liberation are found. || 5 ||

**Example** — The <term>Duration Ghatis</term> are 2;37. Multiplying by 6 gives the degree value 15;42;00. Subtracting this from the <term>Nonagesimal</term> 4s 3° 8' 6" gives the contact <term>Nonagesimal</term> 3s 17° 26' 6". Adding it gives the liberation <term>Nonagesimal</term> 4s 18° 50' 6". From the contact <term>Nonagesimal</term>, the northern <term>Declination Degrees</term> <note>Sanskrit: krantyansha</note> are 22;42;28 and the southern <term>Latitude Degrees</term> <note>Sanskrit: akshansha</note> are 26;33;0; the difference results in the southern <term>Zenith Distance</term> <note>Sanskrit: natansha</note> of 3;50;32. Taking the 22nd part of this zenith distance (0;10;28), squaring it (1;49;33), and adding it to 12, the contact <term>Divisor</term> <note>Sanskrit: hara</note> becomes 13;49;33. The solar motion at the <term>New Moon</term> <note>Sanskrit: amanta</note> is 58;35; applying the negative <term>Motion Adjustment</term> <note>Sanskrit: chalana</note> for the duration of 2;37, the sun at contact is 5s 4° 17' 5". The difference between this and the contact <term>Nonagesimal</term> (3s 18° 2' 6") is 46;54;59. Taking the 10th part (4;39;29), subtracting it from 14 leaves 9;22;31. Multiplying the 10th part and dividing by the divisor, the resulting contact <term>Parallax</term> in Ghatis is 3;8. This parallax is negative (because the Nonagesimal is less than the Sun).

For the liberation <term>Nonagesimal</term>, the northern <term>Declination</term> is 15;26;58 and the southern <term>Latitude</term> is 26;33;0; the difference is the southern <term>Zenith Distance</term> 11;6;2. Its 22nd part is 0;30;16, its square is 00;15;16. Placing 00;15;16 in two places; since 1 does not subtract from 2, adding half (0;7;38) results in 0;22;54. Adding this to 12 gives the <term>Divisor</term> 12;22;54. With positive <term>Adjustment</term>, the clear Sun at liberation is 5s 4° 22' 11". The difference with the liberation <term>Nonagesimal</term> (4s 18° 14' 6") is 0s 16° 8' 5". Subtracting its tenth part (1;36;48) from 14 leaves 12;23;12. Multiplying the tenth part and dividing by the divisor 12;20;6, the result is a negative liberation <term>Parallax Ghati</term> of 1;37 (since the Sun is greater than the Nonagesimal).

Subtracting the <term>Duration</term> 2;37 from the <term>New Moon Ghati</term> 11;10 leaves 8;33; then subtracting the negative contact <term>Parallax</term> 3;8 gives the clear contact time of 5;25. Adding the duration to the new moon (13;47) and subtracting the liberation <term>Parallax</term> 1;37 gives the clear liberation time of 12;10. || 5 ||

# Chapter 6: On Solar Eclipses

The time of immersion <note>original: *sammīlana*, the moment totality begins</note> is found by subtracting the calculated value, and the time of emersion <note>original: *unmīlana*, the moment totality ends</note> is found by adding it. When the parallax <note>term: *lambana* | the apparent shift in position of a celestial body due to the observer's location</note> is applied to these, and combined with the half-duration of totality <note>original: *marda-ardha*</note>, the corrected immersion and emersion times for the middle of the eclipse are established. When the obscured portion <note>term: *grāsa* | literally "the bite" or magnitude of the eclipse</note> of the Sun or Moon is less than one digit <note>term: *aṅgula* | a standard unit of astronomical measurement, 1/12th of the diameter</note>, it should not be predicted <note>because it is too small to be seen by the naked eye</note>. In a lunar eclipse, the Moon appears smoky <note>original: *dhūmra*</note> when the eclipse is small, blackish-brown <note>original: *kṛṣṇa-piṅgala*</note> when half-eclipsed, and tawny or reddish-yellow <note>original: *piṅgala*</note> when fully eclipsed. Specifically: a small eclipse is smoky, a half eclipse is black, and a total eclipse is tawny. The Sun, however, always appears black in all stages of an eclipse. || 6 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

From the duration of totality (*marda*), using the stated method, the moments of immersion and emersion are determined. If the obscured portion (*grāsa*) of the Sun or Moon is less than one digit (*aṅgula*), it is "not to be declared" (not predictable). For the Moon, depending on whether the eclipse is a quarter, a half, or total, the colors are respectively: smoky (grey), black (dark), and tawny (yellowish-red). But the Sun (*arka*), in every type of eclipse, is certainly always black in color. || 6 ||

### The Rationale—

Since the interval between the middle of the eclipse and the moment of immersion is equal to half the duration of totality, and similarly the interval between the middle and emersion is equal to half the duration of totality, it is correct to say these times are derived from the half-duration. As for the colors, the reasoning is simple and follows the traditional authorities which state: "Even if a sixteenth part of the Moon is eclipsed, the nectar-rayed one appears smoky when the cover is slight," etc. || 6 ||

<note>The following paragraph is a Hindi translation of the preceding Sanskrit verses</note>
From the time of liberation <note>end of eclipse</note>, the immersion and emersion times will be found. Due to invisibility, one should not predict an eclipse of less than 1 digit. In small (one quarter), half, and total eclipses, the color of the Moon is respectively smoky (blackish), black, and yellow, while the color of the Sun is always black. || 6 ||

### Now, the calculation for the eclipse at a desired time—

> Multiply the desired time by two, then by the total obscured portion, and divide by the duration between the contact and the end. 
> Add half a unit to find the obscured portion of the Sun at the desired time. || 7 ||

Divide this by the difference in *ghatikas* <note>term: *ghatika* | a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> between the time of contact (9;3) and the time of liberation (16;54), which is 7;51. To the result (2;6), add half a unit (30 *vyaṅgulas*). The result (2;36) is the obscured portion of the Sun at the desired time. The remaining calculations for deflection <note>term: *valana* | the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note> and projection should be done as before. The Sun at the end of the lunar day <note>term: *tithi*</note> corrected by parallax (12;53) is 8s 9° 24' 14". Adding three signs: 11s 9° 26' 14". Adding the degrees of precession: 11s 23° 34' 14". From this, the southern deflection is calculated as 1;30. The middle of the eclipse is 12;53. Midday is 13;3. The "zenith distance" <note>term: *nata*</note> is 0;10 East. From the latitude and other factors, the deflection is 0;14. Multiplied by the equinoctial shadow (5;46) and divided by five, the northern deflection is 0;16. Because it is East, the sum of both is 1;14. Divided by six, the southern deflection is 0;12. The obscured portion 8;6 multiplied by sixty is 486. ## The Madhurī Commentary—

**Doubled** = multiplied by two; **multiplied by the obscuration** = multiplied by the magnitude of the eclipse; **desired** = the desired time in ghatis <note>A ghati is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and so on; **divided by the duration between contact and separation** = divided by the internal ghatis between the moments of first contact and final liberation; **increased by half a unit** = along with a measure of thirty *vyangulas* <note>A vyangula is a fractional unit of a digit/angula; here referring to a specific mathematical offset</note>; **then** at the **desired** = intended; **time** = moment; of the **Sun** = the solar; **obscuration** = the magnitude of the eclipse; **one should know** = it is to be understood. || 7 ||

## Here is the Proof:

Let the value of the half-duration be = *sthi-ardha*; the value of the total duration be = *sthi-gha*; the magnitude of the eclipse = *grā*; and the desired ghatis = *i-dha*. Therefore, by proportion, the desired eclipse magnitude = <gloss>magnitude × desired ghatis / half-duration</gloss>. When the divisor and dividend are both multiplied by two, then the desired magnitude = <gloss>magnitude × desired ghatis × 2 / total duration</gloss>. Here, due to the gradual variation, the Teacher <note>Referring to the original author, Ganesha Daivajna</note> has added half a digit, which is thus proven. || 7 ||

By dividing the product of the desired ghatis, 2, and the eclipse magnitude by the difference in ghatis between the time of contact and the time of liberation, and adding <gloss>1/2</gloss> digit to the quotient, the desired solar eclipse magnitude at that specific time is obtained. || 7 ||

**Example**—Multiplying the product of the assumed desired ghatis (2) and 2, which is 4, by the eclipse magnitude of 9;44,27, we get 38;57,48. Dividing this by 6;45 (the difference between the contact time of 5;25 and the liberation time of 12;10), the quotient is 5;46. Adding 30 *vyangulas* to this, the eclipse magnitude in digits at the desired time of 2 ghatis is 6;16. || 7 ||

> This commentary composed by Yugeshwara and refined by Kapileshwara,
> Known as 'Madhurī', is now completed in this chapter on Solar Eclipses. || 6 ||

Thus ends the Chapter on Solar Eclipses in the first half of the *Madhurī* commentary—which contains new examples and proofs—composed by Pandit Shri Yugeshwara Sharma, son of Pandit Shri Darshana Sharma (a resident of Mijapur village in the Darbhanga district), Head Teacher of the Sanskrit School in Madhesara village in the Muzaffarpur district, and holder of the titles *Jyotishacharya* <note>Master of Astrology/Astronomy</note>, *Jyotistirth*, and *Ayurvedacharya* <note>Master of Ayurveda</note>. || 6 ||

## Chapter 7: On the Group of Months <note>Sanskrit: Masaganadhikara. This chapter deals with calculating time in lunar months for the purpose of predicting eclipses.</note>

### First, the author states the reason for composing this section:

Now, from the group of months, I shall describe a very simple method for the accomplishment of the two eclipses <note>Solar and lunar eclipses</note>; and for the sake of demonstrating the specific wonders of the true Sun, the Node, the lunar days, the dimensions of the celestial bodies, and the magnitude of the obscuration. || 1 ||

Now he speaks of bringing forth the festival <note>The conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon</note> from the group of months. "Now" means following the previous section. From the group of months, by a very light or simple process, the "accomplishment" or calculation of the two eclipses is achieved. For that purpose, I speak of the true Sun, the Node <note>Vipata: the ascending node of the moon, Rahu</note>, and the lunar days <note>Tithis</note>, as well as the "bodies" (the diameters of the discs), the "obscuration" (the extent of the eclipse), and so on, to show the specific wonders. By this, the wonder of the calculators <note>astronomers</note> is produced. || 1 ||

->Madhuri Commentary<-

"Now" = after the statement of the first half; "for specific wonder" = for the sake of greater amazement; "for the accomplishment of the two eclipses" = for the purpose of calculating the eclipses of the Sun and Moon; "by a very simple process" = by a concise and easy method; "from the group of months" = from the collection of months; "true Sun, Node, and lunar days" = the true positions of the Sun, the Moon's node, and the lunar dates; "body" = their discs; "obscuration etc." = the eclipse magnitude and so on; "I shall describe" = I, the author, say. || 1 ||

*I am describing the true Sun, the Node, the lunar day, the disc, and the magnitude of the eclipse etc., through the group of months in a simple manner for the sake of specific wonder and for the calculation of both (Solar and Lunar) eclipses.* || 1 ||

### Now he states the Epochal Constants <term>Kshepaka: a constant value added to a calculation to adjust it to a specific starting date or epoch</term> for these:

The Sun's constant in signs and so on is zero, four, and twenty-one. For the Node, it is eleven, seven, and eighteen. For the "Circle" <note>The Moon's anomaly</note>, it is zero, fourteen, and fifteen. For the weekday and others, it is two and forty-eight and three-quarters. || 2 ||

Now he states the constants. "The constant..." etc. The meaning is clear. || 2 ||

->Madhuri Commentary<-

In "Sun" = for the Sun; "zero" = 0; "four" = 4; "twenty-one" = 21. In "Node" = for Rahu; "eleven" = 11; "seven" = 7; "eighteen" = 18. Thus, in "Circle" = for the Moon's anomaly; "zero" = 0; "fourteen" = 14; "fifteen" = 15. This is the "constant" in "signs and so on" <note>Signs, degrees, and minutes</note>. Now, "two and forty-eight and three-quarters" = 48:45—this is the constant for the "weekday and others" = for the lunar day and the day of the week. || 2 ||

### Here is the Proof:

Just as at the beginning of the Shaka year 1444 <note>1522 CE, the epoch of this text</note> the constants were read as "Eleven, nine, four..." etc. for the Moon, similarly, having brought the planets to the time of the New Moon, he established them as "constants." There, the Node constant is the Moon's constant minus the Rahu constant. He referred to the Moon's mean anomaly by the name "Circle" <note>Vritta</note>. Therefore, the Sun's constant <insert>and</insert> the Moon's constant = (11s 19° 41') - (11s 19° 6') = 35' = 2100" <note>seconds of arc</note> = the remaining seconds to be traversed. Own Commentary: Then, by the method of Nilakantha starting with "From the days past and future," the motion correction for the Sun = 2' 57".

Therefore, Moon's position - Moon's Apogee = Moon's Mean Anomaly <note>Chandra-manda-kendra: the angular distance used to calculate the Moon's equation of center</note> = Circle Position <term>Vritta-kshepa: the specific term used here for the lunar anomaly epoch</term> = (11s 19° 43' 57") - (5s 17° 33') = 6s 2° 10' 57".

Now, according to the method to be described in Verse 7, "The fortnightly motion of the Sun," etc., the fortnightly motion <note>Pakshika-chalanam: the distance traveled in half a lunar month</note> is: for the Sun = 0s 4' 33", for the Node = 0s 5' 20", for the Circle <note>Anomaly</note> = 6s 2' 54", and for the Weekday = 0. 45. 55.
The New Moon positions plus the fortnightly motion become the Full Moon positions. Thus, for the Sun = 0s 4' 16' 57", for the Node = 11s 7' 25' 57", for the Circle = 0s 4' 58' 10", and for the Weekday = 2. 48. 47. Here, Ganesha <note>The author of the Grahalaghava</note> has read the positions as "The position starting with signs..." according to his preference. By this—

It is concluded that this reading is correct and should be considered by the learned. || 23 ||

# Chapter 7: On the Collection of Months

From these <note>referring to previous calculations</note>, the intercalary months <term>Adhimasa; extra lunar months added to synchronize the lunar and solar years</term> belonging to one cycle are found to be 4. Therefore, the total lunar months in one cycle = 132 + 4 = 136. Furthermore, if the total days in a Kalpa <note>a vast cosmic age</note> are determined by the total lunar months of a Kalpa, then what is the number of days for the 136 lunar months of one cycle? The result is the "Days-Collection" <term>Ahargana; the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term> for one cycle = 4016; 9; 36 <note>4016 days, 9 ghatis, 36 palas</note>. Using the method from the 10th verse of the *Chapter on Mean Motions* <note>Madhyamadhikara</note>, the mean Sun originating from one cycle = 11 signs, 28° 20' 25''. When this is cleared of full circles, the constant <term>Dhruva; a fixed starting position for calculations</term> for the Sun, due to a slight difference, becomes 0 signs, 1° 40'. Now, by that same verse, the Moon = 11s 28° 20' 10''. And by the 11th verse of the *Chapter on Mean Motions*, Rahu <note>the Moon's ascending node</note> = 4s 27° 8' 19''. The Moon minus Rahu = (11s 28° 20' 10'') - (4s 27° 8' 19'') = 7s 1° 12' 51''. This is the "Node-less Moon" <term>Vyagu; the Moon's longitude minus the node's longitude</term> = 7s 1° 12' (due to a slight difference).

Furthermore, using the method of the 11th verse of the *Chapter on Mean Motions* with the stated Days-Collection, the Moon's slow apogee <term>Mandoccha; the point where the planet moves slowest</term> = 2s 27° 11' 46'', and the previously calculated Moon = 11s 28° 20' 10''. Therefore, Moon minus Moon's Apogee = (11s 28° 20' 10'') - (2s 27° 11' 46'') = 9s 1° 8' 24''. This is the Moon's Anomaly <term>Chandra-kendra</term> = 9s 1° 8' 00'' (due to a slight difference). Now, the Days-Collection of one cycle divided by seven = 4016 / 7. The remainder is 5; 9; 36, which is the Lunar Day Constant <term>Tithidhruva</term>. Thus, it is proven. || 3 ||

The constants in signs etc. are: Sun = 0s 1° 40' 00'', Node-less Moon = 7s 1° 12' 10'', and Moon's Anomaly = 9s 1° 8' 10''.
<margin>Days, Ghatis, Palas</margin>
The constant for the lunar day and weekday is 5; 9; 36. || 3 ||

### Now he describes the calculation of the Sun and the Node:

> From the doubled collection of months, subtract the signs etc. obtained by dividing by sixty-seven; the result is the Sun.
> The months themselves are the signs; the degrees are the months minus their own third part;
> the minutes are equal to a quarter of the months. This is the Node. || 4 ||

Now he explains the means for the mean Sun and the Node-less Moon. Regarding "From the collection of months": In the Samvat year 1669, Shaka 1534, on Thursday the 15th day of the bright half of Karttika, at 32 ghatis 33 palas; in the Ashvini mansion at 23 ghatis 14 palas; in the Vajra yoga at 54 ghatis 54 palas. The years = 92. Cycles = 8. Intercalary months = 2. Total months = 57. Doubled = 114. Divided by sixty-seven <note>original: "naga-shad" (7 and 6)</note>, the result in signs etc. is 1s 24° 2' 41''. The collection of months <note>57</note> reduced by this becomes the Sun = 7s 8° 57' 19''. The Sun's constant is 0s 1° 40'; multiplied by the cycles <note>8</note> it is 0s 1° 20'. The Sun reduced by this = 6s 26° 37' 19''. The Sun increased by the additive <term>Kshepaka; a correction factor</term> of 0s 4° 21' = 6s 29° 58' 19''.

Now the calculation of the Node. The collection of months = 57. These are the signs = 57. The collection of months = 57. Its third part is 19. The months minus this third part results in the degrees = 38. The collection of months = 57. Its quarter is 14; 15. These are the minutes. Thus, the Node-less Moon in signs etc. = 10s 8° 14' 15''. The constant for the Node-less Moon is 7s 1° 12'. Multiplied by the cycles <note>8</note> it is 8s 9° 36'. The Node-less Moon increased by this = 6s 17° 50' 19''. Increased by the additive 11s 7° 18', the Node-less Moon becomes 5s 25° 8' 19''. || 4 ||

### The "Madhuri" Commentary:

From the doubled "collection of months" (the total number of months), subtract the "signs etc. obtained by sixty-seven" (the signs etc. resulting from dividing by 67). The "reduced collection of months" is the "Sun." "Those" stated "months" are the "signs." The "degrees" are "minus their own third part" (the months minus one-third of themselves). The "minutes" are "equal to a quarter of the months." "This" is the "Node." || 4 ||

## Here is the Proof:

<note>The author is deriving the simplified formulas used in the Grahalaghava, a 16th-century astronomical treatise, by comparing "Kalpa" (vast cosmic cycles) values.</note>

Lunar months in a Kalpa = 53,433,336,000. Total Zodiacal Signs in a Kalpa = 5,184,000,000. Therefore, by the rule of proportion for a Kalpa, the Sun in signs etc. =
$\frac{5,184,000,000 \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{53,433,336,000}$ = $\frac{51,840,000 \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{534,333,36}$ =
= $\frac{65 \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{67}$, due to a slight approximation = $\frac{2 + 65 \times \text{Desired Lunar Months} - 2}{67}$ =
= $\frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} (67 - 2)}{67} = \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 67}{67} - \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 2}{67}$
= Desired Lunar Months - $\frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 2}{67}$. $\therefore$ The first half of the rule is proven.

Now, let the total signs of the descending node <term>Vipata</term><note>The descending node of the moon, often referred to as Rahu or Ketu in Indian astronomy</note> in a Kalpa be considered. Then, by the ratio of the total lunar months in a Kalpa to the total signs of the node, the position of the node in signs etc. for the desired lunar months is =
$\frac{\text{Total Signs of Node} \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{53,433,336,000}$ = Desired Lunar Months ($1 \text{ Sign } + 0^\circ + 40' + 15''$) = 
<br>
-> Sign <- -> Sign <-
Desired Lunar Months ($1 + 0^\circ + \frac{40'}{60} + \frac{15''}{60}$) = Desired Lunar Months ($1 + \frac{2^\circ}{3} + \frac{1'}{4}$)
= Desired Lunar Months { $1 \text{ Sign} + \frac{1^\circ + 2^\circ - 1^\circ}{3} + \frac{1'}{4}$ }
Desired Lunar Months = { $1 \text{ Sign} + (\frac{3^\circ}{3} - \frac{1^\circ}{3}) + \frac{1'}{4}$ } = Desired Lunar Months { $1 + (1^\circ - \frac{1^\circ}{3}) + \frac{1'}{4}$ } =
<br>
-> Sign <-
= $\text{Desired Lunar Months} + (\text{Desired Lunar Months}^\circ - \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months}^\circ}{3}) + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months}^\circ}{4}$. Thus it is proven. || 4 ||

Multiply the <term>Masagana</term><note>The total count of elapsed months</note> by 2 and divide by 67; subtracting the resulting signs etc. from that same month-count gives the remaining signs etc. of the Sun. The position of the node <term>Vipata</term> is the sum of: signs equal to the month-count, degrees equal to the month-count minus its third part, and minutes equal to the fourth part of the month-count. || 4 ||

**Example—** In the Shaka year 1865, Samvat 2000, Year 1351, Shravana month, bright fortnight, Sunday, full moon day, at 49 ghatis and 40 palas; Shravana Nakshatra at 27 ghatis and 39 palas; Saubhagya Yoga at 34 ghatis and 20 palas. On this day, by the method of **"Hya-bdhindro-nitashaka"** etc., the year-count is 423, the cycle is 38, intercalary months <insert>Adhimasa</insert> are 2, and the total month group is 66.

Now, according to the verse, multiplying the month group 66 by 2 gives 132; dividing this by 67 results in 1 sign, 29 degrees, 6 minutes, and 6 seconds. Subtracting this from the month group 66 results in 64 signs, 0 degrees, 53 minutes, and 54 seconds. Dividing these signs by 12, the position of the <unclear>Sun</unclear> <meta>ghost_text</meta> <unclear>or the mean/slow motion</unclear> <insert>now from the month-count subtracted</insert> etc.

Following the method of the 6th verse hereafter, the Sun's constant <note>original: "dhruva"</note> 0 | 14 | 0 | 0 is multiplied by 38 cycles, resulting in 2 | 3 | 20 | 0. Subtracting this from the Sun's position gives 2 | 27 | 33 | 44. By adding the Sun's additive constant <note>original: "kshepa"</note> 0 | 4 | 21 | 00 to this, the Sun's position becomes 3 | 1 | 33 | 44.

The group of months is 66; this is the sign value. Subtracting its third part (22 | 0 | 0) from the month group of 66 leaves a remainder of 44 degrees. Furthermore, the 4th part of the month group, 16 | 30, becomes the minutes and so on. Summing these and dividing the signs by 12, the Node <note>original: "Pata," referring to Rahu</note> in signs etc. is 7 | 4 | 16 | 30. ->Now he describes the calculation of the Moon's anomaly, weekdays, and so on:<-

### Diminished by its own seventh part, the months modulo fourteen; the result increased by one-tenth of the month-group in degrees becomes the anomaly in signs etc.
### The months modulo fourteen, increased by their own half, and further increased by the quotient of ten times the month-group divided by three hundred twenty-seven, gives the day-start (weekday and time). || 5 ||

Now he explains the method for finding the anomaly <note>original: "Vritta," the Moon's mean anomaly</note> and the weekday. Regarding "Diminished by its own seventh part": The months modulo 14 <note>original: "manutasta," 14 is the number of Manus</note> are diminished by their own seventh part in signs etc. (0 | 4 | 17 | 8), resulting in 0 | 26 | 42 | 52. The month group is 57. One-tenth of this in degrees etc. is 5 | 42 | 0. Adding this to the degrees etc. gives 9 | 1 | 24 | 52. The anomaly constant is 9 | 1 | 6. Multiplied by the cycles, it is 0 | 8 | 48. Adding this gives 9 | 10 | 12 | 52. Adding the additive constant 0 | 14 | 51, the resulting anomaly is 9 | 25 | 3 | 52.

Now for the calculation of the weekday etc.: The months modulo 14 (which is 1) increased by its own half (0 | 30) is 1 | 30 | 0. The month group 57 multiplied by ten is 570. Divided by 327 <note>original: "manujai," a numerical code</note>, the quotient is 1 | 44 | 39. Adding this gives the weekday etc. 3 | 14 | 39. The constant for the tithi's weekday is 5 | 9 | 36. Multiplied by the cycles, it is 6 | 16 | 48. Adding this gives 9 | 31 | 23. Adding the additive constant 2 | 48 | 46, the resulting weekday etc. is 5 | 20 | 8. || 5 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary:<-

**Diminished by its own seventh part** = **by its own one-seventh**, **diminished** = **subtracted**, **months modulo fourteen** = **the number of months divided by fourteen**, **signs etc.** = **zodiacal signs and degrees**, **increased by one-tenth of the month-group** = **including one-tenth of the total months**, **becomes the anomaly** = **is the Moon's anomaly**. **Increased by its own half** = **with half of itself added**, **months modulo fourteen** = **months divided by fourteen**, **from ten times the month-group** = **from the total months**, **increased by the quotient** = **including the result of dividing by three hundred twenty-seven**, **day-start** = **the weekday etc. "the weekday additive constant" occurs. || 5 ||**

->Here is the mathematical proof:<-

> "The revolutions of the Moon's apex in an age are 488,203." <note>Latin/Sanskrit source: Surya Siddhanta</note>
> Likewise, "The Moon's revolutions are 57,753,336."

According to the statement in the *Surya Siddhanta*, the Moon's apex revolutions = 488,203; the Moon's revolutions = 57,753,336.
$\because$ Moon's Revs. $-$ Moon's Apex Revs. $=$ Moon's Anomaly Revs. $=$ 57,753,336 $-$ 488,203 $=$ 57,265,133 $=$ the revolutions of the anomaly in an age. "These multiplied by a thousand are the revolutions in a Kalpa," so the anomaly revolutions in a Kalpa = 57,265,133,000. "The lunar months are the difference between the revolutions of the Sun and Moon," so the lunar months in a Kalpa = 53,433,336,000. Therefore, if the Kalpa lunar months give the Kalpa anomaly revolutions, then for the desired lunar months:

What is the result in signs etc. for the anomaly? $=$ $\frac{\text{Kalpa Anomaly Revs. in signs} \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{\text{Kalpa Lunar Months}}$ $=$

## Commentary on the Grahalaghava

$\frac{57265133000 \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{5343336000} = \frac{(1211^\circ 24') \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{14}$ (approximately),

$= \frac{(610^\circ 42') \times \text{Desired Lunar Months}}{7} = \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months}(1 + 6 - 1)}{7} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 42^\circ}{420}$

$= \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} (7 - 1)}{7} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 10^\circ}{10} = \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 7}{7} - \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 1}{7} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 1^\circ}{10}$

$= \text{Desired Lunar Months} - \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months}}{7} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 1^\circ}{10}$. $\therefore$ Thus, the calculation for the <term>Vrutta</term> <note>The 'Vrutta' refers to the Moon's mean anomaly, a key step in finding its true position.</note> is established.

Now, in one lunar month, the <term>Seven-divided Civil Days etc.</term> <note>original: "saptabhakta-savana-dinadi"</note> = 1; 3; 15; 0. Therefore, if these <term>Civil Days</term> <note>A 'Savana' day is a natural solar day from sunrise to sunrise.</note> are obtained in one lunar month, then by proportion, the civil days for the desired lunar months would be: $\frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} (1; 3; 15; 0)}{1} = \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 14 (1; 3; 15; 0)}{14}$

$= \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} (21; 12; 5; 40)}{14} = \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 21}{14} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 25}{14 \times 60} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 40}{14 \times 60 \times 60}$

$= \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 3}{2} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 1^\circ}{327}$ (approximately) $= \text{Desired Lunar Months} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months}}{2} + \frac{\text{Desired Lunar Months} \times 10}{327}$.

Since the number of days is seven, it is appropriate to say "seven-fold," and thus it is proven. || 5 ||

> Subtracting its own <term>Seventh Part</term> <note>saptamsha</note> from the remainder of the months divided by 14, and adding the <term>Tenth Part</term> of the <term>Total Months</term> <note>mashagana</note> in degrees, results in the <term>Vrutta</term>. Adding its own half to the remainder of the months divided by 14, and adding ten times the total months divided by 327, results in the <term>Additive for the Weekday</term> <note>varadika kshepa</note>. || 5 ||

<term>Example</term> — In a group of 66 months, dividing by 14 leaves a remainder of 10. Subtracting the 7th part of 10, which is 1 sign, 25 degrees, 42 minutes, and 51 seconds <note>original: "rashyadi" - signs, degrees, etc.</note>, from the remainder 10, we get 8; 4; 17; 9. Adding to this the 10th part of the 66 months (6 degrees, 36 minutes) gives 8; 10; 53; 9. By adding the <term>Constant</term> <note>dhruva</note> of the Vrutta (9; 11; 6; 0) and the product of 38 <term>Cycles</term> <note>chakra</note> (7; 11; 48; 0) and the <term>Epochal Additive</term> <note>kshepa</note> (0; 14; 51; 0), the Vrutta (the Moon's anomaly) becomes 4 signs, 7 degrees, 32 minutes, and 9 seconds.

Dividing the 66 months by 14 leaves a remainder of 10; adding its half (5 days) gives 15; 0; 0. Adding the 327th part of 660 (which is 66 months multiplied by 10), we get 2 days, 1 minute, and 16 seconds. Adding this to the previous sum gives 17; 1; 16. Finally, adding the weekday constant (5; 9; 36) and the cycle product (0; 4; 8) and dividing the day position by 7, the <term>Weekday result</term> <note>varadi</note> becomes 3; 5; 14. || 5 ||

---

->Now he describes the correction of the constants for the Sun and others produced from the total months:<-

> The Sun generated from the total months is subtracted by its own constant multiplied by the cycles. The others are added to them, and all are combined with their respective additives at the end of the white fortnight <note>The full moon or the end of the bright half of the month.</note> in the desired month. || 6 ||

Now he explains the correction of the constants for the Sun and others produced from the <term>Total Months</term>. The Sun, produced from the total months, should be decreased by its <term>Cycle-multiplied Constant</term>. The others, such as the descending node <note>vipata</note>, should be added to the cycle-multiplied constant. All of these should then be joined with their <term>Respective Additives</term>. These values will then represent the positions at the end of the bright fortnight (Full Moon) of the desired month. || 6 ||
