<header>Chapter on the Mass of Months || 7 ||</header>

# The Madhuri Commentary—

From the mass of months = from the multitude of months, produced = generated, <term>Sun</term> <note>Sanskrit: Ravi</note> = the Sun; by its own, subtracted by the constant multiplied by the cycles = diminished by the constant multiplied by the number of revolutions, the others = the other planets, added = joined with the constant multiplied by the revolutions, then = afterwards, joined with the additive = including their respective additive constants <note>Kshepa: a specific numerical value added to a calculation to align it with a specific epoch</note> "then" they = <term>the ascending node and others</term> <note>Vipata: the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, at the end of the white half of their own month = at the end of the full moon of the desired month, they are = they shall be || 6 ||

# Here is the Proof—

If by one cycle such a planet in the form of a constant is obtained, then by the desired cycle what is obtained? Thus the planet related to the desired cycle is found. However, here the Sun's constant was previously subtracted by twelve signs, therefore the Sun must be made devoid of its own constant. Others must be made inclusive. Furthermore, by adding the planetary additives from the time of the beginning of the text, the planets at the end of the full moon are produced—this is logical and thus proven || 6 ||

In the Sun produced from the mass of months, subtracted by its own constant multiplied by the cycles, and in the <term>Lunar Anomaly</term> <note>Chandra-kendra: the angular distance of the moon from its apogee</note> (the circle) etc., added to their respective constants multiplied by the cycles, by adding their respective additives, the Sun and Lunar Anomaly etc., at the time of the end of the full moon of the desired month are found || 6 ||

# Example—
By the 4th verse, the Sun in signs etc. is 4s 0° 53' 44". In the Sun, or by multiplying 0s 2° 40' 0" by 38 cycles and subtracting 2s 3° 20' 0", then by adding the Sun's additive 0s 4° 21' 0" to 1s 27° 33' 44", the Sun at the end of the month (at the time of the full moon) becomes 2s 1° 54' 44" || 6 ||

# Now he describes their fortnightly motion—

->**In the Sun, the fortnightly motion is zero, fourteen, and thirty-three; in the node, zero, fifteen, and twenty.**<-
->**Six, twelve, and fifty-four in the circle starting with signs; and in the days etc., zero, forty-five, and fifty-five. || 7 ||**<-

Now he describes the motion of the fortnight. "In the Sun, the fortnightly..." etc. The meaning is clear || 7 ||

# The Madhuri Commentary—

In the Sun = in the Sun, zero, fourteen, thirty-three = zero, Indra (fourteen), Deva (thirty-three) 0s 14° 33'. In the node, zero = zero, arrow-moon (fifteen), nails (twenty) = 0s 15° 20'. In the circle = in the Lunar Anomaly, six, twelve, fifty-four = six, Sun (twelve), Yuga-Aksa (fifty-four) 6s 12° 54' starting with signs = signs etc., fortnightly = relating to fifteen days, motion = the motion suitable to be moved, shall be. Then zero = zero, Aksa-Andhi (forty-five), arrow-arrow (fifty-five) = 0. 45. 55 starting with days. In the days etc. = in the lunar days and weekdays etc., the fortnightly motion occurs || 7 ||

# Here is the Proof—

Just as the planet related to the desired month was calculated previously by the fourth verse, so too, having brought the planet for half a month, it is accepted as the "fortnightly motion." By adding these respective motions, they shall be at the time of the new moon. Since previously only the planets at the end of the full moon were calculated, this is proven || 7 ||

0s 14° 33' 00" for the Sun, 0s 15° 20' 00" for the node, and 6s 12° 54' 00" for the Lunar Anomaly is the fortnightly (relating to 15 days) motion in signs etc. And 0. 45. 55 is the fortnightly motion for the days, ghatis, and palas of the lunar date || 7 ||

### ->Now, he describes the six-month motion (adjustment):<-

> The Sun is five, twenty-four, and thirty-eight; the Node <note>Rahu</note> is six, four, and one; the Lunar Anomaly <note>the "Vritta" or epicycle center</note> is five, four, and fifty-three. This is the six-month motion. For the lunar date (tithi), the day-increment is two, eleven, and one. || 8 ||

Now the six-month motion is explained. The verse beginning with "Shara" (five) is clear in its meaning. || 8 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary:<-

In the Sun (Arke) = five <term>Shara</term>, twenty-four <term>Veda-Paksha</term>, thirty-eight <term>Bhujanga-Agni</term>; (5 signs, 24°, 38'). In the Node and Sun (Vyagau) — six, four <term>Krita</term>, one <term>Ku</term> (6 signs, 4°, 1'). In the Lunar Anomaly (Vritte) — five <term>Shara</term>, four <term>Varvai</term>, fifty-three <term>Trishava</term> (5 signs, 4°, 53'). This "beginning with signs" (adi) is the motion (chalana) related to six months (shanmasika). Now for the lunar date (tithe), in the "beginning with days" (dinadye) — two, eleven <term>Bhava</term>, one <term>Bhu</term> (2 days, 11 ghatis, 1 palas). This is the six-month motion for the day-count. || 8 ||

->The Rationale (Upapatti):<-

Here too, using the same logic as the fourth verse, the calculation for the planets over six months is taught as the "six-month motion." The name is literal, meaning "that which occurs in six months." This is established. || 8 ||

The Sun's motion is 5s 24° 38' 00", the Node's is 6s 4° 1' 10", and the Lunar Anomaly's is 5s 4° 53' 10" — these are the motions in signs etc. for 6 months. And for the lunar date, 2d 11g 1p is the motion in days etc. for 6 months. || 8 ||

### ->Now, he describes the calculation for a desired lunar date:<-

> To find the desired lunar date, the dates past or remaining from the Full Moon,
> diminished by their 64th part, is the motion in days.
> Diminished by their 34th part, it is the motion in degrees for the Sun.
> Diminished by their 93rd part and multiplied by thirteen, it is the motion for the Lunar Anomaly. || 9 ||

Now the attainment of the desired lunar date is explained. To achieve the desired lunar date, whether before (prak) or after (pare) the Full Moon, take the number of desired dates and subtract their 1/64th part; this is the motion in days. Subtract their 1/34th part; this is the motion in degrees for the Sun. Then, take those same dates, multiply by thirteen, and subtract their 1/93rd part; this is the motion for the Lunar Anomaly. || 9 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary:<-

Before or after (prak pare) the end of the Full Moon, whatever the number (ya) of lunar dates (tithyah), those diminished by their 64th part (sva-yuga-rasa-lavona) <note>yuga=4, rasa=6; 64</note> are used for the sake of finding the desired date (abhimata-tithi-siddhyai). This is the motion in days (dinadye). "Those same dates" diminished by their 34th part (sva-yuga-guna-lavona) <note>yuga=4, guna=3; 34</note> are the motion in degrees (lavadye) for the Sun (dineshai). Those same dates diminished by their 93rd part (sva-guna-nava-lavona) <note>guna=3, nava=9; 93</note> and [multiplied by thirteen] <note>implied by 'vishwa' in the verse</note> are the motion in degrees for the Lunar Anomaly (vritte). || 9 ||

Let the desired lunar date be represented as 'A. Ti.' According to the method of Bhaskara <note>referring to Bhaskaracharya</note> in the verse "A lunar month consists of...", the measure of civil days in one lunar month is 29;31,50. Therefore, if for thirty lunar dates...

# As before, the result should be positive or negative; but for the Sun's center, that which is other,
# divided by two and diminished by its own sixth part, should be combined with the two. || 10 ||

Now, to determine the clear lunar date (*tithi*), he describes the method for calculating the "Circle Result" (*vṛtta-phala*) and the Sun's center result. "Atyaṣṭi" means seventeen (17). "Aṣṭi" is sixteen (16). "Vṛṣā" is fourteen (14). "Arka" is twelve (12). "Gāvo" is nine (9). "Śarāḥ" is five (5). "Daśau" is two (2). These are the segments (*khaṇḍas*). The Circle is 1s 26° 3' 52". This is the base sine (*bhuja*). Its degrees are 56° 3' 52". Dividing by thirteen gives 4 <note>original: "trīndulavaḥ", referring to the 13-degree divisions used in this system</note>. The sum of the completed segments for this measure is 59. With the remaining unpassed segment 9, the remainder is 3° 3' 52". Multiplied, it is 27' 34" 58"'. Its thirteenth parts (*viśvaśās*) are 2' 7" 17"'. Adding this to the sum of completed segments gives 61' 7" 17"'. As before, in the six signs starting with Aries, the result is positive; in the six starting with Libra, it is negative. Since the Circle's center starts from Aries, the Circle Result is positive 61' 7" 17"'. The Sun is at 6s 29° 58' 19". Subtracting the high apsis (*mandocca*) at 2s 18°, the Sun's center becomes 7s 18° 1' 41". Its base degrees are 48° 1' 41". Divided by thirteen, the result is 3. The sum of the corresponding completed segments is 57. With the next segment 12, the remainder is 9° 1' 41". Multiplied, it is 108' 20" 12"'. Its thirteenth parts are 8' 20" 0"'. Adding this to the sum of completed segments gives 55' 20" 0"'. This is divided by two: 27' 40" 0"'. Subtracting its own sixth part, 4' 36" 40"', leaves 23' 3" 20"'. Because the center is in the Libra group, the Sun's result is negative 23' 3" 20"'. The combination of the two results is positive 38' 3" 57"'. || 10 ||

## Madhuri Commentary—

Atyaṣṭi-aṣṭi-dhṛti-arka-go-śara-daśa = seventeen, sixteen, fourteen, twelve, nine, five, two—these are the segments used in calculating the equation of center (*manda-phala*). By those segments, combined with the thirteenth part of the remainder multiplied by the next segment, one finds the sum corresponding to the thirteenth parts of the Circle's base degrees. As before, according to whether the center is in Aries or Libra, the result is positive or negative; this is the Circle Result. In this way, from the Sun's center, the other (second) result that occurs should be "enveloped" (divided by two) and diminished by its own sixth part. Then, the combination (*saṃskṛti*) of those two results must be performed. || 10 ||

## Here is the Rationale:

By increasing by thirteen degrees within the three signs (90 degrees), one brings forth the results from the Circle's base degrees, subtracting them successively, and multiplying by fifteen, the seven segments are stated. These are approximate. Since 13 x 7 = 91, the wise should consider how seven segments are completed in ninety degrees (three signs) by thirteen-degree increments. Now, if one segment corresponds to thirteen degrees of the base sine, then by proportion, the sum of the completed segments for the desired base degrees should be made. Again, by proportion with the remainder: if the next segment is obtained by thirteen degrees, what is obtained by the remainder? Thus, the product of the remainder and the next segment divided by thirteen, added to the previous sum, is the result of the Circle's base degrees. Furthermore, if by the <term>radius (trijyā)</term> one gets the <term>maximum sine result (parama-phala-jyā)</term>, then what is the result by the <term>sine of the center (kendra-jyā)</term>? For example, <term>radius</term> = 120, the maximum <term>Sun's result (ravi-phala)</term> = 130'. And the maximum <term>Moon's result (candra-phala)</term> = 300'. The <term>center degrees (kendra-aṃśāḥ)</term> = 13°, 26°, 39°, 52°... The <term>sine of the center</term> = 27, 52, 75, 94... Therefore:

<header>Chapter 7: On the Calculation of the Group of Months</header>

260/120 multiplied by fifteen: 260 x 15 / 120 = 33. This is the second result due to a slight difference <note>original: "svalpāntarād", referring to a small mathematical approximation</note>.

Therefore, Second Result - First Result = 33 - 17 = 16 = the second segment. This applies everywhere.

Furthermore, the Moon's Equation = (Sine of Moon's Anomaly x 300) / 120. The Sun's Equation = (Sine of Sun's Anomaly x 130) / 120. If the Sine of the Sun's Anomaly equals the Sine of the Moon's Anomaly, then the ratio of Sun's Equation / Moon's Equation = (Sine of Sun's Anomaly x 130 x 120) / (Sine of Moon's Anomaly x 300 x 120) = 130 / 300 = 13 / 30.

$\therefore$ Sun's Equation = (Moon's Equation x 13) / 30. When the divisor and dividend are reduced by 5/2, then by slight approximation = (Moon's Equation x 5) / 12 = Moon's Equation (6 - 1) / 12 = (6 x Moon's Equation) / 12 - Moon's Equation / 12 = Moon's Equation / 2 - Moon's Equation / (2 x 6). Thus it is proven. || 10 ||

17, 16, 14, 12, 9, 6, and 2 are the <term>segments</term> <note>Khandas: tabular differences used to calculate sines or equations</note> for bringing forth the <term>Manda-phala</term> <note>Equation of Center: the correction needed to account for a planet's elliptical orbit</note>. By these segments, the product of the next segment and the remainder is divided by 13; this is added to the sum of the previous segments corresponding to the quotient obtained by dividing the degrees of the arc by 13. As before (depending on whether the anomaly is in the half-cycles starting with Aries or Libra), the Moon's Equation of Center becomes positive or negative. Similarly, from the Sun's anomaly degrees, calculate the second result, which is the result divided by 2 minus its own 6th part. Then, these two results should be refined. || 10 ||

**Example—** Dividing the degrees of the arc 52° 27' 51" of the <term>Vritta</term> <note>The "circle" or mean anomaly</note> 4 | 7 | 32 | 9 by 13 gives a quotient of 4. Adding the 13th part (0° 19' 36") of the product (4° 10' 29") of the next segment (9) and the remainder (0° 27' 51") to the sum of the 4 passed segments (59), we get 59° 19' 36". Since the anomaly starts from Aries, the Moon's Equation is positive 59° 19' 36".

Subtracting the Sun 3 | 1 | 33 | 44 from its own <term>Mandocca</term> <note>Apogee: the point where the planet is farthest from Earth</note> 2 | 18 | 0 | 0, the Sun's <term>Manda-kendra</term> <note>Mean Anomaly</note> is 11 | 16 | 26 | 16. Dividing its degrees 13° 33' 44" by 13, the quotient is 1. Adding the 13th part (0° 41' 31") of the product (8° 59' 44") of the next segment (16) and the remainder (0° 33' 44") to the passed segment (17), we get 17° 41' 31". Half of this is 8° 50' 45"; subtracting its own sixth part 1° 26' 27" results in 7° 35' 42". Since the Sun's anomaly starts from Libra, this Equation is negative. Subtracting this from the Moon's Equation, the refined result is 51° 43' 54". || 10 ||

---

->**Now he describes the calculation of the divisor—**<-

> The remaining part of the segment of the anomaly, divided by six, is added or subtracted when the anomaly is in the signs starting with Cancer or Capricorn respectively.
> This, combined with thirty and twenty minutes, shall be the divisor; then the <term>Chara</term> <note>Ascensional difference</note> from the Sun should be calculated as previously stated. || 11 ||

Now the method for the divisor is explained. "The remaining part of the segment," etc. The part of the segment to be traversed is 9; divided by six, the result is 1° 30'. With this, the thirty [degrees] and twenty minutes [become] 30° 20'. Because the anomaly is in the six signs starting with Capricorn, it is subtracted, and the divisor becomes 28° 50'. Then the ascensional difference from the Sun must be calculated as stated. The Sun is 6 | 29 | 58 | 19. The precession of the equinoxes is 18° 10'. The Sun with precession is 7 | 18 | 8 | 19. From this, the positive ascensional difference is 84. || 11 ||

->**Madhuri Commentary—**<-

In the "Vritta" = the Moon's mean anomaly; in the signs starting with "Cancer and Capricorn" = when situated in the six-sign groups starting with Cancer or Capricorn; from the "remaining part of the segment" = from the segment of the anomaly yet to be traversed; <insert>divided by six, added or subtracted = respectively increased or decreased by the result of the division by six.</insert>

<header>With the Commentary on Grahalaghava—</header>

The value thirty increased by its own third part <note>original: "sagunāṃśakhavahrayaḥ" - literally 30 plus 1/3 of 1, referring to the constant 30 1/3</note> shall be the **Divisor** (Hara). Then, as previously stated, the **Ascensional Difference** (Chara) and other corrections should be calculated from the Sun. || 11 ||

### Here is the mathematical proof:—

Let the correction minutes of the result be = *fk*, the next segment be = *akh*, the Sun's velocity = 62', the Moon's velocity = 790', and the Moon's apogee velocity = 6'. Therefore, Moon's velocity — Moon's apogee velocity = 790' — 6' = 784' = *ga-am-degrees*, which is the Moon's anomaly velocity (with a slight margin of error). Thus, the segments of the Moon's equation are read in increments of thirty degrees. Therefore, the difference between today's and yesterday's anomaly equation would be the "next segment" (*akh*). Furthermore, because of the previous multiplication by fifteen, that next segment itself, when divided by fifteen to get degrees and multiplied by sixty to get minutes, makes the Moon's velocity correction equal to four times the next segment. Therefore, Moon's velocity correction = 4 × *akh*.

$\therefore$ True Moon velocity = Mean Moon velocity $\pm$ 4 × *akh* = 790 $\pm$ 4 × *akh*. Therefore, the difference in velocity minutes = True Moon velocity — Sun velocity = 790' $\pm$ 4 × *akh* — 62' = 790' — 62' $\pm$ 4 × *akh* = 728 $\pm$ 4 × *akh*. Therefore, by proportion, the **Tithi Correction Ghatis** <term>Ghati: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> =

**Example**—The 6th part of the next segment 9 is 1;30. (Since the anomaly is in Capricorn, subtracting this from 30;20 results in a divisor of 28;50. The Sun is at 3s 15° 33' 44". The **Precession** (Ayanamsha) is 21° 39' 49". From the Tropical Sun at 3s 23° 13' 33", the Ascensional Difference was calculated as 107, which is positive. || 11 ||

### Now he describes the clarification of the Tithi (Lunar Day):—

> The result correction multiplied by ten and divided by the divisor shall be the Ghatis; then the Ascensional Difference,
> which is the characteristic of the Tropical [Sun], then the Vighatikas <term>Vighatika: 1/60th of a Ghati, or 24 seconds</term>, negative if behind and positive if ahead.
> Then the distance in Yojanas <term>Yojana: a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term> reduced by its own quarter; then the Tithi is clarified by these three corrections.
> The corrections in Ghatis should be applied to the Moon and the Sun. || 12 ||

Now, the method for calculating the **True Tithi** (Spashta Tithi). Regarding "The Ghatis": The result correction is 38;3;57. Multiplied by ten, it is 380;39;30. Divided by the divisor 28;50, the result is 13;12 Ghatis, which is positive because the corrections were positive. The Ascensional Difference is 84 positive. Since it is the characteristic of sunset, it becomes negative 84. The distance in Yojanas is 64. Reduced by its own quarter, the **Terrestrial Longitude** (Deshantara) seconds become 48. These are positive because the location is east of the prime meridian. The total correction from these three results is 21;36 positive Ghatis. <unclear>Tithi</unclear> <gloss>Here</gloss> <insert>the correction from the three results</insert> <unclear>becomes</unclear> <gloss>True</gloss> <unclear>Ghatis 21;39 and 14 Palas.</unclear>

<header>Chapter on the Calculation of Months || 7 ||</header>

The correction from the three results <note>The "three results" refer to corrections for the equation of center, the chara (ascensional difference), and deshanatara (terrestrial longitude)</note> in units of time (ghatis) is 12; 36. The Sun, corrected by the same amount in minutes of arc, is 7s 0° 10' 55". The Rahu <note>original: "Vyagu" - the ascending node of the moon</note> is 5s 21° 20' 51". || 12 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

Multiplied by ten = multiplied by 10; divided by the divisor = divided by the denominator; the result of the corrections = the correction process; shall be the time units (nadis/ghatis). Then = thereafter, the calculation of the *chara* <term>chara: ascensional difference, the correction for the varying length of day based on latitude</term> should be performed with reversed signs <note>original: "viloma-samskara" - if the value was positive, make it negative, and vice versa</note>. Then = thereafter, the correction for the terrestrial longitude <term>deshantara: the distance in longitude from the prime meridian, usually Ujjain</term> is negative for places west of the prime meridian and positive for places east of the prime meridian. The terrestrial longitude yojanas <note>a traditional unit of distance</note> minus their own fourth part shall be the time units in *palas* <note>1 ghati = 60 palas</note>. The lunar day <term>tithi</term> corrected by these three results becomes the "true" or "corrected" tithi. In the case of Rahu <note>original: "Vyagu"</note> and the Sun <note>original: "Ushnagu" - the hot-rayed one</note>, minutes of arc equal to the aforementioned correction time units (ghatis) should be applied. || 12 ||

### Here is the Proof (Upapatti):

The reasoning for this correction is easily understood by observing the position of the celestial sphere <note>original: "Gola-sthiti"</note> and is established by the logic of the preceding verses. Now, the calculation of the terrestrial longitude in *palas* is done by proportion. For example: If for the yojanas of the Earth's circumference (4800), the time units of a full day/night in *palas* (3600) are obtained, then what will be obtained for the yojanas of the local terrestrial longitude? Thus, the terrestrial longitude in *palas* is:

= $\frac{\text{Day-Night Palas} \times \text{Longitude Yojanas}}{\text{Earth's Circumference}}$ = $\frac{3600 \times \text{Long. Yoj.}}{4800}$ = $\frac{3 \times \text{Long. Yoj.}}{4}$ = $\frac{\text{Long. Yoj. (4-1)}}{4}$ =

Long. Yoj. (1 — $1/4$) = Long. Yoj. — $\frac{\text{Long. Yoj.}}{4}$ = Longitude in Palas. Thus it is proven. || 12 ||

The correction result multiplied by 10 and divided by the divisor becomes the time units (dandas/ghatis). The *chara* should be considered in reverse (positive as negative, negative as positive). Furthermore, the terrestrial longitude yojanas minus their own fourth part are negative west of the prime meridian and positive to the east. By applying these three corrections, the "true" tithi is found. These same correction units, treated as minutes of arc, should be applied to Rahu and the Sun. || 12 ||

**Example—** The previously mentioned correction result is 51; 43; 54. Multiplying by 10 gives 517; 19; 00. Dividing this by the divisor 28; 50 gives a positive quotient of 18; 7 ghatis (since the correction result was positive). The previously mentioned positive *chara* of 1; 47 ghatis here becomes negative. The terrestrial longitude of Mithila <note>A city in modern-day Bihar/Nepal border</note> is 1; 38 ghatis, which is positive (being east of the prime meridian). Adding the positive units (18; 7 + 1; 38 = 19; 45) and subtracting the negative *chara* (1; 47) results in a total correction of 18; 8 ghatis. Adding this to the tithi of 11; 10 ghatis results in the true tithi of 29; 18 ghatis. Treating the correction units as minutes of arc and adding them to the node (Pata/Rahu) results in the corrected node 10s 7° 28' 38", and adding to the Sun results in the true Sun 3s 15° 51' 52". || 12 ||

### Now he describes the correction of the Sun and Rahu—

> Multiply the result produced from the Sun's own degrees by two;
> make those into minutes of arc and apply them to both to make them true.
> The divisor increased by two-thirds of itself and divided by three <note>original: "Krishanu" - the number 3</note>
> produces the diameter of the Moon in digits <term>angulas</term> and so on. || 13 ||

Now he describes the clarification of the Rahu <note>The ascending node of the Moon</note> and the Sun. "Multiplied by four," etc. The solar correction is 23; 3; 30. Multiplied by four <note>original: "vedaghnam," literally "multiplied by the Vedas," which are four in number</note> it becomes 92; 13; 20. Adding its own twenty-fourth part, 3; 50; 33, the resulting minutes are 96; 3. Because the solar correction is negative, if the solar correction were positive, these minutes should be added to the Rahu and the Sun; if the correction is negative, they should be subtracted. Then those two, the Rahu and the Sun, become "clear" <term>sphuta: the true or corrected position of a planet</term>. After being refined by these minutes, the clear Sun becomes 6s 28° 34' 52". The clear Rahu becomes 5s 23° 44' 48". The divisor 28; 50, when increased by two minus one-third (1; 40), becomes 30; 30. Divided by three <note>original: "krishanu," a poetic term for the number three</note>, the resulting lunar disk in digits <note>original: "angulardyam," half-digits or units of measure for the celestial diameter</note> is 10; 10. || 13 ||

-> The Madhuri Commentary <-

"With its own twenty-fourth part" = including its own 1/24th portion. "Multiplied by the ages" <note>original: "yugaghnam," referring to the four Yugas</note> = multiplied by four. "The result born of the Sun" = the solar correction. "Minutes" = these shall be the minutes of arc. "Them" = those minutes. "Of those two" = of the Sun and Rahu. "Perform" = execute the refinement. Then those two = the Sun and Rahu. "Clear" = they become corrected. "Divided by the fire" = divided by three. "The divisor increased by two minus a third" = the divisor plus two minus one-third ( <gloss>2/3</gloss> ). The resulting lunar disk of the Moon is produced in digits. || 13 ||

-> Here is the Proof <-

By the rule "Eight, two, two, three, twelve, nine, five, eyes," etc., the precise solar correction =
(Moon's correction $\times$ 13) / 30 = [Moon's correction $\times$ (12 + 1)] / 30 = (Moon's correction $\times$ 1/3) / 30 + (Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / 150 = 
(Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / 12 + (Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / (150 $\times$ 3) = (Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / 246 + (Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / (25 $\times$ 6 $\times$ 3).

Now, by that same method, the gross solar correction = (Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / (6 $\times$ 2).

Therefore, the precise solar correction = [(Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / (6 $\times$ 2)] + [(Moon's correction $\times$ 5) / (2 $\times$ 6 $\times$ 25)] = Gross Correction + (Gross Correction / 25). Then, in terms of degrees:

Precise Solar Correction = [Gross Correction + (Gross Correction / 25)] / 15.

Furthermore, the precise solar correction in minutes = [ (Gross Correction + (Gross Correction / 25)) / 15 ] $\times$ 60 =

(Gross Correction + (Gross Correction / 25)) $\times$ 4. Here, in place of twenty-five, due to a small difference, twenty-four is taken.

Therefore, the reading "with its own twenty-fourth part" is correct.

Now, by the previous reasoning, the divisor = (Moon's daily motion - 62) / 24.

$\therefore$ Divisor $\times$ 24 = Moon's daily motion - 62. Therefore, Moon's daily motion = Divisor $\times$ 24 + 62. Then, by the rule "Now the disk of the white-rayed one <note>the Moon</note> is the motion divided by seventy-four," the lunar disk in digits = Moon's daily motion / ...

$\frac{\text{Divisor} \times 24 + 62}{74} = \frac{3 (\text{Divisor} \times 24 + 62)}{74 \times 3} = \frac{\text{Divisor} \times 72 + 186}{74 \times 3}$

$= \frac{2 + \text{Divisor} \times 72 - 2 + 186}{74 \times 3} = \frac{\text{Divisor} \times (74 - 2)}{74 \times 3} + \frac{186}{74 \times 3}$

$= \frac{\text{Divisor} \times 74}{74 \times 3} - \frac{2 \times \text{Divisor}}{74 \times 3} + \frac{186}{74 \times 3} = \frac{\text{Divisor}}{3} + \frac{186}{74 \times 3} - \frac{2 (30।20)}{74 \times 3} =$

$= \frac{\text{Divisor}}{3} + \frac{125।20}{74 \times 3} = \frac{\text{Divisor}}{3} + \frac{1140'}{3} = \frac{\text{Divisor}}{3} + \frac{1 + \frac{5}{3}}{3} = \frac{\text{Divisor} + \frac{5}{3}}{3}$

$= \frac{\text{Divisor} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{5}{3} - \frac{1}{3}}{3} = \frac{\text{Divisor} + \frac{6}{3} - \frac{1}{3}}{3} = \frac{\text{Divisor} + (2 - \frac{1}{3})}{3}$ . Thus, it is proven. || 13 ||

By adding its own 24th part to the Sun's correction <note>original: *phala*</note> in minutes, and multiplying by four, and then applying this to the Sun and the Node <note>original: *vyaguru*</note>, the true Sun and true Node are obtained. By adding 2 minus one-third to the Divisor <note>original: *hara*</note> and dividing by 3, the diameter of the Moon in digits <note>term: *angula* (a traditional unit of measurement)</note> and other units is found. || 13 ||

**Example—** From the 10th verse, the negative solar correction is 35' 42". Adding its 24th part, 0' 17" 59"', results in 0' 54" 41"'. Multiplying this by 4 gives 3' 11" 8"' 44"'. Subtracting this (due to the negative correction) from the corrected Sun 3s 1° 51' 21" results in the true Sun 3s 1° 51' 21" <note>The text shows a calculation where the values remain consistent with the correction applied</note>. Subtracting from the Node 10s 7° 28' 31" results in the true Node 10s 7° 28' 0". Adding the Divisor 28;50 and 1140 <note>representing the constant derived in the proof</note> to get 30;30 and dividing by 3, the Moon's diameter is 10;10 digits. || 13 ||

### Now, he describes the calculation of the diameters of the Sun and the Earth's shadow—

> The Sun's diameter in digits is found by taking 10;50 and adding or subtracting the current solar segment divided by forty, depending on whether the Sun's anomaly is in the half-cycle beginning with Cancer or Capricorn. The Earth's shadow <note>original: *bhūbhā*</note> is the Divisor minus five, increased by its own fifteenth part; to this, add or subtract the solar segment divided by fifty when the anomaly is in the Capricorn or Cancer half-cycles. || 14 ||

Now the method for the Sun's diameter <note>original: *ravivimba*</note> is explained. "Divided by forty": The current segment is 12. Dividing this by 40 gives 0;18. This is applied to the base value 10;50. Since the anomaly is in the Cancer group, it is subtracted: 10;50 - 0;18 = 10;32, which is the Sun's diameter. The Divisor is 28;50. Subtracting five gives 23;50. Adding its fifteenth part (1;36) gives 25;26. For the Earth's shadow, the solar segment 12 divided by fifty gives 0;14. Since the Sun's anomaly is in the Cancer group, it is subtracted, resulting in the Earth's shadow being 25;11. || 14 ||

### The "Madhuri" Commentary—

In one's own anomaly <note>original: *svakendre*</note>, when in the six signs beginning with Cancer or Capricorn, the value 10;50 <note>original: *vyarilavabhavāḥ*</note> is increased or decreased by the current segment divided by forty; this becomes the Sun's diameter in digits. The Divisor minus five, increased by its own fifteenth part, is the Earth's shadow <note>original: *kubhā*</note>. Furthermore, in this Earth's shadow, when the anomaly is in the Capricorn or Cancer groups, the solar segment divided by fifty should be added or subtracted. || 14 ||

# Chapter 7: On the Calculation of Months and Time-Groups
<page-num>145</page-num>

$= \frac{\text{Divisor } \times \text{16}}{\text{15}} - \frac{\text{80}}{\text{15}} \mp \frac{\text{Remaining Fraction}}{\text{50}} \text{ (from the difference of forms) .}$

$= \frac{\text{Divisor } \times \text{16}}{\text{15}} - \frac{\text{16 } \times \text{5}}{\text{15}} \mp \frac{\text{Remaining Fraction}}{\text{50}}$

$= \frac{\text{16}}{\text{15}} (\text{Divisor} - \text{5}) \mp \frac{\text{Remaining Fraction}}{\text{50}} = \text{1} + \frac{\text{1}}{\text{15}} (\text{Divisor} - \text{5}) \mp \frac{\text{Remaining Fraction}}{\text{50}}$

$= (\text{Divisor} - \text{5}) + (\frac{\text{Divisor} - \text{5}}{\text{15}} \mp \frac{\text{Remaining Fraction}}{\text{50}}) = \text{Earth's Shadow Diameter. Thus it is proved. || 14 ||}$

In the centers starting with Cancer <note>Karkyadi: the signs beginning with Cancer</note> and Capricorn <note>Makaradi: the signs beginning with Capricorn</note>, by sequentially adding and subtracting the next fraction of the solar center divided by 40 from 11 minus one-sixth, the solar diameter in digits <term>Angula: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly a finger-breadth</term> is found. By subtracting 5 from the Divisor and adding one-fifteenth of that remainder to itself, the Earth's shadow diameter is found. By sequentially adding and subtracting the 50th part of the next fraction of the solar center in the Capricorn and Cancer centers, the accurate diameter of the Earth's shadow in digits is obtained. || 14 ||

**Example** — In the Capricorn center, dividing the next solar fraction 16 by 40 gives a result of 0;24. Subtracting this from 11;50 results in a solar diameter of 10;26 digits. Subtracting 5 from the Divisor 28;50 leaves a remainder of 23;50. Adding its fifteenth part 1;35 results in 25;25. Adding to this the 50th part of the next fraction 16, which is 0;19 (since it is the Cancer center), the Earth's shadow diameter becomes 25;44 digits. || 14 ||

### Now, the possibility of an eclipse is described—

> Having thus known the time starting with the lunar day, the remainder of the eclipse should be found as before.
> One should observe the eclipse after six months, or six months minus a fortnight, or six months plus a fortnight.
> The eclipse of the Sun and Moon occurs when the degrees of the node-less arm <note>Vyagu-bhuja: the angular distance from the node</note> are less than fifteen; for the Sun, it depends on the southern latitude and whether the end of the lunar day falls during the day or night. || 15 ||

Now the possibility of an eclipse is explained. *Having known*—meaning, having understood the calculation of the lunar day <term>Tithi: a lunar day, 1/30th of a lunar month</term> and so on, the remaining factors like the duration and latitude should be known as in the previous lunar eclipse section. From the occurrence of a solar or lunar eclipse, one should predict another eclipse after six months. Or, one should look for an eclipse after six months minus one fortnight—meaning after five and a half months. Or, look for an eclipse after six months plus one fortnight (fifteen days). Or, look for it in one fortnight. First, where an eclipse occurs, calculate the node-less lunar days and add the "fortnightly motion" <note>Paksha-chalana: the mean motion of planets over 15 days</note>. Observe the eclipse there. If no eclipse occurs there, then add the "six-month motion" to the node-less values. If not there, then subtract the fortnightly motion. If not there, then add the fortnightly motion. Thus, by moving forward, observe the eclipse. There, if the degrees of the node-less arm are less than fifteen, an eclipse of the Sun or Moon may occur. For the Sun, if the node-less arm degrees are southern and within their own range, a solar eclipse occurs. This happens when the lunar day falls within the day-length; if the end of the lunar day occurs at night, then look for a lunar eclipse. Or, it may depend on the transition of day and night. This results in an eclipse at sunrise or sunset. || 15 ||

The phenomena arising from the syzygy <note>the alignment of Sun, Earth, and Moon</note>, and the remainder—namely the duration and so forth—should be determined as before, as in the case of the lunar eclipse. **In six months,** or **six months minus or plus a fortnight** <note>5.5 or 6.5 months</note>, or **in a fortnight (fifteen days),** one should observe the **eclipse of the Sun or Moon.** If the **lunar node's arc ( भुजांश ) is less than fifteen,** one should look for an eclipse. If the **lunar node's arc is less than eight,** it pertains to the **Sun (the hot-rayed one).** If the end of the lunar day occurs **during the day or night,** one should observe the **eclipse of the Sun or Moon** respectively as it falls within that day or night. || 15 ||

### Here is the Derivation:

Based on the variations in the method previously explained for lunar eclipses—"if the node's degrees are small, an eclipse is possible," etc.—the style of calculating an eclipse with a latitude less than fourteen is indicated by the phrase "less than the lunar date (fifteen)." Since a lunar eclipse is never seen during the day, and a solar eclipse is never seen at night, even if an eclipse is possible during those times, it remains invisible to the eye. Thus, it is rightly said that the rest of the derivation is easily understood. || 15 ||

Having calculated the lunar date, latitude, and the disks of the bodies, the remaining matters regarding the eclipse should be calculated according to the previous method. One should consider the possibility of an eclipse six months after a previous eclipse, or six months plus or minus 15 days (i.e., at 5.5 or 6.5 months), or even within 15 days. If the node's arc <note>original: *vyagu-bhujāṃśa*</note> is less than 15, an eclipse is possible. Or, if the southern arc of the node is less than 8, one should consider the possibility of a solar eclipse. If the end of the lunar date occurs when the sun is above the horizon, it is a solar eclipse; if it occurs at night, it is a lunar eclipse. || 15 ||

### Now, the calculation of the magnitude (Grasa) is described:

> This divisor, diminished by three and one-third, multiplied by four, and divided by nine, then subtracted by the degrees of the node's arc, multiplied by eleven and divided by seven, shall be the obscured portion of the Moon (the cool-rayed one) in digits (angulas) and so forth. || 16 ||

Now he describes the calculation of the obscured portion of the Moon. "With a third part": The divisor is 28;50. Subtracted by three and one-third (3;20), it becomes 25;30. Multiplied by four (the Vedas), it is 102;0. Divided by nine, it is 11;20. Subtracted by the node's arc degrees (6;21;12), it is 4;58,48. If it cannot be subtracted by the node's arc, then a lunar eclipse does not occur. Multiplied by eleven (the Bhavas), it is 99;52;48. Divided by seven (the mountains), the result is the obscured portion of the Moon in digits and so forth: 7;58.

### Now, regarding a solar eclipse at sunrise or sunset, he describes the knowledge of the hour angle (nata-ghatika):

> If the solar eclipse occurs at the end of the night or during the night, then the half-day duration combined with those ghatikas <note>units of 24 minutes</note> becomes the hour angle, respectively before or after noon.

If the solar eclipse occurs when a certain number of ghatikas remain in the night or have passed in the night, then the half-day duration added to those ghatikas becomes the morning or afternoon hour angle. At the end of the night, it is the morning hour angle; when the night has passed (into day), it is the afternoon hour angle. || 16 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary:

"Diminished by three and one-third" = subtracted by three plus one-third part. "Multiplied by the Vedas" = multiplied by four. "Divided by the numerals" = divided by nine. "This" = the previously calculated divisor. "By the node's arms" = by the degrees of the node's arc. "Subtracted" = diminished. "Multiplied by the Bhavas" = multiplied by eleven. "Divided by the mountains" = divided by seven. "Of the cool-rayed one" = of the Moon. "Or" = by another method. "Digits and so forth" = the measure of the obscured portion starting with digits. || 16 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary:

**In the east or west:** depending on the hour-angle (time from noon). **Subtract or add one-fourth of the hour-angle at the end of the new moon:** the time of the new moon is decreased or increased by a quarter of the hour-angle. **To the Sun’s position in signs etc.:** the longitude of the Sun. **Corrected by one-sixth of the degrees of the zenith distance:** adjusted by a sixth part of the degrees of the angle from the zenith. **The clear degrees of the Node-Sine:** the precise angular distance from the node. **Subtract from seven:** the value 7 minus the degrees. **Add half of that result:** add half of the remainder to itself. **The rough magnitude of the Sun’s obscuration:** the approximate eclipse measurement in digits. || 17 ||

### Here is the Rationale:

Since understanding a solar eclipse is difficult without calculating <term>Parallax in Longitude (Lambana)</term> and <term>Parallax in Latitude (Nati)</term>, we accept one-fourth of the hour-angle as a rough parallax at the end of the new moon. Adding this to the new moon time and dividing by five yields the result in signs etc. When this is subtracted or added to the Sun's position for the east or west, it yields the <term>Nonagesimal (Vintribha): the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the mid-heaven</term>. Rough latitude parallax is equal to one-fourth of the zenith distance. The corrected latitude is the clear latitude. Thus: Latitude $\pm \frac{\text{Zenith Distance}}{4} =$ Clear Latitude. Now, using the rule "multiply by 11 and divide by 7":

Clear Latitude $= \frac{\text{Node-Sine} \times 11}{7} = \text{Latitude} \pm \frac{\text{Zenith Distance}}{4}$

$\therefore$ Clear Node-Sine $= \frac{(\text{Latitude} \pm \frac{\text{Zenith Distance}}{4}) \times 7}{11} = \text{Node-Sine} \pm \frac{\text{Zenith Distance}}{\frac{44}{7}} = \text{Node-Sine} \pm \frac{\text{Zenith Distance}}{6}$ (due to a small difference) = Clear Node-Sine degrees. Here, the Node-Sine degrees are increased or decreased by one-sixth of the zenith distance. Then...

<header>On the Lati-Grahalaghava—</header>

The Lords of the past nodes are doubled. When the <term>Vyagu</term><note>The Moon's ascending node (Rahu) subtracted from the Sun's position</note> is in Libra or subsequent signs, one is added because six months have already passed; therefore, it is said to be "increased by one" in Libra etc. Likewise, in every cycle (11 years), there are twenty-two Lords of the nodes; when divided by seven, the remainder is one. Thus, the Lord of the past node is the number of past cycles plus the current count. If the Lords exceed seven, the remainder after dividing by seven is the Lord, as there are only seven Lords. This is proven. || 18 ||

By doubling the <term>Vyagu</term>, if the mean position of the <term>Vyagu</term> is in the signs starting from Libra, add 1 and divide by 7; the remainder will be the past Lord of the node starting from Brahma. || 18 ||

**Example—** <term>Vyagu</term> 5s 16° 32' 9", Cycle 38, and the mean position of <term>Vyagu</term> is 5. Therefore:
5 x 2 + 38 = 10 + 38 = 48. $\therefore \frac{48}{7} = 6$ with a remainder of $6$. Therefore, the current Lord of the node is Yama <note>The 6th in the sequence starting from Brahma</note>.

### My verse for naming the Lords of the nodes starting with Brahma—

> Brahma, Chandra, Indra, Kubera, Varuna, Agni, and Yama;
> These are declared the seven Lords of the nodes, increasing every six months.

In the order of a six-month increase, Brahma, Chandra (Moon), Indra, Kubera, Varuna, Agni, and Yama are the 7 Lords of the nodes. || 18 ||

### Now, he describes the calculation of the Moon from the Sun—

> The <term>Tithi</term> multiplied by twelve are the degrees; the Sun increased by that becomes the Moon.
> Then the divisor is twenty-eight and fifty; the motion is increased by two and sixty.
> The Sun's motion is fifty-nine minutes; from that, the past and future <term>Ghatikas</term> 
> of the <term>Nakshatra</term> and <term>Yoga</term> are found from the end of the <term>Tithi</term>. || 19 ||

Now he explains the calculation of the Moon and its motion. Regarding "Tithi": a <term>Tithi</term> is 15. Multiplied by twelve, it becomes 180 degrees. Adding this to the Sun (6s 28° 34' 52"), the Moon becomes 0s 28° 34' 52". Thus, the desired <term>Tithis</term> multiplied by twelve become degrees; the Sun joined with those degrees is the Moon. The divisor is 28; 50. Multiplied by twenty-four (24), it is 692; 0. Adding sixty-two (62), the Moon's motion becomes 754; 0. The Sun's motion is 59 minutes. Then, from the Sun and Moon, the past and future <term>Ghatikas</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> arising from the <term>Nakshatra</term> (lunar mansion) and <term>Yoga</term> (conjunction) are to be calculated. These are from the end of the <term>Tithi</term>. The <term>Nakshatra</term> and <term>Yoga</term> existing at the end of the <term>Tithi</term>—their past and future <term>Ghatikas</term> are from the end of the <term>Tithi</term>. This does not mean from sunrise, because the Sun and Moon are calculated for the end of the <term>Tithi</term>. By subtracting or adding those to the <term>Tithi</term> duration, the <term>Ghatikas</term> of the <term>Nakshatra</term> and <term>Yoga</term> from sunrise are found. From the end of the <term>Tithi</term> 32; 44, the past <term>Ghatikas</term> of the Krittika <term>Nakshatra</term> are 9; 8 and future are 54; 31. For the Variyas <term>Yoga</term>, the past <term>Ghatikas</term> are 46; 28 and future are 12; 33.

Now, the calculation of the Sun's node from the total months. <term>Samvat</term> 1669, <term>Shaka</term> 1534, Vaishakha Krishna 30, Wednesday, <term>Ghatika</term> 26; 8. In Rohini <term>Nakshatra</term>, <term>Ghatika</term> 34; 57. In Dhriti <term>Yoga</term>, <term>Ghatika</term> 42; 29. Cycle 8. Total months 51. Doubled: 102. Divided by 67, the result in signs etc. is 1s 19° 40' 17". Subtracting this from the total months: 9s 14° 19' 43". Subtracting the cycle-multiplied <term>Vyagu</term> 0s 13° 20': 1s 0° 59' 43". Adding the constant 0s 4° 21' 0", the Sun at the end of the full moon is 1s 6° 20' 43". By the fortnightly adjustment, adding 0s 14° 33', the Sun at the end of the new moon is 1s 19° 53' 43".

Now, the calculation of the <term>Vyagu</term> (Node). As stated, at the end of the full moon it is 11s 21° 16' 45". Adding the fortnightly adjustment of 0s 15° 20', the <term>Vyagu</term> at the end of the new moon is 0s 6° 36' 45".

Now, the calculation of the <term>Vrutta</term> <note>A specific astronomical cycle or circle</note>. As stated, at the end of the full moon the <term>Vrutta</term> is 8; 20; 10; 43. Adding the fortnightly adjustment of 6; 12; 54, the <term>Vrutta</term> at the end of the new moon is 9; 2; 5; 37.

# Chapter on the Calculation of Monthly Groups || 7 ||

**Now, the calculation of the weekday and related elements.** As previously stated, the weekday and other values are 3 | 9 | 7 <note>This notation likely refers to the weekday (3 = Tuesday), ghatis, and palas</note>. By applying the correction for the fortnight, 0 | 45 | 99, the values at the end of the new moon (*amānta*) become 3 | 55 | 2. The result of the epicycle calculation is positive: 74 | 22 | 21. The center of the Sun is 0 | 28 | 6 | 17. The solar equation <term>phala: the correction applied to mean planetary positions to get true positions</term> is positive: 14 | 41 | 40. The sum of the two results is positive: 89 | 4 | 1. The remaining segment of the epicycle is 2. The divisor is 30 | 40. The distance from the Sun to the Moon is 108. Following the rule for the "Sāyana" <note>precession-corrected</note> characteristic, the result is positive. The refined result 89 | 4 | 1 multiplied by ten is 890 | 40 | 10. Divided by the divisor 30 | 40, the result in *nadis* <note>units of time, 24 minutes</note> is 29 | 2. Since the refinement is positive, this is added. The terrestrial longitude distance is 64 yojanas; when adjusted, the longitude correction in *palas* is 48. Since the location is east of the prime meridian <note>the "Ujjain line"</note>, this is subtracted. The total refined time from the three corrections is 31 | 38 positive *nadis*. The lunar day (*tithi*) values are 3 | 99 | 3. After applying the three corrections, the true time on Wednesday is 26 *ghatikas* and 40 *palas*. The time equivalent to the three corrections is 31 | 38. The Sun, adjusted by this, is 1 | 20 | 26 | 21. The corrected Rahu <note>the ascending node, "vyaguru"</note> is 0 | 6 | 58 | 23. The solar equation is 14 | 41 | 40. Multiplied by four, it is 58 | 46 | 40. Adding its own 24th part, 2 | 26 | 16, the minutes are 61 | 13 | 36. Since the solar equation is positive, the true Sun adjusted by these positive minutes is 1 | 21 | 26 | 34. The true Rahu is 0 | 7 | 59 | 36. The lunar disc is 10 | 46.

**Now, the calculation of the solar disc.** In calculating the Sun's result, the functional segment is 14. Divided by 40, it is 0 | 21. From the calculation of the sine, it is 10 | 50. Because the center is in Capricorn, it is subtracted, resulting in the solar disc in digits (*angulas*): 10 | 29.

**Now, he describes the calculation of the solar eclipse magnitude.** The end of the new moon is 26 | 40. Midday is 16 | 48. The western hour angle <note>natam: distance from the meridian</note> is 9 | 52. One-fourth of this in signs etc. is 2 | 14 | 0. Because the western hour angle exists, the Sun doubled and added is 4 | 9 | 26 | 34. Its northern declination is 13 | 52 | 22. The southern latitude of the observer is 21 | 26 | 42. After adjusting for declination and latitude, the southern zenith distance is 11 | 34 | 20. One-sixth of this is 1 | 55 | 43 south. The northern arm of Rahu is 7 | 59 | 36. Adjusted by the one-sixth part, the true value is 6 | 3 | 53. Subtracted from seven, it is 0 | 56 | 7. Adding its own half, 0 | 28 | 3, the magnitude of the eclipse in digits is 1 | 24. The mean revolution count of Rahu is 6. The lord of the eclipse-node is Yama. The lunar day (3) multiplied by twelve results in 36 degrees. The Sun added to this becomes the Moon: 1 | 21 | 26 | 34. The lunar velocity is 798. The solar velocity is 59. From the end of the lunar day, the elapsed time of the Rohini nakshatra is 51 | 37, and the remaining time is 8 | 31. For the Dhriti yoga, the elapsed time is 40 | 10, and the remaining time is 19 | 52. || 19 ||

-> Thus ends the solar eclipse calculation from the monthly group. <-

## The Madhuri Commentary —

"The product of the lunar day and the Sun" means the sum of the lunar day multiplied by twelve; these are the degrees. "Joined with that" means added to them; the Sun becomes the Moon. "Then," "joined with sixty-two," "the divisor multiplied by twenty-four"—that becomes the lunar motion. "Fifty-nine minutes"—that becomes the solar motion. "Then," from the Sun and Moon, "from the end of the lunar day," the elapsed and remaining times of the Nakshatra and Yoga should be calculated. || 19 ||

## Here is the Proof —

Let the lunar degrees = L. Let the solar degrees = S. Solar motion = 62'. Then, according to the rule "The degrees of the Moon minus the Sun divided by twelve," the lunar day (*tithi*) = $\frac{\text{L - S}}{\text{12}}$. Therefore, Tithi $\times$ 12 = L - S. Therefore, L = (12 $\times$ Tithi) + S. By reversing the calculation of the divisor, the true lunar motion = (Divisor $\times$ 24) + 62.

The remaining explanation is easy to understand and thus we conclude.

->First, he describes the method for calculating the two eclipses from the almanac—<-

The Sun and Rahu found in the almanac should be adjusted to the exact moment of the end of the phase using the method of "multiplying by elapsed or remaining days." There, the sum of the remaining *Ghatis* at the end of the full moon, or the sum of the elapsed and remaining *Ghatis* of the *Nakshatra*, must be known. The *Dyumana* (length of the day) is also to be understood. Having learned all this from the almanac, I shall describe the two eclipses from them.

# Chapter 8: On the Calculation of the Two Eclipses

Ghati <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> 18:50; Adjusted Ghati 40:26; Total duration of the lunar constellation <term>Bhabhoga</term> 59:16; Length of the day 32:36. At the moment of the full moon's end, the True Sun is at 0s 19° 22' 28", Rahu <note>The ascending node of the moon</note> is at 0s 27° 25' 22", and the Sun minus Rahu <term>Vyagu</term> is 0s 15° 5' 6". ॥ 1 ॥

-> Now he describes the calculation of the lunar eclipse magnitude: <-

> The number 627 <note>original: "tara-shat" (stars-six), a mnemonic for 627</note> divided by the sum of the elapsed and remaining ghatis of the lunar day plus seven, then diminished by the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu, and then increased by its own half and its sixteenth part, results in the obscured portion of the Moon <note>original: "sudhanshu", the nectar-rayed one</note> in digits <term>angulas</term>. ॥ 2 ॥

Now the calculation of the obscured portion is explained. "Stars" etc. The number 627 is divided by the sum of the elapsed and remaining ghatis of the lunar day <note>49:53</note> plus seven. The result in degrees etc. is 12° 36' 41". This is diminished by the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu <note>7° 43' 34"</note>, resulting in 4° 53' 7". This value, increased by its own half <note>2° 26' 33"</note> and its sixteenth part <note>0° 18' 19"</note>, results in the eclipse magnitude in digits: 7:37:59. If the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu cannot be subtracted, then an eclipse is not possible. ॥ 2 ॥

-> The "Madhuri" Commentary <-

**The sum of elapsed and remaining ghatis plus seven** = the sum of the lunar day's ghatis divided after adding seven. **Six hundred and twenty-seven** = the number 627. **Diminished by the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu** = subtracted by the degrees of the Sun minus Rahu. **By its own half and sixteenth part** = with its own half and 1/16th part. **Increased** = added together. Then, of the **Moon** = of the lunar orb. **In digits** = the measure in digits. **Obscured** = the magnitude of the eclipse. ॥ 2 ॥

-> Here is the mathematical rationale: <-

When near the apogee, the velocity and the diameters of the orbs are smaller, while the duration of the lunar day is greater. When near the perigee, the opposite occurs. Therefore, as the diameter increases, the lunar day decreases, and as the diameter decreases, the lunar day increases. Thus, there is a strong inverse relationship between the diameter and the lunar day. Therefore:
(Sum of true diameters / 2) / Mean lunar day = (Sum of mean diameters / 2) / True lunar day.
By cross-multiplication:
(Sum of true diameters / 2) × True lunar day = Mean lunar day × (Sum of mean diameters / 2).
Since the Mean lunar day = 59:4 and the Mean sum of diameters / 2 = 18:56.
Therefore: (Sum of true diameters / 2) × True lunar day = (59:4) × (18:56).
Subtracting (Mean sum of diameters / 2) × 7 from both sides:
(Sum of true diameters / 2) × True lunar day — (Mean sum of diameters / 2) × 7 = (18:56)(59:4) — (18:56) × 7
= (18:56) (52:4).
Dividing both sides by (Sum of true diameters / 2), and assuming (Mean sum / True sum) ≈ 1 for small differences:
185:48 / (Sum of true diameters / 2) = True lunar day — 7.

By rearranging the terms, (Sum of true diameters / 2) = 185:48 / (True lunar day — 7).
By the inverse calculation of the latitude, the degrees of the sum of the true diameters:
= (185:48) × 7 / 11 × (True lunar day — 7) = (8913 / 7) / (True lunar day — 7) = 629 / (True lunar day — 7)
= 627 / (True lunar day — 7) <note>due to a slight approximation</note>.

Then, by the method for lunar eclipses, the magnitude in digits <term>angulas</term> is:
= ( 627 / (True lunar day — 7) — Vyabhuj ) × 11/2
= ( 627 / (True lunar day — 7) — Vyabhuj ) × (11 × 5 / 7 × 5)
= ( 627 / (True lunar day — 7) — Vyabhuj ) × 55/35
= ( 627 / (True lunar day — 7) — Vyabhuj ) × 50/32 <note>approximate</note>.

By dividing 627 by the duration of the <term>Tithi</term><note>A lunar day, here referring to the time taken for the moon to move 12 degrees relative to the sun</note> in <term>Ghatis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> minus 7, and subtracting the <term>Sine of the Node</term><note>original: "Vyaghu-bhuja" - the angular distance from the lunar node</note> from that quotient, then adding half of that result and its sixteenth part to itself, the magnitude of the lunar eclipse in <term>Angulas</term><note>A traditional unit of measure, here used for the "digits" of an eclipse</note> is found. || 2 ||

### Now, the calculation for the diameters of the Moon and the Earth's shadow is stated —

> **The Tithi duration increased by six, dividing 695, gives the Moon's diameter in Angulas.**
> **The Tithi duration decreased by ten, dividing 1322, gives the diameter of the Earth's shadow in Angulas. || 3 ||**

Now the method for finding the measures of the Moon's disk and the Earth's shadow is explained. **"Increased by six"**: The Tithi duration of 56;43 plus six is 62;43. By this, 695 <note>original: "Bana-anka-rtavah" - a mnemonic for 695 using the Katapayadi system</note> is divided; the result is the Moon's diameter in Angulas, 11;4. The Tithi duration 56;43 minus ten is 46;43. By this, 1322 <note>original: "Drig-adri-vaktra-yindavah" - mnemonic for 1322</note> is divided; the result is the Earth's shadow in Angulas, 28;17. || 3 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary —

**The Tithi duration increased by six dividing 695** = 695 divided by the true Tithi duration in Ghatis plus six, **in Angulas** = in the unit of Angulas, etc., **is the Moon's diameter**. **The Tithi duration decreased by ten dividing 1322** = 1322 divided by the true Tithi duration in Ghatis minus ten, **in Angulas** = in the unit of Angulas, etc., **is the Earth's shadow** <note>original: "Kshitibha" - literally 'Earth-shadow'</note>. || 3 ||

### The Rationale —

Let the mean diameter of the Moon = 10;31. Let the mean diameter of the Earth's shadow = 26;40. Let the mean Tithi duration = 59;4. Then, according to the principle "The Sines of the Sun and Moon..." etc., because the motion is primary in calculating the diameters of the Sun, Moon, and Earth's shadow, the relationship between motion and diameter is strong. Therefore:

$\frac{\text{True Moon Diameter}}{\text{Mean Moon Diameter}} = \frac{\text{Mean Tithi Duration}}{\text{True Tithi Duration}}$ . Therefore, True Moon Diameter $\times$ True Tithi Duration = Mean Moon Diameter $\times$ Mean Tithi Duration = (10;31) $\times$ (59;4) <unclear>...</unclear> Therefore, True Moon Diameter $\times$ True Tithi Duration + Mean Moon Diameter $\times$ 6 = Mean Moon Diameter $\times$ ...

### Here is the mathematical derivation:

Let us assume—half the sum of the diameters <note>term: Vimbayogardham (half the sum of the angular diameters of the Moon and the Earth's shadow)</note> = 18;56. The daily motion of the Moon relative to the nodes <note>term: Bhabhoga (the motion of the Moon from the node)</note> by mean measure = 60;52. Then, by the previous logic: (True half-sum / Mean half-sum) = (Mean motion / True motion). Therefore, the True half-sum = (Mean motion × Mean half-sum) / True motion = (60;52 × 18;56) / True motion.

Then, True half-sum × True motion = (60;52 × 18;56). Subtracting 189;40 from both sides: (True half-sum × True motion) - 189;40 = (60;52 × 18;56) - 189;40.
Since 189;40 = Mean half-sum × 10,
Therefore: (True half-sum × True motion) - (Mean half-sum × 10) = (60;52 × 18;56) - (18;56 × 10).
Since True half-sum is approximately Mean half-sum (with a small correction):
True half-sum × (True motion - 10) = 18;56 × (60;52 - 10).
Thus, True half-sum = 18;56 × (50;52) / (True motion - 10).

Therefore, True half-sum = (18;56 × 50;52) / (True motion - 10). Then, by reversing the process for calculating the eclipse magnitude, the degrees of the arc for the true half-sum = (True half-sum × 7) / 11.
= (18;56 × 50;52 × 7) / ((True motion - 10) × 11) = 610 / (True motion - 10) approximately.
Thus, by the rule "those degrees multiplied by the eyes (2) and divided by the mountains (7)," the magnitude of the lunar eclipse in digits <note>term: Angula (a traditional unit of measurement, here used for the 'digits' of an eclipse)</note> and its fractions = (610 / (True motion - 10) - Vyasu <note>note: 'Vyasu' refers to the corrected latitude or distance from the node</note>) × 11 / 7. This is thus proven. || 4 ||

Divide 610 by the daily motion (Bhabhoga) minus 10. From the resulting quotient, subtract the degrees of the latitude (Vyasu). Multiply the remainder by 11 and divide by 7; the result will be the magnitude of the lunar eclipse in digits and fractions. || 4 ||

**Example:** Subtract 10 from the daily motion 59;16, leaving 49;16. Divide 610 by this 49;16 to get the quotient in degrees etc. as 12;22;54. Subtract the latitude degrees 11;57;6 from this, leaving 0;25;48. Multiply this remainder by 11 to get 114;43;48, and divide by 7. The resulting magnitude of the lunar eclipse is 16;23;24 digits. || 4 ||

Remaining time: 12; 99. Total: 64; 49. For the Mula <term>Nakshatra</term> <note>Lunar mansion</note>: elapsed 13; 54, remaining 52; 2. Total: 66; 56. Length of day: 26; 4. At the end of the lunar day, the Sun is at 8; 5; 26; 20. Rahu <note>The ascending lunar node</note> is at 2; 11; 41; 18. The Sun minus Rahu is 5; 23; 49; 2. At the end of the new moon, the eastern <term>natam</term> <note>hour angle or zenith distance</note> is 0; 3. One-fourth of this in signs etc. is 0; 0; 22; 30. Because of the existence of the eastern hour angle, the Sun is reduced to 8; 5; 3; 50. Its southern declination is 23; 43; 40. After applying the latitude correction, the southern zenith distance is 49; 10; 22. One-sixth of this is 8; 11; 43 South. The northern <term>vyagubhujabhaga</term> <note>a specific trigonometric component used in eclipse math</note> is 6; 14; 58. Corrected by the one-sixth part, the clear <term>vyagubhujabhaga</term> becomes 1; 56; 49. || 5 ||

### The Madhuri Commentary —

"Nanda-Veda-Rtavah" = 649 <note>A chronogram where Nanda=9, Veda=4, Rta=6</note>. Divided by the sum of the elapsed and remaining time of the Nakshatra (the total duration), the result is the Moon's disk. "Shara-Aksha-Dvi-Bhuva" = 1255 <note>Shara=5, Aksha=5, Dvi=2, Bhu=1</note>. Divided by the total duration minus fourteen, the result is the Earth's shadow disk in digits (angulas). || 5 ||

### Geometric Proof (Upapatti) —

Let the mean Moon's disk = 10141, Earth's shadow disk = 26155, and the total duration of the Nakshatra = 60; 52. Then, by the previously stated proportion: (True Moon Disk / Mean Moon Disk) = (Mean Duration / True Duration).

$\therefore$ True Moon Disk = (Mean Moon Disk $\times$ Mean Duration) / True Duration = (10141 $\times$ 60; 52) / True Duration = 650 / True Duration = 649 / True Duration (due to a small difference).

Similarly, (True Earth Shadow / Mean Earth Shadow) = (Mean Duration / True Duration). $\therefore$ True Earth Shadow $\times$ True Duration = Mean Earth Shadow $\times$ Mean Duration. Subtracting (26; 55) $\times$ 14 from both sides: (True Earth Shadow $\times$ True Duration) - (26; 55 $\times$ 14) = (Mean Earth Shadow $\times$ Mean Duration) - (26; 55 $\times$ 14) = (26; 55)(60; 52) - (26; 55 $\times$ 14). Or, (True Earth Shadow $\times$ True Duration) - (Mean Earth Shadow $\times$ 14) = 26; 55 (60; 52 - 14; 0). Since True Earth Shadow is approximately Mean Earth Shadow, then: True Earth Shadow (True Duration - 14) = (26; 55)(46; 52). $\therefore$ True Earth Shadow = (26; 55 $\times$ 46; 52) / (True Duration - 14) = 1261 / (True Duration - 14) = 1255 / (True Duration - 14) (due to a small difference) = True Earth Shadow Disk.

By this —

> Divided by the sum of the elapsed and remaining time of the Nakshatra, 650 is the Moon's disk.
> Divided by the time minus fourteen, 1255 is the Earth's shadow in digits.

The scholars should consider that this reading is the most accurate. || 5 ||

Dividing 649 by the sum of the past and future time of the Nakshatra gives the Moon's disk in digits. Dividing 1255 by the total duration minus 14 gives the Earth's shadow disk in digits. || 5 ||

### Now, the calculation of the magnitude of eclipse (Grasa) in a Solar Eclipse:

> Divide one hundred and seventy (170) by the duration of the lunar day (tithi) and add four (4); or, divide two hundred and thirty-three (233) by the duration of the asterism (nakshatra) and add three (3). Subtract the corrected degrees of latitude <note>original: "vyangula-sphuta-lava"</note> from this, multiply by eleven (11), and divide by seven (7). The result is the obscured portion of the Sun in digits. || 6 ||

Now he describes the method for finding the obscured portion of the Sun from the durations of the lunar day and the asterism. **"Divide one hundred and seventy..."** The duration of the lunar day is 64;49. Dividing 170 by this gives a result in degrees of 2;37;22. Adding four gives 6;37;22. Subtracting the corrected degrees of latitude 4;40;37 leaves 1;56;45 <note>The text shows 4;40;37 subtracted from 6;37;22</note>. Multiplying by eleven (11) gives 51;26;47. Dividing by seven (7), the result for the Sun's obscured portion in digits is 7;20;58. 

Using the duration of the asterism 66;56: Dividing 233 by this gives 3;32;9. Adding three gives 6;32;9. Subtracting the corrected degrees of latitude 4;35;16 leaves 1;56;53. Multiplying by eleven (11) gives 50;27;56. Dividing by seven (7), the magnitude of the eclipse by this second method is 7;22. || 6 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

**With four** = added to four; **divided by the lunar day** = divided by the duration of the tithi; **one hundred and seventy** = 170. Or, **with three** = added to three; **two hundred and thirty-three divided by the asterism** = 233 divided by the duration of the nakshatra. **These**, **subtracted by the corrected degrees** = minus the degrees of corrected latitude; **multiplied by eleven** = multiplied by 11; **divided by seven** = divided by 7; **of the Sun** = of the Sun; **the obscured digits** = the digits of the eclipse magnitude. || 6 ||

-> Or, $\frac{\text{True Sum of Radii } \frac{3}{2}}{\text{Sum of Radii } \frac{3}{2}} = \frac{\text{Total Duration of Nakshatra}}{\text{True Total Duration of Nakshatra}} \therefore \text{True Sum of Radii } \frac{3}{2} = \frac{\text{Sum of Radii } \frac{3}{2} \times \text{Total Duration}}{\text{True Total Duration}}$ <-

-> Conversely, the degrees of the base of the true sum of radii $= (\frac{\text{Sum of Radii } \frac{3}{2} \times \text{Total Duration}}{\text{True Total Duration}}) \times \frac{7}{11} = \frac{(10147) (60142)}{\text{True Total Duration}}$ <-

<note>The author uses "Shankara" (a name for Shiva) to represent 11 and "Shaila" (mountain) to represent 7, following the Katapayadi system of numerical notation.</note>

-> By this, the solar eclipse magnitude in <term>Angulas</term><note>Angula: A traditional unit of measure, here used for the "digits" of an eclipse.</note> $= \left\{ \frac{( 4 + \frac{170}{\text{True Tithi Duration}} ) - \text{Vyagu}}{7} \right\} 11$ <-

Add 4 to the result of 170 divided by the <term>Tithi-bhoga</term> (duration of the lunar day), or add 3 to the result of 233 divided by the <term>Bhabhoga</term> (duration of the Nakshatra). From that sum, subtract the true base degrees of the <term>Vyagu</term>. Multiply the remainder by 11 and divide by 7 to obtain the solar eclipse magnitude in <term>Angulas</term> and its fractions. || 6 ||

**Example of a Solar Eclipse:** In the year 1885 of the Samvat era (1750 Shaka era), on the Monday of the New Moon (<term>Amavasya</term>) in the dark fortnight of the month of Kartika. The elapsed time of the Tithi was 44;57 <term>Ghatis</term><note>Ghati: A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>, the remaining time was 19;21, and the total duration of the Tithi was 64;18. For the Vishakha Nakshatra, the elapsed time was 13;41, the remaining time was 51;41, and the total duration (<term>Bhabhoga</term>) was 65;22. The length of the day was 27;00. Based on these, at the moment of the New Moon, the true Sun was at 6s 26° 15' 22", Rahu was at 9s 10° 3' 13", and the <term>Vyagu</term> was 5s 16° 32' 9". Using the previous method for the western hour angle at the New Moon, the true base degrees of the <term>Vyagu</term> were 6;26,35. Dividing 170 by the Tithi duration and adding 4 to the resulting 2;38,38 gives 6;38,38. Subtracting the <term>Vyagu</term> base degrees leaves 00;12,03. Multiplying this by 11 gives 2;12,33, which when divided by 7 yields a solar eclipse magnitude of 00;18,56 <term>Angulas</term>.

By the alternative method: Dividing 233 by the <term>Bhabhoga</term> (65;22) gives 3;34,52. Adding 3 gives 6;34,52. Subtracting the true <term>Vyagu</term> base degrees (6;26,35) leaves 0;08,17 <note>The text says 0;32,36, likely a calculation variant or scribal error</note>. Multiplying by 11 gives 5;58,36, which when divided by 7 yields a solar eclipse magnitude of 00;18,13 <term>Angulas</term>.

# On the Accurate Grahalaghava—
Page 160

### Now, the calculation for the solar disk is stated:

**The value of eleven minus one-sixth <note>original: "virasalavamahēśā", a numerical code where 'Vira' (tastes) = 6 and 'Mahesha' (Shiva) = 11, meaning 11 minus 1/6, or 10° 50'</note> is decreased or increased by one-third of the degrees of the Sun's arm <term>bhujāṃśa: the angular distance from the nearest equinoctial point</term> added to twelve degrees. When the Sun is in the signs starting from Aries or Libra respectively, this yields the disk in digits <term>angulas: a traditional unit of measurement</term>. The remaining elements like duration should be understood as previously described. || 7 ||**

Now the method for bringing forth the solar disk is explained. "With the Sun's degrees": The Sun is at 7s 5° 26' 20". Added to twelve degrees, it becomes 8s 17° 26' 20". Its "arm degrees" <note>the distance from the nearest cardinal point</note> are 77° 26' 20". One-third of these is 25 digits. Because the Sun is in the six signs starting from Libra, these 25 digits are added to the base value of 10° 50' <note>original: "virasalavamahēśā"</note>, resulting in the solar disk of 11° 15'. Having thus determined the obscured portion and so on, the remaining factors like the duration of the eclipse should be known as previously taught. || 7 ||

-> Thus ends the calculation of the two secondary factors of the calendar in the examples of the Grahalaghava. <-

### The Madhuri Commentary:

**In the Sun** = regarding the solar body; **In Aries or Libra** = when in the six signs starting with Aries or the six signs starting with Libra; **Eleven minus one-sixth** = 10;50; **Sun added to its degrees** = the Sun plus twelve degrees; **Equal to one-third of the arm degrees** = equal to 1/3 of the *bhujāṃśa*; **In digits**, respectively; **Decreased or increased** = subtracted or added; **Of this** = of the Sun; **Starting with digits** = the measurement in digits and minutes; **The disk** = the diameter of the solar orb. **Here** = in the solar eclipse; **Remaining** = the rest; **Duration etc.** = the duration and the magnitude of the eclipse; **As before** = according to the method stated for solar eclipses; **Should be known** = one should understand. || 7 ||

### The Mathematical Proof:

"The Sun's slow apogee <term>mandocca: the point where the planet moves slowest</term> is 78 degrees." By the rule "the apogee minus the planet," the Sun's mean anomaly <term>mandakendra</term> = 78° - S <note>where S is the Sun's position</note>. By the rule "the quadrant minus the arm is the cosine," the Sun's cosine position = 90° - 78° + S = 12° + S. These are the arm degrees. Then, by the rule "the cosine degrees of the center multiplied by eleven and divided by thirteen times twenty," the Sun's velocity correction is: $\frac{\text{arm degrees} \times 11}{13 \times 20} - \frac{\text{arm degrees}^2}{5200}$.

Then, when the center is in Cancer, Capricorn, etc., the true velocity of the Sun is: True Velocity $\pm \frac{\text{arm degrees} \times 11}{13 \times 20} - \frac{\text{arm degrees}^2}{5200}$. Then, by the rule "the Sun's velocity plus its eighth part and halved," the solar disk in digits is: (True Velocity $\pm \frac{\text{arm degrees} \times 11}{260} - \frac{\text{arm degrees}^2}{5200}) \times \frac{11}{20 \times 3}$

$= \frac{(59' 8'') \times 11}{20 \times 3} \pm \frac{121 \times \text{arm degrees}}{260 \times 60} - \frac{11 \times \text{arm degrees}^2}{5200 \times 60}$

$= 10' 50'' \pm \frac{121 \times \text{arm degrees}}{15600}$ , with a small difference.

$= 10' 50'' + 10'' - 10'' \pm \frac{\text{arm degrees}}{\frac{156}{211}} = 10' + 60'' - 10'' \pm \frac{\text{arm degrees}}{3}$

with a small difference.

$= 11' - 10'' \pm \frac{\text{arm degrees}}{3} = 11' - \frac{10'}{60} \pm \frac{\text{arm degrees}}{3} = 11 - \frac{1}{6} \pm \frac{\text{arm degrees}}{3}$

# Chapter on Risings and Settings || 9 ||

At the beginning of that, he explains the possibility or impossibility of seeing the Moon on the first day of the bright fortnight <note>Shukla Pratipat</note> in three verses:
> [Verses 1-3: Technical Sanskrit verses describing the mathematical algorithms for lunar visibility, involving corrections for the Sun's position, the terrestrial latitude, and the specific arc of visibility.]

Now, the example for the Chapter on Risings and Settings. There, the knowledge of the Moon's rising on the first day of the bright fortnight is told in three verses. "With the Sun's portion..." etc. In the Shaka year 1632, on Saturday, the 1st of the bright half of Magha, at 7 ghatis <note>1 ghati = 24 minutes</note>. Shravana Nakshatra is at 28;29 ghatis. Siddhi Yoga is at 40;8 ghatis. The Cycle is 8. The total number of days <term>Ahargana: the number of days elapsed since the start of the epoch</term> is 1036. In the morning, the mean Sun is 9s 6° 12' 38".
The Moon is 9s 11° 38' 33". The Apex <note>ucca</note> is 8s 20° 54' 28". Rahu <note>the ascending node</note> is 2s 10° 3' 29". Calculated by the 7 ghatis of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> found in the almanac: The Sun is 9s 6° 19' 31". The Moon is 9s 21° 10' 47".
The Apex is 8s 20° 55' 14". Rahu is 2s 10° 3' 3". The Sun's anomaly <note>mandakendra</note> is 9s 11° 40' 29".
The equation of center <note>mandaphala</note> is positive 0° 41' 27". The corrected Sun is 9s 7° 0' 58". The precession of equinoxes <note>ayanāṃśa</note> is 18° 8'. The ascensional difference <note>cara</note> is positive 106. The true Sun, corrected by the ascensional difference, is 9s 7° 2' 54". The true motion is 61' 10". The Moon, corrected by the three results, is 9s 21° 36' 12". The anomaly is 10s 29° 30' 2". The equation of center is negative 3° 33' 0". The corrected true Moon is 9s 18° 52' 19". The true motion is 739' 1". From these, the lunar day <note>tithi</note> is 1;0;53. Adding these to the 7 ghatis in the almanac, the end of the first lunar day is 7;56.
By these 0;56 ghatis, the values at the end of the lunar day are: Sun 9s 7° 3' 41", Rahu 2s 10° 3' 1".
The Sun without precession is 6s 27° 0' 40". The Sun and the Sun without precession, each increased by twelve degrees, are: Sun 6s 19° 3' 41" and Sun without precession 7s 9° 0' 40". Here, at the end of the first lunar day, make the half-Sun and Sun without precession of that time include the solar portion. Now, the ascensional difference from the Sun without precession alone: The Sun without precession is 7s 9° 0' 40". From this, the ascensional difference is 70. Divided by fifty-six (56), the result is 1;15;0. Because the Sun without precession is in the southern hemisphere, it is negative. This is the first result. || 1 ||
