<header>On the Lallika-Grahalaghava—</header>

The Sun <note>Aruna</note> combined with the precession is 10s 11° 42'. From this, the ascensional difference <term>Chara</term><note>The difference between the time of rising of a celestial body and six hours</note> is 68. By this, the separately placed 212;0 is multiplied, resulting in 89;0;0. The equinoctial shadow <term>Akshabha</term><note>The shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> is 9;45, which doubled is 11;30. Its square is 132;15. The separately placed value is multiplied and divided by this, yielding the result: 0;38;33. Since the Sun, increased by three signs and the precession, has a different celestial hemisphere <term>Gola</term> than the Sun minus the Node <term>Vyagu</term>, this is additive <term>Dhana</term>.

Now for the third result: The Sun combined with six signs and the precession is 4s 7° 11' 42". Its rising time <term>Udaya</term> is 346. Subtracted from 300 <note>original: "Khava-anala"</note>, the difference is 46. Multiplied by 56 <note>original: "Shara-adri-ka"</note>, the result is 4;48;0. Since the rising time of the Sun (with six signs and precession) is greater than 300, it is additive.

Now for the fourth result: Regarding the day-length. The day-length <term>Dyumiti</term> is 26;28. The end of the first lunar day <term>Pratipad-anta</term> is 7;56. Their difference is 18;32. Divided by five <note>original: "Shara"</note>, the result is 3;42;54. Since the day-length is greater than the end of the first lunar day, it is additive.

The correction of these four results: Sum the positives. Sum the negatives. Take the difference between positive and negative. The total correction of the four results is positive 4;53;57. Therefore, at sunset, the Moon is visible. Otherwise, if the correction of the four results were negative, it would be invisible. Thus ends the section on the Visibility of the Moon. || 2-3 ||

### Madhuri Commentary—

-> At the end of the first lunar day <note>original: "Pakshati-kshaye"</note>, in this consideration of the Moon's rising, the Sun and the Sun minus the Node <note>original: "Vyagu-arka"</note> are increased by twelve degrees <note>original: "Sak-amshau"</note>. Then, divided by fifty-six, from the absolute <note>un-precessed</note> Sun minus the Node, that which is the ascensional difference <term>Chara</term> shall be half of the degrees. This, based on the northern or southern hemispheres <term>Gola</term> of the Sun minus the Node and the Sun, make additive or subtractive. || 1 || <-

---

That result is kept separate. Multiplied by the ascensional difference of the Sun increased by three signs and the precession, and divided by the square of twice the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "Dyakshabha-hati"</note>; make that additive or subtractive respectively if the Sun minus the Node is in a different or the same hemisphere. The rising time of the Sun increased by six signs and the precession, when compared to three hundred <note>original: "Khava-anala"</note> and multiplied by twenty-five <note>original: "Shara-adri-ka"</note>, make it additive or subtractive depending on whether the rising time is greater or less than three hundred. || 2 ||

The difference between the day-length and the end of the first lunar day, divided by five <note>original: "Shara"</note>, make it additive or subtractive respectively if the day-length is greater or less than the end of the lunar day. If, in this calculation, the total correction of the four results is positive, then at sunset <note>original: "Tapana-aste"</note>, the Moon <note>original: "Vidhu"</note> is seen; otherwise, it is not seen. || 3 ||

### Rationale <note>Upapatti</note>—

It is assumed: Sine of Latitude <term>Palajya</term> = 110, Radius <term>Trijya</term> = 120, Sine of Declination <term>Jijya</term> = 48, Radius of the diurnal circle <term>Dyujya</term> = 115, Sine of the ascensional difference of the Sun minus Node = <margin>Chavy / 5</margin>. Now, by the rule "the number of lunar days at the end of the first day is 1," <margin>Moon - Sun / 12</margin>. Therefore, Moon - Sun = 12°. Therefore, Moon = Sun + 12°. Since previously the Node <term>Rahu</term> was subtracted from the circle, the Moon with the Node = Moon - Node = Sun - Node + 12° = (Sun minus Node) + 12°. Thus, it is rightly said that the Sun and Sun minus Node are increased by twelve degrees. For this very reason, when the Moon's time-degrees <term>Kalanshas</term> are 12° or more, the Moon is visible at the end of the first lunar day; otherwise, it is invisible. Because at the end of the first lunar day, the interval between the Sun and Moon on the ecliptic is twelve degrees, if the sum of the four results of the visibility correction is positive, the time-degrees will become greater than twelve through that correction, and the Moon will be visible. This is clear.

Now, by the proportion of the corner <note>referring to spherical trigonometry ratios</note>, the Stick <term>Yasti: a calculated functional radius used in projection</term> = $\frac{\text{Day-radius of the pole} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Day-radius}}$. Since the maximum latitude sine = 270, therefore by proportion:

Celestial Latitude <term>Shara</term> = $\frac{\text{Max Lat Sine} \times \text{Sine of Versed Longitude}}{\text{Radius}}$ = $\frac{270 \times \text{Versed Sine}}{120}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine} \times 6}{4}$.

Furthermore, the Corrected Latitude = $\frac{\text{Stick} \times \text{Latitude}}{\text{Radius}}$ = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of Pole Distance}}{\text{Radius} \times \text{Day-radius}}$ $\times$ $\frac{\text{Versed Sine} \times 9}{4}$

= $\frac{9 \times \text{Sine of Pole Distance} \times \text{Versed Sine}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 4}$. Then, following the method of **Bhaskara** <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> starting with "The corrected latitude multiplied by the equatorial shadow..." etc., the units of time for the visibility correction due to latitude <term>Aksha-drik-karma</term> are:

= $\frac{\text{Corrected Lat} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 12}$ = $\frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Versed Sine} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 12}$.

The degrees of latitude visibility correction = $\frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Versed Sine} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 12 \times 60}$

$\frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Versed Sine} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 12 \times 60} \times \frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine}}{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine}}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Declination} \times \text{Sine}}{\text{Radius}} \times$

$\frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Day-radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 12 \times 60 \times \text{Radius}}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Declination} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow}}{12} \times$

$\frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Radius} \times \text{Day-radius} \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Earth-sine}}{\text{Day-radius}} \times \frac{9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60}$.

= $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Ascensional Difference} \times 9 \times \text{Sine Pole Dist} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Radius} \times 4 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Asc. Diff.}}{5} \times \frac{9 \times 110 \times 120}{48 \times 4 \times 115 \times 60}$

= $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Asc. Diff.} \times 11 \times 9}{5520}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Asc. Diff.} \times 99}{5520}$ = $\frac{5520}{99}$ = $\frac{\text{Versed Sine of Asc. Diff.}}{56}$, due to a very small difference. The justification for the positive or negative application is clear from observing the position of the celestial sphere; thus, the calculation of the degrees of ascensional difference is established.

Now, it is assumed: Mean Latitude = $L$. Declination of the planet plus three signs = $D_s$. Its day-radius = $R_s$. Its ascensional difference sine = $S_s$. The ascensional difference = $A_s$. Then, by the previous logic, the Stick = $\frac{\text{Day-radius of Pole} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Day-radius}}$.

The sine of the ecliptic correction = $\frac{\text{Sine of Declination} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Day-radius}}$. The Corrected Latitude = $\frac{L \times R_s}{\text{Radius}}$. The visibility correction due to the ecliptic <term>Ayana-drik-karma</term> =

= $\frac{\text{Equatorial Shadow} \times L \times R_s \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Radius} \times 12 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60}$ = $K$. Therefore, by eliminating the denominator, etc., $L$ = $\frac{K \times \text{Radius} \times 12 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60}{\text{Equatorial Shadow} \times R_s \times \text{Radius}}$

Then, by the method of **Bhaskara** starting with "The product of the corrected deflection..." etc., the ecliptic visibility correction = $\frac{\text{Sine of Deflection} \times L}{\text{Stick}}$

= $\frac{\text{Day-radius} \times K \times \text{Radius} \times 12 \times \text{Day-radius} \times 60 \times \text{Sine of Declination} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Day-radius of Pole} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Equatorial Shadow} \times R_s \times \text{Radius} \times 60}$

Now, the definition of a <term>Tithi</term><note>A lunar day</note> is clearly that at the end of the first lunar day (<term>Pratipada</term>), the distance between the Sun and the Moon is twelve degrees. Now, if from the calculation of the total elapsed days, the sunset and the end of the first lunar day occur simultaneously, then in the time it takes for the twelve degrees of the zodiac sign six places ahead of the Sun to rise after sunset, the Moon's position—which is separated from the Sun by that same amount—will also reach the western horizon. Therefore, if the rising time in <term>Palas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 6 seconds</note> for the sign six places ahead of the Sun is obtained for thirty degrees, then what would it be for twelve degrees? By this proportion, the time in Palas related to the twelve-degree interval between the Sun and Moon is found. These divided by 10 become degrees. Those degrees, separated by 12° of <term>Time-degrees</term><note>Kalansha: degrees of time used to determine visibility</note>, are:

$= 12° \backsim \frac{\text{Rising time of (Sun + 6 signs)} \times 12°}{30° \times 10} = 12° \backsim \frac{\text{Rising time of (Sun + 6 signs)}}{(2 + \frac{1}{2}) \times 10} =$

$= \frac{12° \times 10 \times (2 + \frac{1}{2}) \backsim \text{Rising time of (Sun + 6 signs)}}{(2 + \frac{1}{2}) \times 10} = \frac{300 \backsim \text{Rising time of (Sun + 6 signs)}}{25}$ . 

Therefore, if the rising time is greater than this (300), the results are positive; otherwise, they are negative. If the length of the day and the duration of the first lunar day are equal, then the Moon will certainly rise at sunset on that day. If there is a difference between the length of the day and the lunar day: if 60 <term>Nadis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> yield twelve degrees, then what do the Nadis of the difference between the day-length and the lunar day yield? By this proportion, the resulting degrees are:

$= \frac{(\text{Day length} \backsim \text{Lunar day length}) \times 12°}{60} = \frac{\text{Day length} \backsim \text{Lunar day length}}{5}$ . 

This result is added or subtracted when the day length is greater or less than the lunar day length, because of the certainty or uncertainty of the Moon's rise. Thus, everything is proven. || 1-3 ||

At the end of the first lunar day, add 12 degrees to the calculated Sun and the <term>Vyagu</term><note>A technical term in this system likely referring to a specific planetary longitude or node</note>. Then, divide the <term>Chara</term><note>Ascensional difference</note> degrees produced from the <term>Nirayana</term><note>Sidereal (without precession)</note> Vyagu by 56. Add or subtract this sequentially in the northern and southern hemispheres of the Vyagu. || 1 ||

Divide the product of this and the Chara of the Sun (with precession) by the square of twice the <term>Palabha</term><note>The length of the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>. Understand this to be additive or subtractive depending on whether the Sun and Vyagu are in different or the same hemispheres.

<header>In the Grahalaghava with Commentary—</header>

Regarding the phrase "Lunar day and solar day" etc.: The value for months and other units is placed in two positions: 3 [months], 4 [days], 2 [ghatikas], 29 [palas]. In one place, it is subtracted by fifteen days <note>The term 'tithi-dina' here refers to 15 days, half a lunar month</note>, resulting in 2 | 19 | 2 | 29. In the other place, it is added, resulting in 3 | 19 | 2 | 39. With these months, the setting and rising of the Minister (Jupiter) occur respectively.
To explain: With the value where fifteen days were subtracted—consisting of months, days, and ghatikas—the setting of Jupiter occurs counting from the month of Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note>.
In the other case (where fifteen days were added), it is the rising. This is the meaning. || 43 ||

## The Madhuri Commentary—

**Full of cycles** = including the elapsed cycles (revolutions). **Diminished by the cycles multiplied by thirteen** = minus the cycles multiplied by thirteen. **Doubled** = multiplied by two. **With ten months and the days of Shiva** = joined with ten months and eleven days <note>Shiva/Dhurjati is a numerical symbol for 11</note>. **By the 'ma-s'** = divided by twenty-seven <note>'Ma' refers to the 27 lunar mansions</note>. **Infallible** = subtracted from twenty-seven. **Divided by two** = divided by two. **The collection of months starting with Madhu** = the group of months starting from Chaitra. **Without the face** = starting from the signs (Rashis). This becomes the value. **Separately** = placed in two positions. **By the parts of a lunar day** = by fifteen parts. **Diminished** = subtracted. **When in the signs of the Pot (Libra) or the Goat (Aries)** = when in the six signs starting from Libra or the six signs starting from Aries. **Of this** = of this value starting with signs. **Subtracted or added by the twelfth part of the arm-degrees** = decreased or increased by one-twelfth of the sine of the longitude <note>A correction for the planet's position</note>. **From Madhu** = from the month of Chaitra. **Months and so on** = consisting of months, days, ghatikas, and palas. **In two ways** = in two locations. **Subtracted and added by fifteen days** = decreased and increased by fifteen days. **By those** = by those months. **Respectively** = in order. **Of the Minister** = of Jupiter. **The setting and rising** (the meaning of the word 'respectively' is that the months minus fifteen days indicate the setting, and the months plus fifteen days indicate the rising). These occur. || 43 ||

## Here is the Rationale—

The planet calculated from the sum of months, combined with the epochal constant <term>Kshepa</term> <note>A constant value used to adjust calculations to a specific starting date</note> at the beginning of the text, becomes the true planet at the end of the month. For example, by the proportion of the Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle</note>, the lunar month related to a single conjunction of Jupiter and the Sun is 13 + 3/33. In one cycle (revolution), the lunar months are 13 6/33. From this proportion, the conjunction related to one cycle is = 10 + 13/13 = 10 + (1 + 12 - 1)/13 = 10 + 1/13 * 3/3 - (12 - 1)/13 = 10 + (1 - 1/13) = Remainder + 10. Therefore, if for one cycle this remainder is (1 - 1/13), then for the desired cycles, what is it? The remainder related to the desired cycles = Cycles × (1 - 1/13) = Cycles - (Cycles/13). The sum of months produced by this is = Month-sum + (Cycles - Cycles/13).

Now, this month, combined with the epochal constant at the start of the text (10 months 11 days)/2, becomes: (10 months 11 days)/2 + Month-sum + Cycles - (Cycles/13). Furthermore, as will be explained in the rule "If for Venus it is purified, for Jupiter by thirteen and a half," if one conjunction occurs in 13 + 1/2 months, then by these months, what is the conjunction? The proportion is:
= [ (10 months 11 days)/2 + Month-sum + Cycles - (Cycles/13) ] / 13.5
= [ (5 months + 11/2 days + Month-sum + Cycles - Cycles/13) ] / 27.
Here, after discarding the indication of the number of past conjunctions from the quotient, and subtracting the remainder from the divisor, the lunar months until the next conjunction will be: 13 1/2 - (Remainder/27) = 27/2 - (Remainder/2).

# Chapter 6: On the Rising and Setting of Planets

$= \frac{27 - \text{remainder}}{2}$. And thus, by the previous logic, the Sun below the planet relative to the remaining months $= \frac{65 \times \text{remaining months}}{67}$.

Now, by the logic of the time, the Sun itself is the "Guru" <note>Jupiter</note> from the start of Chaitra <note>the first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note> until the start of Aries, according to the solar degrees accepted by the teacher. By accepting 15 solar degrees and using the ratio, the resulting "arm-result" <term>bhujāṃśaphala: the arc of the sine used in longitude calculations</term> is subtracted or added to the centers of Libra or Aries. Thus, the count of months from the start of Chaitra is determined. Similarly, using the logic from the "True Motion" chapter, the interval for setting occurs in one month, and then rising occurs again. Because the rising and setting of Jupiter occur within a month-count reduced or increased by fifteen days, this reasoning is stated correctly and is proven. || 4 ||

The count of months from the start of Chaitra, in signs and degrees, is calculated as follows: take the sum of the cycles, subtract one-thirteenth of the cycles, multiply by 2, add 10 months and 11 days, divide by 27, subtract the result from 27, and divide by 2. Place this value in two locations. Subtract 15 degrees from one; then, depending on whether the center is in Libra or Aries, sequentially subtract or add one-twelfth of its "arm-degrees" <term>bhujāṃśa</term> to the value in the second location to find the months from Chaitra. By placing this result in two locations and subtracting or adding 15 days, the respective setting <term>asta</term> and rising <term>udaya</term> of Jupiter are found. || 4 ||

**Example** — In the Shaka year 1844, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Jyeshtha, the year-group is 422, the cycle is 38, and the month-group is 52. -> **Mathematical Proof** <-

Revolution of Venus's anomaly in a Kalpa <term>Kalpa|A vast cosmic time cycle</term> = 2,702,388,746.
Lunar months in a Kalpa = 53,433,336,000.
If these lunar months are obtained in a Kalpa's revolutions of Venus, then what is obtained by one revolution? The lunar months for one revolution (the synodic period) = $\frac{53,433,336,000 \times 1}{2,702,388,746} = 19 + \frac{4}{5} = \frac{99}{5}$.

In one cycle (136 revolutions), the lunar months = 136. When divided by this ($\frac{99}{5}$), the remainder for one cycle = ($17 + \frac{17}{99}$). Therefore, if this is the remainder for one, what is it for the desired cycles? The remainder for the desired cycles = ($17 + \frac{17}{99}$) $\times$ cycles.
Months from Chaitra = *mama*. The epochal constant <term>Kshepa|Additive constant at the start of an era</term> for Venus at the start of the text = $\frac{64}{5}$.
Adding these together, if one month is obtained by the Kalpa remainder, what is obtained by the desired remainder? The lunar month = {($17 + \frac{17}{99}$) $\times$ cycles + *mama* + $\frac{64}{5}$} $\times$ 5 = {$\frac{(17 + \frac{17}{99}) \times \text{cycles} + \text{mama}}{99}$} $\times 5 + 64 = \text{Quotient} + \frac{\text{Remainder}}{5}$.
Since the quotient is not needed here, it is discarded. When the remainder is subtracted from the divisor, the lunar months for the next conjunction = $\frac{99}{5} - \frac{\text{Remainder}}{5} = \frac{99 - \text{Remainder}}{5}$. This sum represents the months following Chaitra.
The number of days between the Eastern setting and Western rising of Venus mentioned previously is 73; therefore, half of those days...

### Now, the calculation for the Moon's approximate celestial latitude is stated—

> In the first sign of the Moon's arm minus the Node, the degrees are increased by half themselves; in the second, they are joined with forty-seven.
> In the last, the halved degrees are joined with seventy-seven; the latitude in digits etc. will be in the direction of the Moon minus the Node. || 9 ||

Now the calculation of the Moon's latitude <note>term: "Śara" (arrow/latitude) - the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> is stated. **In the first**: When the "arm-sign" <note>term: "Bhuja" - the arc used to calculate the sine</note> of the Moon minus Rahu <note>The ascending node</note> is in the first sign, the degrees should be increased by their own half; that will be the latitude in digits <note>term: "Angula" - a traditional unit of measure used here for celestial arc</note>. The latitude in digits will be in the **direction** of the globe where the **Moon minus the Node** <note>original: "Vyaguvidhu"</note> is located. In this calculation of latitude, the signs should not be converted to degrees; the degrees below the signs should be taken exactly as they are. For the sake of calculating the Moon's latitude, the Moon and Rahu at the time of the end of the lunar day <note>Tithi</note> as calculated in a solar eclipse are established. Moon: 8s 5° 26' 20". Rahu: 1s 2° 11' 41" 18"'. Moon minus Node: 7s 3° 15' 2". Its "arm" <note>Bhuja</note> is 0s 6° 15' 58". Since the arm is in the first sign, its degrees 6° 15' 58" are increased by their half 3° 7' 29", resulting in a latitude of 9' 22" 27"'. Since the Moon minus Node is in the northern hemisphere, the latitude is North. || 9 ||

This may be a scribal variant.</note>. The **latitude** <note>original: "Viśikha"</note> starting with **digits** will be in the **direction of the Moon minus the Node**. || 9 ||

# Chapter 6: On the Rising and Setting of Heavenly Bodies

### Here is the Proof:—
According to the method to be described later using the mnemonic "Kings, Lunar days, Manus, All-gods" <note>original: "नृपतिथिमनुविश्व"; these are numerical codes: 16, 15, 14, 13</note> and so on, for the arc segments of 30°, 60°, and 90°, the values of the latitude in digits <term>Angulas: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly a finger-breadth</term> are 45, 78, and 90 respectively. Here, the Teacher <note>referring to the author of the original Sanskrit verses</note> has accepted the values 47, 77, and 90 for those same arc segments due to a slight difference in calculation. Now, if for 30 degrees of the arc, a latitude of 47 digits is obtained, then for any desired arc segment, what would it be? By this proportion, the latitude in digits related to the desired arc is:

$\frac{\text{Moon's Node-less Arc} \times 47}{30} = \frac{\text{Moon's Node-less Arc} \times 3}{2}$ (approximately) = Moon's Node-less Arc ($1 + \frac{1}{2}$) = Moon's Node-less Arc

+ $\frac{\text{Moon's Node-less Arc}}{2}$. The difference between the latitude digits at the end of the first and second signs is $47 \sim 77 = 30$. Thus, by proportion, the latitude digits related to the Moon's node-less arc in the second sign = $\frac{30 \times \text{Moon's Node-less Arc}}{30} = \text{Moon's Node-less Arc}$. By adding this to the latitude at the end of the first sign, the latitude digits in the second sign = $47 + \text{Moon's Node-less Arc}$.

Now, $77 \sim 90 = 13$. Again, by proportion, the latitude digits related to the difference = $\frac{13 \times \text{Moon's Node-less Arc}}{30}$

= $\frac{\text{Moon's Node-less Arc}}{2}$ (approximately). By adding this to the latitude at the end of the second sign, the latitude digits for the Moon's node-less arc in the third sign = $77 + \frac{\text{Moon's Node-less Arc}}{2}$.
Thus, it is proven. || 9 ||

If the node-less Moon's arc is in the first sign <note>0° to 30°</note>, add half the arc to itself; if it is in the second sign <note>30° to 60°</note>, add 47 to the arc; and if it is in the third sign <note>60° to 90°</note>, add half the arc to 77. This gives the latitude in digits for the Moon's sphere when the Rahu <note>the North Node</note> is subtracted. || 9 ||

**Example**—At the time of the end of the lunar month mentioned in the solar eclipse, the Moon is at 5 signs, 4°, 21', 59" and Rahu is at 5 signs, 1°, 14', 28". Therefore, the node-less Moon is 0 signs, 3°, 7', 31". Since its arc (3° 7' 31") is in the first sign, adding its half (1° 33' 45") to it (because the node-less Moon is in the Northern hemisphere) results in a Northern lunar latitude of 4° 41' 16" digits. || 9 ||

Now he describes another method for calculating latitude. "Kings..." etc. The node-less Moon is 9 signs, 23°, 49', 2". Its arc segment is 6° 14' 58". Dividing by ten, the completed segment is 0, and the remainder is 6° 14' 58". Multiplying this by the next segment (16) gives 99° 59' 28". Dividing this by ten, the result is 9' 59". Adding this to the sum of previous segments, the latitude in digits is North 9' 59". || 10 ||

# Page 172
### With Commentary on the Grahalaghava

The values 7, 4, and 1 <note>original: "Adrayah, Shrutayah, Vasudha" - using Sanskrit numerical code words where mountains=7, Vedas=4, and Earth=1</note> constitute the nine segments of the latitude <term>shara-khandas; mathematical segments used to calculate the celestial latitude of a planet</term>. By using these segments and the sine of the Moon's longitude minus the node <note>original: "vyagu-vidhu-bhuja"</note>, one calculates the latitude in the same manner as the declination. The direction of this latitude, measured in digits <term>angulas; a traditional unit of measurement</term>, follows the direction of the Moon's pole as determined by the Rahu <note>the ascending node</note> calculation. Alternatively, this is the precise latitude. || 10 ||

->### Here is the Mathematical Proof:<-

The radius <term>trijya</term> is 120. The maximum latitude in digits is 90. Let the sine of the desired Moon-minus-node be "I-Vya-Chan-Jya."
By proportion, the latitude in digits for the desired sine is:
(Maximum Latitude × Sine) / Radius = (90 × Sine) / 120 = (3 × Sine) / 4.
Then, using the method for generating segments, the degrees of the Moon minus the node are taken as: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90.
Their sines are: 21, 41, 60, 77, 92, 104, 113, 118, 120.
Using the previous proportion, the first segment is: (3 × 21) / 4 = 63 / 4 = 16 (approximately).
The second cumulative segment is: (3 × 41) / 4 = 123 / 4 = 31 (approximately).
Therefore, 31 - 16 = 15, which is the second segment. The same logic applies throughout. The rest of the proof is similar to the proof for calculating declination. Thus, it is proven. || 10 ||

The nine segments of the latitude are 16, 15, 14, 13, 11, 9, 7, 4, and 1. Through these, like the calculation of declination, the latitude of the Moon (minus the node) is found in digits and directions.
**Example:** For the Moon's arm-degrees <note>sine-related longitude</note> of 2s 7° 31', dividing by 10 gives a quotient of zero. Thus, the "passed segment" is 0. Multiplying the arm-degrees by the next segment (16) and dividing by 10 results in 5° 0' 1". Since the Moon is in the northern hemisphere, the clear lunar latitude is 5° 0' 1" North. || 10 ||

> A slow-moving planet, if its longitude is less than the Sun's, rises in the East. A fast-moving planet, if its longitude is greater, rises in the West. A slow planet with greater longitude sets in the West, while a fast planet with lesser longitude sets in the East. || 11 ||

Now the author explains the direction of the rising and setting of planets. "A slow-moving planet...": If a planet moves slower than the Sun <note>original: "Ina" - a name for the Sun</note> and its degrees are fewer (meaning it is behind the Sun), it rises in the East. If a planet is further ahead than the Sun and moves faster, it rises in the West. If a planet is ahead of the Sun but moves slower, it sets in the West. If a planet moves faster than the Sun but is behind it in degrees, it sets in the East. This specific behavior applies to Mercury and Venus; it does not apply to others because their motion is always slower than the Sun's. || 11 ||

->### The Madhuri Commentary:<-

Relative to the Sun: a slow-moving planet with fewer signs (located behind the Sun) rises in the East. A fast-moving planet with more signs (located ahead of the Sun) <unclear>if so, then</unclear> rises in the West...

# Chapter on Rising and Setting (Udayasta) || 4 ||

It rises. Thus, a planet with **slow motion** and a **greater longitudinal position** than the Sun <note>original: "laghugah... bhuyan"</note> sets in the **west**. A planet with **fast motion** and a **lesser longitudinal position** than the Sun <note>original: "bhuri-javah... laghuh"</note> sets in the **east**. || 11 ||

-> Here is the mathematical rationale: <-

A planet with slower motion than the Sun and a lesser longitudinal position (located behind the Sun) is capable of being seen in the eastern direction at the end of the night, just before sunrise. Now, a planet with greater motion than the Sun and a greater longitudinal position (located ahead of the Sun) is capable of being seen in the west at the beginning of the night. Furthermore, a planet with slower motion but a greater longitudinal position, even though it is ahead of the Sun, will—due to its slow motion—be overtaken by the Sun and thus sets in the west. Similarly, a planet with faster motion but a lesser longitudinal position, even though it is behind the Sun, will—due to its daily faster motion—overtake the Sun and thus sets in the east. This is clear to the learned and is proven as stated. — The Editor || 11 ||

A planet with slower motion and lesser longitude sets in the east, and a planet with faster motion and greater longitude rises in the west. Similarly, a planet with slow motion and greater longitude sets in the west, and a planet with faster motion and lesser longitude sets in the east. || 11 ||

-> Now he states the degrees of time (Kālāmśas) for the rising and setting of planets: <-

> **Twelve for the Moon, seventeen, thirteen, eleven, nine for the gods' residents, and fifteen. These degrees of time were spoken by the ancients starting from the Moon; for Venus and Mercury when retrograde, they are diminished by one.** || 12 ||

This is the definition of rising and setting caused by the Sun. Now, to understand rising and setting, he states the degrees of time <term>Kālāmśa: the arc of separation from the Sun required for a planet to become visible</term>. **Twelve** etc., are the degrees of time spoken by the ancient teachers starting from the Moon. For the **Moon**, 12. For **Mars** <note>original: "naga-bhuvah" (mountains=7, earth=1)</note>, 17. For **Mercury** <note>original: "guna-candrah" (qualities=3, moon=1)</note>, 13. For **Jupiter** <note>original: "bhu-bhuvah" (earth=1, earth=1)</note>, 11. For **Venus** <note>original: "divisadah" (inhabitants of heaven)</note>, 9. For **Saturn** <note>original: "tithayah" (lunar days)</note>, 15. When **Venus and Mercury** are **retrograde** <term>Vakri: appearing to move backward in the sky</term>, then their stated degrees of time should be made **diminished by one** <note>original: "ksiti-hinah"</note>, i.e., reduced by 1. || 12 ||

-> The Madhuri Commentary: <-

**By the ancients** = by the old teachers; **Twelve** = 12; **Seventeen** = 17; **Thirteen** = 13; **Eleven** = 11; **Nine** = 9; **Fifteen** = 15. These, in order, **from the Moon** (meaning for the Moon and others) are **degrees of time**, so it is **stated**. For the **retrograde** = those with reverse motion, **Venus and Mercury**, the degrees of time are stated as **diminished by one** = minus one. || 12 ||

-> Here is the mathematical rationale: <-

It is based on observation alone. || 12 ||

Ancient teachers have stated the degrees of time for the planets starting with the Moon as 12, 17, 13, 11, 9, and 15 respectively. For retrograde Venus and Mercury, the stated degrees of 9 and 13 are reduced by one, meaning 8 and 12 degrees of time are stated. || 12 ||

-> Now he states the degrees of the Nodes for Mars and others: <-

> **Forty, twenty, eighty, sixty, and ten are, in order, the degrees of the Nodes starting from the son of the Earth (Mars), for Mercury and Venus they are subtracted from the mean and true centers.** || 13 ||

for Jupiter; sixty 60 for Venus; one hundred 100 for Saturn. For Mercury and Venus, the degrees of the nodes <note>Pata: the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> should be decreased by the mean anomaly <note>Shighra-kendra: the "fast center" or anomaly used in calculating planetary positions</note> derived from the daily count of days <note>Ahargana: the number of days elapsed since the beginning of the epoch</note>. || 13 ||

## The Madhuri Commentary —

"Space-oceans" <note>Kha-ambudhaya</note> = forty 40; "Space-twos" <note>Kha-yamah</note> = twenty 20; "Space-serpents" <note>Kha-bhujangah</note> = eighty 80; "Space-limbs" <note>Kha-angamita</note> = sixty 60; "Space-tens" <note>Kha-dasha</note> = one hundred 100. These, starting from the son of the Earth <note>Mars</note>, in order, are the degrees of the nodes. For Mercury and Venus, when these are deprived of the mean anomaly produced from the daily count, the stated node-degrees become the true node-degrees. || 13 ||

## Here is the Proof: —

The node <note>Pata</note> is the intersection of the ecliptic and the planet's orbit. The nodes of Mars and the others are taught as fixed—similar to the statement "the Sun's slow-node <note>apogee</note> is eight degrees etc."—because of their extremely slow motion. Now, because Bhaskara <note>The famous 12th-century mathematician Bhaskaracharya</note> stated that "the node-revolutions of Mercury and Venus are greater than the revolutions of the anomaly," the node-degrees of Mercury and Venus are taught as including the degrees of the mean anomaly. Therefore, it is rightly said that the node-degrees are found by subtracting the mean anomaly. This is proven. || 13 ||

The node-degrees for Mars and the other planets in order are 40, 20, 80, 60, and 100. By subtracting their respective mean anomalies (derived from the daily count) from the node-degrees of Mercury and Venus, the true node-degrees are obtained. || 13 ||

## Now, the calculation of the Planet's Rapid Hypotenuse is stated —

> If the sum of the parts is 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 2; if the anomaly
> exceeds six signs, subtract it from the full circle. Multiply the result
> by the degrees and divide by thirty. Add this to the sum of the parts.
> For Mars [and others], divide by 1, 2, 4, 1, 7 respectively.
> Subtract these from 18, 15, 13, 19, 12. The result is the rapid hypotenuse. || 14 ||

Now, for the purpose of calculating the latitude <note>Shara</note>, the calculation of the rapid hypotenuse <note>Shighra-karna</note> is stated. "Ku-dvi..." etc. On the full moon day of the bright half of the month of Vaishakha, Shaka year 1734 <note>Approximately May 1812 CE</note>, the calculation of the true declination of Mars and the others is performed. There, the final anomalies of Mars and the others are: Mars's anomaly 3|14|55. Mercury's anomaly 11|6|26|17. Jupiter's anomaly 8|21|20|58. Venus's anomaly 3|4|59|52. Saturn's anomaly 2|2|17|0. 

Now, the rapid hypotenuse of Mars is calculated: Mars's anomaly is 3|14|55. The sum of the three segments corresponding to the signs is 6. With the remainder 14|57, the next segment is 4. Multiplied, it is 59|48. Divided by thirty, the result is 0|8|39. Adding this to the sum of segments 6, it becomes 6|8|39. Divided by one, it is 6|8|39. Subtracting this from eighteen 18, the rapid hypotenuse of Mars is 11|51|21. 

From Mercury's anomaly, the result is 2|54|4. Divided by two: 1|27|0. Subtracting this from fifteen 15, Mercury's rapid hypotenuse is 13|37|10. 

From Jupiter's anomaly, the result is 7|9|12. Divided by four: 1|47|18. Subtracting this from thirteen, Jupiter's rapid hypotenuse is 11|12|42. 

From Venus's anomaly, the result is 6|39|58. Divided by one: 6|39|58. Subtracting this from nineteen 19, Venus's rapid hypotenuse is 12|20|2. 

From Saturn's anomaly, the result is 3|9|0. Divided by seven, the result is 0|28|58. Subtracting this from twelve, Saturn's rapid hypotenuse is 11|31|12. || 14 ||

# Chapter on Rising and Setting || 6 ||

If the <term>fast anomaly</term><note>original: "शीघ्र केन्द्र" (shīghra-kendra); the angular distance of a planet from its apogee in its secondary epicycle</note> is greater [than six signs], then by performing <term>circle-purification</term><note>original: "चक्रविशुद्धं" (cakra-viśuddhaṃ); subtracting the value from 12 signs (360 degrees)</note>, take the sum of the equal sign-segments of this [purified value]. To this, add the result of the degrees multiplied by the next segment and divided by thirty. For Mars and the others, divide this respectively by one, two, four, one, and seven. Subtracting these results from eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, nineteen, and twelve respectively, the <term>fast hypotenuse</term><note>original: "शीघ्रकर्ण" (shīghra-karṇa); the distance from the Earth to the planet</note> is obtained. || 14 ||

->### Here is the mathematical proof:—<-

Here, the "fast hypotenuse" refers to the distance of the planet in its secondary epicycle from the center of the Earth. This was calculated by Bhaskara and others using methods such as "the sum of the squares of the cosine and the maximum sine of correction." However, since the discussion of sines and cosines is avoided here, the segments have been read based on the difference between the perigee and apogee across six signs, assuming a radius of 11. ∵ In a radius of "sky-sun" (120), the maximum sine of correction for Mars etc. is 77, 44, 22, 88, 10; therefore, if these are the values in a radius of 120, what would they be in a radius of eleven? In a radius of eleven, the maximum sines of correction for Mars etc. are 7, 4, 2, 8, <gloss>10</gloss>/11. Now, ∵ "Radius + Max Sine = Maximum Fast Hypotenuse at Apogee." Thus, for Mars etc., the maximum fast hypotenuses are 18, 15, 13, 19, 12.

Furthermore, within six signs, at the end of each sign, the cosines for Venus are found to be 19, 11, 0, 11, 23. Therefore, by Bhaskara’s method of "the square root of the sum of the squares of the maximum sine of correction and the radius," the hypotenuses for Venus at the end of each sign in the six-sign arc are 18, 16, 13, 9, 5, 3 (with slight differences). When these are subtracted from the maximum Venus hypotenuse of 19, the remainders are 1, 3, 6, 10, 14, 16. Subtracting these successively from each other, the segments are 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 2. This proves the rule of "the increase of segments by one, two, three, four, four, and two." The rest of the proof is as easy as the proof for calculating declination. Thus, it is proven. || 14 ||

To calculate the fast hypotenuse, the segments are 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, and 2. If the fast anomaly is greater than 6 signs, subtract it from 12 signs. To the sum of the segments corresponding to the remaining signs, add the quotient of the remaining degrees multiplied by the next segment and divided by 30. Divide this by 1, 2, 4, 1, and 7 respectively. Subtracting these quotients from 18, 15, 13, 11, and 12 gives the fast hypotenuses of Mars and the other planets in order. || 14 ||

**Example**—In the Shaka year 1858, year 1344, on the day of the dark half of Kartika, New Moon, Friday, at the total day-count (<term>Ahargana</term>) 3578: the Mean Sun is 6s 28° 50' 17", Mars is 4s 7° 23' 20", Jupiter is 8s 16° 28' 53", and Mean Saturn is 11s 10° 5' 56". Therefore, by the method of "Mean Sun minus the planet's apogee," the fast anomaly of Mars is 2s 21° 26' 57", Mercury's is 11s 7° 41' 17", Jupiter's is 10s 12° 21' 24", Venus's is 2s 27° 1' 14", and Saturn's is 7s 24° 44' 21".

In the fast anomaly of Mars, there are 2 signs; therefore, in the sum of the passed segments 1+2 = 3, add the quotient of the degrees etc. 21° 26' 57" multiplied by the next segment (3), which is 64° 20' 51", divided by 30...

### Now, the calculation of the Celestial Latitude for Mars and others—

> From the planet corrected for slow motion <term>Manda-spashta</term>, subtract its own node <term>Paata</term>. From that alone, find the declination <term>Kranti</term>.
> Multiply by twenty-three and divide by the hypotenuse. For Jupiter, divide again by two.
> For Mars, subtract its own fourth part. This gives the latitude in digits <term>Angulas</term>. The direction is that of the node-subtracted planet.
> Multiplied by three, it becomes minutes of arc <term>Kalika</term>, which is more precise when applied to the declination. || 15 ||

Now the method for calculating the celestial latitude <term>Shara</term> for Mars and others is explained. *From the planet corrected for slow motion...* The slow-corrected **Mars** is 10;3,8,49. Divided by the fast hypotenuse 11;59,12, the result is 45;31,38. As stated, "subtract its own fourth part for Mars," subtracting its fourth part 11;30,24, and because the node-subtracted planet is in the southern hemisphere, the resulting **Southern Latitude** in digits is 34;1,14. Note this specific detail: when Mars's fast hypotenuse is less than eleven, a great difference occurs; therefore, the result obtained by dividing by the hypotenuse should be divided by two before subtracting the fourth part to find Mars's latitude. If the hypotenuse is greater than eleven, the difference is not handled this way.

Slow-corrected **Mercury** is 9;5,3,56. Its node in signs etc. is 10;20,0,0. This is subtracted from the fast anomaly generated from the daily count 11;7,14,50, leaving 11;12,45,10. ### The Madhuri Commentary—

From the absolute (sidereal) position minus its own node, the degrees of declination of the slow-corrected planet are multiplied by twenty-three (3 and 2) and divided by the variable hypotenuse. Then, if it is Jupiter, divide by two (eyes). For Mars, subtract its own fourth part. The direction (North/South) of the latitude is the same as the direction of the planet's hemisphere relative to the node. This latitude in digits, multiplied by three, becomes the latitude in minutes. The declination adjusted by that latitude becomes the **True Declination**. || 15 ||

### Here is the Proof (Rationale):—

| Max Declination | Max Latitude |
| :--- | :--- |
| Current Declination | Current Latitude |

Therefore: Max Declination × Current Latitude = Current Declination × Max Latitude.
Therefore: Current Latitude = (Current Declination × Max Latitude) / Max Declination.

This latitude, relative to the variable hypotenuse, is multiplied by the specific radius and divided by the variable hypotenuse to convert it. Furthermore, this latitude multiplied by the true radius and divided by the specific radius becomes the **Actual Latitude**:

Actual Latitude = (Current Declination × Max Latitude × Radius) / (Max Declination × Variable Hypotenuse) .... (A).

Here, the True Radius = 11, Maximum Declination = 24, and the maximum latitudes in digits for Mars and the others are 37, 50, 25, 50, 50. Therefore, substituting these values into equation 'A', the latitude for Mars and the others is found. For example, the latitude of Mars = (Current Declination × 37 × 11) / (24 × Variable Hypotenuse).

= [Current Declination × 11 (6 + 1/6)] / Variable Hypotenuse = [Current Declination × (66 + 11/6)] / Variable Hypotenuse = (Current Declination × 69) / Variable Hypotenuse (due to a small difference).

# On the Latitudes in the Latika-Grahalaghava

<note>The following equations demonstrate how the author simplifies complex trigonometric ratios into manageable multipliers for calculating planetary latitude.</note>

$$ \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23 \times 3}{4 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23 \times (1 - 1/4)}{\text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23}{\text{Variable Divisor}} - \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23}{\text{Variable Divisor} \times 4} $$

$$ \text{Latitude of Mercury} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 50 \times 11}{24 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 25 \times 11}{12 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times (2 + 1/12) \times 11}{\text{Variable Divisor}} $$

$$ = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times (22 + 11/12)}{\text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23}{\text{Variable Divisor}} \text{ (due to slight difference)} = \text{Latitude of Venus} = \text{Latitude of Saturn.} $$

Because the maximum latitude values for these planets are considered equal in this system.

$$ \text{Similarly, the Latitude of Jupiter} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 25 \times 11}{24 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} = $$

$$ = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23 \times 13}{24 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} = \frac{\text{Desired Declination} \times 23}{2 \times \text{Variable Divisor}} \text{ (taking a slight approximation). The rest of the proof is easy to understand.} $$

Thus, it is proven. || 15 ||

<note>The following is a Hindi explanation of the rule for calculating the celestial latitude (Shara) of Mars and other planets.</note>

Multiply the declination <term>Kranti; the distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</term> of the planets starting with Mars (calculated from their corrected longitudes minus their respective nodes) by 23. Divide this product by the planet's own <term>Shighrakarna; the variable hypotenuse or distance from the Earth to the planet</term>. If the result is for Jupiter, divide it by 2; if for Mars, subtract one-fourth of the value from itself to get the true result. This result is the latitude in <term>Angulas; a traditional unit of measure</term> in the direction of the planet's hemisphere. Multiplying this latitude by three converts it into minutes of arc <term>Kalas</term>. By applying the correction of this latitude to the mean declination, the true declination is obtained. || 15 ||

-> Example <-

From the 10th verse of the chapter on the true positions of the five planets, the corrected longitudes are: Mars 4s 3° 7' 3", Mercury 6s 29° 10' 23", Jupiter 8s 11° 10' 33", Venus 6s 27° 33' 4", and Saturn 10s 24° 49' 31". Now, subtracting the node of 40° from the longitude of Mars, we get the longitude relative to the node as 2s 23° 7' 32" in the northern hemisphere. Using the rule "forty-eighty etc.," the northern declination is 23° 43' 30". Multiplying this by 23 gives 545° 40' 00". Dividing this by the variable hypotenuse of Mars (121; 51, 18), the quotient is 4; 28, 54. Subtracting its fourth part (1; 7, 16, 43), the remaining northern latitude of Mars in Angulas is 3; 15, 0, 11. Similarly, the latitudes of Mercury and other planets should be calculated. Multiplying the latitude of Mars by 3 gives 9' 53" 1"' in minutes, or 1° 15' 31" in degrees. Adding this to the northern declination of Mars results in 2° 45' 9" 1"', which is the true northern declination of Mars. The true declinations of the remaining planets should be calculated in the same way. || 15 ||

# Chapter 6: On Rising and Setting

The position of a planet found in the almanac <note>Panchanga</note> regarding its cycle and other factors should be understood. On that day, the "Fast Anomaly" <term>Shighra-kendra: the angular distance between the planet and the point of its maximum equation</term> of that planet is as stated in the chapter on true positions. Specifically, the degrees of the cycle's setting and so on, divided by thirty, become the signs and degrees of the Fast Anomaly. On the desired day, this should be adjusted using the movement of its own degrees <note>the daily motion of the anomaly</note> by multiplying the elapsed or remaining days. From that adjusted Fast Anomaly, the "Fast Equation" <term>Shighra-phala: the correction for the planet's orbital position relative to the Sun</term> should be calculated as before. This should be applied to the adjusted true planet in a **reverse** manner: if it is additive, make it subtractive; if subtractive, make it additive. That planet then becomes the "Slow-True" planet <term>Manda-spashta: the planet's position corrected only for its own elliptical orbit, before the solar correction</term>. From that, the latitude <note>celestial latitude</note> and other values are derived. The word "and others" refers to the visibility correction <term>Drik-karma</term>.

In the year 1667 of the Vikrama era (Saka 1532), on Thursday, the 8th day of the bright half of the month of Chaitra, the calculation of the "Day-Count" <term>Ahargana: the number of days elapsed since the start of the epoch</term> is performed to determine the setting of Venus.
**Cycle:** 8. **Day-Count:** 757.
**Sun:** 11s 21° 22' 57".
**Fast Anomaly of Venus:** 11s 8° 31' 52".
**Slow Anomaly of the Sun:** 2s 26° 37' 43".
**Slow Equation (Additive):** 2° 10' 31".
**Corrected Sun:** 11s 23° 32' 48".
**Ascensional Difference Factor:** 22.
**True Sun:** 11s 23° 32' 26". **True Motion:** 59' 0".
**Fast Anomaly of Venus:** 11s 8° 31' 52".
**Fast Equation (Subtractive):** 5° 30' 30".
**Corrected Venus:** 11s 16° 51' 47".
**Slow Anomaly:** 3s 13° 8' 13".
**Slow Equation (Additive):** 1° 30' 8".
**Slow-True Venus:** 11s 22° 52' 57".
**Fast Anomaly:** 11s 7° 51' 52".
**Fast Equation (Subtractive):** 5° 37' 48".
**True Venus:** 11s 13° 14' 29". **True Motion:** 74' 53".
From the Slow-True position, the North Declination is 23° 56' 38".
**Fast Hypothenuse:** 18; 14, 4.
**Latitude in digits (South):** 30; 12, 56. || 16 ||

->The Madhuri Commentary<-

On the day when the cycle's setting etc. is found in the almanac, the stated anomaly of the planet is the Fast Anomaly. This should be adjusted for the desired day using the velocity of its own degrees. From that desired Fast Anomaly, the Fast Equation is calculated. This equation is applied to the adjusted true planet in reverse, and the planet then becomes the Slow-True planet. From that Slow-True planet, or by another method, the latitude and other factors are understood. || 16 ||

->The Rationale<-

Since [Slow-True Planet ± Equation = True Planet], it follows that [True Planet ∓ Equation = Slow-True Planet]. The rest of the logic is easy to understand. Thus, it is proven. || 16 ||

On the day the almanac shows the planet's cycle or setting, its anomaly will be equal to the stated Fast Anomaly (using the rule "by thirty..."). By adjusting that anomaly by its motion, one gets the Fast Anomaly for the desired time. By adjusting the true planet by its true motion, and then applying the Fast Equation in reverse, one obtains the Slow-True planet for the desired time. From this Slow-True planet, calculate the latitude and other values using the previously mentioned methods. || 16 ||

The example is straightforward. || 16 ||

### Now, the Zenith Distance for the Visibility Correction:

> Subtract three signs for the East, and add three signs for the West.
> From that planet, the combination of declination and latitude gives the degrees of zenith distance. || 17 ||

Now he describes the calculation of zenith distance <term>Natamsha</term> for the purpose of the visibility correction. For calculating the rising or setting in the East, the declination should be calculated from the true planet minus three signs (90 degrees). For the West, the declination should be <unclear>calculated</unclear> from the planet plus three signs. These, <unclear>corrected</unclear> by the local latitude, become the degrees of zenith distance.
**True Venus:** 11s 13° 14' 29".

<header>With the Commentary on the Grahalaghava—</header>

Because the eastern setting is to be calculated, the value is decreased by three signs: 4s 21° 15' 29". ->Madhuri Commentary<-

In the East (Prāk), subtract three signs (tribha); in the West, add the same to the planet (kheta). From the declination and latitude, the calculation (saṃskāra) results in the degrees of zenith distance (natāṃśāḥ) related to the time of meridian passage. ॥ 17 ॥

->Rationale here:<-

When a planet is on the eastern or western horizon, the rising sign (Lagna) is equal to the planet or the planet plus six signs. When three signs are subtracted from the Lagna, it becomes the "Nonagesimal" <note>original: "vintribhalagna," the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees back from the rising point</note>. Therefore, for a planet on the eastern horizon, subtracting three signs, and for a planet on the western horizon, adding three signs, truly yields the Nonagesimal. By processing the declination of the Nonagesimal and the latitude, the zenith distance is found. Because the Nonagesimal is near the meridian circle, taking this small difference is mathematically sound. ॥ 17 ॥

In the eastern direction, subtract 3 signs, and in the western direction, add 3 signs to the planet. By calculating the declination and latitude from this and processing them together, the zenith distance is obtained. ॥ 17 ॥

Example—Since the eastern setting of Venus is to be calculated, the clear Venus 10s 17° 12' 20" is reduced by 3 signs. Its Southern declination 15° 56' 18" and Southern latitude 26° 10' are added together, resulting in a zenith distance of 42° 6' 18". ॥ 17 ॥

->Now he describes the method for calculating the Visibility Correction <term>Drkkarma: the calculation to adjust a planet's position from the ecliptic to its actual visible position on the horizon</term>-<-

> **Six, seven, eight, nine, twelve, eighteen, and twenty-three are the segments. One should sum the segments corresponding to the tenths of the zenith distance; add to this the product of the next segment and the remainder, divided by ten. Multiply this by the latitude in digits (angulas) and divide by twelve; the resulting minutes are applied to the planet. If the zenith distance and the planet's latitude are in the same or different directions, add or subtract them; in the West, do the opposite. This is the visible planet.** ॥ 18 ॥

Now he explains the calculation of the <term>Drkkarma</term>. "Six, seven..." etc. The zenith distance is 42° 33' 54". One-tenth of this is 4. The sum of the segments up to this is 30. The remainder is 2° 33' 25". The next (fifth) segment is 12. [Calculation follows]: 112° 50' 48" divided by ten is 11° 16' 4". Added to the sum of previous segments (30), it becomes 41° 16' 4". Multiplied by the latitude in digits (30° 2' 9"), it equals 1246° 20' 29". Divided by twelve, the result in minutes etc. for the visibility correction is 103' 92". Since the zenith distance and the latitude are in the same direction, it is added. If the zenith distance and latitude are in the same direction, add; if in different directions, subtract. In the "other" (the West), when calculating setting or rising, the opposite is done: add for different directions and subtract for the same direction. That becomes the "Visible Planet" (Drggraha), the planet after the visibility correction is applied. Clear Venus processed with the visibility correction is 11s 14° 58' 20". ॥ 18 ॥

->Madhuri Commentary<-

Six, seven (shaila), eight, nine, twelve (arka), eighteen (dhrti), and twenty-three (aditija) are the segments (khandas). One must sum the segments equal to the tenths of the zenith distance. To this, add the result of the remainder multiplied by the next segment and divided by ten (asha). Multiply by the latitude in digits (sharangula), divide by twelve (ravi), and the resulting minutes (lipta) are added or subtracted (svarna) to the planet (kheta) based on whether the zenith distance and latitude are in the same or different directions. In the West, do the opposite (vyasta). Then it becomes the Visible Planet (Drggraha). ॥ 18 ॥

<header>Chapter 6: On the Rising and Setting of Heavenly Bodies</header>

# Chapter 6: On the Rising and Setting of Heavenly Bodies

->**The Mathematical Proof**<-

What is this thing called *Visibility Correction* <note>original: *Drik-karma*</note>? It is the "action of sight." In practical terms, when a specific point on the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> appears on the horizon, the actual body of the planet is not necessarily there. This is because the planet sits at the tip of its latitude <note>celestial latitude or *shara*</note> on its own orbit, and latitude is measured along a circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic. Therefore, the planet's body rises either before or after the ecliptic point rises. The interval of time between the rising of the ecliptic point and the rising of the actual planetary body is defined as the *Visibility Correction*.

The proof is stated as follows: When the planet's body is on the horizon, the distance on the ecliptic between the circle passing through the ecliptic poles and the circle passing through the celestial poles is the "Correction in Minutes." The intersection of the horizon and the ecliptic is the "Visible Planet" <note>the projected position</note>. At that time, the north-south distance between the ecliptic position and the planet's body along the secondary circle is the latitude (*shara*); this is the "vertical side" <note>the *koti* of a right triangle</note>. The east-west distance on the ecliptic between the ecliptic position and the visible position is the "base side" <note>the *bhuja*</note>. The distance between the planet's body and the visible position on the horizon is the "hypotenuse." In this triangle, because the polar circle is perpendicular to the ecliptic, the sine of the angle formed is the Radius. The sine of the angle formed by the horizon and the ecliptic is the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal <note>the point 90 degrees from the rising point</note>. Thus, the angle at the planet's body formed by the horizon and the polar circle is the zenith distance of the nonagesimal. Therefore, by the proportion of angles, the minutes of the Visibility Correction are:

(Value of the Base) = 
Latitude minutes × Sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal

=

Latitude in digits × 3 × Sine of the zenith distance
----------------------------------------------------
Gnomon of the nonagesimal

=

Lat. digits × 3 × Sine of zenith distance × 12
----------------------------------------------
Nonagesimal Gnomon × 12

=

Lat. digits × 36 × Sine of zenith distance
------------------------------------------
Nonagesimal Gnomon × 12

.... (a) Here, the scholar Ganesha <note>referring to Ganesha Daivajna, a 16th-century astronomer</note> has calculated the sines for the zenith distance of the nonagesimal in increments of ten degrees. He multiplied these by thirty-six and divided by the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal. He then recorded the differences (tabular segments) as "6, 7, 8..." and so on. If one segment corresponds to ten degrees, then for any desired degrees, the result is found by the sum of the passed segments plus the proportional value of the remaining degrees.

( $\frac{\text{Next Segment} \times \text{Remaining Degrees}}{10}$ ) 

When added, the result becomes the ratio of the sine of the zenith distance to the sine of the altitude, multiplied by thirty-six. Thus, substituting this into formula (a), the value of the Visibility Correction in minutes is:

= $\frac{\text{Lat. digits} \times (\text{Sum of passed segments} + \frac{\text{Next segment} \times \text{Rem. degrees}}{10})}{12}$

Now, it is clear to those learned in the spheres <note>astronomers</note> that if the zenith distance and the latitude are in the same direction, the visible planet is dropped forward from its position; if they are in different directions, the visible planet is elevated <note>moved backward</note>. Thus, the logic for addition and subtraction is easily understood. — *The Editor* || 18 ||

The segments used in calculating the Visibility Correction are 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 18, and 33. Divide the degrees of the zenith distance by 10; take the sum of the segments corresponding to that quotient. To this, add the result of the next segment multiplied by the remaining degrees and divided by 10. Multiply this total by the latitude in digits and divide by 12. The resulting minutes should be added to or subtracted from the planet's position based on whether the zenith distance and latitude are in the same or different directions. In the west, this calculation is applied in reverse. || 18 ||

->**Example**<-

In the previously mentioned zenith distance of 42° 6' 18", dividing by 10 gives a quotient of 4. The sum of the first 4 segments is 30 <note>6+7+8+9=30</note>. The next segment is 12. Multiplying 12 by the remainder 2° 6' 18" gives 25° 15' 56". Dividing this by 10 gives 2° 31' 35". Adding this to the sum (30) gives 32° 31' 35". This value is then multiplied by the latitude in digits, which is 27' 11" 5...

# In the Latiprahlaghava—

The multiplier is 68;30,45. Dividing this by 12, the result (since the <term>zenith distance</term> <note>natāṃśa</note> and the <term>celestial latitude</term> <note>śara</note> are in the same direction) is the positive <term>visibility correction</term> <note>dṛkkarma: a correction applied to a planet's longitude to find its position on the observer's horizon</note> in minutes etc. of 5;42,34. Adding this to the true Venus 11s 7° 22' 20", the <term>apparent planet</term> <note>dṛggraha: the planet's position as it appears on the horizon</note> becomes 11s 7° 18' 22". || 18 ||

### ->Now he describes the knowledge of the time of rising and setting—<-

> One should designate the lesser of the Sun and the apparent planet as the "Sun," and the other as the "Ascendant."
> Between them, the ghatikas <note>units of time equal to 24 minutes</note> should be calculated as before; for the western [rising/setting], this is done with the addition of a half-circle <note>180 degrees or 6 signs</note>.
> These [ghatikas] multiplied by six are the degrees of time. If these are greater than the stated values, the setting is yet to come; if less, it has passed.
> If they are greater than the stated values, the rising has passed; if less, it is yet to come. || 19 ||

Now, having applied the <term>visibility correction</term>, he describes the signs of past or future occurrence to determine the day of the planet's rising or setting. *One should designate the lesser as the Sun*, etc. "Sun" refers to the solar body. The "apparent planet" is the planet to which the <term>visibility correction</term> has been applied. Between these two, the lesser is designated as the "Sun." The one that is greater is designated as the "Ascendant" <note>lagna</note>. Having applied the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>ayanāṃśa</note> to this Sun and Ascendant, the time should be calculated as before, using the method "the portion of the sign to be traversed by the Sun," etc., or if they are in the same sign, by the difference of their degrees.

Later, for calculating the western rising and setting, the time is calculated for the Ascendant and Sun increased by a half-circle (six signs). The result in seconds of arc <note>pala</note> is converted to <term>ghatikas</term>. Those ghatikas multiplied by six become the desired "degrees of time" <note>kālāṃśa</note>. If these desired degrees of time are greater than the previously stated fixed degrees of time, the setting is "to come" <note>gamya</note>; if less, the setting is "past" <note>gata</note>. For rising, if greater, it is "past"; if less, it is "to come."

The Sun is 11s 23° 32' 26". Venus, refined by the <term>visibility correction</term>, is 11s 14° 58' 20". Between these two, Venus is the lesser; it is treated as the "Sun" at 11s 14° 58' 20". With the <term>precession</term> added, it is 0s 3° 6' 20". The other is the Sun-Ascendant at 11s 23° 32' 26". The <term>precession</term> is 18° 8'. The Ascendant with precession is 0s 11° 40' 26". Since these are in the same sign, the difference in degrees is 8° 34' 6". Multiplying this by the rising time of Aries (221), we get 1893;36,6. Divided by thirty, the time is 63. Multiplied by six, the desired degrees of time are 6;18. The stated degrees of time for Venus, with adjustments, are 6;46. || 19 ||

### ->The Madhuri Commentary-<-

<gloss>Of the Sun and the apparent planet</gloss> = of the Sun and the planet corrected for visibility, <gloss>whichever is less</gloss> = the lower value, <gloss>that is the Sun</gloss> = to be treated as the Sun, <gloss>the other</gloss> = the greater planet, <gloss>is designated the Ascendant</gloss> = should be considered so. <gloss>Between them</gloss> = in the interval, <gloss>as before</gloss> = using the logic of the fourth verse in the chapter on the Three Problems, <gloss>there shall be ghatikas</gloss>. <gloss>These</gloss> = ghatikas, <gloss>later</gloss> = in the case of western setting or rising, <gloss>with the addition of a half-circle</gloss> = with six signs added, shall be calculated. The meaning is that for calculating western rising/setting, one should add six signs to the Sun and the apparent planet and then calculate the ghatikas. <gloss>Those</gloss> = ghatikas, <gloss>multiplied by six</gloss> = times six, <gloss>are degrees of time</gloss> = become the degrees of time. <gloss>Than the stated</gloss> = than the mentioned degrees of time, <gloss>if greater, it is past; if less</gloss> = smaller, <gloss>it is to come</gloss> = future; <gloss>this shall be the rising</gloss>. || 19 ||

### ->The Mathematical Rationale-<-

->It is quite simple. || 19 ||<-

Taking the lesser of the Sun and the <term>apparent planet</term> as the "Sun" and the greater as the "Ascendant," the product of 6 and the interval in ghatikas (calculated by the method "the Sun's remaining travel plus the Ascendant's passed time") will be the interval degrees. By comparing whether the interval degrees are greater or less than the stated <term>degrees of time</term>, one should know respectively whether the setting is "to come" or "past." Similarly, if the interval degrees are greater or less than the <term>degrees of time</term>, the rising is respectively "past" or "to come." || 19 ||

**Example** — The <term>apparent planet</term> Venus is 11s 7° 18' 22" and the true Sun is 6s 12° 29' 17". Among these, taking the lesser <term>apparent planet</term> as the Sun and the greater Sun as the Ascendant, and adding the <term>precession</term> of 2° 1' 33" to them... <note>text obscured by digital stamp</note>

# Chapter 6: On Risings and Settings

By adding [the relevant factors], the tropical Sun is 8s 8° 5' 12" and the tropical Ascendant is 7s 11° 2' 17". From these, using the method of **"the portion of the sign to be crossed by the Sun added to the portion already crossed by the Ascendant"** and so on, the desired time is 29 minutes 57 seconds <note>ghatis and palas</note>, which when multiplied by 6 results in the desired time-degrees <term>Kālāṃśa: degrees of time representing the distance between the Sun and a planet required for visibility</term> of 179° 42'. || 19 ||

## Now, the calculation for the number of days is stated —

> Multiply the minutes of the difference between the stated and desired time-degrees by three hundred, and divide by the rising time of the sign occupied by the Sun. For the western horizon, divide by the rising time of the seventh sign from the Sun. Then, divide the result by the difference in daily motion; if the planet is retrograde, divide by the sum of the motions. This gives the days of rising or setting. || 20 ||

Now the calculation of days is explained. **By three hundred <note>literally 'sky-fire-fire' using the Katapayadi system where sky=0, fire=3, fire=3, read backwards as 300</note>...** The stated [required] time-degrees are 8° 44' 30". The desired [actual] time-degrees are 179° 42'. The difference between these is 170° 57'. Its minutes are 10257. Multiplied by three hundred (300) = 3,077,100. Since the eastern rising is being calculated, this is divided by the rising time of the sign occupied by the tropical Sun, which is 221, resulting in 13923.31. Furthermore, if it were a western rising, it should be divided by the rising time of the seventh sign from the tropical Sun. Dividing by the difference between the motions of the Sun and Venus, which is 16' 13", the result is the elapsed days etc. of the setting: 859.28. Counting backwards from the 8th day of the bright half of the month of Chaitra by these 859.28 days, the eastern setting of Venus occurred. The rising or setting of a planet <note>literally 'the one with a cycle'</note> is thus calculated. If the planet is retrograde, then the division should be by the sum of the motions. || 20 ||

### The "Madhuri" Commentary —

**Difference between stated and desired time-degrees =** the difference between the time-degrees read in the tables and the calculated time-degrees of the moment. **Minutes =** arc-minutes. **By three hundred =** by the number 300. **Multiplied =** increased by multiplication. **Divided by the rising of the Sun's sign =** divided by the rising period of the zodiac sign where the Sun is situated. **Furthermore =** in the western direction. **By its seventh =** divided by the rising period of the seventh sign from the Sun's sign. **Then, divided by the difference in speed =** divided by the difference between the daily motion of the Sun and the planet. **In the case of a retrograde planet =** when the planet has backward motion. **By the sum =** divided by the sum of their two motions. Then **the days of rising or setting =** the number of days, **occur. || 20 ||**

### Mathematical Proof —

Let it be assumed that the minutes of the difference in time-degrees = *X*. When these are divided by 6, then the **respiration-units <note>Asu: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> of the difference in time-degrees =** *X* / 6. Let the rising period of the Sun's sign = *R*. Then, by proportion, the minutes of the difference:
**=** (*X* / 6) × (1800 / *R*) **=** (*X* × 300) / *R*.

Then, if one day corresponds to the difference in daily motion, what do the minutes of the difference correspond to? The minutes are multiplied by one and divided by the difference in motion; for a retrograde planet, divided by the sum of motions. The days of rising or setting would be:

| | | |
|----------|----------|----------|
| (*X* × 300) × 1 | *X* × 300 | *X* × 300 |
| ----------------- | = --------- | or, Days of Rising/Setting = ----------- |
| *R* × Diff. Motion | *R* × Diff. Motion | *R* × Sum of Motion |

The rest is easy to understand and thus proven. || 20 ||

Multiply the minutes of the difference between the tabulated time-degrees and the calculated time-degrees by 300. Divide this by the rising period of the sign the Sun is in. Divide that quotient (in minutes etc.) by the difference in daily motion between the Sun and the observed planet to find the days of an eastern rising or setting. To calculate a western rising or setting, one must divide by the rising period of the 7th sign from the Sun's sign. If the planet is retrograde, divide by the sum of their daily motions. || 20 ||

### Example —
The difference between the tabulated clear time-degrees of Venus (8° 44' 30") and the calculated time-degrees (179° 42') is <unclear>170° 57' 30" in minutes</unclear>. Multiplying this by 300 gives <unclear>51292.30</unclear>, which is then divided by the rising period of the sign the Sun is in...

### Now, the difference between the rising and setting of the Moon and Venus is described—

> The difference between three hundred and the rising time, divided by twenty-seven,
> Is added or subtracted depending on whether the rising time is greater or less than three hundred.

Now the author describes the refinement of the time-degrees <note>Kalansha</note> for Venus and the Moon. "The difference": 300. The rising time of the tropical <note>term: Sayana - including the precession of the equinoxes</note> Venus is 221. The difference between these is 79. Their refinement is 2;11,42. A fifth part of this is subtractive: 0;15. The time-degrees of Venus are 9; these are reduced by 14 minutes to 8;46. Again, reduced by two degrees (2), the time-degrees of Venus are 6;46. The equality of observation for rising and setting is calculated by these time-degrees. "Observed by me" means the difference in rising and setting was observed through instrument sightings <note>original: "yantra-vedhadina"</note>. The time-degrees are 6;46. ### Madhuri Commentary—

*Bhavihritam* = divided by twenty-seven; *Khabhragnyudayāntaram* = the difference between the value of three hundred and the rising time; *Prithunodaye* = when the rising value is greater or less than three hundred; *Svarnam* = positive or negative; *Yat* = that which; *Tatsamskritadrikkarmalavatah* = from the visibility correction degrees refined by that; *Prananshena* = by a fifth part; *Samskritah* = refined; *Bhriguchandrayoh* = of Venus and the Moon; *Purvoktah* = previously stated; as read in "The Sun, the mountain, the earth" <note>A mnemonic reference to numerical values in the text</note> etc.; *Kshanalavah* = time-degrees; *Spashtah* = clear/accurate; *Syuh* = they become. *Sugoh* = for Venus; *Dvabhyam* = by two; *Unita* = deprived of/subtracted; the time-degrees become accurate. *Taih* = by those accurate time-degrees; *Udayastadrishtisamata* = there is unity between the observation and the calculation of rising and setting. *Esha* = this; *Maya* = by Ganesha <note>The author of the Grahalaghava</note>; *Lakshita* = observed. || 21 ||

### The Proof—

It is based on observation itself. || 21 ||

Dividing the difference between the rising time of tropical Venus and the tropical Moon and 300 by 27, the quotient should be added or subtracted from the said rising time depending on whether it is greater or less than 300. By refining the visibility correction degrees <note>Drükkarma</note> with this, and then refining the stated center-degrees with a fifth part of that, the accurate time-degrees are found. Furthermore, by subtracting 2 from the accurate time-degrees of Venus, the true accurate time-degrees are obtained. Only through these refined time-degrees does the unity of observation and calculation occur. This I have seen. || 21 ||

### Example—

The rising time in seconds of tropical Venus 2;8,51,12 is 303. The difference between 303 and 300 is 3. Adding this to the visibility correction minutes 5;42,34 gives a positive 8;42,34. Adding a fifth part of this, 1;44,30, to the 9 time-degrees of Venus results in 10;44,30. Subtracting 2 degrees from this, the accurate time-degree of Venus becomes 8;44,30. || 21 ||
